candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ACE-inhibitor fetal toxicity and medication safety action
candidates.educational_objective: Respond promptly to pregnancy detected during lisinopril therapy because current labeling directs discontinuation as soon as pregnancy is detected due to fetal toxicity risk from renin-angiotensin system drugs.

options.A: Continue lisinopril until the second trimester because fetal toxicity is not a concern early in pregnancy.
options.B: Notify the prescriber promptly because current labeling directs discontinuation of lisinopril as soon as pregnancy is detected.
options.C: Reduce the lisinopril dose and continue it because lower exposure removes the fetal toxicity risk.
options.D: Continue lisinopril if blood pressure is controlled because stable maternal pressure prevents fetal toxicity.

candidates.rationale: The current lisinopril boxed warning and Warnings and Precautions §5.1 state that lisinopril should be discontinued as soon as pregnancy is detected because drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus. Therefore the nurse should promptly notify the prescriber so therapy can be changed in accordance with the warning. A incorrectly delays action, while C and D assume that dose reduction or controlled blood pressure eliminates the labeled fetal risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Pregnancy detected during lisinopril therapy requires prompt medication review because the label directs discontinuation as soon as pregnancy is detected due to fetal toxicity risk.
candidates.source_document_title: Lisinopril Tablets prescribing information
candidates.source_locator: Boxed Warning — Fetal Toxicity and Warnings and Precautions §5.1: when pregnancy is detected, discontinue lisinopril as soon as possible; drugs acting directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — surgical-smoke engineering control and occupational exposure prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Use local surgical-smoke evacuation during electrosurgical plume generation to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse into the room.

options.A: To replace the need for general room ventilation during electrosurgery.
options.B: To remove surgical smoke only after it has dispersed into the room air.
options.C: To capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to their source before they disperse.
options.D: To prevent the electrosurgical unit from interfering with physiologic monitoring equipment.

candidates.rationale: NIOSH states that electrosurgical smoke can contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses. General room ventilation alone is not sufficient to capture contaminants generated at the source; local exhaust ventilation such as a smoke evacuator is used to control the plume close to the surgical site, and the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Therefore C is correct. A incorrectly treats local evacuation as a replacement for general ventilation, B waits until contaminants have dispersed rather than capturing them at the source, and D describes a purpose unrelated to surgical-smoke control.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Local surgical-smoke evacuation is an engineering control used to capture hazardous airborne contaminants close to the source and should be active whenever surgical procedures generate airborne particles.
candidates.source_document_title: NIOSH Hazard Controls HC11 — Control of Smoke from Laser/Electric Surgical Procedures
candidates.source_locator: CDC Stacks record description, corresponding to HC11 Hazard/Controls sections: surgical smoke may contain toxic gases and vapors, bioaerosols, cellular material, and viruses; general room ventilation is insufficient; local smoke evacuation captures contaminants near the source; the evacuator should be activated whenever airborne particles are produced. Currentness cross-check: NIOSH Healthcare Respiratory Protection > Surgical smoke (Jan. 15, 2025) directs use of control methods such as ventilation and links this NIOSH publication.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand-hygiene adherence monitoring and feedback
candidates.educational_objective: Use infection-prevention audit data to identify adherence gaps, provide prompt and regular feedback, and support corrective improvement rather than treating measurement as an end in itself.

options.A: Use the results only to identify individual staff for discipline without unit-level improvement feedback.
options.B: Replace infection-prevention education with audit scores because measurement alone changes practice.
options.C: Use the results to identify adherence gaps and provide regular feedback that supports improvement.
options.D: Collect compliance data for reporting purposes without discussing findings or changing practice.

candidates.rationale: CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices identify performance monitoring and feedback as a core practice: facilities should monitor adherence to infection-prevention practices, provide prompt and regular feedback on adherence and related outcomes to healthcare personnel and leadership, and act on surveillance data. Therefore C is correct. A limits monitoring to punishment rather than improvement, B incorrectly substitutes measurement for required education and training, and D disconnects collected data from feedback and corrective action.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Infection-prevention performance monitoring should identify adherence gaps, be paired with prompt and regular feedback, and inform improvement actions; it does not replace education or exist only for reporting or discipline.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — PPE shortage surge-capacity strategies
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish crisis-capacity PPE strategies from conventional and contingency approaches: crisis measures are temporary, higher-risk options for known shortages when supply cannot meet current utilization and should end as adequate supply returns.

options.A: Continue crisis-capacity practices as the routine standard after PPE availability again meets facility needs.
options.B: Move directly to crisis-capacity practices when a future shortage is only anticipated but current PPE supply still meets utilization.
options.C: Use crisis-capacity practices whenever future supply adequacy is uncertain, even before contingency strategies are considered.
options.D: Use crisis-capacity practices temporarily during a known shortage when PPE supply cannot meet current utilization, after considering conventional and contingency approaches.

candidates.rationale: CDC/NIOSH describes three surge-capacity strata. Conventional practices are routine; contingency strategies may be used temporarily during anticipated shortages or uncertainty about future supply; crisis-capacity strategies are higher-risk measures that may be used temporarily during known PPE shortages when supply cannot meet the facility's current utilization rate. Conservation strategies are meant to be considered sequentially, and facilities should promptly resume conventional practices as PPE availability improves. Therefore D is correct. A incorrectly makes crisis practices routine after recovery, while B and C apply crisis measures to circumstances that CDC/NIOSH describes as contingency rather than crisis capacity.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Crisis-capacity PPE strategies are temporary higher-risk measures for known shortages when supply cannot meet current utilization; they follow consideration of lower-risk capacity strategies and should be discontinued as adequate supply returns.
candidates.source_document_title: Conserving Supplies of Personal Protective Equipment in Healthcare Facilities during Shortages
candidates.source_locator: Surge capacity: definitions of Conventional capacity, Contingency capacity, and Crisis capacity. Crisis capacity: temporary during known PPE shortages when supply cannot meet current utilization; highest risk; not routine replacement. PPE supply conservation strategies: contingency then crisis strategies augment conventional strategies and are meant to be considered sequentially; promptly resume standard conventional practices as PPE availability increases.

candidates.educational_objective: Make nursing assignments based on client needs and verified staff competency, using appropriate supervision and resources rather than assuming licensure alone establishes specialty competence.

options.A: Assign the most unstable child because an unrestricted RN license establishes competence for every specialty assignment.
options.B: Give the nurse a full independent PICU assignment without first considering the nurse's competency for the assigned care.
options.C: Assign any available PICU workload and rely on the nurse to request help only after difficulty develops.
options.D: Match assigned care to client needs and the nurse's verified competency, with appropriate supervision and resources for the assigned tasks.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan places assignment, delegation, and supervision under Management of Care. It directs the nurse to identify assignments based on client needs, assign appropriate tasks to personnel with competency to perform them, supervise care provided by others, and evaluate staff ability based on allowable duties, competency, judgment, and decision-making. Therefore D is the safest approach. A incorrectly treats licensure as proof of specialty competence. B omits competency assessment before an independent high-acuity assignment. C delays use of supervision/resources until a problem has already developed.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Safe assignment requires matching client-care needs and tasks to personnel competency and using appropriate supervision; an RN license alone does not establish competency for every specialty task or assignment.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize ICS as a standardized, scalable incident-management structure that integrates command, coordination, resources, personnel, facilities, and communications during emergency response.

options.A: It creates separate command structures for each department so units can manage the incident independently.
options.B: It is a permanent organizational chart that replaces the hospital's routine leadership structure after the incident ends.
options.C: It is limited to police, fire, and emergency medical agencies and is not intended for private-sector organizations such as hospitals.
options.D: It provides a standardized, scalable incident-management structure that integrates command, coordination, personnel, resources, facilities, and communications.

candidates.rationale: FEMA describes the Incident Command System as a standardized approach to command, control, and coordination of incident management. ICS provides a common organizational structure in which personnel from different organizations can work together and integrates procedures, personnel, equipment, facilities, and communications. NIMS principles are scalable, flexible, and adaptable and are used by government, nongovernmental, and private-sector organizations. Therefore D is correct. A contradicts the common coordinated structure, B incorrectly makes an incident-management structure permanent after the incident, and C incorrectly excludes private-sector organizations such as hospitals.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ICS is a standardized incident-management approach that integrates command, coordination, personnel, equipment/resources, facilities, and communications within a common structure; NIMS/ICS principles are scalable and applicable beyond public-safety agencies.

candidates.educational_objective: In telephone triage, recognize new chest pressure with shortness of breath as a possible emergency, prioritize EMS evaluation, and act within authorized nursing protocols rather than making a definitive remote diagnosis or independently prescribing treatment.

options.A: Diagnose acute coronary syndrome from the telephone history and give the caller a definitive cardiac diagnosis.
options.B: Perform a focused assessment, recognize a possible emergency, and direct activation of emergency medical services according to protocol and scope.
options.C: Complete a detailed lifetime health history before deciding whether emergency evaluation is needed.
options.D: Recommend a prescription medication for the chest pressure without an authorized order, protocol, or prescriber involvement.

candidates.rationale: NHLBI identifies chest pressure or discomfort and shortness of breath among heart-attack warning symptoms and advises calling 9-1-1 for emergency medical care even when the person is not certain that a heart attack is occurring. The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan requires prioritization based on acuity, use of referrals/resources, and practice within legal scope. Therefore B is the best nursing action: obtain a focused assessment sufficient to recognize the possible emergency and direct EMS activation according to the applicable protocol and scope. A exceeds the available information by making a definitive remote diagnosis, C delays time-sensitive care, and D recommends prescription treatment without an authorized mechanism.
candidates.source_claim_supported: New chest pressure with shortness of breath can represent a time-sensitive cardiac emergency requiring EMS evaluation; the RN should prioritize acuity and referral within scope rather than provide a definitive telephone diagnosis or unauthorized prescription treatment.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — advocacy, treatment decisions, and referrals
candidates.educational_objective: Support a client's decision to seek additional information before elective treatment by advocating for the client's choice and facilitating appropriate referral and record coordination.

options.A: Discourage another opinion because it may damage the therapeutic relationship.
options.B: Tell the client that only the surgeon can decide whether another opinion may be sought.
options.C: Support the client's stated choice and help coordinate the records or referral process needed for another opinion.
options.D: Advise the client to have the operation first and seek another opinion afterward if concerns remain.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan places advocacy, client rights, and referrals within Management of Care. It directs nurses to discuss identified treatment options and respect client decisions, act as client advocates, advocate for client rights and needs, assess the need for referrals, and identify documents needed when referring a client. Therefore C is the most appropriate response. A discourages the client's informed choice, B incorrectly makes another clinician the gatekeeper for the client's decision to seek additional information, and D defeats the purpose of obtaining another opinion before an elective treatment decision.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nursing advocacy includes respecting client treatment decisions and facilitating appropriate referral/record processes when the client seeks additional information before an elective treatment decision.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — advance directives and health care proxy
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish a durable power of attorney for health care from financial power of attorney and DNR orders: it names a health care agent to act when the person cannot make or communicate health care decisions, within the document and applicable state rules.

options.A: It authorizes an agent to manage only finances and property when the person cannot make decisions.
options.B: It names a health care proxy or agent to make health care decisions if the person cannot make or communicate those decisions, subject to the document and applicable state rules.
options.C: It functions as a do-not-resuscitate order and applies only to resuscitation decisions during cardiopulmonary arrest.
options.D: It transfers all health care decision-making authority to the agent immediately after signing, even while the person remains able to make and communicate decisions.

candidates.rationale: National Institute on Aging guidance describes a durable power of attorney for health care as an advance-directive document that names a health care proxy, representative, surrogate, or agent who can make health care decisions if the person is unable to make or communicate those decisions. The scope and formal requirements can vary by state and by the document. Therefore B is correct. A describes financial/property authority rather than the health care proxy role, C confuses the document with a DNR order, and D incorrectly displaces the decisions of a person who remains able to make and communicate health care choices.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A durable power of attorney for health care names a proxy/agent to make health care decisions when the person cannot make or communicate those decisions; document scope and state rules govern details.

Choosing a Health Care Proxy > What is a health care proxy?: durable power of attorney for health care is the advance directive used to name the proxy; proxy acts when the person cannot make/communicate decisions; state requirements and permitted proxy responsibilities vary.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — DNR scope, advance care planning, and client rights
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that a DNR order addresses cardiopulmonary resuscitation if breathing or heartbeat stops and does not, by itself, discontinue other nonresuscitation treatments.

options.A: A DNR order stops routine medications, diagnostic tests, nursing care, and cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
options.B: A DNR order automatically limits care to comfort measures and withholds all disease-directed treatment.
options.C: A DNR order directs that CPR not be performed if breathing or heartbeat stops; by itself, it does not give instructions to stop treatments outside resuscitation.
options.D: A DNR order withholds chest compressions but requires defibrillation and resuscitation medications during cardiac arrest.

candidates.rationale: Current MedlinePlus guidance defines a DNR as a medical order instructing health care providers not to perform cardiopulmonary resuscitation if the patient's breathing stops or the heart stops beating. It is specific to CPR and does not, by itself, provide instructions for other treatments such as pain medicine, other medications, or nutrition. CPR may include chest compressions, ventilation, electric shock, and resuscitation medicines. Therefore C is correct. A and B improperly extend the DNR to unrelated ongoing treatment, while D incorrectly separates defibrillation and resuscitation drugs from the resuscitation interventions addressed by the DNR.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A standard DNR order is specific to withholding CPR during respiratory or cardiac arrest and does not by itself stop other nonresuscitation treatments; resuscitation encompasses more than chest compressions alone.

candidates.source_locator: Do-not-resuscitate order > introductory definition: instructs providers not to do CPR if breathing stops or heart stops. What is a DNR?: specific about CPR and has no instructions for other treatments such as pain medicine, other medicines, or nutrition. What is Resuscitation?: CPR may include breathing support/chest compressions, electric shock, breathing tubes/oxygen, and medicines.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — legally authorized decision-maker and informed consent
candidates.educational_objective: When a court order specifically grants a guardian authority for a health care decision, recognize that authority within the order and applicable law rather than substituting an unauthorized relative's preference.

options.A: Recognize the guardian's authority for this decision within the court order and applicable law rather than substituting the sibling's preference solely because the sibling is family.
options.B: Let the sibling make the decision because family preference automatically overrides a court order granting health care decision authority.
options.C: Ignore the guardianship because a court-appointed guardian can never be authorized to make health care decisions for an adult.
options.D: Ask whichever relative is physically present to decide because physical presence creates temporary health care decision authority.

candidates.rationale: HHS guidance under 45 CFR 164.502(g) explains that a person authorized under state or other applicable law to make health care decisions for an individual is the individual's personal representative within the scope of that authority; a court-appointed legal guardian is a listed example when the guardian has such legal authority. The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan also requires the nurse to identify the appropriate person to provide informed consent and to address legal rights and responsibilities within scope. Because the stem explicitly states that the court order grants the guardian authority for the decision at issue, A is correct. A sibling's family relationship or physical presence does not by itself supersede that stated legal authority, and court-appointed guardians are not categorically barred from health care decision-making.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A court-appointed guardian who is expressly authorized under the applicable court order/law to make the health care decision at issue has authority within that scope; family relationship or presence alone does not replace the identified legal decision-maker.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — staffing assignments based on client needs, acuity, workload, and nurse competency
candidates.educational_objective: Apply critical-care staffing principles by matching current patient-generated workload and patient characteristics with nurse competency while recognizing that adult critically ill or injured patients generally require approximately one RN for two patients and may require more intensive staffing based on need.

options.A: Base each shift's assignments on current patient-generated nursing workload and nurse competency; staffing plans should anticipate that critically ill or injured patients generally require about one nurse for two patients.
options.B: Use the same routine patient load as a general medical-surgical unit because critical-care acuity does not materially affect staffing needs.
options.C: Assign every critically ill client permanently one-to-one regardless of current needs, therapies, workload, or nurse competency.
options.D: Use a fixed nurse-to-patient ratio as the sole assignment rule without reassessing current workload, patient needs, or nurse competency.

candidates.rationale: AACN's 2024 Standards for Appropriate Staffing in Adult Critical Care state that, for every shift, patient assignments should be based on an accurate assessment of the current nursing workload generated by each patient's needs and should align nurse competency with patient characteristics. AACN also states that organizational staffing plans should anticipate that critically ill or injured patients generally require a ratio of one nurse to two patients. Therefore A is correct. B ignores the higher and changing workload of critical care, C incorrectly makes 1:1 staffing universal and permanent, and D treats a ratio as sufficient without the workload- and competency-based reassessment AACN requires.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Adult critical-care assignments should reflect current patient-generated nursing workload and nurse competency; organizational plans generally anticipate one nurse for two critically ill or injured patients rather than using a ratio as the sole inflexible assignment rule.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — serotonin toxicity differential diagnosis and emergency complication recognition
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome by recognizing the rapid onset after serotonergic change and the characteristic hyperreflexia/clonus pattern of serotonin toxicity.

options.A: Generalized marked rigidity developing over days after exposure to a dopamine-receptor antagonist.
options.B: Hyperreflexia and clonus developing within hours after a serotonergic medication is started, increased, or otherwise altered.
options.C: Flaccid weakness with depressed reflexes after a medication change and no clonus or tremor.
options.D: Fever alone after a medication change without characteristic neuromuscular findings.

candidates.rationale: Serotonin syndrome typically develops rapidly after a serotonergic medication change, often within 6 to 24 hours, and is characterized by neuromuscular hyperactivity, especially hyperreflexia and inducible, spontaneous, or ocular clonus. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome more often develops subacutely over days to weeks after dopamine-receptor antagonist exposure and is characterized by marked rigidity rather than hyperreflexia/clonus. Therefore B most strongly favors serotonin syndrome. A favors NMS, while C and D lack the characteristic serotonin-syndrome neuromuscular pattern.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Rapid onset after serotonergic change with hyperreflexia and clonus strongly favors serotonin syndrome over NMS, which more often has slower onset and marked rigidity.
candidates.source_document_title: Serotonin Syndrome
candidates.source_locator: Pathophysiology/History and Physical: serotonin syndrome usually occurs within 24 hours and most cases present within 6-24 hours after a new serotonergic agent or dose change; Physical Examination: hyperreflexia and muscle clonus are common. Differential Diagnosis > Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome: serotonin syndrome develops within hours and has hyperreflexia/clonus/tremor; NMS develops over days to weeks and shows marked rigidity/slowed neuromuscular response.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — post-anaphylaxis recurrence risk and emergency observation
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that anaphylaxis can recur after apparent initial resolution, supporting continued observation based on the client's clinical course and risk rather than assuming the episode is permanently over.

options.A: Symptoms can recur after initial resolution without another allergen exposure.
options.B: Every client develops a second reaction at the same predictable time after initial recovery.
options.C: A recurrent episode can occur only if the client is exposed to the allergen again.
options.D: Observation is needed only for epinephrine adverse effects because the anaphylactic reaction itself cannot recur after resolution.

candidates.rationale: AAAAI guidance notes that anaphylaxis symptoms may go away and then return a few hours later; this recurrence is commonly described as a biphasic reaction. Continued observation after initial improvement may therefore be appropriate according to the reaction's clinical course and risk. A is correct. Biphasic recurrence is not inevitable or fixed to one exact time, does not require another allergen exposure, and is not simply an adverse effect of residual epinephrine.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Anaphylaxis symptoms can recur after apparent initial resolution without a new allergen exposure, so continued observation may be appropriate based on the clinical course.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — moderate hypothermia management and dysrhythmia prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Manage moderate hypothermia with gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, trunk-focused active external rewarming, and continuous cardiac monitoring because myocardial irritability and dysrhythmias are important risks.

options.A: Encourage vigorous walking to generate heat and apply warming primarily to the hands and feet.
options.B: Handle the client gently, prevent further heat loss, use active external rewarming focused on the trunk, and continuously monitor cardiac status.
options.C: Massage the extremities vigorously and rapidly warm the arms and legs before warming the trunk.
options.D: Apply direct high-temperature heat to numb skin and defer cardiac monitoring until rewarming is complete.

candidates.rationale: A core temperature of 31°C is in the moderate hypothermia range. Current StatPearls/NCBI guidance states that patients with moderate or severe hypothermia should be moved gently because rough movement can increase myocardial irritability and precipitate dysrhythmias. Management includes preventing further heat loss and active external rewarming; efficient heat application is directed to the trunk, axillae, chest, and back, with continuous clinical and cardiac monitoring. Therefore B is correct. Vigorous exercise or massage and rapid peripheral warming can destabilize the client, and direct uncontrolled high heat risks burns and does not replace cardiac monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: At 31°C with altered mentation, moderate hypothermia management includes gentle handling, prevention of further heat loss, active trunk-focused rewarming, and cardiac monitoring; vigorous movement and aggressive peripheral warming are unsafe.
candidates.source_document_title: Hypothermia
candidates.source_locator: Classification/clinical severity: moderate hypothermia is approximately 28-32°C. Treatment/Management: moderate/severe hypothermia requires gentle handling because rough movement can precipitate fatal dysrhythmias; prevent further heat loss; use active external rewarming for moderate hypothermia; heat packs/forced-air warming are applied to trunk/axillae/chest/back; maintain continuous clinical and cardiac monitoring; rapid peripheral warming can contribute to hemodynamic instability.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / StatPearls

candidates.educational_objective: Collect an amikacin trough specimen immediately before the next scheduled dose so the result reflects the lowest serum concentration near the end of the dosing interval.

options.A: Immediately after the dose is administered.
options.B: Halfway through the dosing interval.
options.C: Immediately before the next scheduled dose.
options.D: Only after amikacin therapy has been permanently discontinued.

candidates.rationale: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories ordering guidance states that an amikacin trough specimen should be collected immediately before the next scheduled dose. A specimen collected soon after dosing represents a peak/post-dose context rather than a trough, and a midpoint specimen is not a trough. Therapeutic drug monitoring is performed during therapy, not only after permanent discontinuation. Therefore C is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: An amikacin trough serum concentration should be collected immediately before the next scheduled dose.
candidates.source_document_title: Amikacin, Random, Serum (RAMIK) and Amikacin, Trough, Serum (TAMIK)
candidates.source_locator: RAMIK > Ordering Guidance: peak specimen 30-60 minutes after last dose; trough specimen immediately before next scheduled dose, order TAMIK. TAMIK > Useful For: monitoring adequate clearance near the end of a dosing cycle.
candidates.source_organization: Mayo Clinic Laboratories
candidates.source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories Test Catalog live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A provider orders an amikacin trough concentration. When should the serum specimen be collected?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret diagnostic/laboratory results, identify trends and abnormalities, monitor treatment response, and recognize potential complications related to fluid/electrolyte and acid-base changes.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — DKA acid-base laboratory interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret an increased anion gap in DKA as evidence supporting high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from ketoacids while recognizing that DKA resolution should be assessed with ketone and acid-base criteria rather than the anion gap alone.

options.A: It supports a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from accumulated unmeasured acids such as ketoacids, but it should not be used alone to determine DKA resolution.
options.B: It establishes metabolic alkalosis from excess bicarbonate and shows that ketone-related acidosis has resolved.
options.C: It proves a primary respiratory acidosis from carbon-dioxide retention rather than a metabolic disturbance.
options.D: It independently confirms DKA resolution even if ketones, pH, or bicarbonate remain abnormal.

candidates.rationale: The 2024 international adult hyperglycemic-crises consensus report states that most people with DKA present with a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis because unmeasured ketoacids increase the gap. However, mixed acid-base disorders are common, and hyperchloremic normal-anion-gap acidosis can occur during recovery. The consensus therefore does not recommend the anion gap as a first-line diagnostic or resolution criterion when direct ketone and acid-base measurements are available. A is correct. B describes alkalosis, C incorrectly changes the disturbance to a primary respiratory acidosis, and D incorrectly treats the anion gap as a stand-alone resolution test.
candidates.source_claim_supported: An increased anion gap supports high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from unmeasured ketoacids in DKA but cannot independently establish DKA resolution.
candidates.source_document_title: Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
candidates.source_locator: Diagnosis section: most people with DKA have high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis; anion gap >12 mmol/L indicates high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis consistent with DKA, but mixed disorders and treatment-related hyperchloremic acidosis limit its use. Criteria for resolution: anion gap should not be used as a resolution criterion; direct beta-hydroxybutyrate and pH/bicarbonate are preferred.
candidates.source_organization: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS international consensus panel
candidates.source_version_date: Published June 22, 2024; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: An adult with diabetes has hyperglycemia, elevated ketones, metabolic acidosis, and an increased anion gap. How should the nurse interpret the increased anion gap?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret laboratory findings and trends, recognize risk related to fluid volume/perfusion changes, and integrate diagnostic data with client condition.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — BUN interpretation in volume depletion
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret elevated BUN as a nonspecific finding that can support prerenal azotemia in a volume-depleted client when integrated with clinical status and other renal data rather than treating it as diagnostic by itself.

options.A: The elevation can support a prerenal process related to water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture and other renal data.
options.B: The elevation specifically proves postrenal urinary obstruction regardless of the client's volume status or other findings.
options.C: The elevation demonstrates improved glomerular filtration because BUN rises as renal clearance becomes more efficient.
options.D: The elevation is unrelated to hydration or renal perfusion and should not influence assessment of a volume-depleted client.

candidates.rationale: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories information states that increased BUN can result from prerenal causes such as water depletion from decreased intake or excessive loss and cardiac decompensation/reduced renal perfusion, but BUN can also increase from renal and postrenal causes. It is therefore interpreted with the clinical picture and commonly alongside creatinine rather than as a stand-alone diagnosis. In this volume-depleted client, A is the appropriate interpretation. B overstates specificity for obstruction, C reverses the relationship to clearance, and D incorrectly dismisses the relevance of hydration and perfusion.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Elevated BUN in a clinically volume-depleted client can support a prerenal process from water depletion or reduced perfusion, but BUN is nonspecific and requires contextual interpretation.
candidates.source_document_title: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN), Serum
candidates.source_locator: Clinical Information: increased BUN may be due to prerenal causes including cardiac decompensation and water depletion from decreased intake/excessive loss; renal and postrenal causes are also listed. BUN is frequently requested with serum creatinine to aid differential diagnosis of prerenal, renal, and postrenal hyperuremia.
candidates.source_organization: Mayo Clinic Laboratories
candidates.source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories Test Catalog live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret hemodynamic and diagnostic data, recognize abnormal findings, monitor clients at risk for perfusion compromise, and evaluate trends in clinical status.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — cardiac output/hemodynamic interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize a resting cardiac output of 2.1 L/min as low for an adult while interpreting absolute cardiac output alongside cardiac index, body size, tissue perfusion, and clinical context.

options.A: It is above the usual resting adult range and suggests unusually high forward flow at rest.
options.B: It is below the usual resting adult range and should be interpreted with cardiac index, body size, perfusion findings, and the clinical context.
options.C: It is within the expected resting range for most adults and needs no hemodynamic correlation.
options.D: It is normal solely because the client is critically ill, so no assessment of tissue perfusion is needed.

candidates.rationale: Current StatPearls/NCBI physiology guidance states that resting adult cardiac output generally ranges from 4 to 8 L/min, averaging about 5 L/min. A measured output of 2.1 L/min is therefore below the usual resting range. However, cardiac output alone does not account for body size; cardiac index normalizes output to body-surface area, and hemodynamic measurements must be interpreted with perfusion findings and the overall clinical condition. Therefore B is correct. A and C misclassify the value, while D incorrectly treats critical illness as making a low output normal.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A resting adult cardiac output of 2.1 L/min is below the usual 4-8 L/min range, but absolute CO should be interpreted with cardiac index/body size and clinical perfusion data.
candidates.source_document_title: Physiology, Cardiac Index; Physiology, Cardiac Output
candidates.source_locator: Physiology, Cardiac Index > Introduction/Function: cardiac output as a sole parameter cannot reliably indicate cardiac performance because body size matters; cardiac index normalizes to BSA. Function: resting cardiac output generally 4-8 L/min, average around 5 L/min; normal cardiac index 2.5-4 L/min/m².
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / StatPearls
candidates.source_version_date: Cardiac Index last updated June 8, 2024 and carried in StatPearls 2026 edition; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A critically ill adult has a measured cardiac output of 2.1 L/min at rest. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: conduct risk screening, provide preventive counseling/resources, identify health risks, and support appropriate follow-up/referral for identified needs.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — IPV screening follow-up and supportive intervention
candidates.educational_objective: After a positive IPV screen in a woman of reproductive age, evaluate the finding and connect the patient, when appropriate, with a multicomponent intervention that provides ongoing support rather than relying on brief information alone.

options.A: Provide only a telephone number or brief referral information and end follow-up without ongoing support.
options.B: Require immediate separation from the partner as the standard response regardless of the patient's choices or circumstances.
options.C: Evaluate the positive screen and, when appropriate, provide or refer the patient to an evidence-based multicomponent intervention with ongoing support.
options.D: Take no further action after the positive screen unless visible injury or immediate physical danger is present.

candidates.rationale: The 2025 USPSTF recommendation states that screening benefit depends on what follows a positive screen: patients should be evaluated and, when appropriate, provided or referred to evidence-based interventions that include multiple components and ongoing support. Effective interventions generally involve multiple visits and address a range of emotional, behavioral, health, family, or social needs. Brief counseling or referral information alone, without a multicomponent ongoing intervention, generally did not demonstrate benefit in the reviewed studies. Therefore C is correct. A is too limited, B imposes a single action not established by the USPSTF recommendation, and D fails to provide the evidence-supported pathway after a positive screen.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For women of reproductive age who screen positive for IPV, the evidence-supported pathway is evaluation and, when appropriate, provision/referral to a multicomponent intervention with ongoing support rather than a brief referral alone.
candidates.source_document_title: Intimate Partner Violence and Caregiver Abuse of Older or Vulnerable Adults: Screening
candidates.source_locator: Recommendation Summary/Pathway to Benefit/Clinician Summary: screen women of reproductive age, including pregnant/postpartum women; those who screen positive should be evaluated and, if appropriate, provided or referred to evidence-based interventions with multiple components and ongoing support. Practice Considerations > Interventions for IPV: effective interventions generally include multiple visits and ongoing emotional/behavioral/social support; brief counseling/referral information alone generally did not demonstrate benefit.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)
candidates.source_version_date: Final Recommendation Statement June 24, 2025; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A woman of reproductive age screens positive for intimate partner violence and does not require an immediate emergency response. Which follow-up best reflects current USPSTF evidence?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: recognize mental-health and coping alterations, assess grief/loss responses, provide psychosocial support, and identify findings requiring further mental-health evaluation.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — prolonged grief and bereavement assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize persistent disabling grief at least 12 months after the death of a close person as a pattern that warrants evaluation for prolonged grief disorder while avoiding diagnosis without the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context.

options.A: Normal uncomplicated grief only.
options.B: Prolonged grief disorder.
options.C: Acute stress disorder.
options.D: A manic episode.

candidates.rationale: The American Psychiatric Association states that prolonged grief disorder in adults requires the death of a close person to have occurred at least 12 months earlier and may involve intense longing and/or preoccupation with the deceased together with significant distress or impairment. The client's 14-month timeline and disabling persistent grief pattern therefore warrant evaluation for prolonged grief disorder. B is correct as the condition to evaluate, but the vignette alone does not establish the full DSM-5-TR diagnosis: additional required symptoms, frequency/duration details, differential diagnosis, and whether the grief exceeds expected social, cultural, or religious norms must still be assessed. A underestimates the disabling persistent pattern, while C and D do not fit the described bereavement syndrome.
candidates.source_claim_supported: An adult with persistent intense longing/preoccupation and major functional impairment 14 months after a spouse's death should be evaluated for prolonged grief disorder, although the full DSM-5-TR criteria and cultural context must be assessed before diagnosis.
candidates.source_document_title: Prolonged Grief Disorder; About DSM-5-TR
candidates.source_locator: Prolonged Grief Disorder > Symptoms and Diagnosis: intense longing and/or preoccupation; significant distress/problems in daily functioning; for adults the death must have occurred at least one year earlier; diagnosis additionally requires at least 3 listed symptoms nearly every day for at least the last month and grief lasting longer than expected by social, cultural, or religious norms. About DSM-5-TR confirms PGD is an included diagnosis and criteria require trained clinical judgment.
candidates.source_organization: American Psychiatric Association (APA)
candidates.source_version_date: APA patient/family page physician-reviewed August 2025; DSM-5-TR published 2022 and current in 2026
candidates.stem: An adult's spouse died 14 months ago. The client reports persistent intense longing, preoccupation with the death, and major impairment in daily functioning. Which condition should the nurse recognize as requiring further evaluation?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: therapeutic communication, therapeutic relationships, coping/psychosocial support, and professional boundaries.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic use of self, communication, and boundaries
candidates.educational_objective: Use self-awareness, purposeful presence, empathy, therapeutic communication, and professional boundaries intentionally to advance the client's therapeutic goals rather than creating a social friendship or withdrawing emotionally.

options.A: Use frequent personal self-disclosure to create a friendship and make the relationship less professionally bounded.
options.B: Remain emotionally detached and avoid reflecting on personal reactions so the nurse's self never enters the interaction.
options.C: Use self-awareness, purposeful presence, empathy, therapeutic communication, and professional boundaries to support the client's therapeutic goals.
options.D: Agree with the client's beliefs and decisions automatically even when doing so conflicts with therapeutic goals or professional judgment.

candidates.rationale: Current Open RN/NCBI mental-health nursing guidance describes the therapeutic nurse-client relationship as a purposeful professional relationship focused on client needs and goals. Effective therapeutic communication includes self-awareness, client-centered active listening and empathy, intentional presence, and maintenance of professional boundaries; personal self-disclosure and boundary blurring are identified as barriers. Therefore C best demonstrates therapeutic use of self. A blurs professional boundaries, B rejects the reflective self-awareness and therapeutic presence needed for the relationship, and D substitutes indiscriminate agreement for therapeutic communication and professional judgment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Therapeutic use of self is intentional, self-aware, client-centered professional engagement using empathy, presence, communication, and boundaries to support client goals; friendship-seeking disclosure, detachment, and boundary blurring are nontherapeutic.
candidates.source_document_title: Therapeutic Communication and the Nurse-Client Relationship, 2nd edition
candidates.source_locator: Chapter 2 > Nurse-Client Relationship: therapeutic relationship is compassionate, supportive, professional, establishes trust/rapport with a specific purpose and supports client goals. Therapeutic Communication/Tips for Effective Therapeutic Communication: establish a goal; be self-aware; be client-centered; provide empathy; use active listening; avoid personal self-disclosure; maintain professional boundaries. Common Barriers: lack of awareness of personal biases/feelings and blurring nurse-client boundaries.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / Open RN Nursing: Mental Health and Community Concepts
candidates.source_version_date: 2nd edition published November 1, 2025; currentness live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: Which nursing action best demonstrates therapeutic use of self in a mental health setting?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, printed p.31 > Crisis Intervention: assess potential for violence and use safety precautions; identify the client in crisis; use crisis-intervention techniques to assist coping; guide the client to resources for recovery from crisis. Psychosocial Integrity activity statements also include therapeutic communication and assessment of support systems.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — crisis intervention, safety, therapeutic communication, and resource connection
candidates.educational_objective: Prioritize immediate safety assessment, supportive therapeutic listening, identification of urgent needs, and connection to appropriate resources during early crisis intervention before comprehensive history-taking or long-term treatment planning.

options.A: Complete a comprehensive lifetime psychiatric history before asking about immediate safety concerns.
options.B: Assess immediate safety and urgent needs, use calm supportive listening to understand the crisis, and connect the client with appropriate crisis resources.
options.C: Begin long-term psychotherapy goals before identifying the immediate problem that precipitated the crisis.
options.D: Encourage the client to manage the crisis independently before assessing available supports or urgent risk.

candidates.rationale: Current SAMHSA 988 guidance describes early crisis support as beginning with safety assessment, followed by listening to understand how the problem is affecting the person, providing judgment-free support, and sharing or connecting the person with helpful resources. The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan likewise places crisis intervention in Psychosocial Integrity and includes assessing potential violence/safety, identifying the client in crisis, using crisis-intervention techniques, and guiding the client to recovery resources. Therefore B is the priority. A delays immediate safety assessment, C moves prematurely to long-term treatment goals, and D withholds needed assessment and support during an active crisis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Early crisis support prioritizes safety assessment, understanding the immediate problem through supportive listening, and connection to appropriate resources rather than delaying for comprehensive history or long-term treatment planning.
candidates.source_document_title: 988 Frequently Asked Questions
candidates.source_locator: FAQ sections describing what happens during a 988 call/chat/text: counselor asks about safety, listens and works to understand how the problem is affecting the person, provides personal/judgment-free support, and shares resources or community connections as needed.
candidates.source_organization: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current SAMHSA 988 FAQ live-rechecked August 16, 2026; page content current in 2026 with no separate clinical-version identifier displayed
candidates.stem: A client presents in an emotional crisis but has no immediate medical instability. What should the nurse prioritize early in crisis intervention?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: monitor client response to medications, identify adverse effects/toxicities and interactions, evaluate laboratory data related to therapy, and provide medication-safety teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — amiodarone toxicity surveillance
candidates.educational_objective: Monitor long-term amiodarone for pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, and ocular toxicity using the baseline and ongoing assessments specified in the current FDA label.

options.A: Use serum glucose and hemoglobin A1c as the principal organ-toxicity surveillance throughout therapy.
options.B: Use renal ultrasound and urine protein as the primary tests for the major toxicities of amiodarone.
options.C: Obtain baseline chest imaging and pulmonary-function testing, thyroid studies, and liver aminotransferases; continue pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, and recommended ophthalmic surveillance during therapy.
options.D: After the baseline ECG, no organ-specific surveillance is needed unless the prescribed dose is increased.

candidates.rationale: The current DailyMed/FDA label for oral amiodarone, revised June 2026, requires baseline chest X-ray and pulmonary-function tests, thyroid-function tests, and liver aminotransferases. Pulmonary surveillance includes repeat history, physical examination, and chest X-ray every 3 to 6 months or when symptoms occur; thyroid function and liver transaminases are monitored periodically, and regular ophthalmic examination is recommended during therapy. Therefore C is correct. A and B focus on tests that are not the principal surveillance for amiodarone's major labeled organ toxicities, while D incorrectly omits ongoing organ-specific monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current oral-amiodarone labeling requires baseline pulmonary, thyroid, and hepatic assessment with ongoing surveillance for pulmonary, thyroid, hepatic, and ocular toxicity.
candidates.source_document_title: Amiodarone Hydrochloride Tablets, for oral use
candidates.source_locator: Boxed Warning and Full Prescribing Information §§2, 5.2, 5.3, 5.5, and 5.6: baseline chest X-ray/PFT including diffusion capacity, thyroid-function tests and liver aminotransferases; repeat pulmonary history/physical/chest X-ray every 3-6 months or with symptoms; periodic liver and thyroid monitoring; regular ophthalmic examination during therapy.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
candidates.source_version_date: Updated June 4, 2026; prescribing information revised June 2026
candidates.stem: A client is beginning long-term oral amiodarone therapy for a serious ventricular arrhythmia. Which monitoring plan is most consistent with the current FDA label?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify adverse medication effects, evaluate medication response, reconcile medication changes, and provide accurate client teaching about expected and reportable effects.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ACE-inhibitor/ARB adverse-effect teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients switched from an ACE inhibitor to losartan that cough is less common with losartan than with lisinopril in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, but cough can still occur and should not automatically be dismissed.

options.A: A previous ACE-inhibitor cough makes losartan contraindicated even when there was no angioedema or hypersensitivity.
options.B: Losartan is expected to cause cough at approximately the same frequency as lisinopril in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough.
options.C: Losartan prevents medication-related cough completely, so any cough after the switch must have a nonmedication cause.
options.D: Cough can still occur with losartan, but in controlled trials of patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough it occurred substantially less often with losartan than with lisinopril.

candidates.rationale: The current DailyMed/FDA losartan label reports two randomized controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough. Cough occurred in 17% with losartan versus 69% with lisinopril in one trial and 29% versus 62% in the other; the label also notes postmarketing cases of cough with losartan, including positive rechallenges. Therefore D is correct: losartan can still be associated with cough, but cough was much less frequent than with lisinopril in these trials. A is incorrect because prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a listed contraindication to losartan, B contradicts the trial data, and C falsely treats cough risk as zero.
candidates.source_claim_supported: In patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough, losartan was associated with substantially less cough than lisinopril in controlled trials, although cough can still occur and prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone is not a losartan contraindication.
candidates.source_document_title: Losartan Potassium Tablets, for oral use
candidates.source_locator: Adverse Reactions §6.1 > Cough: two controlled trials in patients with prior ACE-inhibitor cough; Study 1 cough 17% losartan vs 69% lisinopril, Study 2 29% vs 62%; postmarketing cough including positive rechallenges reported. Contraindications §4 lists hypersensitivity and aliskiren coadministration in diabetes, not prior ACE-inhibitor cough alone.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
candidates.source_version_date: Updated January 13, 2026; prescribing information revised January 2026
candidates.stem: A client stopped lisinopril because of a persistent ACE-inhibitor cough and is starting losartan. Which teaching about cough is most accurate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: recognize serious medication adverse effects, monitor therapy, interpret relevant laboratory findings, and intervene for medication-related complications.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — SGLT2 inhibitor ketoacidosis recognition
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that SGLT2-associated DKA can present with only modest hyperglycemia and evaluate compatible symptoms for ketones and metabolic acidosis regardless of the presenting glucose level.

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis, because SGLT2-associated ketoacidosis can occur even when the presenting glucose is below 250 mg/dL.
options.B: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, established solely by the glucose value of 210 mg/dL without additional testing.
options.C: Hypoglycemia, because SGLT2-related ketoacidosis requires glucose above 300 mg/dL.
options.D: Medication intolerance only; ketones and acid-base status do not need evaluation at this glucose level.

candidates.rationale: The current JARDIANCE (empagliflozin) label warns that diabetic ketoacidosis and other ketoacidosis can occur with SGLT2 inhibitors and that blood glucose at presentation may be below the levels typically expected for DKA, including below 250 mg/dL. Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dehydration, and shortness of breath are compatible symptoms. The label directs clinicians to assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting blood glucose and to promptly evaluate if it is suspected. Therefore A is correct. B cannot be established from glucose 210 mg/dL, C falsely requires marked hyperglycemia for SGLT2-associated DKA, and D would inappropriately dismiss a potentially life-threatening adverse effect.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Empagliflozin-associated DKA/ketoacidosis can occur with glucose below 250 mg/dL, so compatible symptoms warrant evaluation regardless of the presenting glucose level.
candidates.source_document_title: JARDIANCE (empagliflozin) tablets, for oral use
candidates.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions §5.1: signs/symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, malaise, dyspnea; blood glucose may be below typical DKA levels (e.g., <250 mg/dL); assess for ketoacidosis regardless of presenting glucose; discontinue and promptly evaluate/treat if suspected.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
candidates.source_version_date: Updated February 17, 2026; prescribing information revised January 2026
candidates.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who takes empagliflozin presents with nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, and fatigue. The blood glucose is 210 mg/dL. Which complication must still be considered?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify medication contraindications/precautions and adverse effects, monitor response, and reduce medication-related risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — tramadol seizure risk
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize tramadol as a medication that can increase seizure risk even at recommended doses, particularly in clients with epilepsy or a seizure history.

options.A: Tramadol raises the seizure threshold and is preferred when analgesia is needed in epilepsy.
options.B: Tramadol can cause seizures even at recommended doses, and the risk may be higher in clients with epilepsy or a history of seizures.
options.C: Seizure risk occurs only with doses below the therapeutic range and is not relevant at recommended doses.
options.D: Concurrent antiseizure medication eliminates the seizure risk associated with tramadol.

candidates.rationale: The current tramadol label states that seizures have been reported in patients receiving tramadol within the recommended dosage range, with higher risk reported above the recommended range. It further states that seizure risk may increase in patients with epilepsy, a history of seizures, or other recognized seizure-risk conditions. Therefore B is correct and the prescription warrants careful prescriber review and monitoring. A reverses the known effect, C contradicts the label, and D incorrectly claims complete risk elimination by antiseizure therapy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Tramadol can cause seizures at recommended doses, and seizure risk may be increased in patients with epilepsy or prior seizures.
candidates.source_document_title: Tramadol Hydrochloride Tablets, for oral use, C-IV
candidates.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions §5.10 Increased Risk of Seizure: seizures reported within recommended dosage range; risk may increase with epilepsy, history of seizures, other seizure risk factors, and certain concomitant medications.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
candidates.source_version_date: DailyMed label updated June 15, 2026; prescribing information revised May 2026
candidates.stem: A client with epilepsy is prescribed tramadol for pain. Why should the nurse recognize this prescription as a significant safety concern?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: apply infection-prevention practices, use disinfection/sterilization principles appropriately, and maintain reusable equipment safely to prevent transmission.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — bronchoscope/endoscope reprocessing and high-level disinfection
candidates.educational_objective: Reprocess a reusable flexible bronchoscope by meticulous cleaning of external surfaces and internal channels followed by at least high-level disinfection before the device is reused.

options.A: Meticulously clean the bronchoscope, including accessible internal channels, and then perform at least high-level disinfection before reuse.
options.B: Use low-level surface disinfection only if the previous client had no known infection.
options.C: Perform high-level disinfection without prior cleaning as long as the disinfectant is circulated through the bronchoscope.
options.D: Reprocess only the exterior surface because the bronchoscope's internal channels do not require the same level of cleaning.

candidates.rationale: Current CDC disinfection guidance states that heat-sensitive flexible endoscopes, including bronchoscopes, must be properly cleaned and at minimum undergo high-level disinfection after each use. CDC further states that meticulous cleaning must precede high-level disinfection or sterilization and that endoscope reprocessing includes cleaning both external surfaces and internal channels before high-level disinfection. Therefore A is correct. B provides an inadequate level of reprocessing, C incorrectly omits the essential cleaning step, and D ignores the internal channels that must also be cleaned and disinfected.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Reusable flexible bronchoscopes require meticulous cleaning, including internal-channel cleaning, followed by at least high-level disinfection after each use before reuse.
candidates.source_document_title: Disinfection of Healthcare Equipment — Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities
candidates.source_locator: Flexible endoscopes/bronchoscopes section: all heat-sensitive endoscopes including bronchoscopes must be properly cleaned and at minimum high-level disinfected after each use. Cleaning section: meticulous cleaning must precede high-level disinfection or sterilization. Reprocessing steps include cleaning external surfaces and brushing/flushing internal channels before high-level disinfection with perfusion of accessible channels.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: CDC web guidance November 28, 2023, based on CDC Guideline for Disinfection and Sterilization in Healthcare Facilities; live currentness rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A reusable flexible bronchoscope has just been used for a client. Which reprocessing step is required before the bronchoscope is used again?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: apply infection-prevention practices, handle contaminated materials safely, and prevent environmental transmission of infectious agents.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — contaminated-linen handling
candidates.educational_objective: Handle contaminated healthcare linen with minimum agitation, contain it at the point of use, avoid sorting or prerinsing it in patient-care areas, and use leak-resistant containment when indicated.

options.A: Sort contaminated linen in the client room before bagging so heavily soiled pieces can be separated early.
options.B: Handle the linen with minimum agitation and contain it at the point of use, using leak-resistant containment when blood or body substances could soak through.
options.C: Shake contaminated linen before bagging to remove loose material and reduce the laundry load.
options.D: Prerinse contaminated linen in the patient-care area before placing it in the transport container.

candidates.rationale: Current CDC environmental infection-control recommendations direct healthcare personnel to handle contaminated textiles with minimum agitation, bag or otherwise contain them at the point of use, avoid sorting or prerinsing them in patient-care areas, and use leak-resistant containment for textiles contaminated with blood or body substances when leakage or soak-through is possible. Therefore B is correct. A and D perform prohibited sorting/prerinsing in the care area, while C increases agitation and potential aerosolization/dispersion of contaminated material.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Contaminated linen should be minimally agitated and contained at the point of use, not sorted or prerininsed in patient-care areas, with leak-resistant containment when blood/body-fluid contamination can leak or soak through.
candidates.source_document_title: Part II. Recommendations for Environmental Infection Control in Health-Care Facilities; Laundry and Bedding
candidates.source_locator: Laundry and Bedding > G.III Routine Handling of Contaminated Laundry: minimum agitation; contain at point of use; do not sort or prerinse in patient-care areas; use leak-resistant containment for blood/body-substance contamination. Laundry and Bedding > Collecting, Transporting, and Sorting reiterates the same principles.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: follow occupational infection-prevention requirements, bloodborne-pathogen precautions, and employee-exposure safety practices.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — occupational bloodborne-pathogen vaccination
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the OSHA requirement that hepatitis B vaccination be offered at no cost to employees with occupational blood/OPIM exposure, subject to defined exceptions.

options.A: Seasonal influenza vaccine.
options.B: Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine.
options.C: Tetanus-diphtheria-pertussis (Tdap) vaccine.
options.D: Hepatitis B vaccine, subject to the standard's stated exceptions.

candidates.rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 requires employers to make hepatitis B vaccine and the vaccination series available to employees with occupational exposure and to provide required medical evaluations/procedures at no cost to the employee. The vaccination must generally be offered after required training and within 10 working days of initial assignment, unless the employee previously completed the series, is demonstrated immune, or the vaccine is medically contraindicated. Therefore D is correct. Influenza, MMR, and Tdap are not the vaccine specifically mandated by the Bloodborne Pathogens Standard for this occupational exposure provision.
candidates.source_claim_supported: OSHA requires hepatitis B vaccination to be made available at no cost to employees with occupational exposure, with specified exceptions for prior vaccination, immunity, or contraindication.
candidates.source_document_title: 29 CFR 1910.1030 — Bloodborne Pathogens Standard
candidates.source_locator: 1910.1030(f)(1)(ii)(A): required evaluations/procedures including hepatitis B vaccine made available at no cost. 1910.1030(f)(2)(i): hepatitis B vaccination offered after training and within 10 working days of initial assignment to employees with occupational exposure unless prior complete series, demonstrated immunity, or medical contraindication.
candidates.source_organization: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current OSHA regulation live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: select and use PPE/respiratory protection appropriately and implement airborne-transmission precautions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — N95 respirator versus surgical mask
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate N95 respirators from surgical masks by recognizing the N95's tight facial seal, fit-testing requirement, and particulate respiratory protection.

options.A: A surgical mask forms a tighter face seal than an N95 and is preferred for inhalation protection from airborne particles.
options.B: A fit-tested N95 is a tight-fitting respirator that filters airborne particles; a surgical mask is loose-fitting and does not provide the same reliable aerosol respiratory protection.
options.C: An N95 and a surgical mask provide equivalent fit and wearer protection from aerosolized particles when both are worn correctly.
options.D: An N95 is intended mainly for splash protection and does not filter small airborne particles.

candidates.rationale: Current CDC/NIOSH healthcare respiratory-protection guidance states that NIOSH Approved filtering facepiece respirators such as N95s are tight-fitting devices that filter at least 95% of airborne particles and require fit testing within a respiratory-protection program. Surgical masks are loose-fitting medical devices that can provide barrier protection against splashes and large droplets but do not provide a reliable level of wearer protection from aerosolized particles because they do not form the same facial seal. Therefore B is correct. A, C, and D misstate the fit or particulate-protection properties of the devices.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A fit-tested N95 provides tight-fitting particulate respiratory protection, whereas a surgical mask is loose-fitting and does not provide the same reliable protection from aerosolized particles.
candidates.source_document_title: Healthcare Respiratory Protection; Fit Testing
candidates.source_locator: Healthcare Respiratory Protection > Overview/Respirators: surgical masks are loose-fitting and do not provide reliable aerosol protection; N95 FFRs tightly fit the face, filter at least 95% of airborne particles, and require fit testing. Fit Testing page: filtering facepiece respirators are tight-fitting and fit testing verifies acceptable face-seal protection.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention / National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (CDC/NIOSH)
candidates.source_version_date: Healthcare Respiratory Protection January 15, 2025; Fit Testing current CDC/NIOSH guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
