candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care: practice within legal scope, recognize professional limitations and legal responsibilities, and provide care consistent with applicable laws/regulations and standards.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — Nurse Practice Act, legal scope, and regulatory discipline
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that practicing outside legal nursing scope can lead to board-of-nursing discipline, with sanctions determined by the applicable Nurse Practice Act, jurisdiction, facts, severity, and disciplinary process rather than an automatic single penalty.

options.A: The board of nursing may impose discipline such as remediation, practice restrictions, suspension, or revocation, depending on applicable law and the facts of the case.
options.B: The consequence is limited to employer counseling because boards of nursing do not enforce Nurse Practice Acts.
options.C: Every scope violation automatically results in permanent license revocation regardless of severity, facts, or jurisdiction.
options.D: Every scope violation automatically produces a criminal conviction before any regulatory investigation or board proceeding occurs.

candidates.rationale: NCSBN explains that state boards of nursing enforce nursing laws and may take disciplinary action when a violation is established. Available board actions vary with state law and the facts and can include remediation or education, reprimand/fines, monitoring or probation, practice restrictions, suspension, and revocation or voluntary surrender. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly denies board authority, while C and D falsely make one severe outcome automatic for every scope violation without investigation, due process, or jurisdiction-specific law.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A Nurse Practice Act/scope violation may lead to board discipline ranging from remediation or restrictions to suspension or revocation, with the actual action depending on state law and case facts.
candidates.source_document_title: Board Action; Discipline; Nurse Practice Act Toolkit
candidates.source_locator: Board Action > Disciplinary Actions: actions vary according to state law and may include monitoring/remediation/education, limitations or restrictions, suspension, revocation/surrender, fines and reprimands. Discipline page: BON investigates alleged NPA violations and may impose discipline if violation found. NPA Toolkit: state Nurse Practice Acts establish BON authority and govern legal nursing practice.
candidates.source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCSBN nursing-regulation guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A nurse practices outside the legal scope authorized by the applicable Nurse Practice Act. Which regulatory consequence is possible?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care: practice within legal/regulatory requirements, recognize professional responsibilities and limitations, and maintain appropriate licensure/credential obligations.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — nursing licensure renewal and jurisdiction-specific regulation
candidates.educational_objective: Before renewing a nursing license, verify the current requirements of the board or nursing regulatory body that issued/governs the license rather than assuming a universal renewal rule.

options.A: Retake the NCLEX at every routine renewal because re-examination is a universal renewal requirement.
options.B: Verify the current renewal requirements of the licensing jurisdiction because licensure and continuing-competency requirements can vary by jurisdiction.
options.C: Use only the renewal requirements from the nurse's state of original licensure even when the active license is issued by another jurisdiction.
options.D: Assume the license remains active indefinitely unless an employer specifically requests renewal.

candidates.rationale: NCSBN states that nursing licensure requirements vary by state/jurisdiction and provides jurisdiction-specific licensure guidance and links to the applicable board of nursing, Nurse Practice Act, and regulations. Renewal is a licensure process governed by the relevant nursing regulatory body; specific continuing-competency, education, timing, fee, and other renewal requirements must therefore be verified for the jurisdiction involved rather than assumed to be universal. B is correct. Routine NCLEX retesting is not a universal renewal requirement, the requirements of an unrelated original state do not govern every other license, and licensure does not remain active indefinitely without satisfying renewal requirements.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nursing-license renewal requirements are jurisdiction-specific and should be verified with the applicable board/regulatory body rather than assumed from another jurisdiction or a universal rule.
candidates.source_document_title: Nurse Licensure Guidance; Licensure; Member Board Profiles
candidates.source_locator: Nurse Licensure Guidance: licensure requirements vary by state and users are directed to state-specific requirements. Licensure page: requirements for each jurisdiction are available in the guidance tool and jurisdiction websites. Member Board Profiles: licensure requirements differ and current state data should be verified against the state Nurse Practice Act/regulations or BON.
candidates.source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCSBN licensure guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A nurse is preparing to renew a nursing license. Which approach is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care: participate in quality-improvement and professional-practice activities, evaluate care against standards, and promote accountability and safe care systems.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — nursing peer review and professional practice evaluation
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate nursing peer review from performance appraisal, informal peer feedback, and credentialing by recognizing its systematic assessment of peer nursing practice against professional standards.

options.A: It is the manager's annual employment-performance appraisal focused on attendance, goals, compensation, and job performance.
options.B: It is informal coworker feedback that is not intended to assess nursing practice against professional standards.
options.C: It is a systematic assessment by nursing peers of the quality and appropriateness of nursing care against professional standards of practice.
options.D: It is the credentialing process used to verify an applicant's education and license before employment.

candidates.rationale: ANA describes nursing peer review as a process in which practicing registered nurses systematically assess, monitor, and make judgments about the quality of nursing care provided by peers as measured against professional standards of practice. The focus is nursing practice and quality improvement, accountability, learning, and identification of practice patterns needing improvement. Therefore C is correct. A describes employment performance evaluation, B describes informal peer feedback, and D describes credential verification rather than peer review.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nursing peer review is a systematic peer assessment of nursing-care quality and appropriateness against professional standards, distinct from employment performance evaluation, casual feedback, or credentialing.
candidates.source_document_title: Peer Review Tip: Distinguishing the Difference Between Peer Review, Peer Evaluation, and Peer Feedback
candidates.source_locator: Peer review section: practicing RNs systematically assess, monitor, and make judgments about quality of nursing care provided by peers as measured against professional standards; focus of peer review is practice, including quality, strengths/weaknesses, evidence for practice change, and patterns requiring more knowledge.
candidates.source_organization: American Nurses Association (ANA)
candidates.source_version_date: ANA consultation article originally published April 2015; current ANA page live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care > Assignment, Delegation and Supervision: identify assignments based on client needs; assign/delegate to personnel with appropriate competency and within allowable duties; evaluate staff ability considering competency, judgment and decision-making; establish priorities based on acuity.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — staffing skill mix, assignment, competency and acuity
candidates.educational_objective: Build a safe nursing skill mix by matching changing patient needs, acuity and workload with the authorized scope, competence, education, experience and available support of the nursing team rather than relying on head count, seniority or preference alone.

options.A: Base the staffing mix primarily on staff seniority and address competency differences after assignments are made.
options.B: Use the same staffing pattern throughout the shift even when patient acuity, workload, and required competencies change.
options.C: Base assignments primarily on staff scheduling preferences once the planned head count has been met.
options.D: Base the staffing mix on patient care needs, acuity, and workload, matched with each staff member's authorized scope or role, education, skills, competencies, experience, and relevant unit/support factors.

candidates.rationale: ANA staffing principles state that appropriate staffing is driven by the needs of the healthcare consumer or population and must account for patient acuity/intensity, workload, required clinical competencies, staff education, skill mix, experience, scope of practice, and characteristics/resources of the practice environment. Staffing plans must also be flexible enough to respond to changes in patient needs and care demands across and within shifts. Therefore D is correct. Seniority alone, a fixed staffing pattern, or scheduling preferences/head count alone do not address the patient- and competency-based factors required for safe staffing.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Safe staffing and skill-mix decisions are dynamic and should match patient needs, acuity and workload with staff scope, education, skills, competencies, experience and relevant unit/resource factors rather than relying on seniority, preferences or fixed head count alone.
candidates.source_document_title: Principles for Nurse Staffing, 3rd Edition; Workforce Management
candidates.source_locator: ANA Principles for Nurse Staffing: staffing decisions are based on the number and needs of healthcare consumers/populations; population needs determine required competencies; staff should practice to license/education/scope/documented competence; staffing plans adjust to changes in care needs across hours/shifts/days. ANA Workforce Management: staffing resources consider patient care needs/acuity/intensity/workload together with staff skill mix, education, competencies, experience, unit variables and available resources.
candidates.source_organization: American Nurses Association (ANA)
candidates.source_version_date: ANA Principles for Nurse Staffing, 3rd Edition (2019) with current ANA staffing guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care: document client care accurately, maintain legal/professional accountability, communicate changes and interventions, and follow organizational/regulatory requirements for records.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — legal nursing documentation and record correction
candidates.educational_objective: Document nursing assessments, interventions, communications, and client responses accurately and promptly after care, and correct charting errors through a traceable approved process without deleting or concealing the original record.

options.A: Document assessments and care objectively, accurately, and promptly after they occur, and correct errors through the approved traceable record process.
options.B: Document planned interventions before they are performed when the nurse expects to complete them by the end of the shift.
options.C: Delete an inaccurate electronic entry so the original information is no longer visible in the record.
options.D: Limit documentation to medications and procedures because client assessments and responses are not part of the legal health record.

candidates.rationale: Current Open RN/NCBI nursing guidance states that the electronic health record is a legal document and that nursing documentation should be objective, factual, professional, accurate, and timely. Care or assessments that were not completed must never be charted as completed, and documentation should occur after the task or as close to the time of care as possible. Electronic charting errors should be corrected using the record's traceable correction process rather than erased or concealed. Therefore A is correct. B is advance/falsified charting, C destroys the audit trail, and D incorrectly excludes assessments and responses from nursing documentation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nursing documentation is part of the legal health record and must be objective, accurate, timely, completed after care, and corrected through a traceable process rather than erased or prospectively falsified.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Fundamentals, 2nd edition — Communication: Documentation; Nursing Management and Professional Concepts — Legal Implications
candidates.source_locator: Nursing Fundamentals > 2.5 Documentation > Legal Documentation: EHR documentation is a legal document; objective/factual/professional; accurate and timely after task; do not chart uncompleted care; electronic errors corrected with details/correction preserved. Nursing Management and Professional Concepts > Documentation: document assessments, observations, communications and actions objectively, timely and accurately, as close to care as possible.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / Open RN
candidates.source_version_date: Open RN Nursing Fundamentals 2nd edition current in NCBI Bookshelf; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care: advocate for client rights and preferences, address ethical dilemmas, use appropriate consultation/resources, support shared decision-making, and coordinate interdisciplinary care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — ethics consultation and interdisciplinary resolution of treatment conflict
candidates.educational_objective: Use healthcare ethics consultation when patients, families, and clinicians face unresolved value-based uncertainty or conflict about an ethically appropriate treatment plan.

options.A: Ask risk management to determine legal liability before clarifying the treatment values and goals in conflict.
options.B: Use a routine discharge-planning conference even though the unresolved issue is an ethical conflict about treatment.
options.C: Request a healthcare ethics consultation to clarify the ethics concern, relevant values and options, and ethically supportable approaches to the disagreement.
options.D: Ask security to resolve the disagreement because treatment-value conflicts are primarily behavioral-management problems.

candidates.rationale: The VA National Center for Ethics in Health Care describes healthcare ethics consultation as a resource when there is uncertainty or conflict about values and what should be done in healthcare. The consultation process clarifies the ethics question, gathers relevant facts and preferences, considers ethically justifiable options, and supports communication and resolution among involved parties. The National Center also states that ethics consultation is not an investigative or misconduct function. Therefore C is correct. A substitutes liability analysis for ethics clarification, B does not address the ethical conflict itself, and D misclassifies a values-based treatment disagreement as a security problem.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A healthcare ethics consultation is appropriate for unresolved conflict or uncertainty about values and what should be done in a complex treatment decision; the service clarifies ethics concerns and ethically supportable options rather than investigating misconduct or determining liability.
candidates.source_document_title: Where do I go for help?; Ethics Consultation CASES Framework
candidates.source_locator: Where do I go for help?: ethics concerns involve uncertainty or conflict about values and judgments about ethically justifiable options; health care ethics questions should be directed to the local Health Care Ethics Consultation Service. ECWeb/CASES framework: clarify ethics question, assemble information, synthesize ethical analysis/options, explain and support the consultation process.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs — National Center for Ethics in Health Care
candidates.source_version_date: Current VA National Center for Ethics in Health Care guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client, family, and healthcare team disagree about the ethically appropriate treatment plan in a complex case. Which resource is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: assess cultural/spiritual influences, use therapeutic and respectful communication, recognize personal bias/assumptions, and provide individualized psychosocially responsive care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — cultural humility, bias awareness and individualized care
candidates.educational_objective: Practice cultural humility through ongoing self-reflection about assumptions, bias and power and by learning from each individual client's cultural identity, experiences, values, beliefs and preferences rather than relying on stereotypes or presumed mastery.

options.A: Apply a previously learned cultural profile to predict the client's preferences without asking about individual differences.
options.B: Avoid reflecting on culture, assumptions, or bias so the nurse's own values cannot influence the interaction.
options.C: Treat completion of cultural-competence training as permanent mastery of the beliefs and preferences of people from that group.
options.D: Use ongoing self-reflection about beliefs, assumptions, bias and power while learning directly from the individual client's experiences, values, beliefs, and preferences.

candidates.rationale: HHS Think Cultural Health's CLAS in Nursing program describes cultural humility through continuing self-awareness and patient-centered learning. Nurses are asked to examine their own beliefs and values and become aware of privilege, power, bias, stereotypes, and assumptions, while also getting to know the individual patient's cultural identity and providing care responsive to that person's experiences, values, beliefs, and preferences. Therefore D is correct. A substitutes stereotyping for individual assessment, B rejects the self-reflection required for humility, and C treats cultural learning as fixed mastery rather than an ongoing process.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Cultural humility in nursing involves ongoing self-awareness of assumptions/bias/power and individualized learning from and responsiveness to the patient's own experiences, values, beliefs and preferences rather than stereotyping or claiming permanent mastery.
candidates.source_document_title: Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Nursing; What is CLAS?
candidates.source_locator: CLAS in Nursing program overview: cultural competency and cultural humility; Course 2 Self-awareness covers beliefs, values, privilege, power, bias and stereotypes; Course 3 learns the patient's cultural identity; Course 4 responds to patient experiences, values, beliefs and preferences. What is CLAS?: respect the whole individual and respond to individual health needs/preferences.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health — Think Cultural Health
candidates.source_version_date: CLAS in Nursing released February 13, 2024; current nursing course and HHS CLAS guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute and chronic endocrine alterations, identify pathophysiologic responses, and intervene appropriately for physiologic instability/complications.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — hyperthyroidism symptom recognition
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the classic hypermetabolic pattern of hyperthyroidism while understanding that symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.

options.A: Weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, and a rapid or irregular heartbeat.
options.B: Weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, and a slowed heart rate.
options.C: Central weight gain, rounded face, purple striae, and proximal muscle weakness.
options.D: Weight loss, hyperpigmentation, salt craving, and persistent hypotension.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK lists weight loss despite increased appetite, rapid or irregular heartbeat, sweating or difficulty tolerating heat, tremor, nervousness, and other hypermetabolic findings among common symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Therefore A is the pattern most consistent with hyperthyroidism. B is more consistent with hypothyroidism, C with hypercortisolism/Cushing syndrome, and D with primary adrenal insufficiency. The item asks for the most consistent symptom cluster, not a definitive diagnosis; thyroid testing is required to confirm hyperthyroidism.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Weight loss despite increased appetite with heat intolerance/sweating and rapid or irregular heartbeat is a characteristic hyperthyroidism symptom pattern, though laboratory testing is needed for diagnosis.
candidates.source_document_title: Hyperthyroidism (Overactive Thyroid)
candidates.source_locator: What are the symptoms of hyperthyroidism?: weight loss despite increased appetite; rapid or irregular heartbeat; sweating/trouble tolerating heat; tremor and other symptoms. Diagnosis section: hyperthyroidism cannot be diagnosed from symptoms alone and is confirmed with thyroid testing.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NIDDK patient/clinical information live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: Which cluster of findings is most consistent with hyperthyroidism?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize endocrine pathophysiology and signs/symptoms of acute or chronic hormone excess/deficiency and differentiate related complications.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — Cushing syndrome versus adrenal insufficiency
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate cortisol excess from primary adrenal insufficiency by recognizing the characteristic Cushing pattern of central/upper-body weight gain, rounded face, and cervicodorsal fat accumulation.

options.A: Diffuse hyperpigmentation with weight loss, salt craving, and persistent hypotension.
options.B: A rounded face with upper-body weight gain and increased fat at the base of the neck or between the shoulders.
options.C: Enlarged hands and jaw with coarse facial features and increased shoe size.
options.D: Cold intolerance, bradycardia, constipation, and generalized weight gain.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK describes common physical changes of Cushing syndrome as weight gain, a round face, increased fat around the base of the neck, and a fatty hump between the shoulders, often with thin limbs, purple striae, bruising, and muscle weakness. In contrast, primary adrenal insufficiency/Addison disease commonly causes weight loss, low blood pressure, salt craving, and skin darkening. Therefore B is the finding most consistent with Cushing syndrome rather than primary adrenal insufficiency. C is more consistent with acromegaly and D with hypothyroidism.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Rounded face with upper-body/neck/upper-back fat accumulation is characteristic of Cushing syndrome, whereas weight loss, hypotension, salt craving and hyperpigmentation favor primary adrenal insufficiency.
candidates.source_document_title: Cushing's Syndrome; Symptoms & Causes of Adrenal Insufficiency & Addison's Disease
candidates.source_locator: Cushing's Syndrome > Symptoms: weight gain, round face, increased fat around base of neck, fatty hump between shoulders, wide purple stretch marks and muscle weakness. Adrenal Insufficiency/Addison's Disease > Symptoms: weight loss, low blood pressure, salt craving; Addison's disease may cause skin darkening.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NIDDK endocrine information live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: Which physical finding is most consistent with Cushing syndrome rather than primary adrenal insufficiency?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: interpret fluid/electrolyte and endocrine alterations, recognize pathophysiologic responses and complications, and manage acute or complex physiologic changes.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — SIAD fluid/electrolyte pattern
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize SIAD as hypotonic hyponatremia with impaired free-water excretion and inappropriately concentrated urine in a generally euvolemic patient after other causes are excluded.

options.A: Free-water loss with hypernatremia and persistently dilute urine.
options.B: Hypovolemic hypernatremia with maximally concentrated urine from an appropriate vasopressin response.
options.C: Hypotonic hyponatremia in a generally euvolemic client with urine that remains inappropriately concentrated rather than maximally dilute.
options.D: Hypertonic hyponatremia with maximally dilute urine caused by complete suppression of vasopressin.

candidates.rationale: Current Endotext guidance describes SIAD as inappropriate antidiuresis in the setting of low plasma osmolality. Persistent vasopressin action impairs free-water excretion, producing dilutional hypotonic hyponatremia; the urine is not maximally dilute, commonly with urine osmolality above 100 mOsm/kg. Patients are generally clinically euvolemic after other causes such as hypovolemia, adrenal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism are excluded. Therefore C is correct. A is more consistent with diabetes insipidus/free-water loss, B describes an appropriate concentrating response to volume depletion rather than SIAD, and D combines non-SIAD tonicity with suppressed vasopressin/maximally dilute urine.
candidates.source_claim_supported: SIAD produces hypotonic dilutional hyponatremia with persistent antidiuresis and urine that remains more concentrated than an appropriate maximally dilute response, typically in a clinically euvolemic patient after competing causes are excluded.
candidates.source_document_title: The Neurohypophysis: Endocrinology of Vasopressin and Oxytocin; Hyponatremia
candidates.source_locator: The Neurohypophysis > Pathophysiology and Diagnosis of SIAD: hypoosmolar plasma with AVP inappropriate for osmolality; urine not maximally dilute, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg indicates AVP action; urine sodium assists differentiation from hypovolemia. Hyponatremia > SIAD diagnostic criteria: hyponatremia, urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg, absence of hypovolemia/hypotension, edema, adrenal failure and hypothyroidism.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / Endotext
candidates.source_version_date: Neurohypophysis chapter updated December 18, 2025; Endotext current in 2026; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: Which laboratory and fluid-balance pattern is most consistent with syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (SIAD)?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize acute GI hemorrhage patterns, assess hemodynamic stability, identify possible bleeding sources and intervene for life-threatening blood loss.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — interpretation of hematochezia and acute GI bleeding source
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret hematochezia as usually indicating lower-GI bleeding while recognizing that brisk upper-GI hemorrhage can also cause hematochezia, especially with hemodynamic instability.

options.A: Hematochezia specifically localizes the source to the rectum regardless of bleeding rate or hemodynamic status.
options.B: Hematochezia usually suggests a lower gastrointestinal source, but a brisk upper gastrointestinal bleed can also present with hematochezia, particularly when the client is hemodynamically unstable.
options.C: Hematochezia is more typical of an upper gastrointestinal source than a lower gastrointestinal source.
options.D: Hematochezia provides no useful localization information because upper and lower gastrointestinal sources are equally likely in all presentations.

candidates.rationale: Hematochezia most often reflects lower gastrointestinal bleeding, but it is not an absolute anatomic localizer. ACG lower-GI bleeding guidance emphasizes that hematochezia accompanied by hemodynamic instability may indicate a brisk upper gastrointestinal source and should prompt evaluation for upper-GI bleeding. Therefore B is correct. A is overly specific, C reverses the usual localization, and D incorrectly states that the finding has no localization value at all.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hematochezia usually suggests a lower gastrointestinal source, but brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding can present with hematochezia, especially when accompanied by hemodynamic instability; it is not an absolute anatomic localizer.
candidates.source_document_title: Management of Patients With Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding: An Updated ACG Guideline
candidates.source_locator: ACG guideline framework for acute overt LGIB and differential evaluation; prior/current ACG guidance explicitly states that hematochezia with hemodynamic instability may indicate an upper-GI source and warrants upper-endoscopic evaluation. ACG current-guidelines page continues to list the February 2023 updated lower-GI bleeding guideline.
candidates.source_organization: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG)
candidates.source_version_date: Am J Gastroenterol. 2023;118(2):208-231; remains the current ACG lower-GI bleeding guideline in 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation: recognize new or worsening neurologic alterations, distinguish complications from transient triggers, and intervene appropriately for acute changes in chronic neurologic disease.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — multiple-sclerosis relapse versus pseudo-relapse
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours in multiple sclerosis as possible relapse requiring evaluation while first assessing for infection, fever, heat, stress, or other pseudo-relapse triggers.

options.A: The symptoms are a pseudo-relapse because any new neurologic symptom lasting more than 24 hours is caused by heat, stress, fever, or infection.
options.B: The symptoms are routine daily fluctuation and do not require assessment when they persist for two days.
options.C: The findings may represent an MS relapse and warrant prompt evaluation, including assessment for infection, fever, heat, stress, or another pseudo-relapse trigger.
options.D: The symptoms establish permanent disease progression because an MS relapse cannot cause new visual or sensory findings.

candidates.rationale: Current U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs multiple-sclerosis guidance describes a relapse as new or worsening neurologic symptoms lasting more than 24 hours that reflect new inflammatory activity and are not better explained by infection, fever, heat, stress, or another pseudo-relapse trigger. Visual and sensory symptoms can occur with MS relapses. New symptoms persisting for two days therefore warrant prompt evaluation by the MS care team, including assessment for pseudo-relapse triggers and other causes; the vignette alone does not establish a definite relapse. Therefore C is correct. A incorrectly labels all prolonged symptoms as pseudo-relapse, B dismisses symptoms that require assessment, and D incorrectly equates a possible relapse with permanent progression.
candidates.source_claim_supported: New visual or sensory neurologic symptoms persisting more than 24 hours in a person with MS may represent relapse and warrant prompt evaluation, but infection, fever, heat, stress and other pseudo-relapse triggers should be assessed before concluding a true relapse.
candidates.source_document_title: Relapse Management for Multiple Sclerosis; What is Multiple Sclerosis?
candidates.source_locator: Relapse Management for Multiple Sclerosis: relapse involves new/worsening MS symptoms lasting >24 hours; contact MS provider for new/worsening symptoms; evaluate for infection and other triggers; pseudo-relapses can occur with infection, stress, and heat. What is MS?: relapse is major worsening of old symptoms or new symptoms lasting at least 24 hours and not caused by infection, fever, or stress.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs — Multiple Sclerosis Centers of Excellence
candidates.source_version_date: Current VA MS guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client with multiple sclerosis develops new visual disturbance and numbness that persist for two days. What is the nurse's best interpretation?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret laboratory results, monitor therapeutic medication effect, recognize abnormal coagulation values and intervene for treatment-related risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — warfarin INR interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret an INR below the prescribed warfarin target range as subtherapeutic anticoagulation and recognize PT/INR as the monitoring test for vitamin K antagonist therapy.

options.A: The INR is below the prescribed therapeutic range and indicates an inadequate anticoagulant effect for this warfarin regimen.
options.B: The INR is within the usual therapeutic range for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin.
options.C: The INR is above the therapeutic range and indicates an excessive anticoagulant effect.
options.D: The INR cannot be used to assess warfarin because vitamin K antagonist effect is monitored with aPTT.

candidates.rationale: Current DailyMed warfarin labeling states that for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation the usual warfarin target is INR 2.5 with a therapeutic range of 2.0 to 3.0, with dosing individualized according to the INR and indication. An INR of 1.4 is therefore below the stated target range and indicates insufficient anticoagulant intensity for this regimen. A is correct. B misclassifies the result as therapeutic, C reverses the direction of abnormality, and D is incorrect because warfarin is routinely monitored with PT/INR rather than aPTT.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For nonvalvular atrial fibrillation treated with warfarin, the usual INR target is 2.5 with range 2.0-3.0; INR 1.4 is subtherapeutic relative to that prescribed range.
candidates.source_document_title: Warfarin Sodium Tablets
candidates.source_locator: Dosage and Administration §2.1 individualized dosing by INR; §2.2 Atrial Fibrillation: in nonvalvular AF target INR 2.5, range 2.0-3.0.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling
candidates.source_version_date: Current DailyMed warfarin labeling live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client taking warfarin for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation has an INR of 1.4. How should the nurse interpret this result when the prescribed target range is INR 2.0–3.0?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential: identify transfusion compatibility risks, verify blood products, and prevent adverse transfusion events through correct interpretation of blood-group information.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — emergency ABO red-cell compatibility
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize group O red cells as the ABO-compatible emergency red-cell choice when recipient ABO type is not yet known, while distinguishing red-cell compatibility from plasma compatibility and avoiding overgeneralization to Rh selection.

options.A: Group O red blood cells lack A and B antigens and can be used for recipients of other ABO groups when emergency red-cell transfusion is required before typing is known.
options.B: Group O red blood cells are universal recipients and can receive red cells from every ABO group.
options.C: Group O red blood cells express both A and B antigens, which makes them compatible with all recipients.
options.D: AB plasma and group O red cells use the same ABO compatibility rule because plasma and red-cell compatibility are interchangeable.

candidates.rationale: AABB states that in an emergency anyone can receive type O red blood cells, which is why people with type O blood are commonly described as universal red-cell donors. This ABO red-cell compatibility principle is different from plasma compatibility; AABB separately notes that individuals of all ABO types can receive AB plasma. Therefore A is correct. B reverses donor/recipient terminology, C incorrectly states that group O red cells express A and B antigens, and D incorrectly treats red-cell and plasma compatibility as interchangeable. Rh selection and other compatibility considerations are outside the deliberately limited ABO-red-cell scope of this item.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For ABO red-cell compatibility, group O red cells can be used in emergencies before a recipient's ABO type is known; this does not mean group O is a universal recipient or that plasma compatibility follows the same rule.
candidates.source_document_title: FAQs About Blood and Blood Donation
candidates.source_locator: About Blood > Most common blood type: in an emergency, anyone can receive type O red blood cells; people with type O blood are known as universal donors. The same section states that individuals of all types can receive type AB plasma, demonstrating component-specific ABO compatibility.
candidates.source_organization: Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies (AABB)
candidates.source_version_date: Current AABB FAQ live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: During an emergency red-cell transfusion before the recipient's ABO type is known, why may group O red blood cells be selected?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort: assist with mobility and transfers, use assistive devices appropriately, and promote safe movement/positioning while preserving client function and comfort.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — safe transfer assessment and assistive equipment
candidates.educational_objective: Before transferring a client, assess mobility and assistance needs and use the appropriate assistive equipment and staffing level for the specific task rather than defaulting to manual lifting.

options.A: Use a gait belt and perform a one-person transfer before determining whether the client can bear weight or how much assistance is needed.
options.B: Manually lift the client's full body weight when the transfer distance is short and a second nurse is nearby.
options.C: Assess the client's mobility and assistance needs first, then use the recommended assistive equipment and number of staff for the transfer.
options.D: Begin the transfer without equipment and add a device only if the client becomes unstable while standing.

candidates.rationale: NIOSH identifies patient handling as a major source of musculoskeletal injury and recommends Safe Patient Handling and Mobility practices that use assistive lifting technology instead of unnecessary high-risk manual handling. VA's current SPHM program specifically uses patient-assessment algorithms to determine mobility/independence, select the safest handling method and equipment, and identify the number of staff needed for each task. Therefore C is correct. A begins a transfer before determining weight-bearing and assistance needs, B relies on manual lifting of full body weight, and D delays equipment selection until instability occurs rather than planning the transfer safely in advance.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Safe transfer planning should begin with assessment of patient mobility/assistance needs and then use appropriate assistive technology and staffing rather than routine manual lifting or waiting for instability.
candidates.source_document_title: About Safe Patient Handling and Mobility; Safe Patient Handling and Mobility (SPHM)
candidates.source_locator: NIOSH SPHM: patient handling is a major WMSD risk; use assistive lifting devices and safe patient-handling programs. VA SPHM: clinical/patient assessment algorithms select the right equipment and number of staff for each handling/mobility task; patient mobility tools assess mobility and degree of assistance and generate task-specific equipment/process recommendations.
candidates.source_organization: CDC/NIOSH; U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
candidates.source_version_date: NIOSH page May 9, 2024; current VA SPHM guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort: assess skin/wounds, provide wound care, monitor comfort/pain and document findings needed to evaluate basic-care interventions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — wound assessment and documentation
candidates.educational_objective: Document a wound comprehensively at baseline using precise location, measurements, wound-bed/periwound characteristics, drainage, pain and other relevant findings so later assessments can be compared accurately.

options.A: Record the wound stage and a photograph only; measurements and drainage characteristics can be added at discharge.
options.B: Record the dressing type and pain score only because wound-bed and surrounding-skin findings are treatment rather than assessment data.
options.C: Delay the baseline description until the first scheduled dressing change so admission findings do not affect later comparisons.
options.D: Record the wound's precise location, size, wound-bed and periwound findings, drainage characteristics, pain, and other relevant assessment findings.

candidates.rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills states that wound assessment and documentation should include the anatomic location, wound type and degree of tissue damage, wound bed, wound size, wound edges and periwound skin, signs of infection, pain, and drainage characteristics. Wounds should be measured on admission and at subsequent dressing changes so progress can be compared over time. Therefore D is correct. A omits key baseline measurements and drainage findings, B incorrectly excludes wound-bed/periwound assessment, and C delays information needed for comparison and care planning.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Comprehensive baseline wound documentation should include precise location, dimensions, wound-bed/periwound findings, drainage, pain and other relevant assessment characteristics, with measurements beginning on admission for later comparison.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Skills — Chapter 20 Wound Care
candidates.source_locator: 20.3 Assessing Wounds: assessment/documentation includes anatomic location, wound type, tissue damage, wound bed, size, edges/periwound skin, signs of infection and pain. Type and Amount of Exudate: document color, consistency and amount. Wound Size: measure on admission and every dressing change. Checklist for Wound Assessment repeats location, dimensions, drainage, periwound, pain and infection findings.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / Open RN Nursing Skills
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCBI/Open RN Nursing Skills content live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: perform medication reconciliation, identify adverse effects/interactions/duplication, monitor medication response, and provide safe medication teaching across transitions of care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — older-adult polypharmacy and comprehensive medication review
candidates.educational_objective: Perform comprehensive medication review in older adults with polypharmacy by reconciling all prescription, OTC and supplement products and assessing ongoing need, interactions, adverse effects, duplication and medication-management burden.

options.A: Review the complete regimen—including prescriptions from all clinicians, OTC products, vitamins and supplements—for adverse effects, interactions, duplication, ongoing need, and medication-management problems.
options.B: Review only medications prescribed by the admitting clinician because drugs from other prescribers are outside the current medication review.
options.C: Stop the oldest medications first because duration of therapy is the primary criterion for deprescribing in polypharmacy.
options.D: Assume the regimen is safe when every drug was prescribed by a licensed clinician, even when several prescribers are involved.

candidates.rationale: The National Institute on Aging notes that older adults often take many medicines, which increases the risk of side effects, drug interactions, duplicate ingredients, and medication-management difficulties. NIA advises patients and clinicians to maintain and review a complete list that includes prescriptions from all prescribers, over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, dietary supplements, and herbal remedies, and to ask whether every medicine is still needed. Therefore A is correct. B creates an incomplete reconciliation, C uses medication age rather than clinical indication/risk as the deprescribing criterion, and D incorrectly assumes multiple valid prescriptions cannot interact or duplicate therapy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Older-adult polypharmacy requires comprehensive review of all prescription and nonprescription products for interactions, side effects, duplication, ongoing necessity and management problems rather than assuming safety because each medication was individually prescribed.
candidates.source_document_title: Taking Medicines Safely as You Age
candidates.source_locator: Medication safety sections: tell providers about all medicines including those prescribed by other doctors, OTC drugs, vitamins, supplements and herbal remedies; mixing products can cause serious problems. Keeping track: maintain a complete list. Do I need to take so many medications?: polypharmacy is a concern in older adults and taking many medications increases side-effect and unintended-problem risk; discuss whether any can safely be reduced/stopped.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute on Aging (NIA), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NIA medication-safety guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: An older adult takes twelve medications prescribed by several clinicians. Which concern should the nurse prioritize during medication review?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: identify fall hazards, implement environmental safety measures, use appropriate assistive supports and prevent injury in high-risk clients.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — older-adult home fall prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Reduce home fall risk in older adults by removing trip hazards, improving lighting, installing grab bars/railings as needed, and supporting safe activity rather than environmental hazards or unnecessary immobility.

options.A: Limit routine walking inside the home so the older adult has fewer opportunities to experience a fall.
options.B: Remove tripping hazards, improve lighting, and install bathroom grab bars or other appropriate home-safety supports.
options.C: Keep familiar throw rugs in walking paths while adding brighter lighting to improve visual contrast.
options.D: Use loose backless slippers indoors because they are easier to remove if balance is lost.

candidates.rationale: Current CDC older-adult fall-prevention guidance recommends making the home safer by removing things that can be tripped over, improving lighting, installing grab bars in and around the tub or shower and next to the toilet, and adding stair railings. CDC also encourages strength and balance activity rather than unnecessary restriction of routine movement. Therefore B is correct. A promotes avoidable inactivity, C leaves a known tripping hazard in place, and D uses insecure footwear that can worsen fall risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Older-adult home fall prevention includes removing trip hazards such as throw rugs/clutter, improving lighting and installing bathroom grab bars/other supports; routine safe mobility should not be restricted solely to reduce opportunities to fall.
candidates.source_document_title: Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures; Information for Older Adults
candidates.source_locator: Preventing a fall or hip fracture > Make your home safer: get rid of trip hazards, add bathroom grab bars, railings on both sides of stairs, improve lighting. Strength and balance exercises are also recommended. Information for Older Adults explicitly identifies throw rugs as trip hazards and recommends brighter lighting and bathroom grab bars.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Preventing Falls and Hip Fractures updated January 27, 2026; current CDC fall-prevention guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide age-appropriate injury-prevention and health-promotion teaching and counsel clients on behaviors that reduce preventable morbidity and mortality.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — adult motor-vehicle injury prevention and seat-belt use
candidates.educational_objective: Teach adults to use a seat belt in every seating position on every trip because consistent restraint use substantially reduces serious crash injury and death and remains necessary even with airbags.

options.A: Reserve seat-belt use mainly for highway travel because short local trips have minimal serious-injury risk.
options.B: Adults seated in the rear seat can omit seat belts when the vehicle has front and side airbags.
options.C: Wear a seat belt in every seating position on every trip, no matter how short, because consistent restraint use substantially reduces serious crash-related injury and death.
options.D: Seat belts are primarily a pediatric intervention and add little protection after a passenger reaches adulthood.

candidates.rationale: Current CDC guidance states that wearing a seat belt is the most effective way to prevent injury or death in motor-vehicle crashes for adults and older children and that seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half. CDC recommends seat-belt use in front and back seats on every trip, no matter how short, and notes that airbags provide added protection rather than replacing seat belts. Therefore C is correct. A limits use based on trip length, B incorrectly treats airbags as a substitute, and D falsely minimizes adult benefit.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Adults should wear seat belts in front and rear seating positions on every trip regardless of length; seat belts reduce serious crash-related injury/death substantially and airbags do not replace them.
candidates.source_document_title: Facts About Seat Belt Use; Seat Belts
candidates.source_locator: Facts About Seat Belt Use > At a glance/Importance/What you can do: seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries/deaths by about half; use on every trip no matter how short; airbags are not a substitute. Seat Belts overview: buckle up—every seat, every trip; adult rear-seat use is also important.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Updated January 27, 2026
candidates.stem: Which statement should a nurse include when teaching an adult about motor-vehicle injury prevention?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide age-appropriate injury-prevention and health-promotion teaching for infants and families, including environmental exposure prevention and anticipatory guidance.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — infant ultraviolet/sun protection
candidates.educational_objective: Protect infants younger than 6 months from ultraviolet exposure primarily with shade, avoidance of direct sunlight and protective clothing, and consult a clinician before using sunscreen.

options.A: Use sunscreen as the primary protection for the infant because shade and clothing provide insufficient ultraviolet protection.
options.B: Provide brief direct midday sun exposure each day because infants younger than 6 months are less susceptible to sunburn.
options.C: Apply an adult sunscreen routinely to all exposed skin before using shade or protective clothing.
options.D: Keep the infant out of direct sunlight when possible, use shade and protective clothing, and ask the pediatrician or another clinician before applying sunscreen.

candidates.rationale: Current FDA guidance states that sunscreen is not generally recommended for infants younger than 6 months because their skin is more vulnerable to sunscreen adverse effects. The best protection is to keep infants out of direct sunlight, use shade and protective clothing when outdoors, and consult a doctor before applying sunscreen to a child younger than 6 months. Therefore D is correct. A and C make sunscreen the primary or routine first-line protection contrary to FDA guidance, while B exposes the infant during peak-intensity sunlight and falsely assumes reduced sunburn susceptibility.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For infants younger than 6 months, FDA recommends avoiding direct sun, using shade and protective clothing, and consulting a clinician before applying sunscreen rather than relying on sunscreen as the primary protective measure.
candidates.source_document_title: Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually; Sunscreen: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun
candidates.source_locator: Should You Put Sunscreen on Infants? Not Usually: FDA/AAP recommend keeping newborns and babies <6 months out of direct sunlight; shade is best protection; protective clothing/hat; check with pediatrician before sunscreen. Sunscreen FAQ: sunscreen is not recommended for infants under six months; keep them out of sun and use protective clothing; ask a doctor before sunscreen.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current FDA infant-sun-protection and sunscreen guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026; FDA sunscreen page reflects June 2026 monograph update
candidates.stem: A parent asks how to protect a 4-month-old infant from ultraviolet exposure. Which teaching is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide community education, identify health risks and warning signs, support early intervention, and connect individuals with appropriate preventive or health-care resources.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — community mental-health literacy and early intervention
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize Mental Health First Aid as an early-intervention community training program focused on recognizing challenges, providing initial support, and connecting people with appropriate help rather than diagnosing or replacing professional treatment.

options.A: Teach community members to recognize mental-health or substance-use challenges, provide initial support, and help connect the person with appropriate professional or community care.
options.B: Teach community members to diagnose psychiatric disorders and independently select definitive treatment plans.
options.C: Train nonclinicians to replace professional services by providing ongoing psychotherapy and medication management.
options.D: Teach participants to avoid responding until a licensed clinician is physically present.

candidates.rationale: Current Mental Health First Aid USA guidance describes MHFA as early-intervention training that teaches people to identify, understand, and respond to signs of mental-health or substance-use challenges, provide an initial level of support, and help connect the person with appropriate professional or other support. MHFA explicitly states that First Aiders do not diagnose mental illness and do not provide therapy or replace professional treatment. Therefore A is correct. B and C assign diagnostic/treatment roles outside the program, while D contradicts the purpose of equipping community members to offer safe initial support before or while professional help is being accessed.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Mental Health First Aid trains community members to recognize and respond to mental-health/substance-use challenges, provide initial support, and connect people with appropriate help; it does not train them to diagnose or replace professional treatment.
candidates.source_document_title: Mental Health First Aid Frequently Asked Questions; About Mental Health First Aid
candidates.source_locator: FAQ: MHFA provides early support by spotting warning signs and acting before problems worsen; First Aiders/Instructors do not diagnose or provide therapy and can connect people to professional help. About MHFA: training teaches how to recognize, understand and respond to mental-health/substance-use challenges and offer the first level of support.
candidates.source_organization: Mental Health First Aid USA / National Council for Mental Wellbeing
candidates.source_version_date: Current MHFA USA guidance live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: What is the purpose of Mental Health First Aid training for community members?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity, printed p.30: provide care for a client experiencing grief or loss; use therapeutic communication techniques; support emotional, mental and social well-being during stressful events.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — grief/loss and developmentally appropriate therapeutic communication
candidates.educational_objective: Use simple, direct, truthful, developmentally appropriate language when explaining death to a young child, and avoid euphemisms such as ‘went to sleep’ that can create confusion.

options.A: Say the grandparent ‘went to sleep’ so the child is protected from distressing details.
options.B: Use simple, direct, truthful words such as ‘died’ and explain concretely, at the child’s level, that the body has stopped working.
options.C: Avoid answering until an adult family member can provide a complete explanation of death.
options.D: Explain death using detailed biological mechanisms so the child receives the same information as an adult.

candidates.rationale: NCI’s PDQ health-professional summary states that when death is discussed with children, explanations should be simple and direct, truthful, and limited to detail the child can understand at the child’s age and developmental stage. It also states that proper words such as ‘died’ and ‘death’ should be used and that euphemisms such as ‘he is sleeping’ can confuse children. Therefore B is correct. A uses a specifically discouraged euphemism, C unnecessarily withholds an honest developmentally appropriate response, and D gives adult-level detail rather than matching the child’s comprehension.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A young child asking about death should receive a simple, direct, truthful, developmentally appropriate explanation using concrete death language rather than euphemisms or adult-level detail.
candidates.source_document_title: Grief, Bereavement, and Coping With Loss (PDQ®)–Health Professional Version
candidates.source_locator: Interventions for Grieving Children > Explanation of death: explanations should be simple/direct, truthful, and matched to age/development; Correct language: use proper words such as died/death and avoid euphemisms such as sleeping because they can confuse children. Page lines 500-508 in current NCI web rendering.
candidates.source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), PDQ Supportive and Palliative Care Editorial Board
candidates.source_version_date: Latest summary update June 26, 2024; regularly reviewed PDQ summary, live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, storage/safe handling, adverse-effect prevention, and client medication teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin storage and medication teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach safe insulin storage: refrigerate unopened insulin at the recommended temperature when possible, never use frozen insulin, protect it from heat/sunlight, and follow product-specific room-temperature limits.

options.A: Keep unopened insulin in a household freezer until first use, then thaw it at room temperature.
options.B: Keep unopened insulin refrigerated at about 36°F to 46°F when possible, never use insulin that has been frozen, and follow the specific product label for room-temperature limits.
options.C: Store unopened insulin at room temperature indefinitely because refrigeration is unnecessary before the first dose.
options.D: Keep insulin near a warm appliance or sunny window so it remains close to body temperature before injection.

candidates.rationale: FDA states that insulin manufacturers recommend refrigeration at approximately 36°F to 46°F; unopened insulin stored this way maintains potency until the labeled expiration date. FDA also states to avoid freezing and not to use insulin that has been frozen, and to keep insulin away from direct heat and sunlight. Room-temperature allowances depend on product and conditions, so the product label should be followed. Therefore B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Unopened insulin should generally be refrigerated at approximately 36°F to 46°F when possible; frozen insulin should not be used, heat/sunlight should be avoided, and room-temperature storage depends on the product and conditions.
candidates.source_document_title: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
candidates.source_locator: Insulin Storage and Effectiveness > Insulin for Injection: refrigerator approximately 36°F to 46°F; unopened refrigerated insulin maintains potency until expiration; avoid freezing/do not use frozen insulin; keep away from direct heat and sunlight.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current FDA web guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client asks how to store unopened insulin at home. Which instruction is most accurate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.14: manage clients with acute or life-threatening physical-health conditions; recognize signs and symptoms of complications and intervene; identify pathophysiology related to acute/chronic conditions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — vesicant extravasation and acute tissue injury
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize burning and swelling during vesicant infusion as possible extravasation with risk of tissue necrosis requiring prompt management.

options.A: Vesicant extravasation usually causes only transient skin discoloration without deeper tissue injury.
options.B: Burning at the site confirms a systemic allergic reaction rather than a local infusion complication.
options.C: Tissue injury is unlikely once the IV catheter is in a peripheral vein, so the infusion can continue while the site is observed.
options.D: Vesicant extravasation can cause severe local tissue injury, including necrosis, so the infusion complication requires prompt recognition and management.

candidates.rationale: NCBI StatPearls defines a vesicant as a drug that can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates into subcutaneous tissue. Reported complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema, and tissue necrosis. Management begins with stopping vesicant administration after extravasation is confirmed. Therefore burning and swelling during a vesicant infusion are urgent because serious local tissue injury can occur; D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Burning and swelling during vesicant infusion are concerning for extravasation, which can cause serious local injury including tissue necrosis and requires prompt management.
candidates.source_document_title: Cancer Chemotherapy
candidates.source_locator: Other Issues > Complications of Extravasation of Vesicants and Management: vesicants can cause tissue necrosis after extravasation; complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema and tissue necrosis; management begins by stopping vesicant administration after confirmation.
candidates.source_organization: NCBI Bookshelf / StatPearls
candidates.source_version_date: StatPearls 2026 edition; article last updated February 27, 2023; live applicability rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: During infusion of a vesicant antineoplastic drug, the client reports burning and swelling at the IV site. Why is this finding urgent?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: controlled substances, safe medication administration, dosage calculations, adverse-effect prevention, monitoring and teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — opioid conversion and overdose prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Use opioid equianalgesic conversions as estimates rather than exact switch doses and reduce the starting dose of the new opioid as clinically appropriate to account for incomplete cross-tolerance and patient variability.

options.A: Use the calculated equianalgesic dose without reduction because conversion factors fully account for cross-tolerance and individual response.
options.B: Increase the calculated dose of the new opioid because incomplete cross-tolerance makes the replacement opioid predictably less potent.
options.C: Treat the conversion as an estimate and generally start the new opioid below the calculated equivalent dose when appropriate because cross-tolerance and individual response vary.
options.D: Match the number and strength of tablets between opioids because equianalgesic estimates are unnecessary when both drugs are oral.

candidates.rationale: CDC states that equianalgesic/MME conversions are estimates and do not account for individual variability. The CDC table cautions not to use the calculated MME dose directly to determine the dose of a new opioid; the new opioid is typically dosed substantially lower to reduce overdose risk from incomplete cross-tolerance and variability. C is therefore the safest principle.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Opioid conversion estimates are not exact switch doses; the new opioid should generally be started below the calculated equivalent dose when clinically appropriate because incomplete cross-tolerance and individual variability increase overdose risk.
candidates.source_document_title: CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022
candidates.source_locator: MME conversion table cautions: equianalgesic conversions are estimates; do not use calculated MME dose directly when converting opioids; the new opioid is typically dosed substantially lower because of incomplete cross-tolerance and individual pharmacokinetic variability. Implementation considerations also advise reducing total daily dosage when changing opioids to account for incomplete cross-tolerance.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication administration, monitoring, adverse effects and client medication teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication deprescribing and patient teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients that transient rebound symptoms can occur when long-term PPIs are stopped and that either tapering or abrupt discontinuation may be considered when deprescribing is appropriate.

options.A: Use an exact eight-week taper for every long-term PPI user because any faster reduction causes permanent pathologic acid hypersecretion.
options.B: Explain that transient rebound upper-GI symptoms may occur after long-term PPI discontinuation and that either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
options.C: Never stop a PPI abruptly because rebound symptoms are uniformly dangerous and cannot be managed clinically.
options.D: Continue the PPI indefinitely after the original indication has resolved because long-term duration alone creates a maintenance indication.

candidates.rationale: AGA Best Practice Advice states that patients who discontinue long-term PPI therapy should be advised that transient upper-GI symptoms may occur from rebound acid hypersecretion and that either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered. Patients without a definitive chronic indication should be considered for a trial of deprescribing. B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: When long-term PPI therapy no longer has a clear indication, deprescribing may be considered; clients should be warned about transient rebound symptoms, and tapering or abrupt discontinuation are both acceptable approaches.
candidates.source_document_title: De-prescribing proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) — Clinical Practice Update
candidates.source_locator: Best Practice Advice 2, 8, and 9: patients without a definitive chronic indication should be considered for deprescribing; warn of transient upper-GI symptoms due to rebound acid hypersecretion; either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
candidates.source_organization: American Gastroenterological Association (AGA)
candidates.source_version_date: Published February 16, 2022; live guidance rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client has taken a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) long term but no longer has a clear ongoing indication. Which deprescribing teaching is most accurate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: review pertinent data before medication administration, monitor medication response/adverse effects, and provide safe medication care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — statin monitoring and hepatic safety
candidates.educational_objective: Know that atorvastatin labeling supports baseline consideration of liver-enzyme testing and repeat testing when clinically indicated rather than routine fixed monthly monitoring for every patient.

options.A: Obtain liver enzymes every month for every client taking atorvastatin regardless of symptoms or prior results.
options.B: Avoid all liver-enzyme testing after atorvastatin is started because transaminase results do not contribute to medication-safety assessment.
options.C: Wait to obtain any baseline liver assessment until symptoms of hepatic injury develop after therapy has already begun.
options.D: Consider liver-enzyme testing before atorvastatin is started and repeat testing when clinically indicated rather than on a fixed monthly schedule.

candidates.rationale: The current DailyMed LIPITOR label states: consider liver-enzyme testing before initiation and when clinically indicated thereafter. It does not require fixed monthly testing for all patients. Therefore D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current LIPITOR labeling advises considering liver-enzyme testing before initiation and repeating testing when clinically indicated, not on a universal fixed monthly schedule.
candidates.source_document_title: LIPITOR — atorvastatin calcium tablet, film coated
candidates.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions §5.3 Hepatic Dysfunction: consider liver enzyme testing before LIPITOR initiation and when clinically indicated thereafter; contraindicated in acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine official drug label
candidates.source_version_date: Updated April 15, 2024

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: controlled substances, safe medication handling, administration and security-related medication practices.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — controlled-substance storage and security
candidates.educational_objective: Apply federal DEA physical-security requirements by storing Schedule II–V controlled substances in securely locked, substantially constructed storage that meets applicable DEA requirements.

options.A: Store Schedule II–V substances on open shelving inside a locked clinic room because the locked room alone satisfies the cabinet requirement.
options.B: Keep Schedule II–V substances in an unlocked medication cart during operating hours when licensed clinicians are working on the unit.
options.C: Use one shared access key for all employees so medications remain available while access restrictions are handled through end-of-day inventory.
options.D: Store Schedule II–V controlled substances in a securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet or other storage meeting applicable DEA security requirements.

candidates.rationale: DEA guidance applying 21 CFR 1301.75(b) states that controlled substances stored at a practitioner's registered location must be kept in a securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet, subject to applicable DEA security requirements. DEA also states that Schedule II–V controlled substances may be stored in a safe or securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet. D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: At a DEA-registered practice location, controlled substances must be secured in storage meeting DEA physical-security requirements, including a securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet under 21 CFR 1301.75(b).
candidates.source_document_title: Controlled Substance Security Q&A — Civil Unrest/Looting Registration Guidance Documents Q&A
candidates.source_locator: Practitioners Q&A: continue to comply with 21 CFR 1301.75(b), which requires all controlled substances to be stored in a securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet. Pharmacy Q&A: Schedule II, III, IV and V may be stored in a safe or securely locked, substantially constructed cabinet.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), Diversion Control Division
candidates.source_version_date: DEA guidance EO-DEA155/EO-DEA165, June 2020; 21 CFR 1301.75(b) applicability live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A DEA-registered outpatient clinic stores Schedule II–V controlled substances on site. Which storage practice best aligns with federal DEA requirements?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: handle biohazardous materials safely, protect from injury, and provide safety/infection-prevention teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — home sharps disposal
candidates.educational_objective: Teach home users to place used needles immediately into an appropriate sharps container and dispose of the filled container according to local/community requirements.

options.A: Recap used needles with two hands and then place them loose in household trash after verifying that each cap is secure.
options.B: Flush used needles down the toilet after injection so household members and sanitation workers cannot contact the sharps.
options.C: Keep used needles on an uncovered rigid tray until several have accumulated, then transfer the group into household trash.
options.D: Place each used needle promptly into an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container when available and follow local disposal requirements when the container is ready for removal.

candidates.rationale: FDA recommends placing used needles and other sharps in a sharps disposal container immediately after use. FDA-cleared containers are preferred when available, and when the container is about three-quarters full, community guidelines should be followed for disposal. Loose sharps should not be placed in household/public trash or flushed down the toilet. D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Used home injection needles should be placed immediately into an appropriate sharps disposal container, preferably FDA-cleared when available, and the container should be disposed of according to local/community requirements.
candidates.source_document_title: Best Way to Get Rid of Used Needles and Other Sharps
candidates.source_locator: Step 1: place all needles and other sharps in a sharps disposal container immediately after use. Step 2: dispose of used sharps containers according to community guidelines. FDA Sharps Disposal Containers page: FDA-cleared containers are recommended; appropriate heavy-duty household containers may be alternatives when cleared containers are unavailable.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current FDA consumer guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
