candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — infection-prevention principles and historical Universal Precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the historical purpose of Universal Precautions: blood/body-fluid precautions applied regardless of a patient's known bloodborne infection status during the HIV/AIDS era.

options.A: Universal Precautions developed during the HIV/AIDS era and applied blood and specified body-fluid precautions to all patients regardless of known infection status.
options.B: Universal Precautions began as a food-safety program and were later transferred to hospitals to address occupational blood exposure.
options.C: Universal Precautions required isolation of every hospitalized patient regardless of diagnosis, symptoms, or anticipated blood exposure.
options.D: Universal Precautions replaced hand hygiene and personal protective equipment with environmental disinfection as the principal control.

candidates.rationale: CDC's historical isolation-guideline table identifies Universal Precautions in 1985–1988 as having developed in response to the HIV/AIDS epidemic and applying Blood and Body Fluid precautions to all patients regardless of infection status. It also included PPE, handwashing, and sharps recommendations. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Universal Precautions were developed in response to HIV/AIDS and applied specified blood/body-fluid precautions regardless of known infection status.
candidates.source_document_title: Appendix A: Table 1. History of Guidelines for Isolation Precautions in Hospitals
candidates.source_locator: Table 1, 1985–88 Universal Precautions row: developed in response to HIV/AIDS epidemic; Blood and Body Fluid precautions applied to all patients regardless of infection status; PPE, handwashing, and sharps recommendations included.

candidates.source_version_date: CDC page updated November 27, 2023; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — staffing, workload, resource use and patient safety
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize inadequate RN staffing as a patient-safety risk associated with missed nursing care and adverse patient outcomes while interpreting staffing evidence with appropriate causal caution.

options.A: Assume lower RN staffing improves safety because fewer nurses reduce handoffs and therefore consistently decrease communication-related errors.
options.B: Recognize inadequate or lower RN staffing as a patient-safety risk associated in observational evidence with missed care, adverse outcomes, and higher mortality.
options.C: Assume staffing does not influence patient outcomes when the number of occupied beds stays constant across the shift.
options.D: Treat RN staffing only as a financial issue because clinical evidence has not linked workload or staffing with patient-safety outcomes.

candidates.rationale: AHRQ PSNet summarizes evidence that appropriate nurse staffing is critical to patient safety. Fewer nurses caring for patients is associated with higher mortality; inadequate staffing can lead to missed nursing care and negative outcomes, and missed care is more prevalent with low staffing. Because much of this evidence is observational and the staffing-outcome relationship is complex, the safest wording is an association rather than an absolute causal claim. B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Lower/inadequate nurse staffing is associated with missed nursing care and adverse patient-safety outcomes, including higher mortality, although the relationship is complex and much evidence is observational.
candidates.source_document_title: Patient Safety Amid Nursing Workforce Challenges
candidates.source_locator: Introduction: appropriate nurse staffing is critical to patient safety; fewer nurses are associated with higher patient mortality. Nursing Workforce Challenges and Patient Safety: inadequate staffing can lead to missed care and negative outcomes; missed care is more prevalent with low staffing; appropriate staffing tends to reduce avoidable harm.
candidates.source_organization: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), Patient Safety Network (PSNet)
candidates.source_version_date: Published April 24, 2024; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A nurse manager evaluates whether reducing registered-nurse staffing could affect patient safety. Which conclusion is most consistent with the evidence base?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: incorporate client cultural practices and beliefs when planning and providing care; use therapeutic communication and support psychosocial needs.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — cultural beliefs/practices and individualized care
candidates.educational_objective: Provide culturally responsive care by eliciting the individual client's beliefs, practices, and preferences rather than stereotyping, and integrate relevant preferences into safe care planning.

options.A: Use a standardized cultural profile to predict preferences instead of asking the individual client about values or practices.
options.B: Exclude cultural practices from the plan whenever biomedical treatment is available, even when the practices are safe.
options.C: Avoid discussing culture or health beliefs so cultural differences cannot influence communication or care planning.
options.D: Ask about the individual client’s cultural values, health beliefs, and preferences and incorporate relevant practices when compatible with safe, effective care.

candidates.rationale: HHS National CLAS Standard 1 calls for effective, understandable, respectful care and services responsive to cultural health beliefs and practices, languages, health literacy, and communication needs. HHS also describes CLAS as respecting the whole individual and responding to the individual's health needs and preferences. D is therefore the culturally responsive approach.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Culturally responsive care should be respectful of and responsive to the individual client's cultural health beliefs, practices, communication needs and preferences rather than relying on stereotypes.
candidates.source_document_title: National Standards for Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services (CLAS) in Health and Health Care
candidates.source_locator: Principal Standard 1: provide effective, understandable and respectful quality care/services responsive to cultural health beliefs and practices, languages, health literacy and communication needs. What is CLAS?: respect the whole individual and respond to the individual's health needs and preferences.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Minority Health
candidates.source_version_date: Current National CLAS Standards; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7: manage conflict among clients and staff; recognize/report ethical dilemmas; utilize resources to promote quality care; protect clients and health care personnel through care-delivery management.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — workplace conflict, safety reporting and organizational response
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize repeated hostile/intimidating workplace behavior as a safety concern that warrants use of the organization’s reporting and investigation process.

options.A: Recognize the repeated hostile and intimidating conduct as a workplace-safety concern and use the organization’s reporting, investigation, and response process.
options.B: Treat repeated verbal and relational aggression as expected socialization unless the new nurse experiences a physical injury.
options.C: Keep the repeated intimidation private between the two nurses because interpersonal hostility is outside workplace-safety processes.
options.D: Delay organizational reporting until probation ends because bullying concerns should be handled informally during orientation.

candidates.rationale: ANA states that incivility, bullying, and workplace violence are serious nursing-workplace issues. ANA defines bullying as repeated intentional hostility or aggression, often involving a power imbalance, and its 2025 position statement calls for a culture of safety with organizational reporting mechanisms, staff training, multidisciplinary investigation, and response. Repeated belittling and intimidation should therefore be addressed through the workplace-safety process rather than normalized. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Repeated hostile/intimidating conduct is a workplace-safety concern; ANA calls for reporting mechanisms, investigation, training and organizational response rather than normalization.
candidates.source_document_title: Workplace Violence Position Statement
candidates.source_locator: Statement of ANA Position: create a culture of safety; develop an organizational plan with a reporting mechanism for all incidents; train staff; investigate incidents through a multidisciplinary committee. ANA Workplace Violence resource: bullying involves repeated intentional hostility/aggression and workplace violence includes harassment and intimidation.
candidates.source_organization: American Nurses Association (ANA)
candidates.source_version_date: Effective March 13, 2025
candidates.stem: A new nurse reports repeated belittling comments, intimidation, and social exclusion by a colleague. How should the charge nurse interpret and address this behavior?

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — role transition, supervision, coaching and professional support
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate the preceptor role from mentorship by recognizing the preceptor’s structured role in clinical transition, coaching, evaluation, and feedback.

options.A: A long-term career adviser who supports professional development but does not participate in clinical orientation or competency feedback.
options.B: An experienced, competent nurse who serves as a role model and resource, coaches the new nurse into the role, evaluates performance, and provides feedback for improvement.
options.C: A disciplinary manager whose primary function is enforcing attendance and employment rules rather than coaching transition into the clinical role.
options.D: A peer selected only for social support who does not observe clinical practice, evaluate performance, or provide role-specific feedback.

candidates.rationale: Open RN describes preceptors as experienced and competent nurses who serve as role models and resources to newly hired nurses, coach them into the nursing role, answer questions, evaluate performance, and provide feedback for improvement. B directly matches this description.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A nursing preceptor is an experienced competent nurse who supports transition into practice through role modeling, coaching, performance evaluation, and feedback.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Management and Professional Concepts, 2nd ed. — Preparation for the RN Role
candidates.source_locator: Chapter 11 Preparation for the RN Role > transition to practice/preceptor role: preceptors are experienced and competent nurses who serve as role models/resources, coach the new nurse into the role, evaluate performance, and provide feedback for improvement.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7: participate in performance improvement projects and quality improvement processes; utilize resources to promote quality client care; practice and advocate for quality care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — quality improvement and data-driven systems improvement
candidates.educational_objective: Describe continuous quality improvement as an ongoing systematic process of setting goals, testing changes, measuring results, learning, and refining care processes.

options.A: End the improvement process once the organization proves that a minimum external standard has been met for the current review period.
options.B: Focus primarily on identifying the individual responsible after an adverse event instead of examining the processes that shaped performance.
options.C: Limit quality-improvement work to external accreditation surveys rather than integrating measurement and testing into routine operations.
options.D: Use an ongoing, systematic, data-driven process that sets goals, tests changes, measures performance, learns from results, and continues improving care processes.

candidates.rationale: AHRQ EvidenceNOW describes quality improvement as a systematic, data-driven process for managing change. It recommends setting improvement goals, identifying and testing changes, selecting measures, collecting and reviewing data regularly, comparing results with goals/benchmarks, and acting on the data. D best represents continuous quality improvement.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Continuous quality improvement is a systematic data-driven process that repeatedly measures performance, tests changes, evaluates results, and acts on learning to improve care processes.
candidates.source_document_title: EvidenceNow Key Drivers and Change Strategies — Key Driver 2: Implement a data-driven quality improvement process
candidates.source_locator: Key Driver 2: QI is a systematic, data-driven process; set goals; identify/test changes; select QI measures; collect/review data regularly; compare results with goals/benchmarks and act on data.

candidates.source_version_date: Current AHRQ EvidenceNOW guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — patient advocacy and interprofessional care planning
candidates.educational_objective: Identify patient advocacy when the nurse communicates and protects a capable client’s stated rights, goals, needs, and preferences within interprofessional care planning.

options.A: Unauthorized prescribing, because communicating the client’s goals independently changes the medical treatment plan.
options.B: Boundary violation, because nurses should not communicate a capable client’s stated preferences to other team members.
options.C: Patient advocacy, because the nurse is helping protect the client’s rights, needs, preferences, and participation in care.
options.D: Case management only, because advocacy for a client’s wishes is outside the entry-level RN role.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan lists 'Advocate for client rights and needs' under Management of Care and also includes interdisciplinary collaboration and updating the client plan of care. Raising a capable client's stated goals during team discussion is therefore an example of patient advocacy. C is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Advocating for client rights and needs and communicating those needs within interprofessional care planning are entry-level RN Management of Care activities.

candidates.source_locator: Management of Care, printed p.7: advocate for client rights and needs; identify/collaborate with multidisciplinary team members; initiate, evaluate and update client plan of care.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed decision-making, client rights and treatment refusal
candidates.educational_objective: Respect an informed treatment refusal by a client with decision-making capacity and complete appropriate communication and documentation processes.

options.A: Respect the capable client’s refusal, communicate it to the responsible clinician or team, and document the relevant informed-decision process according to policy.
options.B: Proceed with the treatment because a capable client’s refusal becomes invalid whenever the clinical team believes the expected benefit is substantial.
options.C: Ask a family member to override the refusal because informed refusal applies only when the healthcare team agrees with the client’s choice.
options.D: Document only the words ‘client refused’ and omit the information provided before the decision because that discussion has no relevance to the record.

candidates.rationale: CMS hospital informed-consent requirements are intended to ensure that patients or their representatives can make fully informed decisions about care. The Patient's Rights Condition of Participation includes informed decision-making, and the scenario establishes that the capable client received relevant information before refusing. The nurse should respect the decision and follow organizational processes for communication and documentation. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A capable patient who has received the relevant information retains decision-making authority; nursing care should respect the informed decision and follow required communication/documentation processes.
candidates.source_document_title: Revisions and Clarifications to Hospital Interpretive Guidelines for Informed Consent
candidates.source_locator: Memorandum summary: informed-consent obligations arise under 42 CFR 482.13(b)(2), 482.24(c)(4)(v), and 482.51(b)(2); hospital policy/process/forms must contain information that allows the patient or representative to make fully informed decisions about care.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — asthma triggers and chronic respiratory management
candidates.educational_objective: Teach that asthma symptoms can be triggered by infections, allergens, exercise, cold air, smoke/poor air quality, and other individual exposures.

options.A: Exercise is the only predictable asthma trigger, so viral infections, smoke, cold air, and allergens do not need consideration.
options.B: Asthma triggers may include respiratory infections, poor air quality or smoke, very cold air, physical activity, and relevant indoor or outdoor allergens, with individual variation.
options.C: Environmental triggers stop influencing asthma after controller therapy is prescribed, making exposure assessment unnecessary.
options.D: Asthma exacerbations occur independently of recognizable exposures, so identifying individual triggers does not help management.

candidates.rationale: NHLBI lists indoor and outdoor allergens, physical activity, respiratory infections, poor air quality, and very cold air among common asthma triggers. Trigger patterns vary among individuals, and identifying/avoiding relevant triggers is part of asthma management. B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Asthma symptoms can be triggered by respiratory infections, allergens, physical activity, poor air quality/smoke-related exposures, and cold air, with patterns varying by individual.
candidates.source_document_title: Asthma — Causes and Triggers
candidates.source_locator: Asthma triggers: indoor/outdoor allergens, physical activity, infections such as colds/flu/COVID-19, poor air quality, and very cold air; managing asthma includes identifying and avoiding relevant triggers.
candidates.source_organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), NIH

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed p.14: recognize clinical manifestations and pathophysiology of acute/chronic physical-health conditions and intervene appropriately.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — peripheral arterial disease and intermittent claudication
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize reproducible exertional calf discomfort relieved by rest as intermittent claudication suggestive of lower-extremity peripheral artery disease.

options.A: Deep vein thrombosis, which is characteristically relieved promptly by rest after a predictable walking distance.
options.B: Restless legs syndrome, which typically produces reproducible ischemic calf pain only during exertion.
options.C: Intermittent claudication from lower-extremity peripheral artery disease, reflecting exertional ischemia.
options.D: A normal effect of aging that does not warrant vascular assessment when symptoms resolve with rest.

candidates.rationale: NHLBI describes intermittent claudication as leg pain, aching, heaviness, or cramping that occurs during walking or stair climbing and goes away after rest; the calf is a common location. This pattern is the most common symptomatic presentation of lower-extremity PAD. C is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Reproducible calf discomfort triggered by walking and relieved by rest is intermittent claudication and strongly suggests lower-extremity PAD.
candidates.source_document_title: Peripheral Artery Disease — Symptoms
candidates.source_locator: PAD Symptoms: pain, aching, heaviness, or cramping in the legs that comes with walking/climbing stairs and goes away after rest is called intermittent claudication; pain is often in the calf.
candidates.source_organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Last updated March 24, 2022; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — rheumatoid arthritis manifestations
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate rheumatoid arthritis from a mechanical osteoarthritis pattern by recognizing symmetric inflammatory small-joint disease with prolonged morning stiffness and possible systemic symptoms.

options.A: Pain mainly with joint use and brief stiffness after rest without persistent inflammatory swelling.
options.B: Symmetric inflammatory involvement of the hands or other small joints with morning stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes and possible fatigue or low-grade fever.
options.C: Symptoms confined to weight-bearing joints with short morning stiffness and mechanical pain as the dominant pattern.
options.D: Arthritis limited to older adults with no autoimmune inflammation or extra-articular features.

candidates.rationale: NIAMS describes rheumatoid arthritis as a chronic autoimmune inflammatory disease that often affects joints symmetrically, commonly involving the wrists, hands, and feet. Typical findings include swelling and warmth, morning or post-rest stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes, fatigue, and occasional low-grade fever. B is the finding more characteristic of RA than a degenerative osteoarthritis pattern.
candidates.source_claim_supported: RA commonly presents with symmetric inflammatory joint involvement, prolonged morning stiffness over 30 minutes, hand/wrist/foot involvement, and possible fatigue or low-grade fever.
candidates.source_document_title: Rheumatoid Arthritis
candidates.source_locator: Overview and Symptoms of Rheumatoid Arthritis: autoimmune inflammatory disease; often symmetrical; wrists/hands/feet commonly affected; stiffness longer than 30 minutes; fatigue and occasional low-grade fever.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (NIAMS), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NIAMS page; live-rechecked August 16, 2026
candidates.stem: A client has symmetric pain and swelling in both hands with prolonged morning stiffness. Which finding is more characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis than osteoarthritis?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: medication indications, administration, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring and teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — colchicine indications and gout therapy
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the labeled role of colchicine in both treatment and prophylaxis of gout flares in adults.

options.A: Colchicine is an antibacterial drug used to eradicate infection in a gouty joint.
options.B: Colchicine is indicated only for acute treatment and has no role in gout-flare prophylaxis.
options.C: Colchicine is indicated for both treatment of acute gout flares and prophylaxis of gout flares in adults.
options.D: Colchicine is primarily a long-term urate-lowering drug whose labeled purpose is to dissolve urate deposits.

candidates.rationale: The current DailyMed colchicine label, updated April 16, 2026, states that colchicine tablets are indicated for both prophylaxis and treatment of gout flares in adults. The drug is not an antibacterial and is not itself the long-term urate-lowering therapy described in D. C is correct.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — therapeutic drug-level interpretation and toxicity monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a properly timed lithium maintenance level within the labeled 0.8–1.0 mEq/L target while integrating clinical response and toxicity assessment rather than relying on the level alone.

options.A: The level is below the labeled maintenance target and proves that the current lithium regimen is clinically ineffective.
options.B: The level is within the labeled maintenance target of 0.8–1.0 mEq/L and should still be interpreted with clinical response and ongoing monitoring.
options.C: The level is above the toxic threshold and requires emergency dialysis even without clinical toxicity.
options.D: The level is unrelated to lithium dosing decisions and therefore provides no useful information during maintenance therapy.

candidates.rationale: The DailyMed lithium carbonate label gives a maintenance-treatment target serum concentration of 0.8 to 1.0 mEq/L. It also states that total reliance must not be placed on serum concentrations alone and that accurate evaluation requires clinical and laboratory assessment. A properly timed level of 0.9 mEq/L is therefore within the labeled maintenance target but must still be interpreted with the client's clinical state and continued monitoring. B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A properly timed serum lithium concentration of 0.9 mEq/L falls within the labeled maintenance target of 0.8–1.0 mEq/L, but clinical assessment and ongoing monitoring remain necessary.
candidates.source_document_title: Lithium Carbonate capsule
candidates.source_locator: §2.4 Dosage for Maintenance Treatment of Bipolar I Disorder: target 0.8–1.0 mEq/L; §2.6 Serum Lithium Monitoring: draw immediately before next dose (about 12 hours after previous dose), do not rely on serum concentration alone, use clinical and laboratory evaluation.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine official drug label
candidates.source_version_date: DailyMed label updated June 24, 2021; current labeling and target live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — therapeutic drug monitoring and digoxin toxicity risk
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a properly timed digoxin concentration within the full clinical context and avoid making dose or toxicity decisions from an isolated serum value alone.

options.A: Interpret the 1.5-ng/mL level as proof of toxicity and give digoxin immune Fab regardless of symptoms, renal function, or electrolyte status.
options.B: Interpret the 1.5-ng/mL level as subtherapeutic and automatically increase the dose without considering the indication or clinical response.
options.C: Interpret the 1.5-ng/mL level in the overall clinical context, including symptoms, renal function, electrolytes, indication, and response, rather than labeling the isolated value automatically therapeutic or toxic.
options.D: Ignore when the level was drawn because the interval between the last digoxin dose and specimen collection does not affect interpretation.

candidates.rationale: The current DailyMed digoxin label states that serum levels below 0.5 ng/mL have been associated with diminished efficacy and levels above 2 ng/mL with increased toxicity without increased benefit. It specifically instructs clinicians to interpret a serum digoxin concentration in the overall clinical context and not to use an isolated value alone to increase or decrease the dose. Levels should be obtained just before the next dose or at least 6 hours after the last dose. Therefore C is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A serum digoxin concentration of 1.5 ng/mL drawn at least 6 hours after the dose should be interpreted with clinical response and toxicity assessment rather than automatically classified as therapeutic or toxic from the isolated number.
candidates.source_document_title: Digoxin tablets
candidates.source_locator: §2.5 Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels: monitor toxicity and clinical response; <0.5 ng/mL associated with diminished efficacy; >2 ng/mL associated with increased toxicity; interpret concentration in overall clinical context; do not use an isolated measurement alone; collect just before next dose or at least 6 hours after last dose.
candidates.source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine official drug label
candidates.source_version_date: Current DailyMed prescribing information; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — therapeutic drug monitoring and seizure-medication toxicity risk
candidates.educational_objective: Use serum phenobarbital concentration as one component of therapeutic exposure, adherence and toxicity assessment while integrating seizure control and adverse-effect findings.

options.A: Treat a concentration within the laboratory reference interval as a replacement for assessing seizure frequency, sedation, and other adverse effects.
options.B: Use the serum concentration only to estimate renal filtration because phenobarbital exposure and toxicity are not reflected by the measured level.
options.C: Avoid serum concentration monitoring because phenobarbital levels have no useful role in assessing therapeutic exposure, adherence, or toxicity.
options.D: Use the serum phenobarbital concentration to support therapeutic-exposure, adherence, and toxicity assessment while also evaluating seizure control and adverse effects.

candidates.rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories lists serum phenobarbital testing as useful for monitoring an appropriate therapeutic concentration and assessing compliance or toxicity. Mayo also states that clinical response correlates strongly with blood concentration. The measured level therefore supports—not replaces—assessment of seizure control and adverse effects. D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Serum phenobarbital concentration is useful for monitoring therapeutic exposure and assessing adherence/toxicity and should be interpreted alongside the client's clinical response and adverse effects.
candidates.source_document_title: Phenobarbital, Serum (PBR)
candidates.source_locator: Useful For: monitoring appropriate therapeutic concentration and assessing compliance or toxicity. Interpretation: clinical response correlates strongly with blood concentration; adult steady-state range described as 20.0–40.0 mcg/mL.
candidates.source_organization: Mayo Clinic Laboratories

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — C-peptide interpretation and endocrine diagnostic monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Use C-peptide as supportive information about residual endogenous insulin secretion in selected insulin-treated patients while integrating clinical history and other diagnostic data.

options.A: It measures average blood glucose over roughly three months and therefore replaces hemoglobin A1c testing.
options.B: It can help assess residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve and must be interpreted with the clinical context and other diagnostic information.
options.C: It determines diabetes type by itself regardless of insulin therapy, clinical history, renal function, or other diagnostic information.
options.D: It measures renal filtration without providing clinically useful information about endogenous pancreatic insulin secretion.

candidates.rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories lists serum C-peptide testing as useful for assessing residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve in selected diabetic patients, including those receiving insulin therapy. C-peptide generally parallels endogenous insulin secretion, but kidney failure and other factors can alter levels and Mayo cautions that interpretation must account for clinical context and assay limitations. B is correct; the test is not an HbA1c substitute and does not classify diabetes by itself.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Serum C-peptide can help assess residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve in selected insulin-treated diabetic patients, but results require clinical-context interpretation and do not independently determine diabetes type.
candidates.source_document_title: C-Peptide, Serum (CPR)
candidates.source_locator: Useful For: assessing insulin secretory reserve in selected diabetic patients receiving insulin therapy, including residual endogenous insulin secretory reserve. Clinical & Interpretive/Cautions: C-peptide reflects endogenous insulin-related changes, is mainly removed by kidneys, and assay/clinical factors affect interpretation.
candidates.source_organization: Mayo Clinic Laboratories
candidates.source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — BNP interpretation in dyspnea and suspected heart failure
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret an elevated BNP as supportive evidence for heart failure in an appropriate clinical context while recognizing that other cardiac and pulmonary conditions can also elevate BNP.

options.A: The elevation specifically proves a pulmonary cause of dyspnea and therefore excludes clinically important heart failure.
options.B: The elevation establishes normal ventricular function because BNP rises only when lung disease is the primary cause of symptoms.
options.C: The elevation has no established role in evaluating dyspnea or suspected heart failure and should not affect the assessment.
options.D: The elevation supports possible heart failure but is not diagnostic by itself because BNP can also rise in other cardiac and pulmonary conditions.

candidates.rationale: Mayo Clinic Laboratories uses BNP in the evaluation of suspected congestive heart failure and provides interpretive ranges that rise with greater heart-failure severity. However, BNP can also be elevated with right-heart failure/cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, acute pulmonary embolism, and acute coronary syndromes. A markedly elevated BNP therefore supports possible heart failure but must be interpreted with the clinical picture. D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A markedly elevated BNP can support suspected heart failure but is not specific to heart failure and requires clinical-context interpretation because other cardiopulmonary conditions can elevate BNP.
candidates.source_document_title: B-Type Natriuretic Peptide, Plasma (BNP)
candidates.source_locator: Interpretation: BNP interpretive levels for CHF; elevations can also occur with right heart failure/cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, acute pulmonary embolism, and acute coronary syndromes.

candidates.source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ophthalmic medication administration
candidates.educational_objective: Demonstrate safe eye-drop instillation by placing drops into the lower conjunctival pocket without touching the bottle tip to the eye or eyelid.

options.A: Touch the bottle tip to the cornea so the medication is delivered directly to the ocular surface and cannot miss the intended site.
options.B: Place the medication on the closed eyelid and wait for it to enter the conjunctival space when the eye is opened.
options.C: Pull the lower eyelid down to create a pocket, instill the prescribed drops into that pocket, and keep the bottle tip from touching the eye or eyelid.
options.D: Rub the closed eye vigorously after each drop because friction improves ocular absorption and decreases contamination of the bottle tip.

candidates.rationale: The National Eye Institute instructs patients to pull the lower eyelid down to create a pocket, hold the bottle tip just above the pocket, and squeeze the prescribed drops into it. To prevent contamination, the bottle tip should not touch the eye, eyelid, or hands. C is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Prescribed eye drops should be instilled into the lower-eyelid pocket while preventing contact between the bottle tip and the eye or eyelid.
candidates.source_document_title: How to Put in Eye Drops
candidates.source_locator: Use eye drops correctly, steps 2–4: pull lower eyelid down to make a pocket, hold tip just above pocket, instill prescribed drops. Prevent infections: do not let bottle tip touch eye or eyelid.
candidates.source_organization: National Eye Institute (NEI), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Last updated December 5, 2024; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized nutrition in chronic kidney disease
candidates.educational_objective: Individualize CKD nutrition recommendations to kidney function, laboratory values, treatment/dialysis status and overall nutrition rather than using universal potassium, phosphorus, protein or fluid targets.

options.A: Restrict potassium and phosphorus to the same low targets for every person with CKD regardless of laboratory results or disease stage.
options.B: Increase protein substantially for every person with CKD, including people who are not receiving dialysis or losing protein.
options.C: Avoid nutrition modifications because dietary sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid intake do not affect CKD management.
options.D: Individualize sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein, and fluid goals to kidney function, laboratory results, treatment status, and nutrition needs.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK states that there is no single meal plan for everyone with CKD and that nutritional needs change as kidney disease advances. Potassium, phosphorus, protein, sodium, and fluid recommendations depend on kidney function, blood-test results, dialysis/treatment status, and nutritional needs. For example, some people with CKD may need moderate protein, whereas people receiving dialysis may need more protein. D is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CKD dietary goals are individualized rather than universal; sodium, potassium, phosphorus, protein and fluid needs vary with kidney function, laboratory findings, treatment/dialysis and nutritional status.
candidates.source_document_title: Healthy Eating for Adults with Chronic Kidney Disease
candidates.source_locator: Why is healthy eating important? nutritional needs change as CKD advances. Nutrient-specific sections: fluid depends on kidney function; potassium goal should be individualized with labs; phosphorus may need adjustment based on blood levels; protein amount should be individualized and dialysis may increase protein needs; sodium limit depends on kidney health. How can I eat healthy with CKD?: no single meal plan for everyone with CKD.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NIDDK guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — glaucoma risk and vision screening
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that glaucoma can be asymptomatic early and that comprehensive dilated eye examination is important for detection in people at increased risk.

options.A: Glaucoma may have no early symptoms, and a comprehensive dilated eye examination can detect disease before additional irreversible vision loss occurs.
options.B: Glaucoma reliably produces severe eye pain before optic-nerve damage, so examination is unnecessary in an asymptomatic high-risk person.
options.C: A routine blood test detects glaucoma earlier than an eye examination and is the preferred test for people at increased risk.
options.D: Glaucoma develops only after severe central vision loss is present, so examination before visual symptoms has little value.

candidates.rationale: NEI states that glaucoma often has no early symptoms, symptoms can progress so slowly that a person may not notice them, and the way to find out whether glaucoma is present is a comprehensive dilated eye examination. NEI's screening statement specifically says detection in higher-risk individuals is best done through a comprehensive dilated eye exam. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Glaucoma may be asymptomatic early, and comprehensive dilated eye examination is the recommended detection approach for individuals at increased risk.
candidates.source_document_title: National Eye Institute Statement on Detection of Glaucoma and Adult Vision Screening; Glaucoma
candidates.source_locator: Detection of glaucoma: detection in higher-risk individuals is best done through comprehensive dilated eye exam. Glaucoma overview: early symptoms often none; symptoms may progress slowly; diagnosis uses dilated eye examination with visual-field testing; early treatment can protect vision.
candidates.source_organization: National Eye Institute (NEI), NIH
candidates.source_version_date: Current NEI guidance; detection statement live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — older-adult driving-safety assessment and counseling
candidates.educational_objective: Evaluate older-driver safety using individualized functional assessment rather than chronological age alone and refer for further driving evaluation when specific concerns are identified.

options.A: Recommend driving cessation solely because of chronological age without first assessing vision, cognition, motor function, or driving-related abilities.
options.B: Assess driving-related vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function and discuss referral for a formal driving evaluation when specific concerns are identified.
options.C: Ignore declining vision or slower reaction time because healthcare professionals have no role in counseling about driving-safety concerns.
options.D: Treat one abnormal office measure as conclusive proof of unsafe driving without considering the broader functional assessment.

candidates.rationale: NHTSA states that decisions about driving ability should never be based on age alone. Its clinician guidance describes assessment of driving-related functional domains including vision, cognition, and motor/sensory function to identify specific concerns and supports referral for additional driving evaluation when indicated. B is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Older-driver fitness should be assessed individually rather than determined by age alone; vision, cognition and motor/sensory function are relevant domains, and further driving evaluation may be appropriate when concerns are identified.
candidates.source_document_title: Older Drivers; Licensing Agency Referrals / Clinician’s Guide to Assessing and Counseling Older Drivers
candidates.source_locator: Older Drivers: decisions about ability to drive should never be based on age alone; changes in vision, physical fitness, reflexes/attention can affect safety. Licensing Agency Referrals: CADReS assesses key functional areas of vision, cognition, and motor/sensory functions and helps identify concerns related to driving; clinicians may refer drivers for additional evaluation.
candidates.source_organization: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA)
candidates.source_version_date: Current NHTSA older-driver guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — body dysmorphic disorder recognition
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize body dysmorphic disorder by the combination of preoccupation with slight or unobservable appearance flaws, repetitive appearance-related behaviors, and clinically significant distress or impairment.

options.A: Obsessive-compulsive disorder, when obsessions and compulsions are present but are not centered on perceived appearance defects.
options.B: Social anxiety disorder, when fear of scrutiny or embarrassment is primary without a persistent perceived appearance flaw.
options.C: Illness anxiety disorder, when fear of having or acquiring serious disease is primary rather than perceived appearance defects.
options.D: Body dysmorphic disorder, characterized by preoccupation with slight or unobservable appearance flaws plus repetitive appearance-related behaviors and clinically significant impairment.

candidates.rationale: StatPearls summarizes DSM-5-TR body dysmorphic disorder as preoccupation with one or more perceived physical defects that are not observable or appear slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, or reassurance seeking, with clinically significant distress or impairment. D directly matches this pattern.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Body dysmorphic disorder is characterized by preoccupation with slight/unobservable perceived appearance defects plus repetitive appearance-related behaviors and clinically significant distress or impairment.

candidates.source_locator: Introduction; History and Physical; Evaluation > Body Dysmorphic Disorder DSM-5-TR Criteria: perceived defects/flaws not observable or slight to others; repetitive behaviors; clinically significant distress or impairment; appearance concern not better explained by eating disorder.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — influenza antiviral timing and medication teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach that indicated influenza antiviral therapy should start as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours for greatest benefit, while recognizing that selected hospitalized, severe, progressive, or high-risk patients may benefit even when treatment begins later.

options.A: Start indicated antiviral treatment as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours for greatest benefit; later treatment can still benefit some hospitalized, severe, progressive, or high-risk patients.
options.B: Wait until at least 48 hours have passed because starting influenza antivirals earlier provides less clinical benefit.
options.C: Delay treatment until influenza symptoms are nearly resolved so medication adverse effects are minimized.
options.D: Use timing only for dosing convenience because antiviral treatment benefit is unrelated to illness duration.

candidates.rationale: CDC's March 10, 2026 clinician guidance states that influenza antiviral treatment provides the greatest clinical benefit when started early, especially within 48 hours of illness onset. It also states that treatment can still provide clinical benefit after 48 hours in hospitalized patients and in patients with severe, complicated, or progressive illness; high-risk patients should receive treatment as soon as possible. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Influenza antiviral treatment is most beneficial when started as soon as possible, ideally within 48 hours, while later treatment may still benefit hospitalized or severe/complicated/progressive illness and treatment is recommended promptly for high-risk patients.
candidates.source_document_title: Influenza Antiviral Medications: Summary for Clinicians
candidates.source_locator: Priority Groups for Antiviral Treatment; Summary of Influenza Antiviral Treatment Recommendations; Antiviral Treatment Efficacy and Effectiveness: greatest benefit when started early, especially within 48 hours; later benefit reported in hospitalized and severe/complicated/progressive illness.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: March 10, 2026
candidates.stem: A client with influenza asks about the importance of antiviral timing. Which teaching is most accurate?

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — fluconazole hepatic toxicity and monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize rising liver tests during fluconazole therapy as a potential hepatic-safety signal requiring monitoring for more severe injury and appropriate escalation if clinical liver disease develops.

options.A: Recognize possible fluconazole-associated hepatic injury and ensure worsening liver injury is monitored when liver tests become abnormal.
options.B: Assume fluconazole has no clinically important hepatic effects even when the client’s liver tests are rising.
options.C: Ignore abnormal liver tests unless blood glucose is also elevated during the antifungal treatment course.
options.D: Assume fluconazole liver injury occurs only after a predictable cumulative dose and therefore cannot occur earlier in therapy.

candidates.rationale: DailyMed fluconazole labeling warns that fluconazole should be used cautiously in patients with liver dysfunction and has been associated with rare serious hepatic toxicity. The label specifically states that patients who develop abnormal liver function tests during therapy should be monitored for more severe hepatic injury; if clinical signs and symptoms consistent with fluconazole-attributable liver disease develop, the drug should be discontinued. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Fluconazole can cause serious hepatic toxicity; patients who develop abnormal liver tests during therapy should be monitored for progression to more severe hepatic injury.

candidates.source_locator: Warnings > Hepatic Injury: caution in liver dysfunction; rare serious hepatic toxicity; no obvious relationship to dose or duration; abnormal liver-function tests require monitoring for more severe hepatic injury; discontinue if attributable clinical liver-disease signs/symptoms develop.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ferumoxytol infusion hypersensitivity precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Administer ferumoxytol over at least 15 minutes with emergency treatment available and observe for hypersensitivity during and for at least 30 minutes after each infusion.

options.A: Administer as an IV infusion over at least 15 minutes with anaphylaxis treatment immediately available, and observe during and for at least 30 minutes afterward.
options.B: Skip post-infusion observation when a previous ferumoxytol dose was tolerated without any adverse reaction.
options.C: Give the entire dose by rapid IV push because faster administration lowers hypersensitivity risk.
options.D: Monitor only for hypoglycemia because serious hypersensitivity is not a labeled ferumoxytol risk.

candidates.rationale: The May 31, 2026 Feraheme label carries a boxed warning for serious hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis. It requires IV infusion over at least 15 minutes when personnel and therapies are immediately available to treat anaphylaxis, and observation for hypersensitivity during and for at least 30 minutes after the infusion, including blood-pressure and pulse monitoring. Reactions can occur even when a previous dose was tolerated. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ferumoxytol must be administered as an IV infusion over at least 15 minutes with anaphylaxis treatment available and requires hypersensitivity observation during and for at least 30 minutes after infusion.

candidates.source_locator: Boxed Warning; §2 Dosage and Administration; §5.1 Serious Hypersensitivity Reactions: infusion over at least 15 minutes; personnel/therapies immediately available; observe during and at least 30 minutes afterward with blood pressure and pulse monitoring; reactions can occur after previously tolerated doses.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — apixaban dosing and anticoagulant monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate apixaban from warfarin by recognizing that apixaban dosing is not routinely titrated to INR and is instead based on labeled indication and patient-specific criteria with ongoing clinical safety assessment.

options.A: No. Apixaban is dosed according to its labeled indication and specified patient factors; routine INR-guided dose titration is not used to monitor its anticoagulant effect.
options.B: Yes. Apixaban uses the same routine INR target and dose-adjustment strategy as warfarin therapy.
options.C: Yes. Apixaban should be held whenever the INR is below 2.0 because a low INR indicates inadequate anticoagulation.
options.D: No monitoring is needed at all because apixaban never requires clinical follow-up or medication-safety assessment.

candidates.rationale: The current ELIQUIS label uses indication-specific fixed dosing and, for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, dose-reduction criteria based on age, body weight, and serum creatinine rather than routine INR-guided titration. The label also states that changes in PT/INR at therapeutic apixaban doses are small, variable, and not useful for monitoring the anticoagulant effect. A is correct; lack of routine INR titration does not eliminate clinical monitoring for bleeding, adherence, interactions, or patient-specific safety factors.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Routine INR-guided titration is not used to monitor apixaban anticoagulant effect; apixaban dosing follows labeled indication and patient-specific criteria.

candidates.source_locator: §2.1 Dosage and Administration: indication-specific dosing and NVAF reduction criteria; §12.2 Pharmacodynamics: PT/INR/aPTT changes are small, variable, and not useful in monitoring apixaban anticoagulant effect; §2.5 notes apixaban affects INR during transition to warfarin.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — apixaban dose-reduction criteria
candidates.educational_objective: Apply the labeled apixaban NVAF dose-reduction rule: 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of the three specified age, weight, and serum-creatinine criteria are present.

options.A: Reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of these criteria are present: age 80 years or older, body weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or greater.
options.B: Reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily whenever any degree of renal impairment is documented, regardless of age or body weight.
options.C: Keep the dose unchanged because age, body weight, and serum creatinine do not affect labeled NVAF dosing.
options.D: Increase the dose whenever serum creatinine reaches 1.5 mg/dL because lower renal clearance requires more drug to maintain effect.

candidates.rationale: Current ELIQUIS labeling recommends 5 mg twice daily for most adults with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation and 2.5 mg twice daily when at least two of three criteria are present: age 80 years or older, body weight 60 kg or less, or serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or greater. A is correct.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12: safely administer medications, identify adverse effects/contraindications, monitor therapeutic response, and provide client education.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — HFrEF beta-blocker initiation during hospitalization
candidates.educational_objective: Initiate an evidence-based HFrEF beta-blocker after clinical stabilization, at a low dose, rather than during ongoing hemodynamic instability or IV inotropic support.

options.A: After the client is clinically stabilized and no longer requires IV inotropic support, with initiation before discharge when appropriate.
options.B: Immediately at a full target dose while marked low-output or hemodynamic instability persists.
options.C: Never, because evidence-based beta-blockers are contraindicated in every client with chronic HFrEF.
options.D: Only after all other guideline-directed HFrEF medications have first been permanently discontinued.

candidates.rationale: The 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart-failure guideline states that evidence-based beta-blockers should be used in HFrEF and can be safely initiated before hospital discharge provided the patient is clinically stabilized and does not require IV inotropic therapy for HF. It also advises caution with initiation after inotrope-requiring hospitalization and allows withholding or dose reduction when marked volume overload or marginal low output is present. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Evidence-based beta-blockers in hospitalized HFrEF should be initiated after clinical stabilization, not during ongoing marked low-output instability or IV inotropic support, and can be started before discharge when appropriate.
candidates.source_document_title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure
candidates.source_locator: §7.3.2 Beta Blockers: safe initiation before discharge if clinically stabilized and not requiring IV inotropic therapy; §9.2 Maintenance or Optimization of GDMT During Hospitalization: caution with initiation after inotropes; consider withholding/reduction with marked volume overload or marginal low cardiac output.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology / Heart Failure Society of America

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — digoxin toxicity reversal
candidates.educational_objective: Identify digoxin immune Fab as the specific antidotal therapy for life-threatening digoxin toxicity such as severe ventricular arrhythmias.

options.A: Digoxin immune Fab (DigiFab), which binds digoxin and is indicated for life-threatening or potentially life-threatening toxicity.
options.B: Protamine sulfate, which reverses unfractionated heparin rather than digoxin toxicity.
options.C: Idarucizumab, which specifically reverses dabigatran rather than digoxin.
options.D: Phytonadione, which reverses vitamin K antagonist effects rather than digoxin toxicity.

candidates.rationale: The current DIGIFAB label indicates digoxin immune Fab for life-threatening or potentially life-threatening digoxin toxicity or overdose, including severe ventricular arrhythmias, progressive bradycardia, high-grade heart block not responsive to atropine, and specified hyperkalemia with rapidly progressive toxicity. A is the specific antidote in this scenario.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Digoxin immune Fab is the specific labeled antidote for life-threatening digoxin toxicity, including severe ventricular arrhythmias.

candidates.source_locator: §1 Indications and Usage: life-threatening or potentially life-threatening digoxin toxicity/overdose, including severe ventricular arrhythmias, progressive bradycardia, high-grade heart block not responsive to atropine, and specified hyperkalemia.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin degludec administration
candidates.educational_objective: Teach adult insulin degludec administration as once-daily subcutaneous dosing with individualized titration and no manual dose conversion between FlexTouch U-100 and U-200 pens.

options.A: Inject insulin degludec subcutaneously once daily; adults may administer it at any time of day, while the dose should still be individualized to metabolic needs and glucose-control goals.
options.B: Inject insulin degludec only by intravenous infusion because subcutaneous administration is not labeled.
options.C: Administer insulin degludec only immediately before meals because its labeled role is rapid prandial glucose control.
options.D: Convert the displayed units when using U-100 versus U-200 FlexTouch pens because the dose window does not show the actual insulin units.

candidates.rationale: Current TRESIBA labeling instructs adults to inject insulin degludec subcutaneously once daily at any time of day and to individualize/titrate the dose based on metabolic needs, blood-glucose monitoring results, and glycemic goals. The label also states not to perform dose conversion between U-100 and U-200 FlexTouch pens because the dose window displays the number of units to deliver. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Adults use insulin degludec subcutaneously once daily at any time of day with individualized dosing; FlexTouch U-100/U-200 pens do not require manual dose conversion.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — nitrate/PDE-5 inhibitor interaction
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the contraindicated interaction between sublingual nitroglycerin and PDE-5 inhibitors such as sildenafil because of severe hypotension risk.

options.A: Do not use sublingual nitroglycerin while taking a PDE-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil because the combination can cause severe hypotension, syncope, or myocardial ischemia.
options.B: Take an extra nitroglycerin dose with sildenafil because PDE-5 inhibitors reduce nitrate effectiveness.
options.C: Use the combination only while standing because an upright position prevents clinically important hypotension.
options.D: Separate sildenafil and nitroglycerin by one hour because this interval eliminates the labeled interaction for all patients.

candidates.rationale: Current nitroglycerin sublingual-tablet labeling contraindicates use in patients taking PDE-5 inhibitors including sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil, and avanafil. Concomitant use can cause severe hypotension, syncope, or myocardial ischemia. A is correct; the label does not establish a universal one-hour interval that makes the combination safe.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: apply principles of infection prevention; protect clients from injury/infection; use equipment safely.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — central-line infection prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Apply CDC-supported central-line infection-prevention practices: aseptic technique, maximal sterile barriers, appropriate chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, and prompt removal when the line is no longer essential.

options.A: Use maximal sterile barriers for insertion, appropriate chlorhexidine skin antisepsis, hand hygiene and site care, and promptly remove the catheter when it is no longer essential.
options.B: Replace all central lines routinely every 24 hours regardless of indication, site condition, or ongoing clinical need.
options.C: Apply topical antibiotic ointment routinely to every central-line insertion site and omit sterile barriers during insertion.
options.D: Keep unnecessary central venous catheters in place until discharge because repeated insertion is always riskier than prolonged dwell time.

candidates.rationale: CDC central-line guidance recommends maximal sterile barrier precautions for CVC/PICC insertion, skin preparation with greater than 0.5% chlorhexidine in alcohol when not contraindicated, hand hygiene and aseptic catheter care, and prompt removal of intravascular catheters that are no longer essential. Routine replacement of CVCs to prevent infection is not recommended. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC supports maximal sterile barriers, chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation, hand hygiene/aseptic care, and prompt removal of unnecessary central catheters as infection-prevention measures.
candidates.source_document_title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections — Summary of Recommendations
candidates.source_locator: Maximal Sterile Barrier Precautions; Skin Preparation; Hand Hygiene/Aseptic Technique; Selection of Catheters/Sites recommendation 10: promptly remove any intravascular catheter no longer essential; Replacement recommendations: do not routinely replace CVCs/PICCs to prevent infection.

candidates.source_version_date: CDC summary page February 28, 2024; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — burn care and isolation precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Apply Standard Precautions to burn care and add pathogen- or syndrome-specific Transmission-Based Precautions when indicated rather than assigning a universal isolation category solely because of the burn injury.

options.A: Apply Standard Precautions to every patient and add Transmission-Based Precautions when an infectious agent or clinical syndrome warrants them; burn injury alone does not create one universal special isolation category.
options.B: Place every patient with a major burn in Airborne Precautions solely because loss of the skin barrier creates airborne transmission risk.
options.C: Use no gloves or gowns for burn wound care unless a culture has already identified a multidrug-resistant organism.
options.D: Use a Protective Environment room for every burn patient because this CDC category was designed for all patients with impaired skin barriers.

candidates.rationale: CDC isolation guidance uses two tiers: Standard Precautions for all patients and Transmission-Based Precautions for patients with known or suspected infectious agents requiring additional measures. CDC also notes that special precautions for burn patients as a universal category are an unresolved issue rather than a blanket isolation recommendation. Protective Environment guidance is specifically directed to allogeneic HSCT patients, not all burn patients. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Burn injury alone does not mandate one universal CDC isolation category; Standard Precautions apply to all patients, with Transmission-Based Precautions added according to suspected or confirmed infection.
candidates.source_document_title: Guideline for Isolation Precautions: Preventing Transmission of Infectious Agents in Healthcare Settings
candidates.source_locator: Precautions to Prevent Transmission: Standard Precautions apply to all patients; Transmission-Based Precautions supplement them for specific suspected/confirmed pathogens. Recommendations section: burn-related special precautions are not established as a universal category; Protective Environment is separately defined for allogeneic HSCT.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: CDC isolation-precautions pages updated November 2023; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — healthcare water-system infection prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Explain the purpose of healthcare water-management programs: identify and control building-water conditions that permit Legionella and other pathogens to grow or spread, particularly in facilities serving vulnerable populations.

options.A: To identify and control conditions that permit Legionella and other waterborne pathogens to grow or spread, especially in complex systems serving vulnerable patients.
options.B: To eliminate the need for routine infection-prevention practices whenever tap water meets municipal drinking-water standards.
options.C: To replace all facility plumbing with sterile disposable tubing because building water systems cannot be managed safely.
options.D: To focus only on water taste and odor because healthcare-associated waterborne infections are not a recognized concern.

candidates.rationale: CDC recommends comprehensive water-management programs for healthcare facilities to reduce Legionella growth and transmission and to help control other waterborne pathogens. Healthcare facilities often have complex water systems and serve patients at increased risk for severe Legionnaires' disease. WMPs identify hazardous conditions, establish and monitor control measures, define corrective actions, and require ongoing verification/validation. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Healthcare water-management programs are used to identify and control conditions that allow Legionella and other waterborne pathogens to grow or spread in building water systems, particularly in facilities serving vulnerable patients.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control, printed p.8: protect clients and healthcare personnel from health/environmental hazards; use equipment safely; follow safety plans and procedures.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — medical-device recall response
candidates.educational_objective: Respond to an FDA device recall by identifying affected equipment and implementing the recall-specific correction or removal instructions rather than assuming every recall requires destruction or continued use.

options.A: Identify affected devices and follow the recall-specific correction or removal instructions and facility policy.
options.B: Discard every recalled device permanently because every FDA recall requires removal and destruction.
options.C: Continue using every recalled device until it fails because recall notices are informational only.
options.D: Ignore the recall unless a patient has already been injured by the exact affected device in use.

candidates.rationale: FDA defines a medical-device recall as a correction or removal action used to address a problem with a device. A recall does not always require permanent removal or destruction; depending on the recall, the action may include inspection, adjustment, repair, relabeling, or another correction. The facility should therefore identify the affected devices and follow the recall-specific instructions and its internal recall process. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: When a device recall affects equipment in use, the facility should identify affected devices and follow the specific FDA/manufacturer correction or removal instructions; recall does not universally mean permanent destruction.
candidates.source_document_title: What Is a Medical Device Recall?
candidates.source_locator: FDA medical-device recall overview: a recall may involve correction or removal; a recall does not always mean a product must be stopped or returned and may require checking, adjusting, fixing, relabeling, or other correction.

candidates.source_version_date: Current FDA medical-device recall guidance; live-rechecked August 16, 2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette
candidates.educational_objective: Apply respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette by covering coughs and sneezes, disposing of tissues, and performing hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.

options.A: Cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, dispose of used tissues, and clean hands after contact with respiratory secretions.
options.B: Cough openly when symptoms are mild because source-control measures are unnecessary in healthcare settings.
options.C: Reuse contaminated tissues during the visit because repeated use reduces unnecessary waste.
options.D: Skip hand hygiene after coughing or sneezing whenever a disposable tissue was used correctly.

candidates.rationale: CDC includes respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette within Standard Precautions. People with respiratory symptoms should cover the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, use and dispose of tissues, and perform hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette includes covering coughs/sneezes, using and disposing of tissues, and hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — safe staffing, workload and resource planning
candidates.educational_objective: Explain why direct-care nurses belong on staffing committees: their frontline knowledge helps align staffing plans with patient acuity, care needs, workload, and staff skills.

options.A: To incorporate frontline knowledge of patient acuity, care needs, workload, and staff skills into unit staffing plans.
options.B: To exclude direct-care nurses from staffing decisions so planning remains entirely administrative.
options.C: To use one fixed staffing number for every shift without considering acuity, workload, or skill mix.
options.D: To transfer staffing decisions to personnel with no direct knowledge of unit-level patient-care demands.

candidates.rationale: ANA describes staffing committees as nurse-led groups that develop unit-level staffing plans based on patient population acuity and needs together with staff skills and experience, and supports substantial direct-care nurse representation. Direct-care nurses contribute frontline knowledge of actual patient-care demands and staffing conditions. A is correct.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — facility emergency action and fire safety
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize core OSHA emergency-action-plan elements, including emergency reporting, evacuation/exit routes, personnel accountability, and assigned rescue or medical duties when applicable.

options.A: Procedures for reporting an emergency, evacuation and exit-route assignments, accounting for personnel, and designated rescue or medical duties when applicable.
options.B: A plan to keep all personnel at their workstations until an external agency arrives, regardless of evacuation instructions or immediate hazards.
options.C: A requirement that only managers know the evacuation route so staff movement can be controlled during an emergency.
options.D: A policy to disable alarms during drills and emergencies so patients are not disturbed by warning signals.

candidates.rationale: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.38 requires an emergency action plan to include, at minimum, procedures for reporting fires or other emergencies; emergency evacuation procedures and exit-route assignments; procedures for critical operations before evacuation when applicable; accounting for employees after evacuation; rescue and medical duties for designated employees; and contact information for plan questions. OSHA also requires an employee alarm system and training/review of the plan. A is correct.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A workplace emergency action plan includes procedures for reporting emergencies, evacuation and exit routes, accounting for personnel, designated rescue/medical duties when applicable, alarm systems, and employee training/review.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — advocacy and client participation in treatment decisions
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate shared decision making from consent-only, patient-alone, and clinician-only decision models.

options.A: The clinician and client review evidence, potential benefits and harms, and the client's values and preferences, then work toward a decision together.
options.B: The clinician obtains consent for a recommended treatment without comparing reasonable alternatives or eliciting the client's preferences.
options.C: The clinician lists available treatments but provides no clinical guidance because the client must make the decision alone.
options.D: The clinician selects the option with the best population-average outcome and informs the client after the decision is made.

candidates.rationale: Shared decision making is collaborative: clinical evidence and clinician expertise are integrated with the client's values, goals, preferences, and circumstances. A describes that process. B is consent without the comparative, preference-sensitive collaboration; C removes clinician guidance; D is clinician-centered decision making.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — case management and continuity
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize case management as individualized coordination of services and transitions across settings.

options.A: Coordinate referrals, services, equipment, and transition needs across settings according to the client's individualized goals and plan of care.
options.B: Perform all bedside procedures personally and leave coordination with community and specialty services to other disciplines.
options.C: Arrange the same standardized services for every client without incorporating individual goals, preferences, or changing needs.
options.D: Postpone resource planning and transition coordination until after the client has already been discharged.

candidates.rationale: Case management emphasizes individualized coordination, continuity, resource linkage, communication, and transitions across the care continuum. A reflects those functions. B narrows the role to direct procedures, C ignores individualized planning, and D delays coordination until after the transition has occurred.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed refusal and client rights
candidates.educational_objective: Apply client-rights principles to informed refusal by a capable adult and support a safe-as-feasible transition plan.

options.A: Respect the informed refusal after ensuring options and foreseeable consequences were discussed, document the discussion, and provide the safest feasible follow-up plan.
options.B: Prevent the client from leaving until the recommended treatment is completed because the healthcare team believes discharge is unsafe.
options.C: Treat the wish to leave as proof of incapacity and detain the client until a psychiatric evaluation authorizes discharge.
options.D: Ask the client to sign a refusal form before discussing alternatives or consequences because the signature alone completes informed refusal.

candidates.rationale: A capable adult may refuse recommended care. The nurse should support an informed refusal process: make sure relevant options and consequences are explained, document the discussion, and reduce harm with feasible follow-up. Capacity is not lost merely because the client chooses differently from the team, and a form is not a substitute for informed discussion.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A patient has rights concerning informed participation and refusal; capable refusal requires communication/documentation rather than automatic detention.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — restraint orders and client rights
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize federal order limits for violent-behavior restraint: no standing/PRN orders, adult renewal up to 4 hours, and earliest-possible discontinuation.

options.A: Standing or PRN orders are not permitted; for an adult, a violent-behavior restraint order may be renewed for up to 4 hours at a time, subject to reassessment and more restrictive state law.
options.B: A PRN restraint order is acceptable whenever the client has a documented history of violent behavior.
options.C: One restraint order may remain active for 24 hours without renewal if staff continue documenting agitation.
options.D: Once the restraint order is written, the restraint must remain in place for the full ordered period even when the unsafe behavior resolves.

candidates.rationale: Federal hospital rules prohibit standing or PRN restraint/seclusion orders. For violent or self-destructive behavior, renewal limits are age-based; for adults 18 or older, each renewal may be for up to 4 hours. Restraint must be discontinued at the earliest possible time and remains subject to monitoring, reassessment, and applicable state law.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Federal hospital rules prohibit standing/PRN restraint orders, set a 4-hour adult renewal maximum for violent/self-destructive behavior, and require earliest-possible discontinuation.
