candidates.source_locator: §5.1 Hypoglycemia: all sulfonylureas including glimepiride can cause severe hypoglycemia; patients must be educated to recognize/manage hypoglycemia; risk increases with deficient caloric intake and specified vulnerable conditions. §1 Indications/Limitations: type 2 diabetes; not for type 1 diabetes or DKA. §2.1: administer with breakfast or first main meal

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication actions, indications and medication-related client education
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — sitagliptin / DPP-4 inhibitor mechanism
candidates.educational_objective: Explain sitagliptin's DPP-4 inhibitor mechanism: prolonged incretin activity produces glucose-dependent increases in insulin and decreases in glucagon.

options.A: It inhibits DPP-4, increasing and prolonging active incretin hormones so insulin release increases and glucagon decreases in a glucose-dependent manner
options.B: It blocks renal SGLT2 transporters so glucose is excreted in the urine
options.C: It directly stimulates pancreatic insulin release independently of the incretin system
options.D: It delays intestinal carbohydrate digestion by inhibiting brush-border alpha-glucosidase enzymes

candidates.rationale: Current sitagliptin labeling states that the drug inhibits DPP-4 and slows the inactivation of incretin hormones such as GLP-1 and GIP. Increased active incretin levels increase insulin synthesis/release and reduce glucagon when blood glucose is normal or elevated. B describes an SGLT2 inhibitor mechanism, C resembles insulin-secretagogue therapy and omits the DPP-4/incretin mechanism, and D describes an alpha-glucosidase inhibitor. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Sitagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor that prolongs incretin activity, increasing insulin and reducing glucagon in a glucose-dependent manner.
candidates.source_document_title: SITAGLIPTIN tablets — Full Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: §12.1 Mechanism of Action: sitagliptin inhibits DPP-4, slows incretin inactivation, increases/prolongs GLP-1 and GIP action, and increases insulin release/decreases glucagon in a glucose-dependent manner
candidates.source_organization: U.S. National Library of Medicine — DailyMed
candidates.source_version_date: DailyMed label updated 2026-05-10

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication actions/indications and medication-related client education
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — acarbose / alpha-glucosidase inhibitor mechanism
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that acarbose lowers postprandial glucose by delaying carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption through alpha-amylase/intestinal alpha-glucosidase inhibition rather than by stimulating insulin secretion.

options.A: It competitively inhibits intestinal alpha-glucosidases and pancreatic alpha-amylase, delaying carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption and reducing postprandial hyperglycemia
options.B: It directly stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release more insulin
options.C: It blocks renal glucose reabsorption so more glucose is excreted in the urine
options.D: It inhibits DPP-4, prolonging endogenous incretin hormone activity

candidates.rationale: Current acarbose labeling states that the drug competitively and reversibly inhibits pancreatic alpha-amylase and membrane-bound intestinal alpha-glucoside hydrolases. This delays carbohydrate digestion and glucose absorption and lowers the postprandial rise in glucose. Acarbose does not enhance insulin secretion. Renal glucose-reabsorption blockade describes SGLT2 inhibitors, while DPP-4 inhibition describes agents such as sitagliptin. Therefore A is the best answer.

candidates.educational_objective: Teach correct basal insulin glargine administration: once-daily subcutaneous dosing at a consistent daily time, without mixing it with other insulins.

options.A: Inject it subcutaneously once daily at any time of day, but at the same time every day
options.B: Use it only as a rapid mealtime bolus when carbohydrate intake is high
options.C: Give it intravenously for acute diabetic ketoacidosis
options.D: Mix it in the same syringe with another insulin before each dose

candidates.rationale: Current LANTUS labeling states that insulin glargine is administered subcutaneously once daily at any time of day, but at the same time each day. It is a long-acting basal insulin rather than a rapid mealtime insulin, it is not recommended for treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis, and the label instructs not to dilute or mix LANTUS with another insulin or solution. candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin pump safety / interrupted insulin delivery
candidates.educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users that interruption of rapid-acting insulin delivery can quickly lead to hyperglycemia and ketosis/DKA, requiring prompt recognition and use of the prescribed backup/troubleshooting plan.

options.A: Because pumps deliver rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin continuously, prolonged interruption can allow hyperglycemia and ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis to develop quickly
options.B: A pump interruption is usually harmless for a full day because long-acting insulin remains under the skin
options.C: Insulin pumps eliminate the need to monitor glucose or respond to high-glucose alerts
options.D: If pump delivery stops, the client should avoid all insulin until the device can be professionally repaired

candidates.rationale: ADA 2026 Standards describe insulin pump therapy as continuous delivery of rapid- or ultra-rapid-acting insulin and specifically note the risk of rapid development of ketosis or diabetic ketoacidosis when insulin delivery is interrupted. Pump users therefore need education on monitoring and an individualized backup/troubleshooting plan. Pumps do not create a long-acting subcutaneous insulin depot, do not eliminate glucose monitoring, and interruption is not a reason to withhold needed insulin. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Insulin pumps provide continuous rapid/ultra-rapid insulin; interruption can rapidly lead to ketosis or DKA, making prompt monitoring and troubleshooting essential.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hemodialysis catheter access / bloodstream-infection prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Use aseptic technique and appropriate catheter-hub disinfection every time a hemodialysis central venous catheter is connected, disconnected, or otherwise accessed.

options.A: Use aseptic catheter-access technique and disinfect the catheter hubs with an appropriate antiseptic before access
options.B: Use clean nonsterile technique because aseptic technique is needed only when the catheter is first inserted
options.C: Skip hub disinfection when the catheter cap appears visibly clean
options.D: Reserve aseptic technique for scheduled dressing changes and use routine handling for dialysis connections

candidates.rationale: CDC dialysis infection-prevention guidance requires adherence to aseptic technique when connecting and disconnecting hemodialysis catheters and during dressing changes. Catheter hubs should be scrubbed with an appropriate antiseptic after the cap is removed and before access, every time the catheter is accessed or disconnected. Maximal sterile barrier precautions are an insertion procedure standard and should not be incorrectly generalized to every routine catheter access. Therefore A is the best answer.

candidates.educational_objective: Safely access an implanted venous port using appropriate skin antisepsis, aseptic technique, and a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle designed for the port septum.

options.A: Use a sterile non-coring (Huber) needle after appropriate site antisepsis and maintain aseptic port-access technique
options.B: Use a standard hypodermic needle because any sharp needle can safely penetrate the port septum
options.C: Use a peripheral IV catheter through the port septum to avoid a needle
options.D: Access the port without skin antisepsis when the overlying skin appears clean

candidates.rationale: FDA device classification identifies the sterile non-coring (Huber) needle as the needle used to access a subcutaneous implanted intravascular infusion port; its tip is designed to enter the septum without damaging it. CDC oncology infection-control guidance directs clinicians to perform hand hygiene, cleanse the port site with an appropriate antiseptic, and insert a non-coring needle while maintaining aseptic access technique. candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — chest tube dislodgement / emergency management
candidates.educational_objective: Respond to accidental chest-tube removal by immediately occluding the insertion site with sterile petroleum/occlusive dressing and rapidly assessing/escalating respiratory care.

options.A: Immediately cover the insertion site with sterile petroleum-impregnated/occlusive dressing, assess respiratory status, and obtain urgent assistance
options.B: Insert the same chest tube back through the tract at the bedside
options.C: Leave the site open to room air until the provider arrives so pleural air can escape
options.D: Clamp the disconnected drainage tubing and delay assessment until a chest radiograph is obtained

candidates.rationale: NCBI nursing guidance states that when a chest tube dislodges from the patient, the nurse should immediately apply pressure to the insertion site and apply sterile petroleum gauze/occlusive dressing. The client then requires prompt respiratory assessment and urgent clinical assistance because recurrent pneumothorax or respiratory deterioration can occur. The nurse should not reinsert the tube, intentionally leave the thoracic opening uncovered, or postpone assessment. Therefore A is the best answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Accidental chest-tube removal requires immediate occlusion of the thoracic insertion site with sterile petroleum/occlusive dressing and urgent respiratory reassessment/escalation.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — tracheostomy airway emergency preparedness
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain immediate bedside access to essential tracheostomy emergency equipment, including a replacement tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction setup, so airway patency and ventilation can be rapidly supported if the tracheostomy becomes obstructed or displaced.

options.A: A replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter setup
options.B: A pulse oximeter, stethoscope, and oxygen tubing, with replacement airway equipment stored on the unit
options.C: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size and tracheostomy ties, without a bag-valve-mask or suction setup
options.D: An oral airway and incentive spirometer, with tracheostomy replacement equipment brought only if decannulation occurs

candidates.rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills states that a replacement tracheostomy tube, an obturator, a bag-valve-mask device, and a suction catheter kit must be available in the room for patient safety. The same chapter also specifies bedside access to the obturator, spare tracheostomy tubes including the same size and one size smaller, and a bag-valve-mask device. Therefore A is the best answer. Monitoring equipment alone does not replace airway-rescue equipment; a same-size spare tube without ventilation and suction capability is incomplete; and oral-airway/incentive-spirometry equipment does not address an acute tracheostomy airway emergency.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Acute-care tracheostomy patients require immediately available airway-rescue equipment including a replacement tracheostomy tube, obturator, bag-valve-mask device, and suction equipment; the chapter also specifies same-size and one-size-smaller spare tubes.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that contract/agency nurses who provide patient care remain subject to the organization's Human Resources requirements, including appropriate orientation to organizational policies, safety content, and assigned duties before safe independent assignment.

options.A: Ensure the nurse is oriented to applicable organizational policies and procedures, key safety content, and the specific duties of the assignment
options.B: Rely on the staffing agency's accreditation as sufficient evidence that no hospital-specific orientation or competency review is needed
options.C: Allow the nurse to begin independent care first and provide unit-specific policies only if an unfamiliar situation occurs
options.D: Limit verification to an active nursing license because the staffing agency is responsible for all other qualifications and competencies

candidates.rationale: The Joint Commission states that Human Resources requirements apply to contract staff who provide patient care and gives orientation to organizational policies and procedures, key safety content, and specific job duties as an example of compliance. It also states that simply contracting with another accredited organization does not itself assure compliance and that the accredited organization remains responsible for applying its requirements to contracted services. Therefore A is the best answer. Agency accreditation alone, delayed orientation, or license verification alone does not address the organization's responsibility to ensure the contract nurse is prepared and competent for the assigned role.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hospitals must apply applicable HR requirements to contract patient-care staff, including appropriate orientation to organizational policies/procedures, key safety content, and specific job duties; agency/traveling nurses are included as contract staff examples.

candidates.educational_objective: For travel or agency nurses, verify required credentials and role-specific competency and provide applicable organizational orientation rather than assuming the staffing agency alone establishes readiness for the hospital assignment.

options.A: Confirm current licensure or required certification, verify qualifications and competency for assigned responsibilities, and complete applicable hospital orientation
options.B: Confirm current licensure and rely on the staffing agency to determine competency and hospital-specific preparation

Agency/traveling nurses are specifically included among examples of contract clinical services. Therefore A is the complete and best answer; the other options omit or improperly defer required elements.

candidates.educational_objective: Make nursing assignments according to each staff member's allowable duties, demonstrated competency, and clinical judgment rather than assuming readiness from residency participation, program completion, or length of employment alone.

options.A: Base the assignment on the RN's demonstrated competency, allowable duties, and ability to use sound clinical judgment for the assigned care
options.B: Assign the same acuity as the most experienced RN because participation in a residency establishes equivalent clinical competence
options.C: Avoid evaluating individual competency until the residency program is completed because the program determines assignment readiness
options.D: Use only the RN's length of employment to determine assignment difficulty, regardless of demonstrated competency

Participation in a residency program does not eliminate the need to evaluate the individual nurse's readiness for a particular assignment. Therefore A is the best answer; the other options substitute program participation, program completion, or tenure for demonstrated individual competency.

candidates.educational_objective: Participate in quality improvement by using client-care data and evidence, collaborating in approved improvement actions, and evaluating whether the intervention improves client outcomes.

candidates.educational_objective: When scope is uncertain, verify the activity against the applicable jurisdiction's nurse practice act and rules and confirm organizational requirements and personal competency before accepting or performing the activity.

options.A: Clarify the activity against the jurisdiction's nurse practice act and rules, applicable organizational policy, and the nurse's education and competence before accepting the assignment
options.B: Perform the activity if another RN on the unit has done it previously, because unit custom establishes legal scope of practice
options.C: Accept the activity whenever a health care provider orders it, because a provider order overrides nursing scope-of-practice limits
options.D: Use the scope rules from the state where the nurse was originally educated, even when practicing under a different jurisdiction's nursing law

candidates.rationale: NCSBN states that nurse practice acts and related rules and regulations guide and govern nursing practice in each jurisdiction. Its Scope of Practice Decision-Making Framework is intended to help determine whether an activity, intervention, or role is permitted under the nurse's education, licensure, and competence while meeting the standards of the applicable nurse practice act and jurisdictional rules. Therefore A is the best answer. Unit custom does not create legal scope, a provider order does not authorize a nurse to practice outside nursing law, and the governing scope is the law and rules of the jurisdiction in which the nurse is practicing rather than the jurisdiction where the nurse was educated.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nursing scope is governed by the applicable jurisdiction's nurse practice act and rules and must be considered together with licensure, education, competence, and organizational requirements when deciding whether an activity may be performed.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that a medication error caught before reaching the client is still a near miss that should be acknowledged and documented according to the facility's established safety process.

options.A: Take no further action because the incorrect dose never reached the client
options.B: Remove electronic messages about the error so the event is not retained in the system
options.C: Follow facility procedure to acknowledge and document the near miss and communicate relevant safety information
options.D: Document that another department caused the error and consider the matter closed

candidates.rationale: The 2026 NCSBN NCLEX-RN Test Plan identifies acknowledging and documenting practice errors and near misses as an entry-level RN safety activity. An error intercepted before reaching the client is still a near miss and should be handled through the facility's established safety process so the event is not concealed and relevant information can be used for safe care. candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate prerenal AKI from intrinsic and postrenal AKI by recognizing that prerenal injury is caused by reduced renal perfusion rather than direct renal tissue injury or urinary obstruction.

options.A: Decreased renal blood flow, such as from intravascular volume depletion or systemic hypotension
options.B: Direct injury to renal tubules from an intrinsic process within the kidney
options.C: Obstruction of urinary outflow causing back pressure in the urinary tract
options.D: Inflammatory injury of the glomeruli causing intrinsic renal dysfunction

candidates.rationale: NCBI StatPearls classifies acute kidney injury as prerenal, intrinsic renal, or postrenal. Prerenal AKI results from reduced blood flow to the kidney, including systemic hypoperfusion such as hypovolemia or hypotension. Direct tubular or glomerular injury is intrinsic renal AKI, while urinary outflow obstruction is postrenal AKI. Therefore A is the only option that describes a prerenal mechanism.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Prerenal AKI is caused by decreased renal perfusion; intrinsic AKI reflects pathology within kidney tissue, and postrenal AKI reflects urinary outflow obstruction.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — urinary calculi/renal colic recognition
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize renal/ureteral calculi by episodic severe flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria, and distinguish this pattern from urinary infection and musculoskeletal pain.

options.A: A ureteral stone causing renal colic
options.B: Acute pyelonephritis
options.C: Acute cystitis
options.D: Lumbar muscle strain

candidates.rationale: NIDDK identifies kidney/urinary stones as a cause of sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen, or groin and hematuria; stone pain may come and go in waves. A stone lodged in the urinary tract can obstruct urine flow and produce severe pain or bleeding, so A best fits the presentation. B can cause back/side/groin pain and bloody urine, but kidney infection more typically includes fever/chills and urinary symptoms such as frequent or painful urination, which are absent here. C commonly causes dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency and lower-abdominal discomfort rather than classic colicky flank-to-groin pain. D may cause back pain but does not explain hematuria or the urinary-tract radiation pattern.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Colicky flank pain radiating toward the groin with hematuria is strongly consistent with urinary stone disease, while fever/dysuria would favor infection and musculoskeletal pain does not explain hematuria.

Kidney Infection > symptoms: fever/chills, frequent or painful urination, back/side/groin pain. Bladder Infection > symptoms: dysuria, urinary frequency/urgency and lower-abdominal discomfort.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antimicrobial therapy adjustment using culture/susceptibility data
candidates.educational_objective: Use urine culture identification and susceptibility data to recognize when empiric broad-spectrum UTI therapy should transition to targeted definitive antimicrobial therapy.

options.A: Continue the same broad-spectrum regimen for the entire course regardless of susceptibility results
options.B: Select an effective antibiotic with a targeted spectrum based on the urine culture identification and susceptibility results
options.C: Stop antimicrobial therapy because a positive culture alone indicates asymptomatic bacteriuria
options.D: Repeat urine cultures daily and delay any treatment adjustment until cultures become negative

candidates.rationale: The 2025 IDSA complicated UTI guideline recommends that, once urine culture identification and susceptibility results are available in a microbiologically confirmed complicated UTI, definitive therapy should use an effective antibiotic with a targeted spectrum rather than continuing empiric broad-spectrum therapy for the full course. Therefore B is correct. A ignores the recommendation to narrow definitive therapy when microbiologic data are available. C is incorrect because the client has a confirmed symptomatic complicated UTI, not asymptomatic bacteriuria. D is not recommended; CDC urine-culture stewardship guidance states that cultures should not routinely be obtained simply to document response when symptoms are resolving.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For confirmed complicated UTI, available culture identification and susceptibility results should guide targeted definitive antimicrobial therapy rather than automatic continuation of broad empiric coverage.
candidates.source_document_title: IDSA 2025 Guideline Update on Complicated Urinary Tract Infections; Urine Culture Stewardship in Patients without Indwelling Urinary Catheters
candidates.source_locator: IDSA 2025 cUTI Guideline > Recommendations on Selection of Antibiotic Therapy > C. Selection of Definitive Antibiotic Therapy: in microbiologically confirmed cUTI, select a definitive effective antibiotic with a targeted spectrum based on urine culture identification and susceptibility as soon as available rather than continuing empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for the complete duration. CDC Urine Culture Stewardship > Inappropriate uses: urine culture to document response to therapy unless symptoms fail to resolve.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — renal diagnostic trend interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret eGFR as an important component of CKD evaluation and GFR categorization while recognizing that CKD classification also includes disease cause and albuminuria.

options.A: eGFR is unrelated to CKD classification once chronic kidney disease has been diagnosed.
options.B: eGFR helps classify kidney function and follow change over time, but CKD classification also considers cause and albuminuria.
options.C: eGFR alone identifies the cause of chronic kidney disease.
options.D: A single eGFR result by itself fully defines CKD prognosis and treatment.

candidates.rationale: KDIGO 2024 classifies CKD by Cause, GFR category, and Albuminuria category (CGA). eGFR is therefore an important measure for classifying kidney function and following change, but it does not independently identify CKD cause or capture albuminuria. B is the only complete interpretation. A incorrectly dismisses GFR classification; C attributes etiologic information to eGFR that it cannot provide; D overstates a single measurement and ignores the multidimensional CKD classification and risk assessment framework.
candidates.source_claim_supported: eGFR is used to categorize kidney function within CKD, but CKD classification and risk assessment are not based on eGFR alone; cause and albuminuria are also integral.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — hemodialysis vascular-access self-care
candidates.educational_objective: Teach daily AV-fistula surveillance for infection findings and the expected blood-flow vibration, with prompt reporting if the vibration is lost.

options.A: I will check the access every day for redness or warmth and make sure I can still feel the usual vibration.
options.B: I only need to check the access on days when I receive dialysis.
options.C: If I cannot feel the usual vibration after dialysis, I can wait until the next scheduled treatment to report it.
options.D: Redness and warmth over the access are expected unless I also develop a fever.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK instructs clients to protect the hemodialysis access, wash the area daily, check for warmth or redness, and confirm the vibration produced by blood flow; the dialysis center should be notified if the vibration cannot be felt. A reflects correct surveillance. B omits daily monitoring, C delays reporting possible loss of flow, and D incorrectly normalizes local infection findings.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Daily AV-access care includes checking for infection and the expected blood-flow vibration and reporting loss of that vibration.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — hemodialysis fluid/volume management
candidates.educational_objective: Use postdialysis weight relative to target dry weight as a clinical indicator of volume management and fluid removal during hemodialysis.

options.A: Assess whether excess fluid removal has brought the client toward the intended volume status
options.B: Determine dialysis solute clearance without using laboratory data
options.C: Diagnose a change in nutritional status from this single treatment
options.D: Determine the vascular-access blood-flow rate

candidates.rationale: NIDDK defines dry weight as the weight after hemodialysis has removed extra fluid and explains that controlling fluid intake helps the client remain at the proper dry weight. Hemodialysis removes excess fluid by ultrafiltration. Comparing the postdialysis weight with the target weight therefore helps assess the client's volume-management result. B is incorrect because solute clearance is not established from weight alone. C overinterprets a single treatment-related weight change, which is largely driven by fluid removal. D requires assessment of the access/dialysis circuit rather than body weight.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Target/dry weight represents the intended postdialysis volume state after excess fluid removal, so postdialysis weight is used to assess volume-management progress rather than solute clearance or access flow.
candidates.source_document_title: Eating & Nutrition for Hemodialysis; Hemodialysis — StatPearls
candidates.source_locator: NIDDK Eating & Nutrition for Hemodialysis > What is my dry weight?: dry weight is the weight after a hemodialysis session has removed all extra fluid. NCBI Hemodialysis > Anatomy and Physiology: ultrafiltration is movement of water across the membrane and is used to achieve fluid removal; session ultrafiltration should balance euvolemia and hemodynamic stability.
candidates.source_organization: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK), NIH; National Library of Medicine — NCBI Bookshelf

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — hemodialysis fluid and sodium self-management
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients on hemodialysis to count liquid-containing foods toward prescribed fluid intake and limit excess sodium because it increases thirst and contributes to fluid-management difficulty.

options.A: I will count foods that are liquid at room temperature, such as soup or gelatin, as part of my fluid intake and limit salty foods that increase thirst.
options.B: Ice cream and gelatin do not count as fluids because they are eaten with a spoon.
options.C: I can drink extra fluid whenever I do not have visible ankle swelling.
options.D: Eating more salty foods will help me tolerate the fluid restriction by reducing thirst.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK explains that excess fluid between hemodialysis treatments can contribute to swelling, blood-pressure changes, cardiac strain, and pulmonary fluid accumulation. Foods that are liquid at room temperature—including soup, gelatin, pudding, and ice cream—contribute to fluid intake. NIDDK also notes that salt increases thirst, so limiting sodium can help clients control fluid intake. Therefore A is correct. B excludes foods that count as fluid, C uses absence of edema as an unsafe substitute for the prescribed plan, and D reverses the sodium-thirst relationship.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hemodialysis fluid-management teaching includes counting foods that contribute liquid and limiting excess sodium because salt increases thirst and excess fluid can cause clinically important complications.
candidates.source_document_title: Eating & Nutrition for Hemodialysis
candidates.source_locator: Why is it important to keep track of how much liquid I eat or drink?: excess fluid consequences and individualized fluid limits; salt makes clients thirsty. What foods count as liquid and why?: foods liquid at room temperature such as soup, gelatin, pudding and ice cream count toward fluid intake.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — CKD risk recognition and early screening
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients with CKD risk factors that early disease can be asymptomatic and that screening includes assessment of both eGFR and urine albumin.

options.A: Kidney screening can wait until swelling or urine changes develop.
options.B: A normal urine appearance rules out early chronic kidney disease.
options.C: Only a serum creatinine level is needed to screen for chronic kidney disease.
options.D: Early kidney disease may have no symptoms, so at-risk clients are screened with kidney-function and urine-albumin testing.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK identifies diabetes and hypertension as major CKD risk factors and notes that early kidney disease may have no symptoms; testing may be the only way to detect it. NIDDK recommends screening people at risk using urine albumin assessment and estimated GFR from serum creatinine. Therefore D is correct. A delays detection until symptomatic disease, B incorrectly relies on urine appearance, and C omits urine albumin, one of the two key CKD markers.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Diabetes and hypertension increase CKD risk; early CKD may be asymptomatic, and at-risk screening uses both urine albumin and eGFR assessment.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — prediabetes lifestyle prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients with prediabetes that modest weight loss achieved through healthier eating plus regular physical activity is an evidence-based strategy to prevent or delay type 2 diabetes.

options.A: Eliminate essentially all carbohydrate foods and avoid structured physical activity until weight normalizes.
options.B: Work toward about 5%–7% weight loss through healthier eating and at least 150 minutes of physical activity each week.
options.C: Rely on vigorous exercise alone without changing eating patterns or body weight.
options.D: Wait to make lifestyle changes until blood glucose reaches the diabetes range.

candidates.rationale: CDC's National Diabetes Prevention Program is based on evidence that people with prediabetes can reduce progression to type 2 diabetes through structured lifestyle change, including healthier eating, modest weight loss of about 5%–7% of body weight, and at least 150 minutes of physical activity per week. B directly reflects those evidence-based targets. A promotes an extreme diet and defers activity; C omits the combined lifestyle approach; D delays prevention until after progression.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For adults with prediabetes and overweight, the CDC evidence-based prevention approach combines healthier eating, approximately 5%–7% weight loss, and at least 150 minutes/week of physical activity.

Prediabetes — Prevent type 2 diabetes: modest 5%–7% weight loss and regular physical activity of at least 150 minutes/week reduce risk.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — hypertension prevention through lifestyle modification
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients with elevated blood pressure that DASH-style eating, sodium reduction, regular physical activity, and healthy weight management are evidence-based measures to prevent or treat hypertension.

options.A: Avoid physical activity until blood pressure returns to normal.
options.B: Follow a heart-healthy pattern such as DASH, reduce sodium, stay physically active, and work toward a healthy weight.
options.C: Lifestyle changes have little role unless antihypertensive medication has already been started.
options.D: Increase sodium intake when exercising so dietary changes do not affect blood pressure.

candidates.rationale: The 2025 ACC/AHA high blood pressure guideline strongly recommends lifestyle changes for prevention and treatment of elevated blood pressure and hypertension, including a heart-healthy eating pattern such as DASH, reduced sodium intake, regular physical activity, and maintaining or achieving a healthy weight. B directly reflects this guidance. A and C contradict the guideline's emphasis on lifestyle intervention, while D reverses the sodium recommendation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current hypertension guidance supports DASH-style eating, lower sodium intake, physical activity, and weight management as core lifestyle measures for elevated blood pressure and hypertension.

candidates.educational_objective: Address ostomy-related body-image and intimacy concerns with open-ended, nonjudgmental communication and offer individualized ostomy and psychosocial support resources when desired.

options.A: It is best to avoid discussing body image until you feel ready to bring it up again.
options.B: Tell me what worries you most about how the ostomy may affect your relationship. We can also discuss ostomy-nurse or support resources if you want them.
options.C: Most people adjust quickly once they learn how to manage the pouch.
options.D: For now, focus on learning pouch care; intimacy concerns can be addressed after physical recovery is complete.

candidates.rationale: NCBI Nursing Skills notes that an ostomy can affect self-esteem, body image, quality of life, and intimacy and that nurses can promote healthy coping through appropriate referrals to a wound/ostomy specialist, social worker, or support groups. Therapeutic communication guidance emphasizes client-centered, nonjudgmental listening and open-ended questions. B acknowledges the concern, invites the client to describe its personal meaning, and offers resources without forcing them. A and D avoid an important psychosocial concern, while C gives premature reassurance and assumes a predictable adjustment course.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ostomy-related body-image and intimacy concerns are legitimate nursing assessment/support needs; therapeutic nursing care invites expression and may include referral to ostomy and psychosocial resources.

candidates.educational_objective: Assess psychosocial coping when dialysis disrupts work, roles, and activities and connect the client with renal social-work or mental-health resources when support is needed.

options.A: Explain that these disruptions are unavoidable and redirect the discussion to the dialysis prescription.
options.B: Advise the client to stop working until adapting emotionally to dialysis.
options.C: Assess the client's coping and emotional concerns and offer referral to the dialysis social worker or mental health support.
options.D: Reassure the client that most people stop feeling overwhelmed after several months of dialysis.

candidates.rationale: NIDDK notes that in-center hemodialysis can require changes in work, home life, activities, and responsibilities and that adjusting to kidney failure and time spent on dialysis can be difficult. It specifically identifies a mental health counselor or social worker as resources to help clients cope. C therefore addresses the client's expressed psychosocial burden with assessment and appropriate support. A minimizes the concern, B makes an unnecessary employment decision for the client, and D gives unsupported reassurance and imposes a fixed adjustment timeline.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Dialysis can substantially disrupt roles and daily life, and clients experiencing psychosocial difficulty should have coping concerns assessed and may benefit from social-work or mental-health support.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — esketamine REMS administration/monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize SPRAVATO REMS requirements for directly observed administration in a certified setting and at least 2 hours of post-dose monitoring, including respiratory assessment.

options.A: Dispense the dose for unsupervised home administration after prior tolerance.
options.B: Administer it in a certified health care setting under direct observation and monitor for at least 2 hours after dosing.
options.C: Discharge immediately if no dissociation occurs during the first 15 minutes.
options.D: Monitor only blood pressure because respiratory monitoring is not required.

candidates.rationale: The March 2026 SPRAVATO label requires administration in a REMS-certified health care setting under direct observation and monitoring for at least 2 hours after each session. Respiratory status must also be monitored for at least 2 hours, including pulse oximetry, with blood-pressure assessment. Thus B is correct; A violates REMS supervision, C shortens required observation, and D omits required respiratory monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: SPRAVATO requires directly observed administration in a REMS-certified health care setting and at least 2 hours of post-dose monitoring, including respiratory-status monitoring.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ketamine respiratory safety and monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that ketamine may preserve pharyngeal-laryngeal reflexes but still requires continuous monitoring and airway readiness because respiratory depression can occur.

options.A: Preserved airway reflexes eliminate the need for respiratory monitoring during ketamine administration.
options.B: Ketamine can still cause respiratory depression, so continuous monitoring and immediate access to airway/resuscitation equipment remain necessary.
options.C: Preserved airway reflexes mean ketamine can be used alone for procedures involving mechanical stimulation of the pharynx.
options.D: Respiratory depression occurs only after the client has completely lost all protective reflexes.

candidates.rationale: The current ketamine hydrochloride injection label states that pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes are not suppressed when ketamine is used alone, but it also warns that respiratory depression may occur, particularly with overdosage or overly rapid administration. The label requires continuous vital-sign monitoring and immediate availability of emergency airway equipment. Therefore B is correct. A and D falsely treat preserved reflexes as proof that respiratory compromise cannot occur. C contradicts the warning to avoid ketamine as the sole anesthetic for procedures involving the pharynx, larynx, or bronchial tree.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ketamine may preserve upper-airway reflexes but can still cause respiratory depression; continuous monitoring and immediate airway support capability remain necessary.
candidates.source_document_title: Ketamine Hydrochloride Injection, for intravenous or intramuscular use, CIII — Full Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Section 2.1 Important Dosage and Administration Information: continuous vital-sign monitoring and emergency airway equipment immediately available. Section 5.3 Respiratory Depression: respiratory depression may occur with overdosage or too rapid administration; maintain oxygenation/ventilation. Section 5.4: pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes are not suppressed when ketamine is used alone; avoid sole use for procedures of pharynx/larynx/bronchial tree. Section 12.2 Pharmacodynamics: dissociative anesthetic state with profound analgesia and preserved pharyngeal-laryngeal reflexes.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — propofol cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway preparedness
candidates.educational_objective: Before propofol MAC sedation, verify continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and immediate airway, ventilation, oxygen, and cardiovascular-resuscitation capability.

options.A: The client can be observed intermittently because propofol rarely affects ventilation.
options.B: Equipment for airway support, artificial ventilation, supplemental oxygen, and cardiovascular resuscitation is immediately available with continuous monitoring.
options.C: The person administering propofol may also perform the surgical procedure if another nurse watches the monitor.
options.D: Airway equipment is needed only if the client has a prior history of difficult intubation.

candidates.rationale: The current propofol prescribing information requires continuous monitoring of sedated patients and immediate availability of equipment for maintaining a patent airway, providing artificial ventilation and supplemental oxygen, and instituting cardiovascular resuscitation. The label warns that hypotension, apnea, airway obstruction, and oxygen desaturation can occur. For general anesthesia or MAC sedation, propofol should be administered only by persons trained in general anesthesia who are not simultaneously conducting the surgical or diagnostic procedure. Therefore B is correct. A understates cardiorespiratory risk, C conflicts with the administration requirement, and D incorrectly limits airway readiness to clients with known difficult airways.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Propofol MAC sedation requires continuous monitoring and immediate airway/ventilation/oxygen/resuscitation capability because clinically important hypotension, apnea, airway obstruction, and desaturation may occur.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — neuromuscular blockade, sedation, and ventilation safety
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that rocuronium causes neuromuscular paralysis without providing anesthesia or sedation and therefore requires adequate anesthesia/sedation plus immediate airway and ventilation capability.

options.A: Rocuronium provides sufficient unconsciousness and analgesia when paralysis begins.
options.B: Adequate anesthesia or sedation must accompany rocuronium, and intubation/ventilation capability must be immediately available.
options.C: The client's ability to move is a reliable indicator of whether pain is controlled after rocuronium is given.
options.D: Mechanical ventilation is unnecessary if oxygen saturation is normal immediately before administration.

candidates.rationale: The current rocuronium bromide injection label states that the drug must be accompanied by adequate anesthesia or sedation and should be used only when facilities for intubation, mechanical ventilation, oxygen therapy, and an antagonist are immediately available. Rocuronium produces neuromuscular blockade; it does not substitute for hypnosis, sedation, or analgesia. Therefore B is correct. A falsely attributes anesthetic/analgesic effects to a neuromuscular blocker. C is unsafe because paralysis prevents movement from being used as evidence of comfort or consciousness. D ignores the predictable respiratory-muscle paralysis for which ventilation capability is required.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Rocuronium is a neuromuscular blocker that requires accompanying anesthesia/sedation and immediate airway/ventilation support capability; paralysis is not evidence of unconsciousness or analgesia.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — sugammadex reversal and post-blockade respiratory/hemodynamic monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: After sugammadex reversal, continue respiratory and hemodynamic surveillance and maintain ventilatory support until adequate spontaneous respiration and airway patency are confirmed.

options.A: Discontinue ventilatory support immediately because sugammadex guarantees complete reversal with the injection.
options.B: Continue respiratory and hemodynamic monitoring and maintain ventilatory support until adequate spontaneous breathing and a patent airway are assured.
options.C: Avoid monitoring heart rate because sugammadex does not cause clinically important bradycardia.
options.D: Expect sugammadex to provide postoperative analgesia while neuromuscular function returns.

candidates.rationale: The current sugammadex label states that ventilatory support is mandatory until adequate spontaneous respiration is restored and the ability to maintain a patent airway is assured. It also warns of marked bradycardia, including rare cardiac arrest, within minutes after administration and of hypersensitivity/anaphylaxis. Therefore B is correct. A assumes immediate guaranteed recovery and removes support too early. C contradicts the hemodynamic-monitoring warning. D assigns an analgesic effect that is not the indication of sugammadex.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium blockade, but respiratory support and monitoring must continue until adequate spontaneous ventilation and airway patency are established; hemodynamic monitoring remains important because marked bradycardia can occur.
candidates.source_document_title: Sugammadex Injection / BRIDION (sugammadex) Injection — Full Prescribing Information

candidates.educational_objective: When intravenous midazolam is used with an opioid for procedural sedation, the nurse prioritizes continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and immediate airway-resuscitation readiness because the combination can cause profound sedation and respiratory depression.

options.A: Give additional midazolam whenever the client becomes less responsive so that amnesia is maintained throughout the procedure
options.B: Continuously monitor respiratory and cardiac status and ensure airway-resuscitation equipment and trained personnel are immediately available
options.C: Use only routine intermittent vital signs because fentanyl provides analgesia and therefore reduces midazolam-related respiratory risk
options.D: Concentrate respiratory monitoring after the procedure because serious respiratory events are not expected while midazolam is being administered

candidates.rationale: Intravenous midazolam can cause respiratory depression, airway obstruction, apnea, and cardiorespiratory arrest. Concomitant opioids such as fentanyl can produce profound sedation and further increase respiratory-depression risk. The client therefore requires continuous respiratory and cardiac monitoring during sedation and recovery, with resuscitative drugs, bag-mask ventilation/intubation equipment, and personnel skilled in airway management immediately available. Additional midazolam should not be given merely to preserve amnesia; dosing must be individualized and titrated to clinical response. Analgesia from fentanyl does not reduce the respiratory risk of the drug combination, and monitoring cannot be deferred until recovery.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current label states that IV midazolam has caused respiratory depression and respiratory arrest; continuous respiratory/cardiac monitoring and immediate resuscitation/airway equipment and skilled personnel are required, and concomitant benzodiazepine-opioid use can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death.

candidates.educational_objective: After flumazenil reversal of benzodiazepine sedation, the nurse continues monitoring for re-sedation because the benzodiazepine effect may persist longer than the reversal effect.

options.A: The recurrent drowsiness confirms that the benzodiazepine has been fully eliminated, so routine discharge preparation can continue
options.B: Re-sedation can occur because the benzodiazepine effect may outlast flumazenil; continue close monitoring and promptly report the change for further management
options.C: The drowsiness indicates opioid withdrawal caused by flumazenil and should be treated by giving another sedative
options.D: The drowsiness is an expected permanent effect of flumazenil and does not require reassessment if oxygen saturation was previously normal

candidates.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine effects, but its reversal may wear off while the benzodiazepine remains active. Re-sedation can therefore occur after an initial response and requires continued clinical monitoring and reassessment; additional prescribed flumazenil may be needed in selected cases. Recurrent drowsiness does not prove drug elimination, flumazenil does not reverse opioids or cause opioid withdrawal, and a prior normal oxygen saturation does not remove the need to reassess a changing level of consciousness.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current label documents re-sedation after successful reversal and states that the major risk is re-sedation when the duration of benzodiazepine effect exceeds that of flumazenil; it also states that flumazenil does not reverse opioids.

candidates.educational_objective: Before deep sedation or anesthesia begins, the nurse verifies that required emergency airway equipment is immediately available and functional; a missing critical airway resource is a safety reason to delay the procedure until corrected.

options.A: Begin the procedure because emergency airway equipment is needed only when a difficult airway has already been predicted
options.B: Proceed if routine oxygen and suction are available, then obtain advanced airway equipment only if ventilation becomes difficult
options.C: Do not begin deep sedation until appropriate emergency airway equipment is immediately available and confirmed functional
options.D: Proceed if the client has no history of difficult intubation because prior uncomplicated anesthesia excludes an unexpected airway emergency

candidates.rationale: Sedation and anesthesia can progress to airway compromise unexpectedly, so appropriate emergency airway and resuscitation equipment must be immediately available and functional before care begins. ASA guidance for sedation/anesthesia settings requires emergency airway equipment to be available and functional, and NCSBN identifies inspection and safe use of client-care equipment as an RN safety responsibility. A previously uncomplicated airway, absence of a predicted difficult airway, or availability of oxygen and suction alone does not eliminate the need for full emergency airway readiness.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ASA states that settings providing sedation/anesthesia must have appropriate safety and resuscitative equipment, including emergency airway equipment, immediately available and functional, and that equipment must be checked/tested at accepted intervals.

candidates.educational_objective: For a hypoxemic adult requiring emergency intubation, anticipate NIV for preoxygenation when it is feasible and tolerated; use other oxygen strategies when NIV is not feasible or appropriate.

options.A: Use conventional oxygen therapy alone because NIV should be avoided before emergency intubation
options.B: Use NIV for preoxygenation when feasible because it reduces peri-intubation hypoxemia more effectively than conventional oxygen therapy
options.C: Avoid preoxygenation and begin intubation immediately because oxygen delivery before laryngoscopy prolongs apnea
options.D: Use high-flow nasal cannula in preference to NIV even when NIV is feasible and tolerated

candidates.rationale: ACEP's January 2026 clinical policy recommends, when feasible, optimizing preoxygenation with noninvasive ventilation rather than conventional oxygen therapy for adults requiring endotracheal intubation in the emergency department. High-flow nasal cannula is an alternative to consider when NIV is not feasible for hypoxemic clients. The stem removes important relative barriers to NIV such as vomiting, decreased consciousness that increases aspiration risk, or inability to cooperate. Preoxygenation is intended to reduce peri-intubation hypoxemia, not to be omitted.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ACEP 2026 recommends NIV over conventional oxygen therapy for preoxygenation when feasible and identifies HFNC as an alternative when NIV is not feasible; the policy notes aspiration/agitation-related relative contraindications to NIV.
candidates.source_document_title: Critical Issues in the Management of Adult Patients Requiring Endotracheal Intubation in the Emergency Department

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postanesthesia transfer readiness and complication assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Use standardized PACU recovery scores as one part of transfer assessment; active complications such as repeated vomiting or surgical-site bleeding require evaluation and management even when the numeric recovery threshold is met.

options.A: Transfer the client because meeting the Aldrete threshold overrides findings not included in the score
options.B: Delay transfer, assess and address the vomiting and bleeding, and communicate the findings because a discharge score does not replace clinical assessment
options.C: Repeat only the activity and consciousness portions of the Aldrete score because postoperative bleeding and vomiting are unrelated to transfer readiness
options.D: Transfer the client and document the vomiting and bleeding for the receiving unit to evaluate after arrival

candidates.rationale: The Aldrete score is a useful standardized measure of physiologic recovery, but the original score focuses on activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, and oxygenation. It does not fully address common postprocedural issues such as pain, nausea/vomiting, and surgical-site bleeding. A client who meets a numeric threshold but has active concerning findings still requires individualized assessment and management before transfer. A standardized score supports—not replaces—clinical judgment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The Aldrete score standardizes physiologic recovery assessment, but the source explicitly notes that the original score does not address pain, nausea/vomiting, or surgical-site bleeding and that broader/individualized discharge assessment remains important.

candidates.educational_objective: A client who loses purposeful responsiveness and develops airway compromise during intended moderate sedation requires immediate recognition of deeper-than-intended sedation and airway rescue with qualified assistance.

options.A: Continue the planned sedation because loss of purposeful response is expected during moderate sedation
options.B: Recognize deeper-than-intended sedation, initiate airway rescue measures within the nurse's training/protocol, and summon qualified assistance immediately
options.C: Wait for spontaneous recovery because intervening with the airway can deepen the level of sedation
options.D: Increase the sedative dose to reduce agitation during airway obstruction before calling for assistance

candidates.rationale: Moderate sedation is intended to preserve purposeful response to verbal commands or light tactile stimulation. A client who no longer responds purposefully and develops airway obstruction has progressed beyond the intended level and requires rescue. ASA guidance emphasizes training in airway maintenance, management of sedation-related complications, and rescue from deeper-than-intended sedation. The nurse should stop treating the situation as routine moderate sedation, support the airway according to training and facility protocol, and summon qualified help.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ASA explicitly requires training in airway maintenance and rescue from deeper-than-intended sedation; ASA sedation definitions describe moderate sedation as maintaining purposeful response to verbal or light tactile stimulation.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — moderate sedation respiratory monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: During procedural sedation, recognize that capnography can reveal hypoventilation before pulse oximetry shows desaturation, particularly with supplemental oxygen; respond to deteriorating ventilation promptly.

options.A: The unchanged oxygen saturation rules out clinically important respiratory depression
options.B: The capnography change can identify inadequate ventilation before oxygen desaturation occurs; assess the airway and ventilation and initiate appropriate support
options.C: Capnography primarily reflects oxygenation, so the pulse oximeter should be used instead to judge ventilation
options.D: The change is expected during moderate sedation and requires no response unless the blood pressure also decreases

candidates.rationale: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, whereas capnography provides information about ventilation through exhaled carbon dioxide. During sedation—especially when supplemental oxygen is being given—oxygen saturation may remain acceptable for a period despite hypoventilation or apnea. A worsening capnographic pattern plus decreasing responsiveness therefore requires immediate airway/ventilation assessment and appropriate respiratory support rather than waiting for desaturation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Capnography assesses ventilatory adequacy during procedural sedation; pulse oximetry measures oxygenation and may lag behind ventilatory compromise, especially when oxygen is supplied.

candidates.educational_objective: The PACU nurse ensures that transfer-of-care communication includes clinically significant intraoperative information and resolves missing data that may affect immediate postoperative management before handoff is completed.

options.A: Accept the incomplete handoff because these details can be reviewed later if the client becomes unstable
options.B: Clarify the missing information with the transferring team before the handoff is completed because it can affect immediate postoperative assessment and care
options.C: Ask the client to provide the missing intraoperative information after fully awakening from anesthesia
options.D: Document that the information was unavailable and omit further follow-up because responsibility transfers to the PACU at arrival

candidates.rationale: Immediate postoperative care depends on an accurate handoff from the operating-room/anesthesia team. Important handoff content includes anesthesia type and duration, medications and IV fluids, estimated blood loss, urine output, drains, and intraoperative complications. Missing information that may change PACU assessment or intervention should be clarified with the transferring team rather than deferred, reconstructed from the recovering client, or simply documented as unavailable.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The chapter states that the PACU RN requires clear, thorough handoff information and lists clinically important intraoperative data needed to manage recovery and complications.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — assignment based on competency
candidates.educational_objective: Charge nurses base assignments on client needs and verified staff competency; specialized monitoring responsibilities should not be assigned independently to personnel whose competency has not been established.

options.A: Assign the RN to monitor moderate sedation independently because an RN license alone establishes competency for every nursing task
options.B: Assign the RN to monitor moderate sedation if the RN agrees to review the policy while the procedure is underway
options.C: Assign the sedation-monitoring responsibility to a nurse whose competency has been verified and give the newly hired RN duties within demonstrated competency
options.D: Assign the RN independently and ask an unlicensed assistive person to observe the client's respiratory status

candidates.rationale: Safe assignment requires matching client needs and task complexity with the staff member's allowable duties, demonstrated competency, and ability to exercise appropriate judgment. A professional license does not establish competency for every specialized unit responsibility. When competency for moderate-sedation monitoring has not yet been validated under the facility's process, the charge nurse should assign that responsibility to a qualified nurse and give the newly hired RN work within verified competency. An unlicensed assistive person cannot substitute for the qualified nurse responsible for sedation monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: NCSBN directs the RN to assign/delegate based on client needs and personnel competency and to evaluate allowable duties, competency, and judgment before assignment.

candidates.educational_objective: When adjunct technology is part of the facility RSI-prevention process, complete it before wound closure even when the manual count is correct.

options.A: Allow closure because a correct manual count makes RF verification unnecessary
options.B: Complete the required RF verification before final wound closure and communicate any discrepancy
options.C: Skip RF verification if the scrub person and surgeon verbally confirm the count
options.D: Allow closure and perform RF verification after the client leaves the OR

candidates.rationale: Manual counts can be falsely reassuring. AORN recommends adjunct technology as a supplement when used and directs completion of the manual count and adjunct verification before wound closure according to manufacturer instructions and facility policy. Verbal agreement does not replace the established verification process, and post-closure verification is too late for its prevention purpose.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AORN supports adjunct technology as a supplement to manual counting and states to complete both before wound closure when adjunct technology is used.

candidates.educational_objective: For a lateralized procedure such as eye surgery, verify that required site marking is completed by the appropriately accountable licensed practitioner before the procedure and involve the patient whenever possible.

options.A: Proceed because eye surgery does not require site marking when the consent names the correct eye
options.B: Pause progression and ensure the licensed practitioner accountable for the procedure completes the required site-marking process before the procedure
options.C: Mark the left eye independently so the operating schedule is not delayed
options.D: Proceed to the final time-out because the time-out replaces site marking for paired organs

candidates.rationale: Joint Commission site-marking requirements apply when more than one possible procedural location exists and an incorrect site would affect safety or quality; eye surgery is specifically listed as a common example. The site is marked before the procedure by the licensed practitioner ultimately accountable for and present at the procedure, with the patient involved whenever possible. The nurse should therefore pause progression and ensure the required process is completed rather than independently marking outside the defined process or treating the time-out as a substitute.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — Informed Consent
candidates.educational_objective: A signed form alone does not establish informed consent; unresolved client questions require clarification before the nurse verifies consent and care proceeds.

options.A: Continue because the signature confirms informed consent is complete
options.B: Pause progression, notify the appropriate provider, and ensure the client's questions are addressed before verifying consent
options.C: Explain all procedure-specific risks, benefits and alternatives independently and rely on the original signature
options.D: Ask a family member to explain the procedure so it can proceed

candidates.rationale: Informed consent is more than a signature. NCSBN 2026 expects the RN to participate in obtaining informed consent and verify that the client receives education and consents to care and procedures. The client's unresolved questions show the process is not adequately complete for the nurse to simply proceed. The nurse should pause progression, communicate the concern to the appropriate provider, and ensure questions are addressed before verifying consent rather than independently substituting for the provider responsible for procedure-specific disclosure or relying on family explanation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: NCSBN explicitly includes RN participation in informed consent and verification that the client received education and consents.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed consent and decision-making capacity
candidates.educational_objective: Before relying on informed consent, verify that the client can meaningfully understand and decide; when current decision-making capacity is impaired, pause elective care and follow the appropriate provider/surrogate consent process.

options.A: Ask the client to sign immediately because the procedure is already scheduled
options.B: Do not obtain a new consent signature from the client in the current state; notify the appropriate provider and follow the consent process for a client who cannot presently demonstrate decision-making capacity
options.C: Ask any available family member to sign because family presence automatically creates legal authority to consent
options.D: Proceed without consent because administration of procedural sedation creates an emergency exception

candidates.rationale: Valid informed consent requires the ability to understand relevant information, consider alternatives, and make a voluntary decision. The stem establishes that the client is currently drowsy, confused, and unable to explain the procedure or alternatives, so the nurse should not treat a new signature obtained in that state as adequate informed consent. The appropriate provider should be notified and the applicable process for decision-making incapacity and an authorized surrogate, if needed, should be followed. A family member is not automatically a legally authorized surrogate, and routine elective care does not become an emergency merely because sedation has already been administered.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AMA identifies decision-making ability as a required element of informed consent; NCSBN defines the RN role as participating in and verifying informed consent rather than treating a signature alone as sufficient.

candidates.educational_objective: Use preoperative briefings to identify anticipated changes in the surgical plan and close resource gaps before the procedure begins, especially when conversion to an open procedure is possible.

options.A: Begin the procedure because conversion can be discussed only if it actually becomes necessary
options.B: Use the briefing to communicate the resource gap and ensure required open-procedure equipment is available before the case begins
options.C: Wait until conversion is requested, then leave the room to locate the needed equipment
options.D: Omit the concern from the briefing because equipment availability is unrelated to team communication

candidates.rationale: AORN team-communication guidance identifies briefings as a tool for creating a shared mental model and situational awareness. AORN minimally invasive surgery guidance specifically notes that discussing possible conversion to an open procedure during the preoperative briefing allows the team to identify and gather needed resources in advance and anticipate intraoperative changes. Starting without required resources or waiting until an urgent conversion is underway creates avoidable delay and risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AORN supports preoperative briefing to create shared situational awareness and specifically recommends discussing possible open conversion so the team can identify and gather resources in advance.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — malignant hyperthermia emergency management
candidates.educational_objective: When malignant hyperthermia is suspected, promptly activate the MH response, stop triggering anesthetics, provide 100% oxygen with hyperventilation, and administer dantrolene rather than delaying for fever or laboratory confirmation.

options.A: Continue the volatile anesthetic while applying cooling measures first, then reassess the end-tidal CO2 before obtaining specific treatment
options.B: Activate the malignant-hyperthermia response: discontinue triggering agents, obtain the MH cart/dantrolene, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, and administer IV dantrolene promptly
options.C: Treat the tachycardia with a calcium-channel blocker and delay dantrolene until the core temperature becomes markedly elevated
options.D: Reduce minute ventilation to avoid respiratory alkalosis while waiting for confirmatory laboratory testing before treating

candidates.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia is a rapidly progressive hypermetabolic emergency. MHAUS directs teams to discontinue volatile triggering agents and succinylcholine, call for help and obtain the MH cart/dantrolene, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen to lower carbon dioxide and flush volatile anesthetic, and give IV dantrolene promptly. Treatment should not wait for severe hyperthermia or confirmatory testing. Cooling may be needed, but it must not distract from dantrolene and treatment of hypercarbia/acidosis. Calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil or diltiazem can have dangerous interactions with dantrolene and are not the response to prioritize here.
candidates.source_claim_supported: MHAUS directly lists discontinuation of triggers, urgent dantrolene access/administration, 100% oxygen hyperventilation, and team activation as immediate management of an acute MH event.
candidates.source_document_title: Managing A Crisis — Emergency Treatment for An Acute MH Event
candidates.source_locator: Managing A Crisis — Emergency Treatment for An Acute MH Event: discontinue volatile agents/succinylcholine; get dantrolene/MH cart and call for help; hyperventilate with 100% oxygen; give IV dantrolene. MHAUS hyperthermia recommendation: dantrolene/hyperventilation should not be delayed by cooling.

candidates.educational_objective: Acute agitation during emergence requires immediate safety and physiologic assessment for reversible causes before labeling it emergence delirium.

options.A: Assume emergence delirium is self-limited and observe without additional assessment
options.B: Promptly assess airway, breathing/oxygenation, circulation, vital signs, pain, and other reversible causes of acute confusion while protecting the client from injury
options.C: Administer an additional sedative immediately before assessing for hypoxia, hypercarbia, or medication effects
options.D: Diagnose malignant hyperthermia from agitation alone and begin the MH protocol without evaluating for other findings

candidates.rationale: Agitation and confusion during emergence are nonspecific. Important differentials include hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypoglycemia, hypotension, pain, medication effects, and other acute conditions. PACU recovery also requires assessment of breathing, circulation, consciousness, and oxygenation. Protect the client from injury while promptly assessing physiology and reversible causes rather than assuming a benign phenomenon or reflexively adding sedation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Postoperative agitation/delirium requires assessment for physiologic/metabolic causes; postanesthesia recovery monitoring includes breathing, circulation, consciousness and oxygenation.

candidates.source_locator: Postoperative Delirium — Differential Diagnosis: hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypoglycemia, hypothermia, stroke, seizure, acidemia/electrolyte disturbances; vital signs promptly. ASA After surgery — monitor breathing, circulation, consciousness, oxygen.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — preoperative aspiration-risk assessment
candidates.educational_objective: When a preoperative client reports breaking prescribed fasting instructions, communicate the finding and obtain anesthesia/procedural reassessment before elective anesthesia proceeds because aspiration risk may be increased.

options.A: Continue routine preparation because fasting affects comfort but not anesthesia safety
options.B: Pause routine progression and promptly notify the anesthesia/procedural team so aspiration risk and the anesthesia plan can be reassessed
options.C: Tell the client to induce vomiting so the procedure can remain on schedule
options.D: Cancel the procedure independently without communicating with the anesthesia or procedural team

candidates.rationale: Fasting instructions before sedation or general anesthesia are intended to reduce regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents. A client who reports not following the prescribed fasting instructions requires reassessment by the anesthesia/procedural team before elective care proceeds. The nurse should communicate the new information and pause routine progression rather than ignore the risk, induce vomiting, or independently make the final procedural decision. No universal fasting interval is inferred from the stem; management depends on the clinical situation and anesthesia plan.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ASA explains that fasting before sedation/general anesthesia is used to reduce regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration and that anesthesia-specific guidance should direct preoperative intake decisions.

candidates.source_locator: Why would having food in your stomach make you less safe? — gastric contents can regurgitate and enter airway/lungs; fasting is used before general anesthesia or sedation to reduce aspiration. Adult Checklist — follow presurgery diet/fasting directions and ask anesthesiologist for guidance.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postanesthesia airway complication assessment
candidates.educational_objective: New post-extubation stridor with respiratory deterioration is an airway emergency cue; prioritize airway/oxygenation support and rapid escalation rather than assuming a single diagnosis.

options.A: Assume laryngospasm is the diagnosis and wait for spontaneous resolution before reassessing the airway
options.B: Treat the finding as possible upper-airway obstruction: immediately assess and support oxygenation/ventilation, summon airway-qualified assistance, and prepare for escalation such as reintubation if obstruction is significant
options.C: Offer oral fluids to soothe airway irritation and reassess after the client has swallowed
options.D: Transfer the client from the recovery area because post-extubation stridor is an expected finding after general anesthesia

candidates.rationale: Post-extubation stridor indicates clinically important upper-airway narrowing and is not specific for laryngospasm. Post-intubation laryngeal edema is a common cause, while laryngospasm, angioedema/anaphylaxis, foreign body, hematoma, and vocal-cord problems are among the differential diagnoses. With increasing work of breathing and falling oxygen saturation, the priority is immediate airway and oxygenation/ventilation support with rapid escalation to airway-qualified personnel; prompt reintubation may be required when significant obstruction is suspected. Oral intake and transfer are unsafe during active airway compromise, and diagnostic labeling should not delay stabilization.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Post-extubation stridor can reflect laryngeal edema or other upper-airway causes and significant obstruction may require prompt reintubation; the clinical priority is airway/oxygenation management rather than diagnosing laryngospasm from stridor alone.
candidates.source_document_title: Extubation; Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema
candidates.source_locator: Extubation — Management of Post-extubation Stridor: oxygen/CPAP options when stable and prompt reintubation if significant airway obstruction is suspected. Post-Intubation Laryngeal Edema — Differential Diagnosis and Consultations: laryngeal edema as common cause of post-extubation stridor; differentiate from laryngospasm, angioedema/anaphylaxis, foreign body, hematoma, vocal-cord palsy.
