candidates.educational_objective: When a client reports possible awareness during general anesthesia, acknowledge and document the experience, notify the anesthesia team, and support appropriate follow-up rather than dismissing the report or assigning blame.

options.A: Reassure the client that the memory must have been a dream because awareness cannot occur during general anesthesia
options.B: Acknowledge the report and distress, document the client's description, notify the anesthesia team for evaluation, and facilitate follow-up or counseling as appropriate
options.C: Tell the client that the report proves an anesthesia error occurred and advise immediate legal action
options.D: Avoid discussing the memory because reviewing the experience is likely to create psychological harm

candidates.rationale: Intraoperative awareness with explicit recall is rare but recognized during intended general anesthesia. ASA advises patients who believe awareness occurred to describe the experience to their anesthesiologist, and notes that the event can be disturbing or traumatic and that some patients benefit from counseling. The nurse should therefore take the report seriously, support the client, preserve the client's account, and ensure anesthesia evaluation and appropriate follow-up. The report should not be dismissed as impossible or a dream, but it also does not by itself prove negligence or a specific error.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ASA recognizes anesthesia awareness as a rare event under general anesthesia and recommends reporting the experience to the anesthesiologist; counseling may benefit distressed patients.
candidates.source_document_title: Anesthesia Awareness (Waking Up) During Surgery
candidates.source_locator: What happens if you have anesthesia awareness during surgery? — varied recall during general anesthesia; describe the experience to the anesthesiologist after surgery; some patients benefit from counseling for confusion/stress

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — perioperative hypothermia prevention and monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: When perioperative temperature is falling under general anesthesia, use appropriate active warming and continued temperature monitoring rather than passive insulation alone or delayed treatment.

options.A: Continue passive blankets alone because active warming is not recommended during general anesthesia
options.B: Initiate the facility's appropriate active-warming strategy and continue temperature monitoring, minimizing unnecessary interruptions to warming
options.C: Stop temperature monitoring once warming begins because a warming device prevents further hypothermia
options.D: Delay warming until the postoperative phase because intraoperative warming has little effect on perioperative hypothermia

candidates.rationale: AORN's updated Patient Temperature Management guideline emphasizes active warming because it is more effective than passive insulation alone at raising temperature and preventing hypothermia during general anesthesia. The guideline also emphasizes maintaining warming through the intraoperative and postoperative phases and minimizing unnecessary interruptions. Temperature assessment continues because warming does not eliminate monitoring needs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AORN states active warming is more effective than passive insulation alone during general anesthesia, recommends warming across perioperative phases, and supports ongoing temperature monitoring.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — preoperative airway-risk assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret Mallampati classification as one component—not a stand-alone rule-out test—of difficult-airway assessment and maintain appropriate airway preparedness even when the Mallampati class appears favorable.

options.A: Agree because a low Mallampati class reliably rules out a difficult airway
options.B: Recognize that Mallampati is only one airway predictor; other anatomic and clinical features must also be considered and difficult-airway readiness remains necessary
options.C: Disregard the Mallampati finding completely because it has no relationship to airway difficulty
options.D: Interpret Mallampati class I as evidence that mask ventilation and emergency airway access will also be uncomplicated

candidates.rationale: The Mallampati classification is a useful component of preoperative airway assessment, and higher classes are associated with greater intubation difficulty. However, its sensitivity and predictive accuracy are limited when it is used alone. Airway evaluation should integrate other features such as mouth opening, neck mobility, mandibular/thyromental anatomy, prior difficult-airway history, and the broader clinical context. A low Mallampati class therefore does not guarantee easy intubation, mask ventilation, or rescue airway access.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Mallampati is associated with intubation difficulty but is an unreliable stand-alone screening tool and should be interpreted with other airway features and overall clinical context.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — preoperative OSA risk screening and monitoring planning
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a high-risk STOP-BANG result as a perioperative risk signal—not a definitive OSA diagnosis—and communicate it so anesthesia and postoperative respiratory monitoring can be individualized.

options.A: The screening result confirms OSA, so no further clinical evaluation is needed
options.B: The result identifies increased likelihood of OSA and perioperative respiratory risk; communicate it to the anesthesia/procedural team and incorporate it into risk planning and postoperative monitoring
options.C: The result is unrelated to anesthesia because STOP-BANG is used only after a sleep-study diagnosis has already been made
options.D: The result should be ignored unless the client develops apnea while awake in the preoperative area

candidates.rationale: STOP-BANG is a screening and risk-stratification tool, not a diagnostic sleep study. A high-risk result suggests increased probability of clinically important OSA and should be communicated during perioperative planning. OSA risk is relevant because affected or high-risk surgical clients can have greater respiratory and other postoperative complications, particularly when sedatives, anesthetics, and opioids are involved. The screen should therefore inform assessment and monitoring rather than be treated as definitive diagnosis or ignored until overt apnea occurs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: STOP-BANG screens for OSA probability rather than establishing diagnosis; high-risk screening status is clinically relevant to perioperative complication risk and postoperative planning.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — perioperative cardiovascular risk assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Use RCRI as one component of stepwise perioperative cardiovascular risk assessment; do not treat an elevated score as an automatic stress-test indication or a diagnosis of coronary disease.

options.A: Agree because any elevated RCRI requires stress testing before noncardiac surgery
options.B: Recognize that RCRI is one validated tool in stepwise perioperative cardiovascular assessment; additional testing depends on the overall clinical picture, functional capacity, surgical risk, and whether testing would change management
options.C: Disregard RCRI because validated risk-prediction tools are no longer used in perioperative assessment
options.D: Interpret RCRI as a diagnostic test for obstructive coronary artery disease rather than a perioperative risk tool

candidates.rationale: The 2024 AHA/ACC perioperative guideline recommends stepwise cardiovascular assessment for noncardiac surgery. Validated tools such as RCRI or NSQIP inform decisions but do not diagnose coronary disease or automatically mandate stress testing. Stress testing is reserved for selected patients when perioperative risk is elevated, functional capacity is poor or unknown, and the result would affect management; routine testing in low-risk situations can create unnecessary delay and over-testing.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AHA/ACC guidance uses RCRI as a validated perioperative risk tool within broader stepwise assessment and does not make an elevated score an automatic stress-test indication.
candidates.source_document_title: 2024 AHA/ACC/ACS/ASNC/HRS/SCA/SCCT/SCMR/SVM Guideline for Perioperative Cardiovascular Management for Noncardiac Surgery

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpretation of anesthesia monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret BIS as an adjunct rather than a stand-alone measure of consciousness; unexpected values require correlation with signal quality, medications, and the client's overall physiologic/anesthetic context.

options.A: The lower BIS value proves the client is more deeply unconscious and can be used by itself to guide anesthetic depth
options.B: The BIS value should be interpreted with the raw signal/quality indicators and the client's overall anesthetic and physiologic data because neuromuscular blockade and other factors can alter processed EEG values
options.C: A BIS change after neuromuscular blockade confirms intraoperative awareness
options.D: BIS replaces standard monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and anesthetic delivery whenever it is available

candidates.rationale: BIS is a processed EEG-derived adjunct for assessing hypnotic depth, but its value is not a direct or infallible measure of consciousness. Neuromuscular blockade can lower BIS by reducing electromyographic activity even without a corresponding increase in anesthetic effect. Other drugs, hypothermia, neurologic conditions, device interference, and signal quality can also affect BIS. Current reviews therefore emphasize interpreting processed EEG in the full clinical context and not substituting it for comprehensive physiologic and anesthetic monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: BIS is a processed EEG adjunct with clinically important limitations; neuromuscular blockade can decrease BIS independently of consciousness, and BIS should be interpreted with comprehensive monitoring rather than used alone.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpretation of preoperative physical-status assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret ASA Physical Status as a standardized description of preanesthesia systemic disease, not a stand-alone surgical-risk or cancellation rule; ASA III denotes severe systemic disease.

options.A: Yes. ASA III by itself means the procedure should not proceed
options.B: No. ASA III indicates severe systemic disease; the classification communicates preanesthesia health status and must be considered with the procedure and other risk factors rather than used alone to decide whether surgery is too dangerous
options.C: No. ASA III means only mild systemic disease and essentially the same risk as a healthy client
options.D: Yes. ASA III means systemic disease that is a constant threat to life

candidates.rationale: ASA Physical Status III describes severe systemic disease. The ASA system is intended to assess and communicate preanesthesia medical comorbidities; it is not by itself a complete perioperative-risk model or a rule for canceling surgery. Risk is interpreted with factors such as procedure type, frailty and the overall clinical picture. A constant threat to life corresponds to ASA IV.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ASA III denotes severe systemic disease; ASA PS describes preanesthesia comorbidity and is combined with other clinical/procedural factors rather than used alone as a risk/cancellation decision.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — diagnostic tests and preprocedure risk assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that preoperative diagnostic testing should be individualized to the client's condition and planned procedure rather than applied as an identical routine panel to all clients.

options.A: Preoperative testing is selected according to the client's history, comorbidities, examination findings, planned procedure, and specific risks rather than by using one identical test panel for every client
options.B: All surgical clients should receive the same laboratory and diagnostic tests so that no individual risk assessment is needed
options.C: The client's age alone determines which preoperative tests are appropriate, regardless of health history or procedure
options.D: Preoperative testing has little relationship to anesthesia or surgical risk and is mainly performed for administrative purposes

candidates.rationale: Preoperative assessment is individualized. History, comorbidities, physical findings, the planned procedure, and identified risks help determine which laboratory or diagnostic tests are clinically useful. A universal panel for every client can produce unnecessary testing and does not replace individualized assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Preoperative tests are used within a broader health assessment, and additional/specialized testing depends on the client's medical history and surgical procedure.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — postanesthesia airway protection
candidates.educational_objective: Use individualized positioning and airway-support measures to reduce aspiration or obstruction risk in a drowsy postanesthesia client.

options.A: Keep the client flat and supine regardless of secretions so that positioning does not influence the airway
options.B: Position the client laterally or turn the head to the side as clinically appropriate and keep suction available while continuing respiratory assessment
options.C: Place the client prone because prone positioning is required after general anesthesia
options.D: Sit the client fully upright immediately even if the client's level of consciousness does not allow safe maintenance of that position

candidates.rationale: In a markedly drowsy client without a positioning contraindication, lateral or head-turned positioning can help secretions drain away from the airway while the nurse continues close respiratory assessment and has suction available. Postanesthesia care remains individualized; no single position is appropriate for every surgical client.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Airway assessment and protection are immediate priorities during postanesthesia recovery; positioning must be adapted to the client's clinical and surgical context.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — pain assessment and evaluation
candidates.educational_objective: Reassess pain, function, and treatment effects after an analgesic at an interval appropriate to the intervention rather than relying on a fixed universal time or physiologic signs alone.

options.A: Document the medication as given and wait until the next shift to assess the client's response
options.B: Reassess pain and function at a time appropriate to the medication's route and expected onset or peak, and evaluate for adverse effects
options.C: Reassess only if the client requests another dose because the original pain score already established the need for treatment
options.D: Use changes in heart rate and blood pressure instead of asking the client about pain because physiologic signs are more reliable than self-report

candidates.rationale: Evaluation is part of the nursing process. After a pain intervention, the nurse reassesses whether the intervention achieved the client's comfort and functional goals and whether adverse effects occurred. The timing should reflect the route and expected onset/peak rather than an arbitrary universal interval. Self-report remains central when the client can communicate.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Pain interventions require reassessment for effectiveness, with timing individualized to the medication route/onset/peak rather than one universal interval.

candidates.source_locator: Comfort — Evaluation: regularly evaluate intervention effectiveness; after analgesics reassess in about an hour or another time frame based on route, onset, and peak; follow up if ineffective

candidates.blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort — comfort measures, mobility and postoperative care
candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — postoperative pulmonary hygiene and comfort
candidates.educational_objective: Use pain control and coached pulmonary-hygiene measures to improve lung expansion and secretion clearance after surgery.

options.A: Encourage prescribed pain-control measures, then coach deep breathing and coughing while the client splints the incision as appropriate
options.B: Ask the client to avoid coughing and deep breathing until the incision is pain free so the wound is not stressed
options.C: Keep the client on strict bed rest because mobility and deeper respirations increase the risk of atelectasis
options.D: Use leg exercises as the primary intervention for lung expansion and secretion clearance

candidates.rationale: Postoperative pulmonary care includes adequate pain control plus deep breathing/coughing and other prescribed lung-expansion measures. Splinting can reduce incisional discomfort during coughing. These measures promote ventilation and secretion clearance and reduce atelectasis risk; they complement, rather than replace, mobilization and other prescribed prophylaxis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Postoperative respiratory care uses lung-expansion/secretion-clearance measures, with splinting and pain management supporting participation.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — health promotion, risk reduction and client education
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — tobacco cessation before surgery
candidates.educational_objective: Teach that preoperative smoking cessation reduces perioperative risk and should be encouraged before elective surgery and during recovery.

options.A: Quitting before surgery can reduce breathing and wound-healing complications, so stopping now and remaining smoke-free through recovery is beneficial
options.B: Smoking affects long-term health but has no meaningful relationship to postoperative respiratory or wound complications
options.C: It is better to continue smoking until after surgery because stopping beforehand increases surgical complications
options.D: Only clients with diagnosed chronic lung disease benefit from stopping smoking before surgery

candidates.rationale: Smoking increases perioperative pulmonary and wound-healing risk. The American College of Surgeons advises clients to quit before surgery and remain smoke-free during recovery; earlier cessation provides time for physiologic benefit.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Preoperative smoking cessation improves surgical recovery and reduces wound and respiratory risk.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — client education and risk reduction before procedures
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — preoperative fasting education
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients to follow individualized preanesthesia fasting instructions and report deviations because fasting requirements are not identical for every client.

options.A: I will follow the specific eating and drinking instructions from my surgical and anesthesia team and will tell them if I do not follow those instructions exactly
options.B: Everyone having anesthesia follows one identical fasting schedule, so my medications and medical conditions do not affect the plan
options.C: If I accidentally eat or drink outside the instructions, I should not mention it unless I develop nausea
options.D: Fasting instructions are mainly for convenience and do not affect aspiration risk during anesthesia or deep sedation

candidates.rationale: Preprocedure fasting reduces aspiration risk during anesthesia or deep sedation. Instructions can vary with intake, procedure, anesthesia plan, medications and conditions affecting gastric emptying. Clients should follow individualized instructions and disclose deviations so the anesthesia team can reassess safety.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Clients should follow their specific fasting instructions and disclose deviations because aspiration risk and the appropriate plan vary with clinical circumstances.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — preoperative optimization
candidates.educational_objective: Identify prehabilitation as proactive preoperative optimization of functional capacity and modifiable risks.

options.A: Begin individualized exercise and nutrition optimization before surgery, with other risk-reduction support such as smoking cessation or psychosocial preparation as indicated
options.B: Wait until a major postoperative functional decline occurs before starting exercise or nutrition interventions
options.C: Avoid activity before surgery so the client can conserve all physical capacity for the postoperative period
options.D: Use prehabilitation only as a substitute for postoperative rehabilitation and routine perioperative care

candidates.rationale: Prehabilitation aims to improve functional reserve before surgery. Programs may include exercise, nutrition optimization, psychological support, education and other modifiable-risk interventions. It complements rather than replaces routine perioperative and postoperative care.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Prehabilitation occurs before surgery and may include exercise, nutrition and other support to improve functional reserve.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication, coping and anxiety
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — preoperative anxiety and therapeutic communication
candidates.educational_objective: Use open-ended, individualized therapeutic communication to assess preoperative anxiety before providing support or facilitating further education.

options.A: There is nothing to worry about because anesthesia is safe, so try not to think about it
options.B: Tell me what concerns you most about the anesthesia so we can address the questions and support you before the procedure
options.C: It is better not to discuss anesthesia now because talking about risks will usually make anxiety worse
options.D: Everyone feels the same before surgery, so your anxiety does not require individual assessment

candidates.rationale: Therapeutic communication begins by inviting the client to describe the specific concern and by listening without minimizing or making guarantees. The nurse can then reinforce appropriate preoperative information, use calming/supportive strategies, and ensure questions requiring detailed anesthesia risk-benefit discussion are addressed by the anesthesia provider.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Preoperative nurses assess and address anxiety using active listening, empathy, therapeutic communication and appropriate education/support.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — coping mechanisms, anxiety reduction and therapeutic interventions
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — coping with preoperative anxiety
candidates.educational_objective: Support client-selected, low-risk nonpharmacologic coping strategies for preoperative anxiety.

options.A: Choose a relaxation strategy that fits you, such as slow breathing or listening to preferred calming music, and practice it while waiting
options.B: Try not to ask any more questions because information generally worsens preoperative anxiety
options.C: Suppress signs of fear so the surgical team will not think you are too anxious for the procedure
options.D: Avoid all coping activities until after surgery because preoperative relaxation has no role in anxiety management

candidates.rationale: Nonpharmacologic coping strategies can be individualized to client preference. Relaxation techniques such as slow breathing and preferred music may reduce preoperative anxiety, while accurate information and supportive communication can reduce uncertainty. The nurse should not encourage suppression, avoidance, or discourage questions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Preoperative anxiety coping can include individualized relaxation, breathing, music and information/support.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Management of Care — informed consent, client rights and advocacy
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — informed consent and decision-making capacity
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish emotional distress from impaired decision-making capacity during informed consent.

options.A: Assume the client lacks decision-making capacity because visible anxiety automatically invalidates consent
options.B: Provide emotional support, verify that the client's understanding and voluntary choice remain intact, and continue the consent process according to policy
options.C: Sign the consent form for the client because anxiety makes the client's own signature invalid
options.D: Ask a family member to make the decision even though the client demonstrates understanding and can communicate a voluntary choice

candidates.rationale: Anxiety or emotional distress can interfere with understanding and therefore deserves assessment and support, but anxiety alone does not establish incapacity. Decision-making capacity centers on the ability to understand relevant information, evaluate options, and communicate a voluntary decision. In this stem the client demonstrates those abilities, so the nurse should support the client and verify the process rather than substitute another decision-maker.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Emotional distress warrants assessment but does not itself revoke capacity when the client can understand, evaluate and communicate a voluntary decision.
candidates.source_document_title: Informed Consent — StatPearls
candidates.source_locator: Informed consent requires assessing understanding and voluntary decision-making; emotional distress may affect understanding; capacity involves understanding/retaining information, evaluating options and communicating a decision

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — acute confusion/delirium, cognitive changes and therapeutic management
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — postoperative delirium
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize hypoactive postoperative delirium and initiate appropriate screening and evaluation rather than relying on agitation as the defining sign.

options.A: Use a validated delirium screening approach and assess for reversible contributors because delirium can present with hypoactive, quiet symptoms
options.B: Document normal postoperative fatigue because delirium requires agitation or combativeness
options.C: Wait until hallucinations develop before assessing for delirium
options.D: Assume the change is permanent cognitive decline because delirium does not usually have an acute onset

candidates.rationale: Postoperative delirium is an acute change in mental status and may be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed. Hypoactive delirium can appear as withdrawal, lethargy, inattention, or altered level of consciousness and is easily missed. Older surgical adults should be screened with a validated approach and evaluated for contributing causes rather than waiting for agitation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Older postoperative clients may have hypoactive delirium without agitation and should be screened using validated tools.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — support systems, client preferences and coping
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — support-person involvement
candidates.educational_objective: Individualize family/support-person involvement according to the client's preferences, privacy needs and perioperative safety requirements.

options.A: Support each client's stated preference when clinically and operationally feasible, while protecting privacy and explaining any perioperative restrictions
options.B: Require family presence for both clients because support persons uniformly reduce anxiety in every surgical client
options.C: Exclude family for both clients because family presence has no psychosocial role in perioperative care
options.D: Allow family presence based only on the family's preference rather than the client's wishes

candidates.rationale: Perioperative psychosocial care is individualized. Family or other support persons may help some clients cope with anxiety, but not every client wants or benefits from the same arrangement. The nurse should center the capable adult client's preference, protect privacy, and follow clinical and facility restrictions rather than treating family presence as universally required or prohibited.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Perioperative nursing care and psychosocial support should be individualized to client preferences and values; family involvement is included when appropriate.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — adverse effects, contraindications and monitoring
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — anticoagulant renal safety
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize acute renal failure as a safety change requiring prompt dabigatran discontinuation review per labeling.

options.A: Continue the same dabigatran regimen because acute changes in renal function do not affect dabigatran exposure
options.B: Notify the prescribing clinician; current labeling directs discontinuation of dabigatran in acute renal failure and consideration of alternative anticoagulant therapy
options.C: Increase the dabigatran dose because renal failure lowers the medication's anticoagulant exposure
options.D: Use the INR alone to determine the routine dabigatran dose because INR is the preferred assay for dabigatran activity

candidates.rationale: Dabigatran exposure increases as renal function worsens. Current U.S. labeling directs assessment of renal function and discontinuation of dabigatran if acute renal failure develops, with alternative anticoagulation considered. INR is not the preferred assay for dabigatran activity.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Acute renal failure while taking dabigatran requires discontinuation and consideration of alternative anticoagulation.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — perioperative anticoagulant interruption
candidates.educational_objective: Verify perioperative apixaban interruption against current bleeding-risk guidance.

options.A: Question and clarify the plan because current U.S. labeling recommends stopping apixaban at least 48 hours before elective procedures with moderate or high clinically significant bleeding risk
options.B: Accept the plan because current apixaban labeling uses 24 hours for every elective procedure regardless of bleeding risk
options.C: Tell the client to stop apixaban permanently because any invasive procedure contraindicates future anticoagulation
options.D: Arrange routine heparin bridging for every client during the apixaban interruption because bridging is always required

candidates.rationale: Current apixaban labeling specifies at least 48 hours of interruption for moderate/high bleeding-risk elective procedures and at least 24 hours for low-risk procedures. Bridging during the short interruption is not generally required, and therapy is restarted once adequate hemostasis is established.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Apixaban interruption depends on procedural bleeding risk, with a 48-hour minimum for moderate/high-risk elective procedures.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — rivaroxaban administration
candidates.educational_objective: Teach the dose-specific food requirement for rivaroxaban 20 mg without incorrectly applying it to every rivaroxaban strength.

options.A: Take the 20 mg dose with food at approximately the same time each day because food improves absorption of this dose
options.B: Continue taking the 20 mg dose fasting because food substantially reduces rivaroxaban absorption
options.C: All rivaroxaban strengths must be taken fasting, so avoid meals for several hours after every dose
options.D: The relationship to food is unimportant for every rivaroxaban dose and indication

candidates.rationale: Current rivaroxaban labeling specifies that 15 mg and 20 mg tablets should be taken with food. For DVT/PE treatment, the 20 mg once-daily maintenance dose is taken with food at approximately the same time each day. Food increases exposure to the 20 mg dose; lower strengths such as 10 mg may be taken with or without food depending on the indication.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Rivaroxaban 20 mg requires administration with food for appropriate exposure; food requirements differ by dose.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — edoxaban renal-function limitation
candidates.educational_objective: Identify the edoxaban NVAF limitation in clients with CrCl greater than 95 mL/min and question an unsafe prescription.

options.A: Administer edoxaban as prescribed because higher creatinine clearance improves its stroke-prevention efficacy
options.B: Question the prescription because current U.S. labeling states edoxaban should not be used for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation when CrCl is greater than 95 mL/min
options.C: Reduce the edoxaban dose by half because every CrCl above 95 mL/min requires dose reduction rather than a different anticoagulant
options.D: Hold all anticoagulation permanently because a high CrCl is a contraindication to anticoagulant therapy in general

candidates.rationale: Edoxaban has a boxed limitation for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: it should not be used when creatinine clearance exceeds 95 mL/min because efficacy for prevention of ischemic stroke was reduced compared with warfarin in this group. Renal function therefore must be assessed before initiation. This restriction is specific to edoxaban use for NVAF and does not mean anticoagulation itself is contraindicated.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For NVAF, edoxaban should not be used when CrCl exceeds 95 mL/min; renal function must be assessed before therapy.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — dosage adjustment, anticoagulant monitoring and adverse-effect prevention
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — argatroban in hepatic impairment
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize hepatic impairment as a major argatroban dosing and monitoring consideration in HIT.

options.A: Question the order because hepatic impairment substantially reduces argatroban clearance and current labeling recommends a lower initial dose with close aPTT-guided titration
options.B: Administer the usual initial infusion because argatroban is eliminated primarily by the kidneys and hepatic impairment does not affect exposure
options.C: Replace argatroban with unfractionated heparin because heparin is preferred when HIT has already been diagnosed
options.D: Administer argatroban without coagulation monitoring because direct thrombin inhibitors do not require laboratory titration in HIT

candidates.rationale: Argatroban is an approved nonheparin anticoagulant for adult HIT. In moderate or severe hepatic impairment, clearance is markedly reduced and current labeling recommends a lower initial infusion with careful aPTT monitoring and titration. For HIT, aPTT is used to monitor therapy. Heparin should not be restarted simply because hepatic impairment is present.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Argatroban is indicated for adult HIT; hepatic impairment requires lower starting dose and careful aPTT titration.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — fondaparinux renal safety
candidates.educational_objective: Identify severe renal impairment as a contraindication to fondaparinux for VTE prophylaxis/treatment.

options.A: Administer the medication because renal function does not materially affect fondaparinux clearance
options.B: Question the order because fondaparinux is contraindicated for VTE prophylaxis or treatment when CrCl is less than 30 mL/min
options.C: Administer the medication intramuscularly to reduce accumulation in renal impairment
options.D: Double the dose because severe renal impairment reduces the anticoagulant effect of fondaparinux

candidates.rationale: Fondaparinux is substantially eliminated by the kidneys. Current labeling contraindicates VTE prophylaxis/treatment when CrCl is below 30 mL/min because reduced clearance increases anticoagulant exposure and bleeding risk. It is given subcutaneously, not intramuscularly.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Fondaparinux is contraindicated for VTE prophylaxis/treatment when CrCl is less than 30 mL/min.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — enoxaparin reversal
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that protamine provides incomplete reversal of enoxaparin and requires continued bleeding and adverse-reaction monitoring.

options.A: Protamine completely neutralizes all enoxaparin anti-factor Xa activity, so further bleeding assessment is unnecessary
options.B: Enoxaparin reversal is incomplete; anti-factor Xa activity may persist, so the nurse must continue assessing bleeding and the client's response while also watching for protamine reactions
options.C: Protamine has no clinically meaningful effect on enoxaparin and therefore should never be used for enoxaparin-associated bleeding
options.D: Once protamine is started, severe hypotension or anaphylactoid reactions are no longer relevant safety concerns

candidates.rationale: Protamine can largely neutralize enoxaparin, but current labeling states that anti-factor Xa activity is never completely neutralized and reaches only about 60% maximal neutralization. Ongoing bleeding assessment remains necessary. Protamine itself can cause severe hypotension and anaphylactoid reactions, so administration requires appropriate monitoring and resuscitation capability.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Protamine incompletely reverses enoxaparin anti-Xa activity and carries important infusion-reaction risk.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — warfarin pharmacogenetics and INR monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Explain the limited but useful role of warfarin pharmacogenetic information while preserving the requirement for INR-guided dosing.

options.A: Genotype information can help inform the initial warfarin dose, but the dose still must be individualized and adjusted using INR monitoring and clinical factors
options.B: That is correct; once CYP2C9 and VKORC1 are known, INR monitoring is no longer necessary
options.C: Genetic results are used only to determine blood type and have no relationship to warfarin dosing
options.D: Genotype results determine a fixed lifelong dose that should not be changed for medications, diet, illness, or INR results

candidates.rationale: Warfarin dose requirements vary with clinical and genetic factors. Current labeling states that known CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes may be considered when choosing the initial dose, but therapy still requires close INR monitoring and subsequent individualized dose adjustment. Genotype does not define a fixed dose or replace monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CYP2C9/VKORC1 information can inform initial warfarin dosing but does not replace INR-guided individualized therapy.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication administration and client education
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — LMWH self-administration
candidates.educational_objective: Teach evidence-based enoxaparin prefilled-syringe self-injection technique.

options.A: Expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe before injecting so no air enters the subcutaneous tissue
options.B: Inject deeply into a skin fold of the abdomen, alternate sites, and avoid rubbing the site after the injection
options.C: Give the medication intramuscularly in the deltoid because muscle absorption is more predictable
options.D: Use the same abdominal site each day to reduce variation in anticoagulant effect

candidates.rationale: Current enoxaparin labeling instructs subcutaneous administration into an abdominal skin fold, alternation of injection sites, and no rubbing after injection to reduce bruising. The air bubble in a prefilled syringe should not be expelled because doing so can cause loss of medication. Intramuscular administration is not recommended.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Enoxaparin self-injection technique includes deep subcutaneous abdominal administration, site rotation, retention of the prefilled-syringe air bubble and no rubbing afterward.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication monitoring and client education
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — DOAC monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish the absence of routine coagulation-test titration for apixaban from the need for ongoing clinical safety follow-up.

options.A: Apixaban is not routinely titrated with PT, INR, or aPTT because these tests do not reliably measure its anticoagulant effect, but you still need clinical follow-up for bleeding risk, medication interactions, and organ function as indicated
options.B: That is correct; apixaban requires no clinical or laboratory follow-up once the first dose is taken
options.C: You should obtain a daily INR and adjust the apixaban dose to the same therapeutic INR range used for warfarin
options.D: Routine aPTT is the preferred test for adjusting every apixaban dose

candidates.rationale: Apixaban has predictable dosing and is not routinely adjusted using PT, INR, or aPTT; labeling notes that changes in these tests are small, variable, and not useful for monitoring its anticoagulant effect. This does not eliminate the need to assess for bleeding, interacting medications, adherence, and renal or hepatic changes when clinically indicated.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — C. difficile contact precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Apply current CDC duration guidance for C. difficile contact precautions and question premature discontinuation.

options.A: Clarify the plan because CDC recommends maintaining contact precautions for at least 48 hours after diarrhea resolves, and facilities may continue them longer through hospitalization
options.B: Discontinue precautions immediately because C. difficile precautions end with the first formed stool
options.C: Continue precautions for life because a prior C. difficile infection permanently requires isolation
options.D: Use contact precautions only during toileting because transmission does not occur from the client's environment

candidates.rationale: CDC acute-care guidance updated in May 2026 recommends maintaining contact precautions for confirmed C. difficile infection for at least 48 hours after diarrhea has resolved, with longer continuation up to the duration of hospitalization in some settings. C. difficile spores can contaminate the environment, so precautions are not limited to toileting encounters.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — VRE/MDRO precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Apply setting-specific CDC precautions for known VRE colonization in an acute-care hospital.

options.A: Use Standard Precautions plus Contact Precautions for the known target-MDRO colonization according to the hospital's infection-control program
options.B: Use Airborne Precautions because VRE is primarily transmitted through airborne droplet nuclei
options.C: Use no precautions because colonization cannot contribute to healthcare transmission
options.D: Use Droplet Precautions alone and omit Standard Precautions

candidates.rationale: CDC MDRO guidance for acute-care hospitals recommends routine Contact Precautions for patients infected with target MDROs and for patients previously identified as colonized, while Standard Precautions remain foundational. VRE is transmitted mainly through direct or indirect contact, including contaminated environmental surfaces and equipment, not through the airborne route.
candidates.source_claim_supported: In acute-care hospitals, known colonization with a target MDRO such as VRE calls for Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions under CDC guidance.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — CRE containment
candidates.educational_objective: Apply current CRE infection-control and interfacility communication practices to prevent transmission.

options.A: Maintain Isolation and Contact Precautions and ensure the receiving facility is notified of the client's CRE colonization status
options.B: Discontinue transmission-based precautions because colonized clients cannot transmit CRE
options.C: Use Airborne Precautions because CRE is primarily spread by airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: Withhold the CRE information from the receiving facility unless the client develops a symptomatic infection

candidates.rationale: Current CDC CRE guidance recommends Isolation and Contact Precautions in acute-care settings and emphasizes communication of CRE infection or colonization status during interfacility transfer. Colonized clients can contribute to transmission, and CRE spreads mainly through contact with contaminated hands, wounds, stool, equipment, or the healthcare environment rather than the airborne route.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Acute-care CRE colonization requires targeted contact-based precautions and communication during transfer.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — S. aureus decolonization
candidates.educational_objective: Explain the purpose and limits of targeted S. aureus nasal decolonization in high-risk surgical care.

options.A: The protocol reduces S. aureus carriage at common body sites and is used to lower infection risk in selected high-risk settings; it does not replace standard infection-prevention measures
options.B: The protocol cures any bloodstream or deep surgical infection that may already be present without systemic treatment
options.C: Every person colonized with MRSA should receive mupirocin indefinitely regardless of clinical setting or resistance concerns
options.D: Once decolonization is started, hand hygiene and other perioperative infection-control practices are no longer necessary

candidates.rationale: CDC recommends targeted S. aureus decolonization/pathogen-reduction strategies in selected high-risk settings, including certain surgical populations. Intranasal mupirocin or another nasal antistaphylococcal agent is commonly paired with chlorhexidine cleansing to reduce carriage and infection risk. It is not universal indefinite therapy, does not treat established invasive infection by itself, and does not replace core infection-control practices.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Targeted nasal decolonization can reduce S. aureus carriage/infection risk in selected high-risk surgical settings but is not universal or a substitute for infection-control practices.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — SSI surveillance
candidates.educational_objective: Apply current NHSN surveillance rules when a surgical-site infection progresses to a deeper tissue level during the surveillance period.

options.A: Keep the original superficial-incisional classification because the first classification can never be changed
options.B: Edit the event to reflect the deepest tissue level that meets SSI criteria—deep incisional in this case—and update the event date according to NHSN instructions
options.C: Automatically classify the event as organ/space because any progression beyond superficial tissue is organ/space infection
options.D: Remove the event from NHSN surveillance because an SSI that changes tissue level is no longer reportable

candidates.rationale: NHSN requires the entire SSI protocol to be followed. If a superficial-incisional SSI progresses and meets criteria at a deeper tissue level during the designated surveillance period, the event type and date are edited to reflect the deepest tissue level where SSI criteria are met. Deep-incisional and organ/space definitions are distinct; progression does not automatically make an event organ/space.
candidates.source_claim_supported: NHSN SSI classification is a surveillance/reporting framework and requires updating the event to the deepest tissue level meeting criteria during the surveillance period.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — central-line necessity review
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize prompt removal of a no-longer-needed central venous catheter as a key CLABSI-prevention strategy distinct from insertion-bundle elements.

options.A: Promptly communicate that the catheter is no longer necessary and facilitate removal according to the care plan and facility process
options.B: Leave the catheter in place indefinitely because infection risk does not increase with unnecessary catheter days
options.C: Replace the catheter routinely with a new central line solely to prevent infection, even though central access is no longer needed
options.D: Keep the catheter until discharge because insertion-site care eliminates the infection risk of an unnecessary line

candidates.rationale: Central-line infection prevention includes both safe insertion and limiting unnecessary catheter exposure. CDC guidance emphasizes appropriate site selection, maximal sterile barrier precautions and chlorhexidine skin preparation during insertion, and prompt removal of central catheters that are no longer essential. Routine replacement solely to prevent infection is not recommended.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Prompt removal of unnecessary central catheters reduces exposure risk and is part of comprehensive CLABSI prevention; insertion and maintenance measures are distinct components.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand-hygiene monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret electronic hand-hygiene monitoring as a quality-improvement tool with useful reach but important measurement limitations.

options.A: Use the system to broaden monitoring and identify adherence patterns, but interpret its data with knowledge of what behaviors the system can and cannot detect and validate findings with other methods when needed
options.B: Treat electronic compliance percentages as a perfect measure of every CDC hand-hygiene indication and of the quality of hand-cleaning technique
options.C: Stop all other auditing or feedback because electronic monitoring eliminates measurement limitations and observer bias completely
options.D: Assume a detected dispenser activation proves that hand hygiene occurred at every clinically indicated moment and was performed correctly

candidates.rationale: Electronic monitoring can expand the volume and continuity of adherence data and may reduce some limitations of episodic direct observation. However, monitoring systems differ in what they detect and may not capture every clinical indication, technique quality, or context. Infection-prevention programs should use standardized monitoring, understand method limitations, validate data, and provide feedback rather than treating any single metric as perfect ground truth.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Electronic monitoring can support hand-hygiene quality improvement, but monitoring methods require validation and should not be treated as flawless measurement of all hand-hygiene behavior.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — discontinuing isolation precautions
candidates.educational_objective: Use pathogen-specific CDC duration criteria when deciding when Transmission-Based Precautions can be discontinued.

options.A: Use the organism- or condition-specific duration criteria in current CDC guidance and applicable facility or public-health requirements rather than applying one fixed isolation period to every infection
options.B: Discontinue precautions after the same 24-hour period for every infectious diagnosis regardless of transmission risk
options.C: Require negative cultures for every infectious disease before any Transmission-Based Precautions can be stopped
options.D: Continue all Transmission-Based Precautions indefinitely because infectious shedding cannot be estimated clinically

candidates.rationale: CDC states that Transmission-Based Precautions remain in effect while transmission risk persists or for the recommended duration of illness, and Appendix A provides disease-specific type and duration guidance. Some conditions use a defined treatment interval, others the duration of illness, and selected infections use microbiologic clearance or additional jurisdictional criteria. No single time or universal negative-test rule applies to all pathogens.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — HIPAA record amendment rights
candidates.educational_objective: Protect client rights by recognizing the HIPAA right to request amendment of inaccurate or incomplete health information and using the formal record-correction process.

options.A: Explain that the client has the right to request an amendment or correction through the covered entity's process and help route the request appropriately rather than independently deleting the existing record
options.B: Delete the entry immediately and remove any trace of the original documentation because HIPAA requires records to be rewritten when a client disagrees
options.C: Tell the client that HIPAA gives no right to request correction of inaccurate or incomplete health information
options.D: Advise the client to wait until a lawsuit is filed because medical-record corrections can be requested only during legal proceedings

candidates.rationale: The HIPAA Privacy Rule gives individuals the right to request amendment of protected health information in a designated record set. A covered entity must have a process to receive and act on the request; it may grant or deny the amendment under specified conditions and, if denied, the individual may submit a statement of disagreement. The bedside nurse should facilitate the formal process rather than erase or rewrite the existing record outside authorized documentation procedures.
candidates.source_claim_supported: HIPAA gives individuals a federal right to request amendment of designated-record-set PHI; amendment follows a formal covered-entity process rather than ad hoc deletion.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — EMTALA emergency access
candidates.educational_objective: Protect emergency-care access by applying EMTALA requirements for medical screening, stabilization, and non-delayed care regardless of ability to pay.

options.A: Ensure the client receives an appropriate medical screening examination without delaying it for payment or insurance issues, and proceed with stabilization or appropriate transfer if an emergency medical condition is identified
options.B: Delay the medical screening examination until the client provides proof of insurance or pays a deposit
options.C: Direct the client to an outpatient clinic solely because the client is uninsured, without an emergency medical screening examination
options.D: Explain that EMTALA protections apply only to Medicare beneficiaries rather than to all individuals who present for emergency evaluation

candidates.rationale: EMTALA requires Medicare-participating hospitals with emergency services to provide an appropriate medical screening examination when an individual presents requesting examination or treatment for a possible emergency medical condition, regardless of insurance status or ability to pay. If an emergency medical condition exists, the hospital must provide stabilizing treatment within its capability or an appropriate transfer. Insurance questions may be asked only if they do not delay examination or treatment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: EMTALA creates federal emergency screening/stabilization obligations independent of insurance or ability to pay for individuals presenting to covered hospital emergency departments.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — protected workplace-safety reporting
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize federal anti-retaliation protection for employees who engage in protected workplace-safety reporting under OSH Act Section 11(c).

options.A: Section 11(c) of the OSH Act prohibits retaliation for protected workplace-safety activities such as raising safety concerns or filing an OSHA complaint, and a worker who experiences retaliation should contact OSHA promptly
options.B: Employers may discipline workers solely for filing a workplace-safety complaint because reporting hazards is not a protected activity
options.C: OSHA whistleblower protections guarantee a promotion or financial reward whenever a worker reports a hazard
options.D: Section 11(c) protects only physicians and does not apply to other covered employees such as nurses

candidates.rationale: OSHA states that Section 11(c) of the Occupational Safety and Health Act prohibits retaliation against employees for exercising protected workplace-safety rights, including raising safety concerns with an employer, filing a safety and health complaint with OSHA, participating in an OSHA inspection, or reporting a work-related injury or illness. A worker who believes retaliation occurred should contact OSHA promptly because filing deadlines apply. Protection does not guarantee a reward or immunity from legitimate nonretaliatory employment actions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Covered employees are protected from employer retaliation for specified workplace-safety activities under OSH Act Section 11(c); retaliation complaints are subject to filing requirements.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — reporting suspected abuse in long-term care
candidates.educational_objective: Respond to suspected resident abuse in a federally certified nursing facility by protecting the resident and initiating required reporting without delaying for independent proof.

options.A: Report the allegation immediately through the facility's required process and to the officials specified by federal and applicable state requirements rather than waiting to prove that abuse occurred
options.B: Wait until the nurse personally completes a full investigation and obtains definitive proof before any report is made
options.C: Document the observation only in the resident's record and take no further reporting action
options.D: Confront the staff member privately and keep the incident within the unit unless the resident later develops an injury

candidates.rationale: Federal long-term-care requirements at 42 CFR 483.12 require facilities to protect residents from abuse and to ensure alleged violations involving abuse, neglect, exploitation, mistreatment, or misappropriation are reported promptly to required facility and governmental officials. Reporting is triggered by an allegation; staff should not delay required reporting while attempting to prove the case independently. The facility must also investigate and protect the resident while the allegation is addressed.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Federally certified nursing facilities must promptly report allegations of abuse and protect residents; reporting cannot be postponed until staff independently prove the allegation.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — client rights, privacy/confidentiality, and appropriate handling of protected health information
candidates.educational_objective: Protect client confidentiality by declining curiosity-driven requests for PHI from workforce members who lack a legitimate job-related need; same-employer status or system access does not itself authorize disclosure.

options.A: Share the diagnosis because both nurses are members of the same hospital workforce.
options.B: Share only the diagnosis because limiting the disclosure to one fact satisfies the minimum-necessary standard.
options.C: Share the diagnosis after confirming that the other nurse has active access credentials for the electronic health record.
options.D: Decline to disclose the diagnosis because the request has no legitimate job-related purpose.

candidates.rationale: D is correct. The HIPAA Privacy Rule requires covered entities to use role-based policies that limit workforce access to protected health information (PHI) to persons who need the information to perform their job duties, and the minimum-necessary standard generally limits uses, disclosures, and requests to what is reasonably necessary for the permitted purpose. A curiosity-driven request from a workforce member who is not involved in the client’s care does not become appropriate merely because the requester works for the same hospital, asks for only one fact, or has active system credentials. Disclosures to or requests by a health care provider for treatment are exempt from the minimum-necessary standard, but this scenario expressly involves curiosity rather than a treatment purpose. Therefore A, B, and C do not establish a legitimate basis for disclosure.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Covered entities must limit workforce access to PHI according to job duties and apply the minimum-necessary standard where required; treatment-purpose disclosures/requests are an explicit exception, which does not convert a curiosity request into a treatment purpose.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — client rights and access to health information
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that HIPAA generally gives individuals access to PHI in designated record sets and, when PHI is maintained electronically, a right to an electronic copy in a readily producible requested format, subject to limited denial grounds.

options.A: The hospital may provide only a paper copy whenever paper is easier for staff to produce.
options.B: The client generally may receive an electronic copy in a requested readily producible format, subject to limited grounds for denial.
options.C: The client must explain why the records are needed before an electronic copy can be released.
options.D: Electronic access is optional under HIPAA and depends entirely on the hospital’s internal policy.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. Under 45 CFR §164.524, individuals generally have a right to access PHI about themselves in a designated record set. When the PHI is maintained electronically, the individual generally has a right to an electronic copy; if the requested electronic form and format are readily producible, the covered entity must provide that form and format, and otherwise must provide a readable alternative electronic format agreed to by the individual and covered entity, subject to the limited grounds for denial in §164.524(a). A is incorrect because a covered entity generally cannot substitute paper merely because it is easier when an electronic copy is required and a readily producible electronic format is available. C is incorrect because an individual is not required to state a purpose for exercising the right of access. D is incorrect because the access right arises from HIPAA and is not left entirely to facility discretion.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Individuals generally have a right to access PHI in designated record sets; if PHI is maintained electronically, they generally have a right to an electronic copy in the requested readily producible form and format, or an agreed readable alternative electronic format, subject to limited denial grounds.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — legal accountability and secure handling of controlled-substance prescribing credentials
candidates.educational_objective: Protect the integrity of controlled-substance prescribing by refusing to use or enter a prescriber’s EPCS authentication factor; the prescribing practitioner must personally complete the required authentication and electronic signature.

options.A: Enter the authentication factor after the prescriber verbally confirms the medication order.
options.B: Enter the authentication factor if the nurse first verifies the medication and dose on the screen.
options.C: Decline and have the prescribing practitioner personally complete the required authentication and electronic signature.
options.D: Ask a second licensed nurse to enter the authentication factor so two nurses verify the prescription.

candidates.rationale: C is correct. DEA’s Electronic Prescriptions for Controlled Substances (EPCS) requirements make the prescribing practitioner’s two-factor authentication credential the practitioner’s legal electronic signature. DEA states that the practitioner must retain control of the authentication factors, must not share a password or other knowledge factor, and must not allow another person to use the token or enter the practitioner’s identification means to sign controlled-substance prescriptions. Verbal confirmation of the order, nurse verification of the medication, or use of a second nurse does not authorize another person to complete the prescriber’s authentication. The prescriber must personally perform the required authentication and signature.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For EPCS, the prescribing practitioner must personally use the required authentication credential to legally sign the controlled-substance prescription and may not allow another person to use or enter the practitioner’s authentication factors.

candidates.educational_objective: Report clinically meaningful near misses through the organization’s safety-event system so system contributors can be identified and corrected before a similar event causes harm.

options.A: Submit a near-miss report so the event can be analyzed for contributing system vulnerabilities.
options.B: Do not report the event because the incorrect dose never reached the client.
options.C: Record that a medication error harmed the client and take no further reporting action.
options.D: Request disciplinary action against the dispensing staff member before submitting any report.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AHRQ identifies near misses as patient-safety events worth reporting and describes effective reporting systems as supportive, systems-oriented, responsive, and focused on learning. Reporting an intercepted tenfold-dose error allows the organization to examine contributing processes before a similar event reaches a client. B is incorrect because the absence of harm does not eliminate the safety value of reporting a near miss. C is incorrect because no incorrect dose reached or harmed the client, and clinical documentation should not falsely state that harm occurred. D is incorrect because beginning with individual punishment can suppress reporting and bypass analysis of system contributors; a just culture can still address unsafe or reckless behavior separately when warranted.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Near misses are valid patient-safety events for reporting; supportive, systems-oriented reporting enables learning from events and identification of latent safety problems rather than limiting reporting to events that caused harm.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — right-sided heart failure and systemic venous congestion
candidates.educational_objective: Link jugular venous distention, dependent edema, and abdominal congestion in right-sided heart failure to impaired right-ventricular forward flow and systemic venous backup.

options.A: Systemic venous blood backs up because the right ventricle cannot move blood forward effectively.
options.B: Left atrial pressure rises and forces fluid primarily into the pulmonary alveoli.
options.C: Acute bronchial smooth-muscle constriction traps air in the distal airways.
options.D: Loss of plasma protein in the urine lowers oncotic pressure as the primary problem.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. In right-sided heart failure, impaired right-ventricular pumping causes blood returning from the body to back up in the systemic venous circulation. The resulting venous congestion contributes to jugular venous distention and fluid accumulation in dependent tissues and the abdomen. B describes the pulmonary-congestion mechanism more characteristic of left-sided failure. C describes obstructive airway physiology and does not explain systemic venous distention. D can cause generalized edema in nephrotic states but does not explain the right-heart-failure pattern of jugular venous congestion in this stem.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Right-sided heart failure causes systemic venous backup and congestion, producing findings such as peripheral/abdominal edema; venous congestion is mechanistically distinct from pulmonary alveolar congestion caused by elevated left-sided filling pressures.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpreting serial laboratory trends during hemorrhagic shock resuscitation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a worsening base deficit after traumatic hemorrhage as a nonspecific sign that may indicate persistent metabolic acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion, requiring reassessment alongside other perfusion and bleeding data.

options.A: It supports concern for persistent tissue hypoperfusion and should prompt reassessment of bleeding and resuscitation response.
options.B: It primarily reflects hyperglycemia and should be interpreted as a marker of inadequate glucose control.
options.C: It specifically demonstrates acute kidney injury and can be used independently of the overall clinical picture.
options.D: It indicates improved perfusion because a larger base deficit reflects correction of metabolic acidosis.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Base deficit derived from blood-gas analysis is an indirect marker of global metabolic acidosis and can reflect impaired tissue perfusion in traumatic hemorrhage when other causes of metabolic acidosis are not present. A worsening trend should therefore increase concern for persistent hypoperfusion and be interpreted together with the client’s overall clinical status and response to resuscitation. B is incorrect because base deficit is not a measure of blood glucose. C is incorrect because base deficit is nonspecific and does not independently diagnose acute kidney injury. D reverses the physiologic meaning: a larger base deficit corresponds to more, not less, metabolic acidosis. Current trauma guidance notes that lactate is the preferred sensitive test for estimating bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion when available, with base deficit serving as a suitable alternative.
candidates.source_claim_supported: In bleeding trauma, base deficit is a nonspecific indirect marker of global metabolic acidosis due to impaired perfusion and can be used to help estimate/monitor shock when interpreted in context and when other causes of acidosis are considered.
candidates.source_document_title: The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition
candidates.source_locator: Recommendation 10 and rationale, ‘Blood lactate and base deficit’ — lactate recommended to estimate/monitor bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion; base deficit suitable when lactate unavailable; base deficit provides an indirect estimate of global tissue acidosis due to impaired perfusion when other causes such as renal failure or hyperchloremia are absent; negative base excess is termed base deficit

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — serial troponin interpretation in suspected acute coronary syndrome
candidates.educational_objective: Do not use a single non-elevated high-sensitivity troponin obtained very early after symptom onset to rule out myocardial infarction; continue serial troponin assessment and clinical/ECG evaluation using a validated chest-pain pathway.

options.A: The single early troponin result excludes acute myocardial infarction, so further cardiac evaluation is unnecessary.
options.B: The client should continue the acute coronary syndrome evaluation, including serial high-sensitivity troponin testing according to the facility’s validated clinical pathway.
options.C: A normal initial troponin establishes a noncardiac cause of the chest pressure even if symptoms persist.
options.D: Troponin testing has little role in acute chest-pain evaluation unless ST-segment elevation is already present on the ECG.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is the preferred biomarker for myocardial injury, but interpretation depends on symptom timing, the assay, serial change, ECG findings, and the overall clinical picture. Rapid rule-out strategies can be unreliable in very early presenters because troponin may not yet have risen; therefore an initial non-elevated result obtained about 1 hour after symptom onset does not by itself exclude myocardial infarction. A and C incorrectly treat one early value as definitive. D is incorrect because serial high-sensitivity troponin is central to evaluating suspected acute coronary syndrome even when ST-segment elevation is absent.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A single non-elevated high-sensitivity troponin obtained very early after symptom onset cannot independently exclude acute MI; serial hs-cTn testing integrated with timing, ECG, and clinical assessment is the recommended approach in suspected ACS.
candidates.source_document_title: 2021 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain; 2022 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Acute Chest Pain
candidates.source_locator: 2021 Chest Pain Guideline Perspectives — serial assessment of cardiac troponin I or T is the preferred biomarker strategy and high-sensitivity cTn is preferred; 2022 ACC Expert Consensus key points — serial hs-cTn measurements are essential for MI confirmation and rapid hs-cTn algorithms can fail in very early presenters; interpretation depends on symptom onset and clinical data

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — lactate interpretation and occult hypoperfusion after trauma
candidates.educational_objective: Use elevated and serial lactate values as adjuncts to detect and monitor tissue hypoperfusion in trauma, recognizing that apparently reassuring vital signs do not reliably exclude occult shock.

options.A: The near-baseline vital signs exclude clinically important tissue hypoperfusion.
options.B: The elevated lactate supports concern for occult tissue hypoperfusion and should be trended with the client’s clinical response to resuscitation.
options.C: The elevated lactate specifically identifies acute kidney injury as the cause of the abnormal result.
options.D: The lactate value can be ignored because trauma-related shock is assessed reliably by blood pressure and heart rate alone.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. In traumatic hemorrhage, blood lactate is a sensitive marker used to estimate and monitor the extent of bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion. Vital signs may not reliably reflect injury severity, particularly in penetrating trauma, so an elevated lactate despite near-baseline blood pressure and heart rate can support concern for occult hypoperfusion. Serial lactate values can also help evaluate response to therapy. Lactate is not specific to one cause, so it must be interpreted with the overall clinical picture. A and D incorrectly treat vital signs as sufficient to exclude shock, and C incorrectly assigns a nonspecific biomarker to a single diagnosis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: In bleeding trauma, lactate is a sensitive adjunct for estimating and monitoring tissue hypoperfusion, and can reveal occult hypoperfusion when routine vital signs appear relatively reassuring; serial values should be interpreted with the clinical context.
candidates.source_document_title: The European guideline on management of major bleeding and coagulopathy following trauma: sixth edition
candidates.source_locator: Recommendation 10 and rationale, ‘Blood lactate and base deficit’ — blood lactate is recommended as a sensitive test to estimate/monitor bleeding and tissue hypoperfusion; serial measurements help evaluate response; lactate may be particularly important in penetrating trauma because blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate do not reliably reflect injury severity

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — hemoglobin interpretation and restrictive red-blood-cell transfusion practice
candidates.educational_objective: Apply a restrictive red-blood-cell transfusion strategy in hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, using hemoglobin together with symptoms and clinical context rather than transfusing simply to normalize the laboratory value.

options.A: A transfusion is routinely indicated because any hemoglobin value below the normal reference range requires red blood cells.
options.B: A restrictive strategy is appropriate; this hemoglobin value alone does not automatically require transfusion, and the overall clinical context should guide the decision.
options.C: Transfusion should be given until the hemoglobin returns to the normal range for a healthy adult.
options.D: Hemoglobin concentration should not be considered when clinicians decide whether red-blood-cell transfusion is appropriate.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. The 2023 AABB international guideline recommends a restrictive red-blood-cell transfusion strategy for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, considering transfusion when hemoglobin is less than 7 g/dL for most such adults. It also emphasizes the overall clinical context, signs and symptoms, patient preferences, and alternatives to transfusion. Therefore, an asymptomatic, stable medical client with a hemoglobin of 7.4 g/dL does not require transfusion solely because the value is below the normal reference range. A and C incorrectly use the normal hemoglobin range as a transfusion target. D is incorrect because hemoglobin is an important component of the decision, although it is not the only factor. Different thresholds may be selected for specific populations such as cardiac surgery, orthopedic surgery, or preexisting cardiovascular disease.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, AABB recommends a restrictive RBC-transfusion strategy, generally considering transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL while individualizing the decision to symptoms and clinical context; selected populations may use different restrictive thresholds.
candidates.source_document_title: Red Blood Cell Transfusion: 2023 AABB International Guidelines
candidates.source_locator: Recommendation 1 / PubMed abstract — for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, recommend a restrictive strategy and consider transfusion when hemoglobin is <7 g/dL; thresholds of 7.5 g/dL may be selected for cardiac surgery and 8 g/dL for orthopedic surgery or preexisting cardiovascular disease; Conclusions — consider overall clinical context and alternatives
