candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — safe management of a chest-tube drainage system
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain a closed chest-tube drainage system upright and below chest level, with unobstructed tubing, to support safe drainage and reduce the risk of backflow or impaired evacuation.

options.A: Move the drainage unit to an upright position below the level of the client’s chest and ensure the tubing can drain without obstruction.
options.B: Leave the drainage unit on the bed because its height does not affect drainage as long as the tubing remains connected.
options.C: Clamp the chest tube routinely before moving the drainage unit to prevent air from entering the pleural space.
options.D: Raise the drainage unit above chest level so gravity prevents excessive pleural fluid loss.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. A closed chest-tube drainage system should be maintained upright and below the level of the client’s chest to facilitate gravity drainage and help prevent fluid from flowing back toward the pleural space. The nurse should also keep the tubing positioned so drainage is not obstructed. B and D place the system at an inappropriate height. C is incorrect because routine clamping is not required simply to reposition the drainage unit and can obstruct the intended evacuation pathway; chest-tube handling should follow the specific drainage-system instructions and agency policy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Closed chest-tube drainage systems should be kept upright and below the client’s chest to facilitate drainage, with safe system management following the device manufacturer’s directions and agency policy.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Advanced Skills — Chapter 6: Manage Chest Tube Drainage Systems
candidates.source_locator: Chapter 6, section 6.2 ‘Basic Concepts,’ Closed Chest Tube Drainage System: drainage system must be maintained upright below the patient’s chest to facilitate drainage; section also directs nurses to follow agency policy and manufacturer directions for setup, monitoring, and use

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — tracheostomy emergency equipment and airway preparedness
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain immediate tracheostomy emergency readiness by ensuring same-size and smaller spare tubes, functioning suction, and equipment for oxygenation/manual ventilation are available before an airway emergency occurs.

options.A: A spare tracheostomy tube of the same size only, with routine oxygen equipment available elsewhere on the unit
options.B: A spare tracheostomy tube one size larger, with suction requested only if secretions become difficult to clear
options.C: Spare tracheostomy tubes of the same size and one size smaller, functioning suction, and immediately available equipment for oxygenation and manual ventilation
options.D: Standard nasal cannula supplies only because airway emergencies should be managed through the upper airway rather than the tracheostomy

candidates.rationale: C is correct. Adult tracheostomy emergency guidance emphasizes having essential airway equipment immediately available with the client. At minimum, spare tracheostomy tubes of the same size and one size smaller should be at the bedside, and functioning suction must be available. Equipment for oxygenation and manual ventilation must also be immediately accessible because obstruction or displacement can rapidly compromise ventilation. A is incomplete because a smaller backup tube and airway-rescue equipment are needed. B is incorrect because a larger tube is not the recommended backup and suction should be ready before an emergency occurs. D is unsafe because emergency oxygenation may need to be delivered through the face, the stoma, or both depending on the airway anatomy and problem.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For an adult with a tracheostomy, emergency preparedness includes same-size and one-size-smaller spare tracheostomy tubes at bedside, suction, and immediately available airway/oxygenation equipment so obstruction or displacement can be managed without delay.
candidates.source_document_title: Emergency Care (Adults) — Essential Emergency Equipment; Basic Care (Adults) — Kit Checklist and Daily Checks

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — aseptic central-venous-catheter dressing care
candidates.client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
candidates.educational_objective: For central-line dressing changes, maintain aseptic technique with hand hygiene, appropriate skin antisepsis, and a sterile dressing; do not assume sterile gloves or maximal sterile barrier precautions are universally required for every routine dressing change.

options.A: Perform hand hygiene, maintain aseptic technique, cleanse the site with an appropriate antiseptic, and apply a sterile catheter-site dressing; either clean or sterile gloves may be used for the dressing change.
options.B: Use clean technique without attention to asepsis because the central catheter was inserted under sterile conditions.
options.C: Wear sterile gloves, but omit skin antisepsis if the insertion site has no redness or drainage.
options.D: Use maximal sterile barrier precautions with cap, sterile gown, full-body drape, and sterile gloves for every routine dressing change.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends hand hygiene before and after dressing an intravascular catheter, maintenance of aseptic technique during catheter care, skin antisepsis during dressing changes, and use of a sterile gauze or sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. For routine intravascular-catheter dressing changes, CDC states that either clean or sterile gloves may be worn. B is incorrect because aseptic technique remains necessary during catheter care. C is incorrect because skin antisepsis is part of dressing-change care even when the site appears normal. D confuses routine dressing changes with central-line insertion, for which maximal sterile barrier precautions are recommended.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC requires hand hygiene and aseptic catheter care, appropriate antiseptic skin preparation during central-line dressing changes, and a sterile catheter-site dressing; either clean or sterile gloves may be used for routine intravascular-catheter dressing changes, whereas maximal sterile barrier precautions apply to central-line insertion rather than routine dressing changes.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — postoperative abdominal support, comfort, mobility, and realistic client teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that postoperative abdominal binders may improve comfort and mobility but should not be presented as proven prevention for wound dehiscence or incisional hernia, and they do not replace wound assessment.

options.A: Yes. Abdominal binders are proven to prevent wound dehiscence after open abdominal surgery.
options.B: The binder may improve comfort and support movement, but evidence has not established that it prevents wound dehiscence or incisional hernia.
options.C: No. Abdominal binders increase postoperative pain and should not be used during mobilization.
options.D: The binder replaces the need to assess the incision while it is being worn.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. Updated abdominal-wall closure guidance from the European and American Hernia Societies states that evidence does not establish a reduction in burst abdomen/wound dehiscence or incisional hernia from postoperative abdominal binders, although limited evidence suggests they may reduce postoperative pain without compromising pulmonary function. More recent randomized-trial meta-analysis also supports short-term improvements in pain and mobility. A overstates an unproven preventive benefit. C contradicts evidence suggesting pain and mobility benefits in some clients. D is incorrect because a binder is an adjunct for comfort/support and does not replace ongoing incision and skin assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Postoperative abdominal binders may provide short-term comfort/pain and mobility benefits, but current evidence does not establish prevention of wound dehiscence/burst abdomen or incisional hernia and does not support presenting the binder as a substitute for routine wound assessment.
candidates.source_document_title: Updated guideline for closure of abdominal wall incisions from the European and American Hernia Societies

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — community overdose prevention and naloxone education
candidates.educational_objective: Teach community members that naloxone is a bystander-administered opioid-overdose reversal medication used during a suspected overdose as part of an emergency response that includes activating emergency services and continued observation/support.

options.A: I can give naloxone if I suspect an opioid overdose, call emergency services, support breathing as able, and stay with the person until help arrives.
options.B: Naloxone prevents an opioid overdose if it is taken before someone uses opioids.
options.C: Once naloxone is given and the person awakens, emergency evaluation is no longer needed.
options.D: Only health professionals should administer naloxone because bystanders should not use it.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies expanded community access to naloxone as an overdose-prevention strategy because bystanders can administer this opioid-overdose reversal medication and potentially save a life. CDC advises administering naloxone when an opioid overdose is suspected, calling 911, supporting breathing/keeping the person awake as able, placing the person on the side to reduce choking risk, and staying until emergency assistance arrives. B is incorrect because naloxone does not prevent an overdose when taken in advance. C is incorrect because the response to a suspected overdose includes emergency assistance even if the person responds to naloxone. D is incorrect because CDC states that anyone can carry and administer naloxone.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Community naloxone access enables lay bystanders to reverse suspected opioid overdose and is paired with emergency response actions; naloxone is not prophylactic and community members do not need to be health professionals to administer it.
candidates.source_document_title: Preventing Opioid Overdose; What to Do If You Think Someone Is Overdosing; Naloxone Frequently Asked Questions

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — community harm reduction and prevention of bloodborne infection
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that comprehensive syringe services programs reduce injection-related infectious-disease risk while connecting participants to testing, vaccination, and treatment services without requiring abstinence or increasing illegal drug use.

options.A: SSPs provide sterile injection equipment and link people to testing, treatment, and other services; they are associated with lower HIV and hepatitis C transmission without increasing illegal drug use or crime.
options.B: SSPs are intended to replace substance-use-disorder treatment so participants do not need referral to treatment programs.
options.C: SSPs reduce infection risk mainly by requiring participants to stop injecting drugs before receiving sterile equipment.
options.D: SSPs are used primarily to identify people who inject drugs for law-enforcement referral rather than to provide prevention services.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes syringe services programs as community-based prevention programs that provide access to sterile syringes and safe disposal, infectious-disease testing and vaccination, and linkage to treatment for infections and substance use disorder. CDC reports that comprehensive SSPs are associated with reduced HIV and hepatitis C incidence and do not increase illegal drug use or crime. B is incorrect because SSPs complement, rather than replace, treatment and linkage services. C is incorrect because abstinence is not a prerequisite for receiving harm-reduction services. D is incorrect because SSPs are public-health prevention programs, not primarily law-enforcement referral programs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Comprehensive SSPs are community-based harm-reduction programs that reduce infectious-disease transmission risk, provide sterile equipment and other preventive services, and link participants to care; CDC states that these programs do not increase illegal drug use or crime.
candidates.source_document_title: Strengthening Syringe Services Programs (SSPs); Infectious Diseases in Persons Who Inject Drugs

Infectious Diseases in PWID repeats safety/effectiveness and prevention role

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — recognize and respond to clients at risk for self-harm/suicide and provide a safe therapeutic environment; integrated clinical judgment and safety processes
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — suicide-risk screening and follow-up in behavioral health care
candidates.educational_objective: Use a validated suicide-risk screening tool for clients whose primary reason for care is a behavioral health condition, then complete evidence-based follow-up assessment and safety planning according to the result and clinical presentation.

options.A: Screen the client for suicidal ideation using a validated screening tool and follow an evidence-based assessment process if the screen is positive.
options.B: Skip suicide screening unless the client spontaneously states an intent to die.
options.C: Use an informal conversation only, because validated tools are not required when behavioral health is the primary reason for care.
options.D: Assume that universal suicide-risk screening is required for every hospital patient regardless of the reason for care.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The Joint Commission’s current suicide-risk performance goal requires screening patients being evaluated or treated primarily for a behavioral health condition for suicidal ideation using a validated screening tool and using an evidence-based process for further assessment when indicated. B is incorrect because the standard does not require waiting for spontaneous disclosure. C is incorrect because a validated screening tool is specifically required for this population. D is incorrect because the Joint Commission does not require universal screening of all hospital patients regardless of presentation. Separately, the USPSTF has concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine the balance of benefits and harms of universal suicide-risk screening in asymptomatic adults in primary care, reinforcing the need to avoid an unsupported universal claim.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Joint Commission standards require validated suicide-ideation screening for patients whose primary reason for care is a behavioral health condition and evidence-based follow-up assessment when indicated; the requirement is not universal for every hospital patient.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — provide a safe therapeutic environment, recognize and respond to risk for self-harm/suicide, and use therapeutic communication and evidence-based psychosocial interventions
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — collaborative suicide safety planning
candidates.educational_objective: Develop suicide safety plans collaboratively with the client by identifying warning signs, internal coping strategies, social supports, and professional/crisis resources rather than relying on a no-harm contract as the primary safety intervention.

options.A: Ask the client to sign a no-harm contract promising not to attempt suicide and use the signed promise as the primary safety intervention.
options.B: Collaboratively identify the client’s warning signs, internal coping strategies, supportive people or places, and professional or crisis resources to use during a suicidal crisis.
options.C: Give the client a crisis telephone number without developing individualized coping steps or support contacts.
options.D: Create the safety plan for the client without participation so discussing warning signs does not reinforce suicidal thoughts.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. The Safety Planning Intervention is a collaborative, patient-centered approach that creates step-by-step actions for use before or during a suicidal crisis. Core components include recognizing warning signs, using internal coping strategies, seeking social support, and contacting professional or crisis resources; current VA suicide-prevention guidance also recommends safety planning over traditional no-harm contracts, which lack research support. A is incorrect because a no-harm contract is not an evidence-based substitute for assessment and collaborative planning. C is incomplete because a crisis number alone does not provide the individualized sequence of coping and support steps that defines a safety plan. D is incorrect because collaboration with the client is a defining feature of the intervention rather than a risk to be avoided.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Collaborative safety planning uses individualized warning signs, coping strategies, social supports, and professional/crisis resources and is recommended over no-harm contracts, which are not supported by research as a suicide-prevention intervention.
candidates.source_document_title: Crisis Response Planning and Safety Planning; The Safety Planning Intervention

The Safety Planning Intervention — Steps 1–5 identify warning signs, internal coping, social contacts, family/friends for help, and professionals/agencies

candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — suicide postvention, grief support, and systems-based safety review
candidates.educational_objective: After a suicide death, support affected clients, families, and staff through organized postvention while participating in a separate systems-focused review of contributing factors to reduce future risk.

options.A: Avoid discussing the death with affected people unless they independently request help, because organized follow-up may intensify grief.
options.B: Focus the response on identifying which individual clinician should be blamed before offering staff or client support.
options.C: Provide immediate and ongoing support and referral resources to people affected by the suicide while the organization separately reviews contributing system factors to reduce recurrence risk.
options.D: Limit the response to completion of the client’s medical record because emotional support and event review are outside the organization’s role.

candidates.rationale: C is correct. Suicide postvention is an organized response after a suicide that supports healing, reduces harmful effects of exposure, and helps reduce suicide risk among affected people; current Suicide Prevention Resource Center guidance recommends immediate and long-term support tailored to those exposed. Separately, Joint Commission patient-safety policy expects organizations to examine root causes and contributing factors of sentinel events and make improvements to reduce recurrence risk. A is incorrect because effective postvention is proactive rather than limited to people who independently seek help. B is inconsistent with a systems-based safety response and can impede support and learning. D omits both the psychosocial needs of people exposed to the suicide and the organization’s patient-safety review responsibilities.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Postvention provides proactive immediate and long-term support to people exposed to a suicide; healthcare organizations also use systems-focused analysis of serious safety events to identify contributing factors and reduce recurrence rather than substituting blame for learning.
candidates.source_document_title: Provide for Immediate and Long-Term Postvention; Sentinel Event FAQs and Sentinel Event Policy and Procedures

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; monitor diagnostic/therapeutic data, recognize unreliable or discordant findings, and use monitoring technology safely
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — safe use and interpretation of continuous glucose monitoring technology
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients using CGM to interpret sensor glucose trends while retaining access to blood glucose monitoring for circumstances in which sensor data may be inaccurate, unavailable, or clinically discordant.

options.A: The sensor tracks glucose values and trends over time, but I still need access to a blood glucose meter when the CGM reading may be inaccurate or unavailable.
options.B: The CGM measures my A1C continuously, so I no longer need to review daily glucose patterns.
options.C: Every CGM directly measures glucose in arterial blood, so sensor readings always match a finger-stick value exactly.
options.D: Once I start CGM, blood glucose testing is never needed again, even when symptoms do not match the sensor reading.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Continuous glucose monitoring uses a sensor to provide repeated glucose information and trends; FDA device classifications describe CGM systems as detecting trends and tracking patterns in interstitial glucose. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend that people using CGM still have access to blood glucose monitoring for situations such as suspected CGM inaccuracy, sensor warm-up or transmission disruption, calibration when required, or rapidly changing glucose. B is incorrect because CGM does not continuously measure A1C. C is incorrect because commonly used CGM systems measure interstitial glucose, and sensor values are not guaranteed to match capillary blood glucose exactly. D is incorrect because CGM does not eliminate the need for backup blood glucose testing in all circumstances.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CGM provides repeated sensor glucose values and trend information, generally reflecting interstitial glucose; users still need access to conventional blood glucose monitoring for specified backup and confirmation situations rather than assuming CGM eliminates blood glucose testing.
candidates.source_document_title: Diabetes Technology: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; FDA Continuous Glucose Monitor Device Classification
candidates.source_locator: ADA 2026 Section 7, recommendations 7.10–7.12 and CGM discussion — people using CGM must have access to BGM for suspected inaccuracy, warm-up, transmission disruption, calibration when needed, supply delays, or rapidly changing glucose. FDA product classifications MDS/QCD — CGM detects trends/tracks patterns in interstitial glucose using a sensor and displays glucose values

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — semaglutide product indications and medication teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish FDA-approved indications among semaglutide products and recognize Wegovy as an approved option for long-term weight reduction in eligible adults rather than assuming semaglutide is used only for diabetes.

options.A: Wegovy is an FDA-approved semaglutide product for reducing excess body weight and maintaining weight reduction long term in eligible adults when used with reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
options.B: Semaglutide is approved only for type 2 diabetes, so using Wegovy for obesity is necessarily off-label.
options.C: All semaglutide products have identical FDA indications, so the product name and formulation do not matter.
options.D: Wegovy is used to treat acute hypoglycemia in adults who do not have diabetes.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current Wegovy prescribing information identifies semaglutide as a GLP-1 receptor agonist and includes reduction of excess body weight and long-term maintenance of weight reduction among its FDA-approved indications for eligible adults, in combination with reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity. B is incorrect because Wegovy has FDA-approved non-diabetes indications. C is incorrect because semaglutide products are labeled for different indications and are not simply interchangeable on the basis that they contain the same active drug; for example, Ozempic is labeled for adults with type 2 diabetes and specific cardiovascular and kidney-risk indications. D is incorrect because semaglutide is not an acute treatment for hypoglycemia.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Wegovy and Ozempic contain semaglutide but have distinct FDA-labeled indications; current Wegovy labeling includes long-term weight reduction/maintenance for eligible adults, so semaglutide is not restricted to diabetes treatment.
candidates.source_document_title: WEGOVY (semaglutide) Prescribing Information; OZEMPIC (semaglutide) Prescribing Information

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; provide medication education, monitor for adverse effects, and promote safe medication administration
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — sulfonylurea hypoglycemia risk and administration teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients taking glipizide that clinically significant hypoglycemia can occur and that extended-release glipizide is administered with breakfast or the first meal of the day according to the prescription.

options.A: This medication can cause severe hypoglycemia, so learn the signs of low glucose and take the extended-release dose with breakfast or the first meal of the day as prescribed.
options.B: This medication rarely lowers glucose enough to cause symptoms, so routine hypoglycemia education is unnecessary.
options.C: The main expected effect is weight loss, and low blood glucose is not a clinically important risk.
options.D: Take the medication at bedtime without regard to meals because food timing does not affect how it should be administered.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current glipizide extended-release labeling states that all sulfonylureas, including glipizide, can produce severe hypoglycemia and directs clinicians to educate clients to recognize and manage hypoglycemia. The label also directs administration with breakfast or the first meal of the day. B and C minimize a clearly labeled safety risk. D conflicts with the labeled administration instructions. Risk is higher in some populations and with certain concomitant glucose-lowering medications, so individualized monitoring remains important.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Glipizide extended-release can cause severe hypoglycemia and requires patient education about recognition/management; the labeled administration timing is with breakfast or the first meal of the day.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — pioglitazone contraindication and heart-failure risk
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the boxed-warning heart-failure risk of pioglitazone and clarify a new order before initiation in a client with established NYHA class III or IV heart failure.

options.A: Administer the medication because heart failure is not a labeled concern with pioglitazone.
options.B: Clarify the prescription because initiating pioglitazone in established NYHA class III or IV heart failure is contraindicated.
options.C: Give the medication and monitor only for hypoglycemia because fluid retention is not expected with this drug class.
options.D: Administer the medication because thiazolidinediones are preferred when a client has symptomatic heart failure.

candidates.rationale: B is correct. Pioglitazone carries a boxed warning for congestive heart failure. Current labeling states that thiazolidinediones can cause or exacerbate heart failure through fluid retention, that pioglitazone is not recommended in symptomatic heart failure, and that initiation in established NYHA class III or IV heart failure is contraindicated. The nurse should therefore clarify the new order before administering the first dose. A and C ignore the boxed-warning risk, and D reverses the label’s recommendation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Pioglitazone can cause fluid retention and exacerbate congestive heart failure; initiation is contraindicated in established NYHA class III or IV heart failure and the drug is not recommended in symptomatic heart failure.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — rapid-acting insulin administration timing
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients using subcutaneous NovoLog to administer it within 5 to 10 minutes before a meal and to follow product-specific insulin instructions rather than assuming all insulin-aspart formulations have identical timing.

options.A: I should inject NovoLog within about 5 to 10 minutes before I begin eating.
options.B: I should inject NovoLog 30 to 60 minutes before every meal because all mealtime insulins require the same lead time.
options.C: I should wait until at least 1 hour after finishing the meal before injecting NovoLog.
options.D: The timing does not matter because NovoLog is a long-acting basal insulin.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NovoLog labeling directs subcutaneous injection within 5 to 10 minutes before a meal. B incorrectly generalizes timing from slower-acting insulin formulations. C delays a rapid-acting mealtime insulin beyond the labeled timing. D is incorrect because NovoLog is a rapid-acting insulin analog, not a long-acting basal insulin. Insulin-aspart products are not interchangeable for meal timing solely because they share the same active molecule; for example, Fiasp labeling allows dosing at the start of a meal or within 20 minutes after starting it.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Subcutaneous NovoLog is labeled for injection within 5 to 10 minutes before a meal; meal timing is product-specific and should not be generalized across all insulin-aspart formulations.
candidates.source_document_title: NOVOLOG (insulin aspart) Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Dosage and Administration, Section 2.2 — subcutaneous NOVOLOG should be injected within 5 to 10 minutes before a meal; FIASP Section 2.2 used only to verify that insulin-aspart product timing differs

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — glucagon mechanism and treatment failure in glycogen depletion
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that glucagon requires hepatic glycogen stores to raise blood glucose and may be ineffective after prolonged starvation or other glycogen-depleting states, requiring glucose treatment instead.

options.A: Glucagon depends on adequate hepatic glycogen stores to raise blood glucose, and prolonged poor intake may reduce those stores.
options.B: Glucagon lowers blood glucose by increasing insulin secretion, so persistent hypoglycemia is the expected therapeutic response.
options.C: Glucagon works only by supplying exogenous glucose directly into the bloodstream, so it cannot be used without an IV line.
options.D: Glucagon is ineffective in severe hypoglycemia whenever the client has diabetes.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current glucagon-for-injection labeling states that glucagon raises blood glucose by activating hepatic glucagon receptors, stimulating glycogen breakdown and release of glucose from the liver. Adequate hepatic glycogen is therefore necessary for the antihypoglycemic effect. Clients with depleted glycogen stores, including those in starvation states, may respond poorly and should be treated with glucose. B reverses glucagon’s effect. C is incorrect because glucagon does not supply glucose directly and can be administered without IV access. D contradicts its labeled indication for severe hypoglycemia in people with diabetes.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Glucagon raises glucose by mobilizing hepatic glycogen; depleted hepatic glycogen can make glucagon ineffective, and glucose should be used in such circumstances.
candidates.source_document_title: Glucagon for Injection Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions, Section 5.4 ‘Lack of Efficacy in Patients with Decreased Hepatic Glycogen’; Clinical Pharmacology, Section 12.1 ‘Mechanism of Action’ — glucagon activates hepatic receptors, stimulates glycogen breakdown and glucose release; adequate hepatic glycogen is required

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — extended-release metformin administration and titration
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients starting extended-release metformin to take it with the evening meal, swallow the tablet whole, and follow gradual dose titration based on glycemic response and tolerability rather than self-escalating the dose.

options.A: Take the prescribed starting dose with the evening meal, swallow the tablet whole, and expect dose increases to be made gradually based on glycemic control and tolerability.
options.B: Crush the extended-release tablet and take it on an empty stomach so the medication is absorbed more quickly.
options.C: Double the dose after the first day if the blood glucose remains above goal because weekly titration is unnecessary.
options.D: Take the entire daily dose only when symptoms of hyperglycemia occur rather than on a regular schedule.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current metformin extended-release labeling directs administration with the evening meal, requires the tablets to be swallowed whole rather than crushed, cut, or chewed, and specifies gradual dose increases in 500-mg weekly increments based on glycemic control and tolerability. Gastrointestinal adverse effects such as diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, and abdominal pain are common, making tolerability clinically relevant during titration. B, C, and D conflict with the labeled administration schedule and extended-release formulation instructions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Extended-release metformin is taken with the evening meal, swallowed whole, and titrated gradually according to glycemic control and tolerability; gastrointestinal adverse effects are common.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — IV insulin in severe diabetic ketoacidosis
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize continuous IV insulin as the recommended approach for severe DKA while understanding that selected uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA can be managed with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin under an appropriate protocol.

options.A: Continuous IV insulin is appropriate for severe DKA, with protocol-based monitoring and adjustment as ketoacidosis resolves.
options.B: All DKA, including uncomplicated mild DKA, must be treated with continuous IV insulin in an intensive care setting.
options.C: IV insulin eliminates the need to monitor potassium because insulin does not affect serum potassium during DKA treatment.
options.D: Regular human insulin is the only insulin formulation that can ever be administered intravenously, which is why it must be used for every DKA case.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care state that severe DKA is managed with continuous intravenous insulin infusion using a fixed-rate or validated nurse-driven protocol. The 2024 international hyperglycemic-crisis consensus similarly identifies continuous IV short-acting insulin as the preferred approach for severe or complicated DKA, while uncomplicated mild or moderate DKA may be treated with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin analogs in appropriate settings. C is unsafe because IV regular insulin labeling requires close glucose and potassium monitoring due to risks including hypoglycemia and hypokalemia. D is false: the rationale for IV treatment in severe DKA is clinical severity and titratable continuous insulin delivery, not a claim that regular insulin is the only insulin product approved for IV use.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Severe DKA is appropriately treated with continuous IV insulin using a validated protocol; selected uncomplicated mild/moderate DKA can be treated subcutaneously; IV regular insulin requires close glucose and potassium monitoring.
candidates.source_document_title: Diabetes Care in the Hospital: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report; NOVOLIN R Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: ADA 2026 Section 16, DKA/HHS management — severe DKA: continuous IV insulin infusion; mild uncomplicated DKA may use subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin. 2024 Consensus Report, ‘Insulin’ — IV short-acting insulin preferred; subcutaneous rapid-acting analogs effective for uncomplicated mild/moderate DKA. NOVOLIN R Section 2.2 — IV administration under medical supervision with close blood glucose and potassium monitoring

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control; use infection-prevention practices when handling client-care equipment and blood-contaminated devices
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — shared blood glucose meter reprocessing
candidates.client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
candidates.educational_objective: When a blood glucose meter must be shared, use a device intended for professional multi-patient use and clean and disinfect it after every client according to manufacturer instructions; do not share a meter lacking validated reprocessing instructions.

options.A: Use a meter designed for professional multi-patient use and clean and disinfect it after every client according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
options.B: Wipe the meter once at the end of the shift because a new lancet is used for each client.
options.C: Share any over-the-counter home glucose meter as long as visible blood is wiped away between clients.
options.D: Continue sharing the meter even if the manufacturer provides no validated cleaning and disinfection instructions.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends assigning blood glucose meters to individual patients whenever possible. If a meter must be shared in a health care or congregate setting, it should be a device designed for professional use and must be cleaned and disinfected after every use according to the manufacturer’s instructions. If the manufacturer does not specify how the device should be cleaned and disinfected, the meter should not be shared. B is insufficient because contamination can occur with each use. C is incorrect because over-the-counter home meters are not automatically suitable for professional multi-patient use. D directly contradicts CDC guidance.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Shared glucose meters require validated cleaning and disinfection after every patient use and should be designed for professional multi-patient use; meters without manufacturer reprocessing instructions should not be shared.
candidates.source_document_title: Considerations for Blood Glucose Monitoring and Insulin Administration
candidates.source_locator: Blood glucose meters — whenever possible assign a meter to one person; if sharing is necessary, select a device designed for professional use and clean and disinfect after every use per manufacturer instructions; if the manufacturer does not specify cleaning/disinfection, do not share the meter

candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — home sharps disposal
candidates.client_need: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
candidates.educational_objective: Teach home injection users to place sharps immediately in an appropriate puncture-resistant disposal container and follow local requirements for final disposal rather than discarding loose needles in trash, recycling, or toilets.

options.A: I will place used needles immediately in an FDA-cleared sharps container when possible; if one is unavailable, an appropriate heavy-duty plastic household container may be used, and I will follow local disposal rules.
options.B: I can place loose needles in the household trash as long as I wrap each needle in tissue first.
options.C: I should flush used needles down the toilet so no one in the home can reach them.
options.D: I should put loose needles in the recycling bin because metal sharps can be separated during recycling.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. FDA recommends placing used needles and other sharps immediately into an FDA-cleared sharps disposal container when possible. If an FDA-cleared container is unavailable, an appropriate heavy-duty plastic household container with required safety features may be used as an alternative, and final disposal must follow community guidelines. Loose sharps should not be placed in household/public trash or recycling and should never be flushed down the toilet. B, C, and D therefore create preventable needlestick and infection risks.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Home users should immediately contain used sharps in an FDA-cleared sharps container when possible, may use an appropriate heavy-duty household plastic container when needed, and must follow local disposal rules; loose sharps should not enter trash, recycling, or toilets.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies; safely administer parenteral medications, evaluate response, and educate clients about injection technique
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin injection-site rotation and lipodystrophy
candidates.educational_objective: Teach insulin users to avoid lipodystrophic or lumpy injection areas, rotate injection sites appropriately, and monitor glucose closely when moving injections from affected to unaffected tissue because insulin absorption may change.

options.A: Stop injecting into the abnormal area, rotate sites within an appropriate region, and monitor glucose more closely when changing to unaffected tissue.
options.B: Continue using the lumpy area because lipodystrophy improves insulin absorption and reduces glucose variability.
options.C: Massage the thickened area immediately after each injection so insulin enters the bloodstream more rapidly.
options.D: Use only the same exact skin spot for each dose because changing sites is the main cause of lipodystrophy.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current insulin labeling instructs clients to rotate injection sites to reduce lipodystrophy and localized cutaneous amyloidosis and to avoid injecting into areas that are thickened, pitted, or lumpy. Repeated injections into affected tissue have been associated with hyperglycemia, while a sudden change from affected to unaffected tissue can increase the risk of hypoglycemia; closer glucose monitoring is therefore appropriate during the change. B and D reverse the purpose of site rotation. C is not a recommended strategy for correcting abnormal injection-site tissue and introduces unpredictable absorption rather than addressing the cause.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Insulin injection sites should be rotated and abnormal lipodystrophic/amyloid areas avoided; moving from chronically affected tissue to unaffected tissue can alter insulin effect and requires closer glucose monitoring.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — safe insulin storage and pump-supply planning during travel
candidates.educational_objective: When traveling with insulin-pump therapy, keep insulin and essential pump supplies in carry-on luggage, protect insulin from extreme heat and freezing, and plan enough medication and equipment for possible delays.

options.A: I will keep my insulin and pump supplies in my carry-on luggage and protect the insulin from extreme heat and freezing.
options.B: I will pack all insulin in checked luggage because cargo storage keeps medication at a controlled temperature.
options.C: I will place insulin directly against frozen ice packs because freezing does not affect insulin potency.
options.D: I only need the exact amount of insulin for the planned travel time because delays do not affect supply planning.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. FDA guidance for insulin-pump travel advises packing pump supplies, including insulin, in carry-on luggage rather than checked baggage because checked items can be delayed, lost, or damaged. FDA insulin-storage guidance also warns that extreme temperatures reduce insulin effectiveness and specifically states not to use insulin that has been frozen and to keep it away from direct heat and sunlight. C is therefore unsafe. B falsely assumes checked baggage protects medication. D ignores FDA travel guidance to plan adequate medication and supplies for possible travel delays.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Air travelers using insulin pumps should carry insulin and pump supplies in carry-on luggage, plan for travel delays, and protect insulin from extreme heat and freezing because temperature extremes can reduce potency.
candidates.source_document_title: Insulin Pumps: Tips for Using Your Insulin Pump at Home; Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency

FDA Insulin Storage and Effectiveness: extreme temperatures reduce effectiveness; avoid freezing; do not use frozen insulin; keep away from direct heat and sunlight

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — glucagon emergency-kit storage and readiness
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain glucagon emergency readiness by checking and replacing expired kits, storing unreconstituted glucagon correctly, avoiding freezing, and preparing the medication only when it is needed for use.

options.A: We will check the expiration date, replace the kit before it expires, keep it in its original package at room temperature, and not freeze it.
options.B: We can continue to use the kit after its expiration date as long as the powder still looks normal.
options.C: We should mix the powder and diluent now so the medication is ready whenever an emergency occurs.
options.D: We should store the kit in the freezer because freezing preserves glucagon potency.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA/DailyMed labeling for glucagon for injection states not to use the product after the expiration date, to store the unreconstituted kit at controlled room temperature, not to freeze it, and to keep it in the original package protected from light. Once the powder is reconstituted, the solution should be used immediately and any unused portion discarded. B, C, and D each conflict with those labeled storage and handling instructions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Glucagon emergency kits should not be used after expiration, should be stored unreconstituted at controlled room temperature without freezing and protected in the original package, and should be used immediately after reconstitution rather than premixed for later use.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide client education that promotes preventive self-care and reduces risk of chronic-disease complications
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — preventive diabetic foot self-care
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients with diabetic neuropathy or loss of protective sensation to inspect their feet every day so painless skin injuries or preulcerative changes can be identified and treated early.

options.A: Inspect both feet every day, including the soles and between the toes, because neuropathy can allow minor injuries to go unnoticed; use a mirror or ask for help if needed.
options.B: Check the feet only after walking long distances because painless injuries are unlikely during normal daily activity.
options.C: Rely on pain to identify early ulcers because diabetic neuropathy usually increases sensitivity to foot injury.
options.D: Inspect the feet once a month unless an open wound is already visible.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend daily surveillance for early foot problems, particularly in people with loss of protective sensation, using visual inspection, palpation, or an unbreakable mirror when needed. Diabetic peripheral neuropathy can reduce or eliminate protective pain sensation, allowing minor trauma to go unrecognized and progress to ulceration or infection. B, C, and D delay detection and incorrectly rely on pain or infrequent inspection.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Loss of protective sensation can make foot trauma painless or unrecognized, and current ADA guidance recommends daily foot surveillance for early problems, with mirror or caregiver assistance when needed.
candidates.source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin-pump infusion-site care
candidates.educational_objective: Teach insulin-pump users to inspect and rotate infusion sites and to change infusion sets according to the specific device manufacturer’s instructions rather than relying on a universal change interval.

options.A: I will inspect the infusion site for skin problems, rotate sites, and change the infusion set according to my pump manufacturer’s instructions.
options.B: I should keep using the same infusion site until insulin delivery stops because routine site rotation is unnecessary.
options.C: A pump infusion site does not need skin assessment because infection occurs only with insulin injections, not infusion sets.
options.D: I should use a fixed universal change interval even if the instructions for my specific infusion set recommend something different.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care identify appropriate care and rotation of insulin infusion sites as part of safe insulin administration and note pump-site infection and other skin complications as recognized problems. FDA guidance instructs pump users to follow pump-specific directions for when to change infusion sets and rotate infusion sites. B and C ignore known infusion-site complications. D is incorrect because change timing is device- and infusion-set-specific rather than a single universal interval for every product.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Safe insulin-pump use includes appropriate infusion-site care and rotation, recognition of site complications, and following manufacturer-specific instructions for infusion-set changes rather than a universal replacement interval.

FDA ‘Using your insulin pump’ — follow pump-specific instructions for when to change infusion sets and rotate infusion sites

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; initiate appropriate referrals and collaborate with interprofessional resources to meet client needs
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — referral for diabetes self-management education and support
candidates.educational_objective: Refer clients with diabetes to DSMES for individualized education and support in self-care skills, problem-solving, goal setting, and sustainable health behaviors beginning at diagnosis and at other critical times of need.

options.A: A diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES) service, where a trained diabetes care and education professional can provide individualized self-management education, goal setting, and problem-solving support.
options.B: A scheduling office whose role is limited to arranging follow-up appointments without providing diabetes self-management education.
options.C: A specialist whose primary role is to independently prescribe all diabetes medications in every state regardless of professional licensure or scope-of-practice law.
options.D: No referral is indicated because DSMES is intended only for clients who have already developed a diabetes complication.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care advise all people with diabetes to participate in DSMES. DSMES supports informed decision-making, self-care behaviors, problem-solving, active collaboration with the health care team, goal setting, and behavior-change strategies, and it should be provided at diagnosis and again at other critical times. B does not meet the client’s educational and behavioral needs. C makes an invalid universal scope-of-practice claim; prescribing authority depends on the professional’s license and applicable law, not the diabetes-education credential alone. D is incorrect because diagnosis itself is a recommended time for DSMES.
candidates.source_claim_supported: DSMES is a person-centered educational and behavioral-support intervention for people with diabetes and is recommended beginning at diagnosis; it helps build self-management skills, problem-solving, and sustainable behavior change.
candidates.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; coordinate referrals and collaborate with interprofessional team members based on client needs
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized specialty referral in diabetes
candidates.educational_objective: Coordinate diabetes specialty referrals according to the client’s actual complications, comorbidities, treatment complexity, and support needs rather than applying a universal referral rule or laboratory cutoff.

options.A: Arrange referrals according to the client’s complications, comorbidities, treatment complexity, and individual needs rather than assuming every client with diabetes requires the same specialist.
options.B: Refer every adult with diabetes to endocrinology at diagnosis because specialty care is universally required regardless of clinical needs.
options.C: Use a single hemoglobin A1C value as a universal rule that automatically determines whether endocrinology referral is required.
options.D: Avoid specialty referral once diabetes is diagnosed because primary care alone should manage all diabetes-related complications.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care emphasize individualized, team-based diabetes care and recommend specialist referrals as appropriate for complications, comorbidities, treatment burden, and other person-specific needs. The standards do not establish one universal endocrinology referral threshold for every adult with type 2 diabetes, nor do they require endocrinology referral for every diagnosis. B and C impose unsupported universal rules. D is incorrect because diabetes-related complications often require collaboration with appropriate specialists such as endocrinology, nephrology, cardiology, ophthalmology, podiatry, behavioral health, or other professionals depending on the clinical problem.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current ADA standards support individualized specialist referral based on complications, comorbidities, treatment burden, and client needs rather than a universal endocrinology referral requirement or single A1C cutoff.
candidates.source_document_title: Improving Care and Promoting Health in Populations: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026; Comprehensive Medical Evaluation and Assessment of Comorbidities: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; coordinate discharge planning, referrals, client education, and continuity of care during transitions
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — DSMES referral during transition to a new insulin regimen
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that DSMES is an ongoing process and should be reassessed and provided at critical times such as diagnosis, unmet goals, new complicating factors, and major transitions in treatment or care.

options.A: A new referral for diabetes self-management education and support is appropriate because major treatment and care transitions are critical times to reassess education and support needs.
options.B: Repeat DSMES is unnecessary because evidence-based diabetes education is intended to occur only once at diagnosis.
options.C: DSMES should be repeated only if the client specifically requests printed educational materials.
options.D: A new insulin regimen does not change self-management needs, so prior education should be considered permanently sufficient.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend DSMES at diagnosis, annually and/or when treatment goals are not being met, when complicating factors develop, and when transitions in life and care occur. A hospital discharge with a new insulin regimen represents a meaningful treatment and care transition that can change self-management skills and support needs. B and D incorrectly treat education as a one-time event. C is too narrow because DSMES is an interactive, person-centered process that includes problem-solving and behavior support rather than only printed information or client-initiated requests.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current ADA standards treat DSMES as ongoing support that should be revisited at defined critical times, including major treatment and care transitions rather than only at initial diagnosis.
candidates.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; coordinate accessible services, referrals, continuity, and technology-supported care based on client needs
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — telehealth access to diabetes self-management education
candidates.educational_objective: Use telehealth or digital DSMES to reduce access barriers when appropriate while preserving individualized in-person assessment and follow-up when clinically needed.

options.A: Offer telehealth or another appropriate digital DSMES option if it meets the client’s needs and preferences, while maintaining necessary clinical follow-up.
options.B: Discontinue DSMES because education is effective only when delivered face to face.
options.C: Use telehealth as a complete replacement for all in-person medical evaluation regardless of the client’s clinical condition.
options.D: Delay further education until the client can reliably travel to the clinic because remote delivery does not address access barriers.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend offering DSMES through telehealth and/or digital interventions to meet individual preferences, reduce access barriers, and improve satisfaction. Telehealth can expand access but does not automatically replace every in-person examination or other clinically necessary care. B and D contradict the guideline’s support for remote DSMES. C overstates telehealth by treating it as a universal substitute for all in-person clinical assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current ADA standards support telehealth/digital delivery of DSMES to reduce access barriers and meet individual preferences without establishing that remote care universally replaces all in-person clinical evaluation.
candidates.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide client education using methods appropriate to learning needs and evaluate understanding of self-care
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — health literacy and teach-back for diabetes self-management
candidates.educational_objective: Use plain language and teach-back or show-me techniques to confirm that clients can understand and perform self-management tasks rather than relying on yes/no statements of understanding.

options.A: Ask the client to show how to perform the glucose check and explain the key steps in the client’s own words, then reteach any unclear points using plain language.
options.B: Ask only, “Do you understand?” and document successful teaching if the client answers yes.
options.C: Provide a detailed written handout using medical terminology and avoid further discussion so the client can study independently.
options.D: Repeat the same explanation word for word at a faster pace so the client hears the information again.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AHRQ’s Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit recommends clear, plain-language communication and teach-back/show-me methods to confirm understanding. Teach-back asks the client to explain information in the client’s own words, while show-me can verify performance of a health task. A simple yes/no question does not reliably demonstrate understanding. Written materials can reinforce teaching but should be easy to understand and are not a substitute for interactive confirmation. Repeating unclear information without adapting it does not address the communication problem.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AHRQ recommends plain-language communication and teach-back/show-me methods to verify understanding and performance rather than assuming a yes response proves comprehension.
candidates.source_document_title: Health Literacy Universal Precautions Toolkit, 3rd Edition — Communicate Clearly and Use the Teach-Back Method
candidates.source_locator: Tool 4 ‘Communicate Clearly’ — use plain language, simple pictures/models, and clear communication; Tool 5 ‘Use the Teach-Back Method’ — ask patients to state in their own words what they need to know or do; show-me confirms ability to perform specific instructions

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — provide individualized health education and nutrition-related self-management support that respects client values and preferences
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — culturally responsive diabetes nutrition education
candidates.educational_objective: Provide culturally responsive diabetes nutrition education by incorporating the client’s usual foods and preferences into an individualized eating plan that supports metabolic and nutrition goals.

options.A: Work with the client and, when appropriate, a registered dietitian nutritionist to build an individualized eating plan that incorporates cultural food preferences while meeting metabolic and nutrition goals.
options.B: Advise the client to stop eating all traditional foods because culturally familiar eating patterns are incompatible with diabetes management.
options.C: Give the same standardized meal plan used for every client so cultural preferences do not influence diabetes education.
options.D: Avoid discussing food preferences because medical nutrition therapy should focus only on carbohydrate grams and not on the client’s usual eating pattern.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care state that there is no one-size-fits-all eating pattern for diabetes and recommend individualized medical nutrition therapy and meal planning based on current eating patterns, metabolic goals, personal and cultural preferences, access to food, and other person-specific factors. DSMES should also be culturally and socially appropriate. B, C, and D conflict with person-centered nutrition care and can create unnecessary barriers to sustainable self-management.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current ADA guidance recommends culturally responsive, individualized diabetes nutrition planning that incorporates usual eating patterns and personal/cultural preferences rather than requiring abandonment of traditional foods or use of a universal meal plan.
candidates.source_document_title: Facilitating Positive Health Behaviors and Well-being to Improve Health Outcomes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; identify barriers to care, coordinate referrals/resources, support continuity, and advocate for access to prescribed treatment
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — financial barriers and equitable access to diabetes technology
candidates.educational_objective: Identify and address financial or insurance barriers to diabetes technology early by coordinating coverage and support resources to reduce avoidable interruption of effective therapy.

options.A: Assess the financial and insurance barrier, notify the diabetes care team, and connect the client with appropriate coverage, social-service, or lower-cost support resources before access is interrupted.
options.B: Assume technology access depends only on personal preference and continue the plan without addressing cost or coverage.
options.C: Tell the client to stop using diabetes technology permanently because financial barriers cannot be modified by the care team.
options.D: Wait until the client has already run out of sensors before discussing access because insurance status is not relevant to treatment planning.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care direct clinicians to assess financial barriers, health insurance, and health care access as social determinants that can affect diabetes management and to collaborate with the care team and social-service resources to reduce cost-related barriers. ADA also recognizes geographic and socioeconomic variation in diabetes-technology adoption and emphasizes continued access to devices and supplies. B, C, and D fail to address a modifiable barrier that can disrupt evidence-based care.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Financial, insurance, socioeconomic, and access barriers can affect diabetes care and technology use; current ADA guidance requires assessment of such barriers and collaborative efforts to preserve access to evidence-based treatment and supplies.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; coordinate individualized plans of care, communicate treatment changes, and support continuity across settings
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized school diabetes plan after treatment change
candidates.educational_objective: Coordinate safe school diabetes care by ensuring the student’s individualized DMMP is updated whenever the diabetes regimen changes and that relevant trained school personnel can follow the current monitoring, treatment, and emergency instructions.

options.A: Obtain and implement an updated individualized Diabetes Medical Management Plan (DMMP) that reflects the student’s current monitoring, insulin, hypo/hyperglycemia, and emergency-care instructions.
options.B: Continue using the prior DMMP until the next school year because diabetes plans are updated only annually.
options.C: Replace the individualized DMMP with the school’s general diabetes policy because one district-wide plan is sufficient for every student.
options.D: Keep the revised diabetes instructions only for the school nurse and avoid communicating applicable emergency procedures to trained school personnel.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current ADA school guidance states that each student with diabetes should have an individualized DMMP developed by the health care professional in collaboration with the student and parent or guardian. The DMMP is the basis for school diabetes care and emergency planning and should be updated annually or whenever the student’s regimen, self-management level, or school circumstances change. B delays a required update after a treatment change. C ignores the individualized medical orders. D is unsafe because appropriate school personnel need training and access to the instructions necessary to provide care and respond to emergencies.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Students with diabetes require an individualized DMMP that guides monitoring, treatment, and emergency care at school and should be updated when the diabetes regimen or relevant circumstances change.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — reinforce preventive screening and early detection practices for chronic disease complications
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — diabetic retinopathy screening
candidates.educational_objective: Teach adults with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes that retinopathy screening begins at diagnosis even when vision is normal because clinically important retinal disease may be asymptomatic.

options.A: A dilated comprehensive eye examination is recommended at the time type 2 diabetes is diagnosed because diabetic retinopathy can be present without noticeable vision symptoms.
options.B: Eye screening should begin only after blurred vision or other visual symptoms develop.
options.C: Diabetic retinopathy always causes early pain or obvious visual changes, so symptom monitoring is sufficient.
options.D: Routine eye examination is unnecessary in type 2 diabetes unless the client first develops a foot or kidney complication.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care recommend that people with type 2 diabetes receive an initial dilated and comprehensive eye examination by an ophthalmologist or optometrist at the time of diabetes diagnosis. Retinopathy may be advanced or vision-threatening while the person remains asymptomatic, so waiting for vision changes can delay detection and treatment. B and C incorrectly rely on symptoms. D adds an unsupported requirement for another complication before eye screening.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Type 2 diabetes warrants an initial dilated comprehensive eye examination at diagnosis, and absence of visual symptoms does not exclude clinically important diabetic retinopathy.
candidates.source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — diabetic gastroparesis and diagnostic exclusion
candidates.educational_objective: Suspect diabetic gastroparesis in a client with compatible upper gastrointestinal symptoms and erratic glycemia while recognizing that medication-related and structural causes must be excluded before confirming the diagnosis.

options.A: Diabetic gastroparesis is a possible cause, but medication effects and organic causes of impaired gastric emptying should be excluded before the diagnosis is established.
options.B: The symptom cluster confirms diabetic gastroparesis, so no further evaluation for other causes is necessary.
options.C: Gastroparesis is unlikely because delayed gastric emptying does not affect glycemic variability in people using insulin.
options.D: The symptoms indicate gallbladder disease rather than diabetic autonomic neuropathy whenever nausea and early satiety occur together.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ADA Standards of Care state that gastroparesis should be suspected in people with erratic glycemic management or upper gastrointestinal symptoms when another cause has not been identified, but gastrointestinal neuropathies are diagnoses of exclusion. Reversible or iatrogenic causes—including medications that impair gastrointestinal motility—and organic causes such as gastric outlet obstruction or peptic ulcer disease should be considered before a diagnosis or specialized gastric-emptying testing is pursued. B overdiagnoses a nonspecific symptom cluster. C is incorrect because gastroparesis can contribute to glucose variability by disrupting the relationship between nutrient absorption and glucose-lowering therapy. D falsely assigns a single alternative diagnosis without evaluation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Diabetic gastroparesis can present with upper gastrointestinal symptoms and erratic glycemia, but it is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring consideration of medication-related and structural causes before confirmation.
candidates.source_document_title: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — overnight glucose-pattern assessment before insulin intensification
candidates.educational_objective: Evaluate recurrent fasting hyperglycemia with overnight glucose data before increasing basal insulin so the nurse can distinguish an early-morning rise from unrecognized nocturnal hypoglycemia and avoid an unsafe assumption of Somogyi rebound.

options.A: Overnight glucose data to determine whether the morning rise occurs without nocturnal hypoglycemia and to identify any unrecognized overnight lows.
options.B: Only the fasting glucose value because overnight glucose patterns do not affect interpretation of morning hyperglycemia.
options.C: Whether the client has been told that every high morning glucose value represents a Somogyi rebound from nocturnal hypoglycemia.
options.D: Only the most recent A1C because an A1C value can identify whether overnight hypoglycemia occurred on a specific night.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Morning hyperglycemia should be interpreted in the context of the overnight glucose pattern before insulin is intensified. Continuous glucose monitoring can document the early-morning rise associated with the dawn phenomenon and, importantly, reveal whether nocturnal hypoglycemia occurred. The dawn phenomenon is not preceded by nocturnal hypoglycemia. The classic Somogyi rebound theory proposes morning hyperglycemia after an overnight low, but modern CGM-era evidence has challenged how often this actually occurs; it should not be assumed from a fasting value alone. B and C risk inappropriate insulin adjustment, and D cannot establish the glucose pattern of a specific night.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Overnight glucose monitoring helps evaluate recurrent fasting hyperglycemia and detect nocturnal hypoglycemia; dawn phenomenon occurs without preceding nocturnal hypoglycemia, while routine assumption of Somogyi rebound is not supported by modern evidence.
candidates.source_document_title: StatPearls: Dawn Phenomenon; StatPearls: Somogyi Phenomenon; Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
candidates.source_locator: Dawn Phenomenon — Evaluation: CGM is the most effective way to document early-morning hyperglycemia and ensure no nocturnal hypoglycemia; dawn phenomenon is not preceded by hypoglycemia. candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — fructosamine interpretation when A1C is unreliable
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret serum fructosamine as an intermediate-term glycemic marker covering roughly 1 to 3 weeks and recognize its usefulness when altered red blood cell survival limits A1C interpretation.

options.A: Fructosamine reflects intermediate glycemic control over roughly the previous 1 to 3 weeks and can be useful when red blood cell survival makes A1C unreliable.
options.B: Fructosamine reflects only the glucose concentration at the moment the blood sample is collected.
options.C: Fructosamine reflects approximately the same red-cell-based glycemic interval as A1C and is affected by red blood cell survival in the same way.
options.D: Fructosamine is primarily a six-month measure of glycemia and is therefore less responsive to recent changes than A1C.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Mayo Clinic Laboratories describes serum fructosamine as a measure of intermediate glycemic control over approximately the previous 1 to 3 weeks and identifies it as useful for monitoring people with shortened red blood cell survival, when A1C may be misleading. Fructosamine measures glycated serum proteins, largely glycated albumin, rather than glycated hemoglobin. B confuses fructosamine with a point-in-time glucose measurement. C incorrectly treats fructosamine as red-cell dependent. D reverses its clinical time window.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Serum fructosamine reflects intermediate glycemic control over approximately 1–3 weeks and can be useful when shortened red blood cell survival makes A1C unreliable.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — free and total insulin interpretation with suspected anti-insulin antibodies
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a marked difference between total and free insulin as evidence that can suggest anti-insulin antibodies while avoiding the unsupported conclusion that antibodies necessarily explain all glycemic variability.

options.A: The pattern raises suspicion for anti-insulin antibodies that bind circulating insulin, but the laboratory finding must be interpreted with the clinical picture.
options.B: The finding proves that anti-insulin antibodies are the sole cause of the client’s glucose variability and excludes all other causes.
options.C: A difference between free and total insulin indicates that the client is not receiving any exogenous insulin.
options.D: Anti-insulin antibodies increase the free insulin fraction by preventing insulin from binding in circulation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Mayo Clinic Laboratories states that people treated with exogenous insulin may develop anti-insulin antibodies and that a significant difference between total and free insulin after ultrafiltration suggests their presence. These antibodies can bind insulin, reducing the unbound bioactive fraction, but Mayo also notes that insulin antibodies may or may not affect insulin activity and metabolism. Therefore the finding supports suspicion and possible confirmatory antibody testing rather than proving that antibodies are the sole explanation for glycemic variability. B overstates causality. C is unrelated to the laboratory pattern. D reverses the effect of antibody binding.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A substantial discrepancy between total and free insulin after ultrafiltration can suggest anti-insulin antibodies; antibody binding can reduce the bioactive free insulin fraction, but the presence of antibodies does not by itself prove the cause of all glucose variability.
