'Preeclampsia with Severe Features' lists the defined severe-feature criteria. Preeclampsia and High Blood Pressure During Pregnancy FAQ — diagnosis section: high blood pressure is confirmed and urine, liver, kidney, and platelet testing may be used; severe features are separately enumerated. Serum uric acid is not included among these diagnostic or severe-feature criteria.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — accurate recognition and monitoring of obstetric blood loss
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that quantitative obstetric blood-loss measurement improves measurement accuracy compared with visual estimation, especially at larger losses, while remaining one component of a broader hemorrhage-recognition and response process rather than a stand-alone outcome guarantee.

options.A: Quantitative methods are more accurate than visual estimation, which tends to underestimate larger blood losses, but quantitative measurement alone has not been proven to improve clinical outcomes.
options.B: Visual estimation is generally more accurate than weighing or calibrated collection, so quantitative methods are mainly useful for documentation.
options.C: Quantitative blood loss is recommended only for cesarean births because vaginal births cannot be measured reliably.
options.D: Quantitative measurement eliminates the need to assess cumulative bleeding, vital signs, symptoms, and other clinical evidence of hemorrhage.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ACOG states that quantitative methods are more accurate than visual estimation for determining obstetric blood loss and that visual estimation is more likely to underestimate actual blood loss when volumes are high. ACOG also cautions that the effect of quantitative measurement by itself on clinical outcomes has not been demonstrated. B reverses the evidence. C is incorrect because ACOG recommends multidisciplinary quantitative-assessment protocols for both vaginal and cesarean births. D is incorrect because blood-loss measurement is one component of hemorrhage recognition and does not replace cumulative assessment or the client's clinical status.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Quantitative blood-loss measurement is more accurate than visual estimation for obstetric blood loss, visual estimation tends to underestimate high-volume loss, and quantitative measurement should be integrated with broader hemorrhage assessment rather than treated as a stand-alone guarantee of improved outcomes.

candidates.source_locator: Recommendations and Conclusions: quantitative methods are more accurate than visual estimation; visual estimation more often underestimates actual blood loss at high volumes and overestimates at low volumes; effectiveness of quantitative measurement on clinical outcomes has not been demonstrated; protocols should address both vaginal and cesarean births. candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — immediate nursing intervention for uterine atony/postpartum hemorrhage
candidates.educational_objective: When uterine atony is suspected postpartum, perform fundal massage by stabilizing the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other, and integrate the maneuver into the immediate hemorrhage response.

options.A: Support the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis with one hand while firmly massaging the fundus with the other.
options.B: Use both hands on the fundus and apply forceful downward pressure without stabilizing the lower uterine segment.
options.C: Massage only the lower uterine segment above the symphysis pubis and avoid direct contact with the fundus.
options.D: Delay uterine massage until the uterus remains boggy after all prescribed uterotonic therapy has been completed.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance describes fundal massage by placing one hand on the uterine fundus while the other supports the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; firm fundal pressure is then used to stimulate contraction. Supporting the lower segment also reduces the risk of uterine inversion during the maneuver. B is incorrect because forceful downward pressure on an unsupported uterus is not the described technique. C is incorrect because the therapeutic massage is directed to the fundus while the lower segment is supported rather than massaged in place of the fundus. D is incorrect because uterine massage is a first-line response when uterine atony is identified and is used as part of the immediate postpartum-hemorrhage response rather than being postponed until uterotonics are exhausted.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For postpartum uterine atony, fundal massage is performed with one hand on the fundus and the other supporting the lower uterine segment near the symphysis pubis; therapeutic uterine massage is part of the immediate first-response treatment of postpartum hemorrhage rather than a delayed measure.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postpartum surveillance using serial vital-sign assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Monitor postpartum vital signs most closely during immediate recovery and progressively extend the interval only when the client remains stable, while continuing systematic assessment for hemorrhage, hypertensive disorders, infection, and other postpartum complications.

options.A: Assess vital signs closely during the immediate recovery period, then lengthen the interval as the client remains stable and according to agency policy.
options.B: Obtain one complete set of vital signs after birth and repeat them only if the client reports new symptoms.
options.C: Use the same fixed assessment interval throughout the entire postpartum stay regardless of stability or elapsed time since birth.
options.D: Omit routine vital-sign assessment after an uncomplicated birth because postpartum hemorrhage is identified primarily by vaginal bleeding alone.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance describes frequent maternal vital-sign assessment during the immediate postpartum recovery period, with intervals becoming less frequent as recovery progresses and the client remains stable; ongoing frequency is also governed by orders and agency policy. WHO likewise recommends regular maternal assessment during the first 24 hours, including pulse and temperature from the first hour after birth and blood pressure shortly after birth. B and D are unsafe because postpartum assessment is ongoing rather than symptom-triggered only, and maternal complications may first appear through vital-sign or other assessment changes. C is incorrect because monitoring intensity appropriately changes with postpartum phase, stability, and local policy rather than remaining at one fixed interval.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Maternal vital signs and related postpartum findings require regular assessment beginning immediately after birth, with close monitoring in early recovery and less frequent assessment only after stability is established and according to policy.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — postpartum perineal hygiene and comfort
candidates.educational_objective: Teach postpartum perineal care using gentle warm-water cleansing, patting dry, frequent sanitary-pad changes, and hand hygiene while avoiding unnecessary fragranced or antiseptic additives unless specifically directed.

options.A: I can use warm water from a peri-bottle after voiding or bowel movements, pat the area dry, change sanitary pads frequently, and wash my hands before and after pad changes.
options.B: I should avoid cleansing the perineum between showers because repeated contact with water delays healing.
options.C: I should add antiseptic or fragranced products to the peri-bottle routinely so the wound remains sterile.
options.D: I can leave the same sanitary pad in place unless it becomes completely saturated because frequent pad changes irritate the wound.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI postpartum nursing guidance describes using a peri-bottle filled with warm water to gently cleanse and soothe the perineal and rectal area after voiding and bowel movements, followed by gentle drying. Current postnatal-care guidance also emphasizes good perineal hygiene, including regular cleansing, frequent sanitary-pad changes, and hand hygiene before and after pad changes. B is incorrect because gentle cleansing is part of routine postpartum care. C is incorrect because additives or medicated products should not be placed in cleansing water unless specifically directed; routine fragranced or antiseptic products are unnecessary. D is incorrect because frequent sanitary-pad changes are part of recommended perineal hygiene and allow ongoing observation of lochia and wound condition.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Postpartum perineal self-care includes gentle warm-water cleansing with a peri-bottle, gentle drying, frequent sanitary-pad changes, and hand hygiene; routine additives are not required unless directed.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postoperative/postpartum surveillance after cesarean birth
candidates.educational_objective: After cesarean birth, integrate routine postpartum surveillance with postoperative assessment of the incision, pain, bowel/bladder function, and mobility, and promote ambulation when clinically appropriate to support recovery and reduce complication risk.

options.A: Assess the incision, uterine fundus, lochia, pain, bowel and bladder function, and extremities; assist with ambulation when clinically appropriate and permitted.
options.B: Focus assessment on the abdominal incision because uterine tone and lochia are not clinically relevant after a cesarean birth.
options.C: Keep the client on bed rest until discharge to protect the incision and avoid provoking postoperative pain.
options.D: Delay incision assessment until discharge teaching unless the client first reports drainage or wound pain.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. A client who has had a cesarean birth requires both routine postpartum assessment and additional postoperative assessment. Current NCBI nursing guidance includes evaluation of the uterine fundus, lochia, bladder, bowel function, extremities, pain, and the cesarean dressing/incision. Early ambulation is also encouraged when clinically appropriate because it supports postoperative recovery and circulation. B is incorrect because cesarean birth does not eliminate the risk of uterine atony or postpartum hemorrhage; fundal and lochia assessment remain essential. C is incorrect because routine prolonged bed rest is not recommended and can impede recovery. D is incorrect because the incision is assessed during hospitalization for dressing condition, approximation, and signs of infection rather than only when symptoms are volunteered or at discharge.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Post-cesarean nursing care combines routine postpartum assessment with surgical-incision and postoperative assessment, pain management and clinically appropriate early mobility; fundal and lochia assessment remain necessary after cesarean birth.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — risk-based preeclampsia prevention with low-dose aspirin
candidates.educational_objective: Teach that clinician-directed low-dose aspirin is preventive therapy for pregnant clients at increased preeclampsia risk, is started after 12 weeks under current U.S. guidance, and supplements rather than replaces ongoing prenatal surveillance.

options.A: Low-dose aspirin is recommended after 12 weeks for clients at high risk because it reduces the risk of preeclampsia and related morbidity; it does not guarantee prevention.
options.B: Low-dose aspirin is used to treat an acute rise in blood pressure, so it should be taken only when the client's blood pressure is elevated.
options.C: Low-dose aspirin is recommended routinely for every pregnant client regardless of individual preeclampsia risk factors.
options.D: Once aspirin is started, routine blood-pressure and prenatal surveillance for preeclampsia are no longer necessary.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current USPSTF recommendation advises low-dose aspirin 81 mg/day after 12 weeks of gestation for pregnant persons at high risk for preeclampsia; chronic hypertension is one listed high-risk factor. ACOG and SMFM support this risk-based recommendation and advise initiation between 12 and 28 weeks, optimally before 16 weeks, with daily use until delivery unless contraindicated or otherwise directed. Aspirin lowers risk; it does not guarantee prevention. B is incorrect because this is preventive therapy, not an as-needed antihypertensive treatment. C is incorrect because the national recommendation is risk-based rather than universally required for every pregnant person, although some practices may use broader implementation based on their patient population. D is incorrect because aspirin prophylaxis does not replace routine prenatal assessment and blood-pressure monitoring. FDA safety communication also specifically recognizes clinician-directed low-dose 81 mg aspirin as an exception to its general NSAID pregnancy warning.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Low-dose aspirin 81 mg/day after 12 weeks is recommended as preventive medication for pregnant persons at high risk of preeclampsia, including those with chronic hypertension; it reduces risk but does not replace ongoing prenatal surveillance or function as an as-needed antihypertensive.

candidates.source_locator: USPSTF Recommendation Summary/Clinician Summary: prescribe low-dose aspirin 81 mg/day after 12 weeks to pregnant persons at high risk; chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor. ACOG Practice Advisory — USPSTF 2021 Recommendation/Implementation Considerations: 81 mg/day for high-risk individuals, initiated 12–28 weeks, optimally before 16 weeks, continued daily until delivery. FDA NSAID pregnancy safety communication footnote: clinician-directed low-dose 81 mg aspirin is an exception to the general NSAID warning.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — purpose and individualized delivery of prenatal care
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that prenatal care supports maternal-fetal monitoring, screening, education, counseling, and social-resource assessment throughout pregnancy, while the frequency and format of visits may be individualized according to current risk and care needs.

options.A: Prenatal care provides ongoing maternal and fetal monitoring, screening and testing, education, and support, while the visit schedule can be adjusted to the client's medical and social needs.
options.B: Prenatal care is mainly beneficial for clients already classified as high risk; uncomplicated pregnancies require little routine monitoring or education.
options.C: Prenatal care is effective only when every pregnant client follows the same fixed number and timing of in-person visits regardless of risk or preferences.
options.D: Once telehealth is available, in-person prenatal visits are generally unnecessary because physical examinations and laboratory testing can be completed remotely.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current ACOG guidance describes prenatal care as including medical care, screening tests, monitoring of maternal and fetal health, counseling, education, and help with social support and community resources. ACOG's 2025 Clinical Consensus on tailored prenatal care states that visit frequency and monitoring may be individualized according to medical and social needs rather than using one rigid schedule for everyone. B is incorrect because routine prenatal care is relevant to both average-risk and high-risk pregnancies. C is incorrect because ACOG now specifically supports tailored visit schedules for appropriate clients. D is incorrect because telehealth can supplement prenatal care, but in-person visits remain necessary when physical examination, laboratory testing, imaging, or other hands-on services are required.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ongoing prenatal care provides maternal-fetal monitoring, screening/testing, education and support, while current ACOG guidance permits tailoring visit frequency and modality to medical, social and individual care needs.

'What is tailored prenatal care?' and 'How often should I expect to go into the office?': care is individualized by complication risk, preferences and health needs. ACOG Clinical Consensus, Tailored Prenatal Care Delivery — Frequency: visit frequency and monitoring schedule may be tailored to medical and social needs; targeted schedules can provide equivalent outcomes for selected average-risk individuals.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — postpartum depression screening during infant preventive care
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that postpartum depression screening is a routine, repeated component of early well-child care because timely identification and referral can support the birth parent, infant, and parent-infant relationship; a positive screen requires further assessment rather than serving as a diagnosis by itself.

options.A: Repeated screening during early well-child visits creates opportunities to identify postpartum depression and connect the parent with further evaluation, treatment, and support that can benefit the parent-infant dyad.
options.B: A positive screening score allows the pediatric team to make a definitive psychiatric diagnosis without further clinical evaluation.
options.C: Screening is needed only when the infant has feeding, growth, or developmental problems that already suggest parental depression.
options.D: Once screening is completed at the 2-month visit, additional postpartum depression screening during later early-infancy well visits is unnecessary.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends routine postpartum depression screening of the birth parent with a validated tool at the infant's 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits. Repeated screening provides multiple opportunities to identify depression, initiate support, and arrange referral or treatment when indicated; perinatal depression can affect the parent, infant, and parent-infant relationship. B is incorrect because a screening result identifies risk and the need for further evaluation rather than establishing a psychiatric diagnosis by itself. C is incorrect because AAP recommends routine screening at specified well-child visits rather than waiting for infant problems or overt parental symptoms. D is incorrect because AAP specifically recommends repeated screening through the 6-month well-child visit.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AAP recommends routine repeated postpartum depression screening with a validated tool at 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits to identify parents who may need further evaluation, treatment, referral, and support for the parent-infant dyad.
candidates.source_document_title: Incorporating Recognition and Management of Perinatal Depression Into Pediatric Practice; Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule; Integrating Postpartum Depression Screening in Your Practice in 4 Steps
candidates.source_locator: AAP Clinical Report — Recommendations: routine PPD screening should be integrated into well-child visits at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months; screening should use a validated tool and positive findings should lead to intervention/referral. AAP Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule — Maternal Depression Screening: screening at 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month visits. AAP implementation guidance — Screening: birth parent should be screened at the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-infant visits using a validated tool.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: recognize changes in psychosocial functioning, assess clients experiencing stress or mental-health symptoms, provide therapeutic support, and facilitate appropriate referrals.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — recognition of childbirth-related PTSD and referral for assessment/support
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize persistent trauma-specific intrusion, avoidance, and hyperarousal symptoms after a traumatic birth as possible childbirth-related PTSD and facilitate timely mental health assessment and support without confusing the presentation with postpartum blues or psychosis.

options.A: The pattern is consistent with possible childbirth-related posttraumatic stress disorder and warrants further mental health assessment and support.
options.B: The symptoms represent uncomplicated postpartum blues and require only reassurance because trauma-focused assessment would be unnecessary.
options.C: The symptoms establish postpartum psychosis because any severe distress after birth indicates impaired reality testing.
options.D: The symptoms are an expected response to emergency delivery and should not be assessed unless they persist beyond the first postpartum year.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ACOG recognizes that a traumatic birth experience can result in postpartum posttraumatic stress disorder and recommends attention to psychological well-being as part of postpartum care. The client's recurrent intrusive memories/nightmares, avoidance of trauma reminders, hyperarousal/startle symptoms, persistence beyond one month, distress, and functional interference match major PTSD symptom domains and warrant further assessment rather than dismissal. B is incorrect because postpartum blues does not adequately explain this persistent trauma-specific pattern. C is incorrect because postpartum psychosis involves severe disturbance in reality testing such as delusions or hallucinations; those findings are not present here. D is incorrect because clinically significant trauma symptoms should be addressed when identified rather than deferred for months. A screening result or symptom pattern does not by itself replace a formal diagnostic evaluation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Traumatic childbirth can be followed by postpartum PTSD; persistent intrusion, avoidance and hyperarousal symptoms lasting beyond one month and causing functional impairment should prompt further mental health assessment and support rather than routine reassurance.
candidates.source_document_title: Optimizing Postpartum Care; Implementing Perinatal Mental Health Screening; PTSD Basics / PTSD and DSM-5
candidates.source_locator: ACOG Optimizing Postpartum Care — Comprehensive Postpartum Visit: traumatic birth experience can cause postpartum PTSD and postpartum care should assess psychological well-being. ACOG Implementing Perinatal Mental Health Screening — screening tools include PTSD instruments and all perinatal patients should receive mental-health screening. VA National Center for PTSD, PTSD Basics/PTSD and DSM-5: symptom domains include intrusion/re-experiencing, avoidance, negative cognition/mood, and hyperarousal; PTSD requires symptoms lasting more than one month with clinically significant distress or functional impairment.
candidates.source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG); U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs National Center for PTSD
candidates.source_version_date: ACOG Committee Opinion No. 736, May 2018, current page accessed 2026-08-17; ACOG perinatal mental-health implementation page current 2026; VA National Center for PTSD current pages updated 2025-2026
candidates.stem: Six weeks after an emergency birth that the client describes as terrifying, the client reports recurrent unwanted memories and nightmares about the delivery, avoids reminders of the hospital, is easily startled, and says these symptoms interfere with sleep and daily functioning. candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: provide therapeutic communication, recognize and support grief and loss, respect cultural and spiritual preferences, and facilitate psychosocial resources for clients and families.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — individualized bereavement care after perinatal loss
candidates.educational_objective: Provide person-centered bereavement care after stillbirth by acknowledging the loss, individualizing support to family preferences and cultural or religious needs, offering opportunities for contact and memory-making if desired, and facilitating ongoing support resources.

options.A: Offer individualized emotional support, ask about cultural or religious preferences, and give the parents the option to spend time with and hold the baby if they wish.
options.B: Use the same predetermined bereavement plan for every family so that emotionally difficult decisions are removed from the parents.
options.C: Avoid mentioning or acknowledging the baby unless the parents initiate the conversation because discussing the loss may intensify grief.
options.D: Move the family away from the maternity setting immediately and minimize staff contact so they can begin grieving without clinical involvement.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ACOG recommends individualized bereavement care after stillbirth that recognizes each family's personal, cultural, and religious needs, includes clear communication and ongoing emotional support, and gives parents the opportunity to hold the baby and participate in cultural or religious activities if desired. B is incorrect because grief responses and preferences vary and bereavement care should not be standardized into one inflexible approach. C is incorrect because sensitive acknowledgment, communication, and recognition of parenthood are components of bereavement care. D is incorrect because families may benefit from ongoing emotional and practical support and referral to bereavement, peer-support, or mental-health resources; staff should not withdraw solely because a loss has occurred.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Bereavement care after stillbirth should be individualized, compassionate, culturally responsive, communicative, and supportive; parents should be offered opportunities to hold the baby or participate in meaningful activities if they desire rather than having one response imposed on them.
candidates.source_document_title: Management of Stillbirth; Supporting Patients Through Stillbirth Care: Toolkit for Health Care Professionals
candidates.source_locator: Management of Stillbirth — 'What support services and clinical counseling should be offered to the patient with a stillbirth?': emotional support, individualized bereavement care recognizing personal/cultural/religious needs, good communication, shared decision making, recognition of parenthood, ongoing emotional/practical support, and referral when advisable. Evaluation/Autopsy section: parents should be given the opportunity to hold the baby and perform cultural or religious activities. Supporting Patients Through Stillbirth Care toolkit — Overview/Conversations at Points of Care: no single standard approach; care should be personalized, compassionate, and adapted to unique needs and circumstances, with emotional support and remembrance options.
candidates.source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
candidates.source_version_date: ACOG Obstetric Care Consensus No. 10, March 2020, current page accessed 2026-08-17; ACOG stillbirth-care toolkit current page accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of pharmacologic principles, therapeutic response, medication effectiveness, and factors that can alter antimicrobial treatment response.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antimicrobial resistance mechanisms and treatment response
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that bacterial antibiotic resistance can arise through multiple microbial defense mechanisms—reduced entry, efflux, drug inactivation, target alteration, or pathway bypass—and that resistance belongs to the microorganism rather than the client's body.

options.A: Bacteria may restrict drug entry, pump the drug out, enzymatically change or destroy it, alter its target, or bypass the drug's effect.
options.B: Antibiotic resistance occurs because the client's body becomes resistant to the medication rather than because the microorganism changes.
options.C: All resistant bacteria use the same defense mechanism, so identifying the antibiotic class predicts the exact resistance mechanism.
options.D: Resistance develops only after a bacterium has personally been exposed to the antibiotic; resistance traits cannot spread between microorganisms.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes several antimicrobial-resistance mechanisms, including restricting antibiotic access, pumping the drug out, changing or destroying the drug with enzymes, changing the drug target, and bypassing the drug's effects. B is incorrect because antimicrobial resistance refers to the germ's ability to defeat the drug; it does not mean the patient's body has become resistant. C is incorrect because microorganisms can use multiple different resistance mechanisms. D is incorrect because resistance traits encoded in microbial DNA can spread to other germs, including germs that were not themselves exposed to the antimicrobial. Appropriate antibiotic use helps limit selection pressure and spread, but antibiotic exposure is not the only way a resistant organism can acquire a resistance trait.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Bacteria can resist antibiotics through several distinct microbial mechanisms, including reduced access, efflux, enzymatic drug modification/destruction, target alteration, and pathway bypass; resistance traits can spread between germs and do not represent resistance of the patient's body.
candidates.source_document_title: About Antimicrobial Resistance; How Antimicrobial Resistance Happens
candidates.source_locator: About Antimicrobial Resistance — 'How antimicrobial resistance happens' and 'Spread of germs and resistance mechanisms': resistance mechanisms include restricting antibiotic access, getting rid of antibiotics through pumps, changing or destroying antibiotics with enzymes, changing antibiotic targets, and bypassing antibiotic effects; resistant germs can share resistance mechanisms with other germs. '5 things to know': antimicrobial resistance means germs defeat antimicrobial drugs; it does not mean the body is resistant to them. How Antimicrobial Resistance Happens — At a glance: drug resistance occurs when bacteria no longer respond to the drug designed to kill them.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: About Antimicrobial Resistance dated January 31, 2025; How Antimicrobial Resistance Happens dated April 2, 2026; current pages accessed 2026-08-17
candidates.stem: A nursing student asks how bacteria can remain viable despite exposure to an antibiotic that previously inhibited them. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of medication mechanisms, therapeutic use, effectiveness, adverse effects, and safe administration.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — piperacillin-tazobactam mechanism and antimicrobial stewardship
candidates.educational_objective: Describe piperacillin-tazobactam as a penicillin-class antibacterial plus beta-lactamase inhibitor: piperacillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases and does not eliminate the need to use susceptibility information when available.

options.A: Piperacillin inhibits bacterial cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases that can inactivate beta-lactam antibiotics.
options.B: Tazobactam is the primary bactericidal component, while piperacillin mainly prevents renal elimination of tazobactam.
options.C: The combination is an antiviral regimen whose activity depends on blocking viral nucleic-acid replication.
options.D: Tazobactam eliminates all clinically important beta-lactamase-mediated resistance, so culture and susceptibility data do not affect therapy.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current DailyMed prescribing information states that piperacillin exerts bactericidal activity by inhibiting bacterial septum formation and cell-wall synthesis, while tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor with little clinically relevant antibacterial activity by itself. B reverses the roles of the two components. C is incorrect because piperacillin-tazobactam is an antibacterial combination, not an antiviral drug. D is incorrect because tazobactam inhibits specified classes of beta-lactamases rather than every resistance mechanism, and the label directs clinicians to consider culture and susceptibility information when available when selecting or modifying therapy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Piperacillin provides bactericidal cell-wall synthesis inhibition, while tazobactam inhibits certain beta-lactamases; the combination remains subject to organism susceptibility and culture-guided modification when data are available.
candidates.source_document_title: Piperacillin and Tazobactam for Injection, Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Section 1 Indications and Usage: combination of piperacillin, a penicillin-class antibacterial, and tazobactam, a beta-lactamase inhibitor; Section 1.6 Usage: consider culture and susceptibility information when available. Section 12.4 Microbiology — Mechanism of Action: piperacillin inhibits septum formation and cell-wall synthesis; tazobactam has little clinically relevant antibacterial activity itself and inhibits specified beta-lactamases.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
candidates.source_version_date: Current DailyMed professional label with recent major change September 2024; current label accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply medication knowledge to safe antimicrobial therapy, evaluate medication effectiveness, and support appropriate medication use.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — antimicrobial stewardship and carbapenem conservation
candidates.educational_objective: Apply antimicrobial stewardship by using infection site and susceptibility data to select an effective preferred agent and conserving carbapenems when narrower recommended therapy is active, rather than treating ESBL status alone as an automatic indication for meropenem.

options.A: Nitrofurantoin is a preferred option; although carbapenems can be effective, avoiding them when an effective narrower option is available helps preserve their activity for infections with fewer treatment choices.
options.B: Meropenem should be preferred whenever an ESBL-producing organism is identified, regardless of infection site or susceptibility to other recommended agents.
options.C: Carbapenems have no activity against ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, so meropenem susceptibility should be considered a laboratory error.
options.D: Once ESBL production is identified, antimicrobial susceptibility results no longer influence antibiotic selection.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current IDSA 2026 antimicrobial-resistance guidance lists nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole as preferred options for uncomplicated cystitis caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales when active. Carbapenems can be effective alternatives, but their use is discouraged when an effective preferred option is available because limiting carbapenem use preserves their activity for future infections in which treatment options may be more restricted. B overgeneralizes carbapenem use without considering infection site and other susceptible agents. C is false because ESBL-producing Enterobacterales generally remain susceptible to carbapenems. D is incorrect because the IDSA guidance assumes in-vitro activity of selected agents and repeatedly uses susceptibility results to guide therapy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis with nitrofurantoin susceptibility, nitrofurantoin is preferred and carbapenem use should generally be conserved; ESBL status does not replace infection-site and susceptibility-guided antimicrobial selection.
candidates.source_document_title: IDSA 2026 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial Resistant Gram-Negative Infections; Meropenem for Injection Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance — Section 1, ESBL-producing Enterobacterales, Question 1.1: nitrofurantoin and TMP-SMX are preferred for uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis; fluoroquinolones and carbapenems are effective alternatives but their use is discouraged when preferred agents are active because limiting them preserves activity for future infections. Section 1 introduction: ESBL-E generally remain susceptible to carbapenems and treatment suggestions assume in-vitro activity. DailyMed Meropenem — Section 1 Usage: use for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria.
candidates.source_organization: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA); U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
candidates.source_version_date: IDSA 2026 AMR Guidance published July 27, 2026; DailyMed meropenem label updated November 14, 2025; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of medication indications, therapeutic effects, and safe antimicrobial therapy.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ceftriaxone use in bacterial meningitis
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize ceftriaxone as an antibacterial with an FDA-labeled role in meningitis caused by specified susceptible organisms and understand that empiric therapy should be reassessed as culture and susceptibility data become available.

options.A: Ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin antibacterial with an FDA-labeled indication for meningitis caused by susceptible Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, or Streptococcus pneumoniae.
options.B: Ceftriaxone is not used for central nervous system infections because therapeutic drug concentrations cannot be achieved in cerebrospinal fluid.
options.C: Ceftriaxone is an antiviral agent and is selected when viral meningitis is the leading diagnosis.
options.D: Once ceftriaxone is started, culture and susceptibility information should not be used to modify therapy.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling lists ceftriaxone as indicated for meningitis caused by susceptible H. influenzae, N. meningitidis, or S. pneumoniae. B is incorrect because the drug is specifically labeled for meningitis and the label documents measurable cerebrospinal-fluid concentrations. C is incorrect because ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin antibacterial, not an antiviral. D is incorrect because the label directs clinicians to consider culture and susceptibility information when available when selecting or modifying antibacterial therapy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ceftriaxone is a cephalosporin antibacterial FDA-labeled for meningitis caused by specified susceptible organisms; culture and susceptibility results should inform modification of therapy.
candidates.source_document_title: Ceftriaxone for Injection, USP Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Section 1 Indications and Usage: use for infections caused by susceptible bacteria and consider culture/susceptibility data when available. Section 1.8 Meningitis: indication for meningitis caused by Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, or Streptococcus pneumoniae. Clinical Pharmacology/CSF data document ceftriaxone concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: provide medication education and recognize adverse effects and precautions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Doxycycline adverse-effect teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients taking doxycycline that photosensitivity may cause exaggerated sunburn and that direct sunlight or ultraviolet exposure should be limited according to the product warning.

options.A: Doxycycline can cause photosensitivity with an exaggerated sunburn reaction.
options.B: Doxycycline predictably causes permanent skin discoloration in every client exposed to sunlight.
options.C: Sunlight prevents doxycycline absorption, so exposure makes each dose ineffective.
options.D: The advice is only for comfort because doxycycline has no clinically important skin or light-related adverse effects.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current DailyMed labeling warns that tetracyclines, including doxycycline, can cause photosensitivity manifested by an exaggerated sunburn reaction and advises limiting sun exposure. B overstates tissue hyperpigmentation as universal and sun-dependent. C is not a labeled mechanism. D contradicts the photosensitivity warning.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Doxycycline can cause photosensitivity with exaggerated sunburn reactions and patients should limit sun exposure.
candidates.source_document_title: Doxycycline Hyclate Delayed-Release Tablets Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Warnings and Precautions, Section 5.3 Photosensitivity: photosensitivity manifested by an exaggerated sunburn reaction has been observed with tetracyclines; limit sun exposure. Adverse Reactions also lists photosensitivity.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Medication allergy and TMP-SMX contraindication
candidates.educational_objective: Before administering trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, identify prior hypersensitivity to sulfamethoxazole or other sulfonamide antibacterial components as a contraindication and hold/clarify the medication rather than performing a supervised rechallenge independently.

options.A: Hold the medication and clarify the prescription because known hypersensitivity to sulfonamides is a contraindication.
options.B: Administer the medication because the trimethoprim component prevents sulfonamide hypersensitivity.
options.C: Administer the first dose and monitor because prior anaphylaxis is only a concern with nonantibiotic sulfonamides.
options.D: Give the medication with food because food prevents recurrence of sulfonamide hypersensitivity.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current DailyMed labeling lists known hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or sulfonamides as a contraindication to sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim. A prior anaphylactic reaction to sulfamethoxazole directly meets that contraindication, so the nurse should not administer the dose until the prescription is clarified. B, C, and D do not remove the labeled hypersensitivity risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Known hypersensitivity to sulfamethoxazole/sulfonamides is a labeled contraindication to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

candidates.source_locator: Contraindications: sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim is contraindicated with known hypersensitivity to trimethoprim or sulfonamides. Warnings: serious and potentially fatal hypersensitivity reactions have been reported.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: understand medication indications, effectiveness, and safe antimicrobial selection.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Nitrofurantoin for uncomplicated cystitis
candidates.educational_objective: Use nitrofurantoin appropriately for susceptible uncomplicated lower urinary infection and avoid extrapolating its role to invasive or renal-parenchymal infection.

options.A: Nitrofurantoin is a preferred oral option for uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis when active, whereas broader agents such as carbapenems can often be conserved for more complicated or invasive infections.
options.B: Nitrofurantoin is preferred because it reliably treats bloodstream infection and renal-parenchymal infection from ESBL-E.
options.C: Nitrofurantoin should be selected regardless of susceptibility testing because urinary isolates cannot develop resistance to it.
options.D: Nitrofurantoin is mainly a respiratory antibiotic and its use for cystitis is off-label.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current IDSA 2026 AMR guidance lists nitrofurantoin as a preferred treatment option for uncomplicated cystitis caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales when appropriate. The same guidance suggests reserving carbapenems and several broader agents for complicated UTI or invasive ESBL-E infection when effective uncomplicated-cystitis options are available. B overstates nitrofurantoin's role beyond lower urinary infection. C ignores the need to consider organism susceptibility and clinical context. D is false; nitrofurantoin is an established urinary antibacterial.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Nitrofurantoin is a preferred option for susceptible uncomplicated ESBL-E cystitis and should not be generalized as therapy for invasive ESBL-E infection.
candidates.source_document_title: IDSA 2026 Guidance on the Treatment of Antimicrobial Resistant Gram-Negative Infections
candidates.source_locator: Section 1, Question 1.1: nitrofurantoin is a preferred option for uncomplicated cystitis caused by ESBL-E; broader agents including carbapenems are typically effective but are suggested to be reserved for cUTI and other invasive ESBL-E infections when effective uUTI alternatives exist. Treatment suggestions assume in-vitro activity of selected agents.
candidates.source_organization: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA)

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: evaluate medication orders, prepare/administer medications safely, and provide medication education.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — fosfomycin administration teaching
candidates.educational_objective: Teach correct administration of oral fosfomycin tromethamine for acute uncomplicated cystitis: one prescribed sachet is dissolved in water and taken as a single oral dose rather than repeated daily or swallowed dry.

options.A: Dissolve the contents of one prescribed sachet in water and take it as a single oral dose.
options.B: Take one sachet every day until urinary symptoms completely resolve.
options.C: Swallow the dry granules directly because mixing with water reduces absorption.
options.D: Expect the medication to be administered only by intravenous infusion for uncomplicated cystitis.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current DailyMed labeling states that for women 18 years of age and older with uncomplicated urinary tract infection (acute cystitis), the recommended dose is one sachet of fosfomycin tromethamine granules for oral solution. The contents must be dissolved in water and taken orally. The label also warns not to use repeated daily doses for a single episode because repeated dosing did not improve clinical or microbiologic success and increased adverse events. B therefore gives an unsupported multidose regimen. C contradicts the preparation instructions. D is incorrect because this labeled product is an oral granule formulation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For labeled treatment of acute uncomplicated cystitis in adult women, fosfomycin tromethamine granules are administered as one oral sachet dissolved in water; repeated daily dosing for the same episode is not recommended.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — amphotericin B toxicity monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: During conventional amphotericin B therapy, monitor renal function and electrolytes—especially potassium and magnesium—because nephrotoxicity and electrolyte disturbances are important treatment risks.

options.A: Monitor renal function frequently and monitor serum electrolytes, especially potassium and magnesium.
options.B: Monitor only hepatic enzymes because clinically important renal effects are not associated with amphotericin B.
options.C: Monitor serum glucose alone because amphotericin B toxicity is primarily caused by hyperglycemia.
options.D: Stop routine laboratory monitoring after the first tolerated infusion because cumulative renal toxicity is not a concern.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current DailyMed label for conventional amphotericin B recommends frequent monitoring of renal function and regular monitoring of serum electrolytes, particularly potassium and magnesium. Renal adverse effects include decreased renal function, azotemia, renal tubular abnormalities, acute renal failure, and electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. B, C, and D omit the major labeled renal and electrolyte risks. Monitoring should continue throughout therapy and results are used to guide dosage decisions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Conventional amphotericin B can cause clinically important renal dysfunction and electrolyte abnormalities, requiring frequent renal-function monitoring and regular potassium/magnesium monitoring during therapy.
candidates.source_document_title: Amphotericin B for Injection, USP Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Precautions — General: frequent monitoring of renal function is recommended because of nephrotoxicity risk. Precautions — Laboratory Tests: monitor renal function frequently and regularly monitor serum electrolytes, particularly magnesium and potassium; laboratory results should guide subsequent dosage adjustment. Adverse Reactions — Renal/Altered Laboratory Findings: decreased renal function, azotemia, acute renal failure, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia are reported.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — voriconazole visual adverse effects
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize abnormal vision, color-perception changes, and photophobia as labeled voriconazole adverse effects and ensure visual-function monitoring when treatment extends beyond 28 days.

options.A: These are recognized voriconazole-associated visual disturbances; if therapy continues beyond 28 days, visual function should be monitored.
options.B: These findings indicate an expected improvement in visual acuity and require no further assessment.
options.C: These findings prove irreversible blindness and require the nurse to tell the client that vision loss will be permanent.
options.D: These findings are unrelated to voriconazole because the medication has no labeled visual adverse effects.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current DailyMed labeling states that voriconazole-associated visual disturbances are common and can include abnormal vision, color-vision changes, and photophobia. The label also reports prolonged visual adverse reactions such as optic neuritis and papilledema and directs monitoring of visual acuity, visual field, and color perception if treatment continues beyond 28 days. B and D contradict the label. C overstates the prognosis; the label does not say that these symptoms prove permanent blindness, and a controlled 28-day study showed retinal and visual changes returning to normal after therapy ended, while prolonged postmarketing events have also been reported.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Voriconazole can cause visual disturbances including abnormal/color vision and photophobia; treatment beyond 28 days requires monitoring of visual function, and visual symptoms should not be characterized as uniformly permanent or benign.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: use measures that reduce infection-related risk and support safe evidence-based care; related activities include infection prevention and quality/safety practices.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hospital antibiotic stewardship
candidates.educational_objective: Describe hospital antibiotic stewardship as a patient-safety and resistance-prevention system that measures antibiotic use, implements evidence-based prescribing interventions, and tracks outcomes rather than simply maximizing or minimizing antibiotic exposure.

options.A: Measure antibiotic use and resistance, implement interventions such as audit-and-feedback or preauthorization, and improve appropriate antibiotic use to protect patients and combat antimicrobial resistance.
options.B: Increase broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing for all admitted clients so treatment begins before an indication is established.
options.C: Eliminate antibiotic therapy whenever possible, including for infections in which antibiotics provide a clear clinical benefit.
options.D: Limit stewardship activities to outpatient settings because inpatient antibiotic prescribing is outside the CDC Core Elements.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC defines antibiotic stewardship as the effort to measure and improve how antibiotics are prescribed and used. Its hospital Core Elements include action strategies such as prospective audit and feedback or preauthorization, tracking of antibiotic prescribing and outcomes including resistance patterns and C. difficile infection, reporting, and education. The goal is appropriate antibiotic use that improves patient care and combats antimicrobial resistance—not indiscriminate expansion or elimination of antibiotic therapy. D is incorrect because CDC has a specific hospital stewardship framework applicable to hospitals of all sizes.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hospital antibiotic stewardship programs measure and improve antibiotic use through structured interventions, tracking, reporting and education to improve patient care, reduce avoidable antibiotic harms, and combat antimicrobial resistance.
candidates.source_document_title: Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs; Core Elements of Antibiotic Stewardship
candidates.source_locator: Hospital Core Elements — At a glance/Overview: hospital programs promote appropriate antibiotic use to improve patient care and combat antimicrobial resistance. Action: use interventions such as prospective audit and feedback or preauthorization. Tracking: monitor antibiotic prescribing, intervention impact, C. difficile infections, and resistance patterns. Core Elements overview: stewardship is the effort to measure and improve antibiotic prescribing and use to advance patient safety and outcomes.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: CDC pages dated September 15, 2025 and September 10, 2025; current pages accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: obtain specimens using appropriate infection-related procedures and support timely evidence-based management of suspected infection.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — culture collection and antimicrobial sequencing in sepsis
candidates.educational_objective: In suspected adult sepsis, obtain blood cultures promptly and ideally before antimicrobials while ensuring that diagnostic sampling does not create avoidable delay in emergency treatment; use resulting microbiology to refine therapy.

options.A: Collect the blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before the first antimicrobial dose, while avoiding unnecessary delay of emergency sepsis treatment.
options.B: Delay antimicrobial therapy until final blood-culture identification and susceptibility results are available.
options.C: Give the first antimicrobial dose before collecting blood cultures because prior antibiotic exposure improves culture yield.
options.D: Cancel the blood cultures once empiric antibiotics are ordered because culture results no longer affect treatment decisions.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign adult guideline recommends collecting blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobial therapy in adults with possible, probable, or definite sepsis or septic shock. The same guideline emphasizes that sepsis and septic shock are medical emergencies and treatment and resuscitation should begin immediately. B is unsafe because definitive culture results are not required before empiric treatment when sepsis warrants antimicrobials. C reverses the recommended order and antibiotic exposure can reduce microbiologic recovery. D is incorrect because microbiologic diagnosis and susceptibility results support later antimicrobial de-escalation or narrowing.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For adults with suspected or confirmed sepsis, blood cultures should be collected promptly and ideally before antimicrobials, without allowing diagnostic sampling to undermine immediate emergency management; microbiology should later guide de-escalation.
candidates.source_document_title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
candidates.source_locator: Diagnostics — Blood culture recommendation: for adults with possible, probable, or definite sepsis or septic shock, collect blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before administration of antimicrobial therapy. Fluid resuscitation/initial management good-practice statement: sepsis and septic shock are medical emergencies and treatment/resuscitation should begin immediately. Antimicrobial therapy: de-escalate/narrow therapy when microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility profile are available.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: support evidence-based infection management and practices that reduce avoidable antimicrobial exposure and infection-related risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — antimicrobial de-escalation
candidates.educational_objective: When microbiology identifies a susceptible pathogen in sepsis, support antimicrobial de-escalation by discontinuing unnecessary agents or narrowing therapy rather than continuing avoidable broad empiric coverage.

options.A: Discontinue unnecessary agents or narrow the regimen to therapy directed at the identified susceptible pathogen.
options.B: Continue every empiric antimicrobial for the full course even when culture data show that several agents are unnecessary.
options.C: Broaden therapy further after susceptibility results identify a narrower active option.
options.D: Ignore microbiology results because de-escalation is recommended only when cultures remain negative.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends antimicrobial de-escalation when a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility profile are available. The guideline defines de-escalation as discontinuing unnecessary antimicrobial therapy or narrowing the spectrum when appropriate. B and C do the opposite of de-escalation. D is incorrect because the strongest de-escalation recommendation specifically applies when microbiologic diagnosis and susceptibility are available; the guideline also separately suggests de-escalation in selected culture-negative cases.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current adult sepsis guidance recommends antimicrobial de-escalation after microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility data, using discontinuation of unnecessary agents or spectrum narrowing as appropriate.
candidates.source_document_title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
candidates.source_locator: Antimicrobial Therapy recommendation: for adults with sepsis or septic shock, recommend de-escalation over no de-escalation when a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility profile are available. Remarks: de-escalation involves discontinuing unnecessary antimicrobial therapy or narrowing antimicrobial spectrum where appropriate. Separate conditional recommendation supports de-escalation even when no pathogens are identified on final cultures.
candidates.source_organization: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine, Surviving Sepsis Campaign
candidates.source_version_date: Published March 23, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: use infection-control and microbiologic information to support safe, evidence-based care and antimicrobial stewardship.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — interpreting facility antibiograms
candidates.educational_objective: Use the hospital antibiogram as an aggregate summary of local organism-antibiotic susceptibility patterns to inform empiric therapy while still incorporating infection site, patient factors, and patient-specific culture/susceptibility results when available.

options.A: Aggregate local susceptibility percentages for organism-antimicrobial combinations that can help guide empiric antibiotic selection.
options.B: The current patient's individual allergy history and prior adverse drug reactions.
options.C: A definitive susceptibility result for the current patient's infecting organism before that organism has been cultured.
options.D: Hospital medication acquisition costs without microbiologic susceptibility information.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's NHSN Antimicrobial Resistance guidance describes a facility-wide antibiogram as a table of calculated percent susceptible values for organism-antimicrobial combinations and states that antibiogram data can be used to guide empirical antimicrobial therapy. B is patient-specific history, not antibiogram data. C overstates what aggregate surveillance can provide; the antibiogram does not replace patient-specific culture and susceptibility testing. D describes financial information rather than a microbiology susceptibility summary.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A hospital antibiogram summarizes aggregate local antimicrobial susceptibility percentages and can inform empiric antimicrobial selection, but it is not an individual patient's susceptibility test.
candidates.source_document_title: FAQs: Antimicrobial Resistance (AR) Option; MDRO Management — Summary of Recommendations
candidates.source_locator: NHSN AR Option FAQ Q9: facility-wide antibiogram displays calculated percent susceptible (%S) for each organism-antimicrobial combination; NHSN/CLSI antibiograms can be used to guide selection of empirical antimicrobial therapy. MDRO Management V.A.3.a: hospitals and LTCFs should review local susceptibility patterns (antibiograms) to foster appropriate antimicrobial use.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), National Healthcare Safety Network
candidates.source_version_date: CDC NHSN AR FAQ dated 2025/current page accessed 2026-08-17; MDRO recommendations current page accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: maintain specimen integrity, use proper infection-related collection practices, and participate in safety/quality improvement.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — blood-culture contamination quality monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret a lower blood-culture contamination rate as evidence of fewer probable contamination events and improved collection quality, while recognizing that contamination monitoring does not by itself prove perfect bloodstream-infection detection.

options.A: Fewer cultures are being classified as probable contaminants, which supports improved collection quality and reduces the risk of false-positive results leading to unnecessary antibiotics.
options.B: The lower contamination rate proves that all bloodstream infections are now being detected correctly and no other collection-quality measures are needed.
options.C: The rate is unrelated to preanalytic collection practices and therefore has little value for quality improvement.
options.D: A lower contamination rate means fewer true bloodstream infections are being diagnosed and indicates that cultures should be collected less carefully.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies blood-culture contamination rate as a patient-safety and laboratory-quality measure used to monitor collection practices. Contamination by skin commensals can produce false-positive results that lead to unnecessary antibiotic therapy and prolonged hospitalization. CDC states that monitoring contamination and single-set rates helps reveal gaps in blood-culture collection and supports improvement of standardized practices. B overclaims what one quality metric can prove. C contradicts CDC's quality-measure purpose. D confuses contamination with true bacteremia.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Blood-culture contamination rate is a quality measure of probable contamination events and collection practices; reducing contamination reduces false-positive risk and avoidable antibiotic exposure, but the metric does not prove complete diagnostic accuracy by itself.
candidates.source_document_title: Prevent Adult Blood Culture Contamination; Primary Measure: Blood Culture Contamination Rate; Report and Take Action
candidates.source_locator: Prevent Adult Blood Culture Contamination — Why it is important: skin commensals can cause false-positive cultures leading to unnecessary antibiotic therapy and prolonged hospitalization; best practices improve diagnosis and reduce contamination. Primary Measure — Overview: BCC rate calculates the relative incidence of contaminated blood cultures and is important for maintaining quality practices. Report and Take Action — monitoring BCC and single-set rates provides insight into collection practices and reveals gaps requiring mitigation.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Division of Laboratory Systems
candidates.source_version_date: CDC quality-tool pages current through March 31, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: use aseptic technique, maintain invasive devices safely, and implement measures to prevent healthcare-associated infection.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — CAUTI prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Prevent CAUTI by limiting indwelling catheter use to valid indications, maintaining a continuously closed and unobstructed drainage system, and reassessing daily for prompt removal rather than using routine antimicrobial prophylaxis or unnecessary system disconnections.

options.A: Verify that a valid indication remains, maintain an intact closed drainage system with unobstructed flow, and remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed.
options.B: Disconnect the drainage tubing daily for routine cleaning and reconnect it after the tubing has air-dried.
options.C: Continue the catheter for staff convenience when the client is incontinent even if no other clinical indication remains.
options.D: Use routine systemic antibiotics and antiseptic meatal cleaning while the catheter remains in place to prevent bacteriuria.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends inserting urinary catheters only for appropriate indications, leaving them in place only as long as needed, maintaining a closed drainage system after aseptic insertion, keeping urine flow unobstructed, and using quality-improvement processes such as daily review to identify catheters that can be removed. B breaks the closed system without a clinical indication. C is specifically listed as inappropriate catheter use when the catheter substitutes for incontinence care. D is incorrect because CDC does not recommend routine systemic antimicrobials for CAUTI prevention and recommends routine hygiene rather than antiseptic periurethral cleaning while the catheter is in place.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CAUTI prevention requires appropriate catheter indication, aseptic insertion, maintenance of a closed unobstructed drainage system, and prompt removal when no longer needed; routine antimicrobial prophylaxis and antiseptic meatal cleaning are not recommended.
candidates.source_document_title: Clinical Safety: Preventing Catheter-associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTIs); Guideline for Prevention of Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infections — Summary of Recommendations
candidates.source_locator: Clinical Safety recommendations: use urinary catheters only when needed, place using aseptic technique/sterile equipment, maintain the closed sterile drainage system, and remove as soon as no longer needed. Summary of Recommendations I.A: insert only for appropriate indications and leave only as long as needed; III.A and III.B: maintain a closed drainage system and unobstructed urine flow; III.F and III.G: do not routinely use systemic antimicrobials or antiseptic periurethral cleaning for CAUTI prevention; IV.A: use QI strategies including daily review of continued need and removal of unnecessary catheters.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: implement measures to prevent healthcare-associated infection and maintain clients receiving invasive respiratory support safely.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — VAP prevention and positioning
candidates.educational_objective: For mechanically ventilated adults without a contraindication, use 30–45-degree head-of-bed elevation as one component of VAP-prevention care while avoiding unsupported claims that this intervention alone reduces mortality or duration of ventilation.

options.A: Maintain head-of-bed elevation at approximately 30–45 degrees as an essential prevention practice.
options.B: Keep the client routinely supine because head-of-bed elevation has been shown to increase VAP rates.
options.C: Elevate the head of the bed only after VAP is diagnosed because positioning is a treatment rather than a prevention measure.
options.D: Use head-of-bed elevation as a substitute for other ventilator-prevention practices because it has been proven to reduce mortality and ventilation duration by itself.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current SHEA/IDSA/APIC acute-care prevention guidance lists head-of-bed elevation to 30–45 degrees as an essential practice for mechanically ventilated adults. The supporting meta-analysis found an association with lower VAP rates, but evidence quality was low and the guidance notes no demonstrated difference in duration of mechanical ventilation or mortality. B and C contradict the prevention recommendation. D overstates the evidence and incorrectly treats one prevention measure as a replacement for a broader ventilator-safety strategy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Head-of-bed elevation to 30–45 degrees is an essential VAP/VAE prevention practice for mechanically ventilated adults, with evidence suggesting lower VAP rates but not proven mortality or ventilation-duration benefit.
candidates.source_document_title: Strategies to Prevent Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia, Ventilator-Associated Events, and Nonventilator Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia in Acute-Care Hospitals: 2022 Update; CDC Management and Prevention Guidelines
candidates.source_locator: 2022 Update, Section 4 — Recommended strategies to prevent VAP/VAE in adult patients, 'Elevate the head of the bed': elevate head of bed to 30–45 degrees, Quality of Evidence LOW; meta-analysis found lower VAP rates but no difference in mechanical-ventilation duration or mortality. CDC Management and Prevention Guidelines — Healthcare-acquired pneumonia: lists the SHEA/IDSA Strategies to Prevent VAP 2022 Update as current prevention guidance.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: perform hand hygiene and implement Standard Precautions to prevent transmission of infectious agents.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — hand hygiene and MDRO transmission
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that hand hygiene helps control antimicrobial resistance by interrupting transmission of resistant organisms, while antimicrobial stewardship separately addresses unnecessary or suboptimal antimicrobial exposure.

options.A: Hand hygiene reduces person-to-person transmission of germs, including antimicrobial-resistant organisms, and works alongside antimicrobial stewardship.
options.B: Hand hygiene directly reverses bacterial resistance genes after the organism contacts alcohol-based sanitizer.
options.C: Hand hygiene replaces the need for antimicrobial stewardship because transmission control alone prevents resistance from developing.
options.D: Hand hygiene has little effect on resistant-organism spread because MDRO transmission occurs independently of healthcare workers' hands.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC states that cleaning hands reduces the spread of germs, including those resistant to antibiotics, and identifies healthcare workers' hands as an important route of MDRO transmission. Infection prevention and antimicrobial stewardship address different parts of the resistance problem and are complementary. B is incorrect because hand hygiene removes or kills organisms; it does not genetically reverse resistance. C is incorrect because CDC separately emphasizes preventing spread and improving antibiotic/antifungal use. D contradicts CDC evidence that MDROs can be carried from one person to another via healthcare personnel's hands.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hand hygiene interrupts transmission of antimicrobial-resistant germs in healthcare settings and complements, rather than replaces, antimicrobial stewardship.
candidates.source_document_title: Clinical Safety: Hand Hygiene for Healthcare Workers; Epidemiology of MDROs; Antimicrobial Resistance: Causes and How It Spreads
candidates.source_locator: Clinical Safety — Why it matters: hand hygiene reduces spread of germs, including those resistant to antibiotics. MDRO Epidemiology — Important concepts in transmission: epidemiologic evidence shows MDROs are carried person-to-person via healthcare personnel's hands and hand-hygiene adherence is an important control component. AR Causes and How It Spreads — prevention requires stopping spread, slowing development, improving antimicrobial use, and preventing infections.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: CDC hand-hygiene page dated February 27, 2024; AR causes/spread page dated September 25, 2025; current pages accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members, coordinate transitions of care, and assess the need for referrals and resources.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — infectious-diseases review and discharge coordination for OPAT
candidates.educational_objective: Before a client begins OPAT, coordinate infectious-diseases expert review so the indication, antimicrobial choice, route, and outpatient plan are reassessed rather than assuming inpatient IV therapy should automatically continue after discharge.

options.A: Ensure infectious-diseases expert review occurs before OPAT is initiated.
options.B: Arrange OPAT without specialist review because the route of therapy alone determines whether outpatient treatment is appropriate.
options.C: Assume IV therapy must continue if it was started in the hospital, even when expert review identifies an effective oral alternative.
options.D: Delay all discharge planning until the entire antimicrobial course is completed in the hospital.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current IDSA OPAT guideline recommends infectious-diseases expert review before initiation of OPAT. The rationale includes antimicrobial stewardship: expert review can identify cases in which parenteral therapy is unnecessary, an oral regimen is appropriate, or antimicrobial therapy itself should be modified. B bypasses the recommended review. C incorrectly treats the inpatient IV route as fixed rather than reassessing whether OPAT is needed. D is incorrect because OPAT is specifically a model for completing appropriate parenteral therapy outside the hospital in selected patients.
candidates.source_claim_supported: IDSA recommends infectious-diseases expert review before OPAT is initiated, in part to reassess whether parenteral therapy, the selected antimicrobial, and the outpatient plan are appropriate.
candidates.source_document_title: IDSA 2018 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Outpatient Parenteral Antimicrobial Therapy
candidates.source_locator: Antimicrobial Stewardship, Question XVII, Recommendation 17: all patients should have infectious-diseases expert review prior to initiation of OPAT (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence). Rationale: expert review can curtail unnecessary OPAT and may identify patients for whom oral or no antimicrobial therapy is appropriate; ID review may occur through traditional consultation, an ID care-transition/OPAT stewardship team, or a collaborative pharmacist/ID-physician model.
