candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: identify and collaborate with multidisciplinary team members and participate in quality-improvement systems to promote safe client care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — multidisciplinary antimicrobial stewardship
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize antimicrobial stewardship as a multidisciplinary care-management function in which trained pharmacy expertise participates in program leadership, antimicrobial review, and active prescribing interventions rather than being limited to medication dispensing.

options.A: Use physician-pharmacist stewardship leadership, with trained pharmacy expertise participating in program management and interventions such as prospective audit and feedback or preauthorization.
options.B: Limit the pharmacist to medication dispensing and exclude pharmacy expertise from antimicrobial-use decisions.
options.C: Assign stewardship responsibility to nursing alone and avoid collaboration with physicians or pharmacists so accountability remains with one discipline.
options.D: Use pharmacy expertise only after an antimicrobial course is complete because stewardship interventions should not influence active prescribing.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's current Hospital Core Elements identify accountability and pharmacy expertise as core stewardship components and note that many effective programs are co-led by a physician and pharmacist. CDC also recommends active stewardship interventions such as prospective audit and feedback or preauthorization. Current 2026 multi-society guidance likewise describes stewardship as multidisciplinary and emphasizes clinical infectious-diseases, pharmacology, microbiology, quality-improvement, communication, and program-evaluation skills. B and D improperly reduce the pharmacist to a dispensing role. C conflicts with the collaborative program structure recommended by CDC.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current stewardship guidance supports active physician-pharmacist leadership and trained pharmacy participation in antimicrobial-use interventions and program management rather than a dispensing-only role.
candidates.source_document_title: Core Elements of Hospital Antibiotic Stewardship Programs; Priorities for Hospital Core Element Implementation; Guidance for the Knowledge and Skills Required for Antimicrobial Stewardship Leaders
candidates.source_locator: CDC Hospital Core Elements — Accountability/Pharmacy Expertise: appoint a leader or co-leaders such as a physician and pharmacist responsible for program management and outcomes; Action: implement prospective audit and feedback or preauthorization. CDC Priorities — Accountability: co-leadership by physician and pharmacist is an effective model; Pharmacy/Stewardship Expertise: leaders should have ID specialty, certificate, or other stewardship training. 2026 SHEA/SIDP/PIDS/IDSA Guidance — Introduction: antimicrobial stewardship is coordinated, multidisciplinary work requiring clinical ID, pharmacology, microbiology, quality-improvement, communication, and measurement skills.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: collaborate with multidisciplinary team members, participate in quality-improvement systems, and use organizational resources to promote safe client care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — role of infection-prevention program leadership
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize infection-prevention program leadership as an ongoing systems role that integrates surveillance, policy implementation, performance monitoring and feedback, and healthcare-personnel education rather than functioning only during outbreaks.

options.A: Coordinate HAI and pathogen surveillance, monitor adherence to infection-prevention practices, support current evidence-based policies, and provide or coordinate staff education and feedback.
options.B: Provide routine bedside assignments as the primary function and become involved in infection prevention only during declared outbreaks.
options.C: Track infection rates but avoid participating in policy, staff education, or performance-improvement activities because those functions belong exclusively to unit managers.
options.D: Focus only on employee illness records and exclude patient-care infection risks and healthcare-associated infections from the program.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices call for qualified personnel to manage facility infection-prevention programs. Core program activities include monitoring healthcare-associated infections and transmission, monitoring adherence to infection-prevention requirements, providing feedback, ensuring current evidence-based policies and procedures, and providing job-specific education and training. B incorrectly limits the role to outbreak response. C fragments functions that CDC treats as components of the infection-prevention program. D confuses a facility-wide infection-prevention program with occupational health alone.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A facility infection-prevention program is managed by qualified IPC personnel and includes ongoing surveillance, evidence-based policy support, staff education, monitoring of practice adherence, feedback, and response to identified transmission risks.
candidates.source_document_title: CDC's Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices for Safe Healthcare Delivery in All Settings; Isolation Precautions — Fundamental Elements Needed to Prevent Transmission
candidates.source_locator: Core Practices Table — Leadership Support: assign qualified individuals trained in infection prevention and control to manage the facility IPC program. Education and Training: provide job-specific IPC education and current evidence-based written policies/procedures. Performance Monitoring and Feedback: monitor adherence to IPC practices and infection incidence, provide regular feedback, and use surveillance to detect transmission. Isolation Precautions, Surveillance for HAIs: surveillance is an essential ongoing systematic activity for identifying infections, clusters, and indications for change.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: collaborate with multidisciplinary teams, participate in quality-improvement and safety activities, and coordinate responses to changes affecting groups of clients.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — collaborative healthcare outbreak investigation
candidates.educational_objective: Participate in outbreak response as a systematic, collaborative process of case verification and finding, descriptive and analytic epidemiology, hypothesis testing, and timely implementation of evidence-informed control measures.

options.A: Verify the diagnoses and outbreak, alert key partners, define and find cases, analyze data by person/place/time, develop and test hypotheses, and implement control measures as evidence becomes available.
options.B: Select the most likely source immediately and design all control actions around that assumption without systematic case finding or data analysis.
options.C: Wait until the cluster becomes large before beginning an investigation because smaller clusters do not warrant epidemiologic assessment.
options.D: Keep the investigation within the public-health team and avoid collaboration with facility clinicians, laboratory personnel, and infection-prevention staff.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes outbreak and healthcare-associated infection investigations as systematic, multistep processes that include verifying the diagnosis and outbreak, communicating with key partners, establishing case definitions, identifying and counting cases, organizing data by person, place, and time, formulating and testing hypotheses, implementing control measures, and communicating findings. Steps may occur concurrently, and preliminary control measures may be appropriate before the entire investigation is complete. B anchors prematurely without evidence. C is incorrect because even a single unusual healthcare-associated case can trigger a full investigation depending on the disease and setting. D conflicts with CDC's emphasis on collaboration among public-health officials, facility staff, clinicians, laboratories, and other stakeholders.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Healthcare outbreak investigations use a systematic, collaborative sequence of diagnosis/outbreak verification, case definition and finding, descriptive analysis, hypothesis development/testing, control measures, and communication; steps may overlap and smaller signals can still warrant investigation.
candidates.source_document_title: CDC Field Epidemiology Manual — Conducting a Field Investigation; Healthcare Settings
candidates.source_locator: Conducting a Field Investigation — Investigation/Ten Steps: systematic multistep approach; diagnosis/outbreak confirmation may occur together; early collaboration is important; Step 6 notes control measures can be implemented at any point and modified as evidence evolves. Healthcare Settings — Field Investigation: verify diagnosis, confirm HAI outbreak, alert key partners, establish case definitions, identify/count cases, organize person/place/time data, formulate/test hypotheses, perform infection-control assessment/control measures, follow up and communicate findings.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: understand legal/regulatory requirements and coordinate care with public-health systems when communicable-disease control measures apply.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — legal/public-health distinction between quarantine and isolation
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish quarantine, which applies to people exposed to a contagious disease who may become ill, from isolation, which separates people who are sick with a communicable disease from those who are not sick, while recognizing that legal authority varies by jurisdiction.

options.A: Quarantine separates or restricts movement of people who were exposed to a contagious disease to see whether they become ill; isolation separates people who are sick with a quarantinable communicable disease from people who are not sick.
options.B: Quarantine and isolation are legally identical terms that apply only to people with confirmed symptomatic infection.
options.C: Quarantine applies only after laboratory confirmation of infection, whereas isolation is used for people who were merely exposed.
options.D: Quarantine has no public-health legal basis in the United States and can be used only as an informal voluntary suggestion.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's current legal-authorities guidance defines quarantine as separating and restricting movement of people exposed to a contagious disease to determine whether they become sick, whereas isolation separates sick people with a quarantinable communicable disease from people who are not sick. B and C reverse or collapse the two concepts. D is incorrect because isolation and quarantine have established state and federal legal authorities; however, the exact legal authority and procedures depend on jurisdiction and circumstance.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC distinguishes quarantine as restriction of exposed persons who may become ill from isolation of sick persons; both have established public-health legal foundations, with implementation depending on applicable authority.
candidates.source_document_title: Legal Authorities for Isolation and Quarantine; Laws and Regulations Governing the Control of Communicable Diseases
candidates.source_locator: Legal Authorities for Isolation and Quarantine — Isolation and Quarantine: isolation separates sick people with a quarantinable communicable disease from people who are not sick; quarantine separates and restricts movement of people exposed to a contagious disease to see if they become sick. The page also describes isolation/quarantine as police-power functions. Laws and Regulations Governing the Control of Communicable Diseases — federal authority is implemented under Title 42 and relevant regulations, while state/local authorities also exist.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Port Health
candidates.source_version_date: Legal Authorities page dated May 15, 2024; laws/regulations page dated May 18, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: coordinate referrals and community/public-health resources, maintain confidentiality, and support continuity of care for clients and contacts.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — TB contact investigation and confidentiality
candidates.educational_objective: During a TB contact investigation, identify and evaluate exposed contacts promptly, arrange appropriate testing/follow-up, and preserve the index client's confidentiality rather than disclosing the client's identity to contacts.

options.A: Identify people who were exposed while the client could transmit TB, notify and assess those contacts, arrange testing or follow-up as indicated, and protect the index client's identity during notification.
options.B: Tell each contact the index client's name so the contact can personally verify the exposure history before testing.
options.C: Notify only contacts who have already developed symptoms because asymptomatic exposed people do not need assessment.
options.D: Use an unstructured public announcement instead of identifying specific exposed contacts because individual contact assessment has little role in TB control.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC describes TB contact investigation as quickly identifying, assessing, and managing people exposed to a person with infectious TB. Contacts are notified that they may have been exposed and may need TB testing and, depending on results, treatment. CDC also states that the index patient's personal and medical information is kept confidential and that contacts are not told the name of the person with active TB disease. B violates that confidentiality principle. C is incorrect because exposed contacts are assessed even if they are asymptomatic. D discards the targeted case-and-contact process used to interrupt transmission.
candidates.source_claim_supported: TB contact investigation identifies, notifies, assesses, and manages exposed contacts while protecting the index patient's identity and arranging testing/follow-up even before contacts develop symptoms.
candidates.source_document_title: Exposure to Tuberculosis
candidates.source_locator: Contact investigations can help limit the spread of TB: contact tracing is the process of quickly identifying, assessing, and managing people exposed to disease; health departments/contact tracers notify contacts about exposure and precautions/testing. 'The information you share ... is kept confidential': patient information is kept private. 'What to expect if you have been named as a contact': the health care worker tells the contact they may have been exposed but, to maintain privacy/confidentiality, does not tell the name of the person with active TB disease; contacts should obtain TB testing and additional evaluation as indicated.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Division of Tuberculosis Elimination

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: collaborate with public-health and interprofessional resources, follow reporting systems, and contribute to coordinated responses during emergencies and communicable-disease events.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — public-health coordination for cross-border infectious threats
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize global health security as coordinated cross-border preparedness, detection, reporting, and response under the International Health Regulations rather than isolated national action or unilateral WHO control of domestic health measures.

options.A: Cross-border health threats require countries to maintain capacities to detect, report, and respond to significant public-health events and to coordinate when international spread is possible.
options.B: Countries should manage infectious threats independently because sharing surveillance information across borders is outside current international health frameworks.
options.C: International health-security systems apply only after a pandemic has been declared and have no role in earlier outbreak detection or reporting.
options.D: WHO can unilaterally impose any clinical or public-health measure inside a country once an international event is reported.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The International Health Regulations (IHR), as amended in 2024 and in force for most States Parties since September 19, 2025, provide the global framework for preventing, preparing for, detecting, reporting, and responding to public-health threats that can cross borders. B and C contradict the IHR emphasis on surveillance, notification, preparedness, and coordinated response before and during international emergencies. D is incorrect because WHO serves a coordinating and technical role under the IHR and does not have authority to force health measures on countries or populations.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current IHR support national capacities and international coordination for preparedness, detection, reporting, and response to public-health threats with cross-border implications while preserving national authority over domestic health measures.
candidates.source_document_title: International Health Regulations (2005), as amended in 2014, 2022 and 2024; Amended International Health Regulations Enter into Force
candidates.source_locator: WHO International Health Regulations topic page — current amended IHR text and functions supporting surveillance, assessment, information sharing, technical assistance, and emergency coordination. September 19, 2025 news release — IHR guide States Parties' rights and obligations concerning public-health risks, recognize that threats cross borders, and require coordinated global action; amendments strengthen national coordination and emergency response. WHO Q&A on amendments — WHO cannot force lockdowns or other health measures on a country's population.
candidates.source_organization: World Health Organization (WHO)
candidates.source_version_date: Current amended IHR in force from September 19, 2025 for applicable States Parties; WHO news release September 19, 2025; current pages accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute complications and intervene; apply pathophysiology and emergency-care knowledge to deteriorating musculoskeletal conditions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and escalation of septic arthritis
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize an acute hot, swollen, severely painful monoarticular joint with systemic findings as possible septic arthritis requiring urgent arthrocentesis-based evaluation and prompt treatment rather than routine observation.

options.A: Suspect septic arthritis and escalate for urgent diagnostic evaluation, including synovial-fluid aspiration, because delayed treatment can rapidly damage the joint.
options.B: Assume osteoarthritis because a single knee is involved and arrange routine nonurgent follow-up.
options.C: Treat the presentation as a muscle strain because fever is commonly caused by uncomplicated periarticular injury.
options.D: Wait for the joint swelling to become chronic before pursuing aspiration because acute septic arthritis is usually self-limited.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Septic arthritis is an orthopedic emergency that commonly presents as acute monoarticular pain, swelling, warmth, limited motion, and sometimes fever. Synovial-fluid evaluation by arthrocentesis is a crucial diagnostic step, and early diagnosis and treatment are important to preserve joint function. B does not fit the acute febrile inflammatory presentation. C does not adequately explain an acutely inflamed joint with fever. D is unsafe because untreated septic arthritis can progress rapidly and should not be observed until chronic.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Acute severe monoarticular inflammation with fever should raise urgent concern for septic arthritis; synovial-fluid aspiration is central to diagnosis and delay risks rapid joint damage and systemic complications.
candidates.source_document_title: Septic Arthritis; Ultrasound-Guided Arthrocentesis
candidates.source_locator: Septic Arthritis — Introduction: orthopedic emergency; early diagnosis/treatment are crucial. History and Physical: classic acute monoarticular pain, fever, swelling and reluctance/reduced joint movement. Evaluation: suspected septic arthritis includes arthrocentesis and synovial-fluid analysis; Pearls: arthrocentesis should be pursued without delay. Ultrasound-Guided Arthrocentesis — Introduction: septic arthritis is the critical monoarticular arthropathy to confirm/treat; synovial fluid analysis remains the diagnostic gold standard and prompt antibiotics/orthopedic involvement follow when findings support infection.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute complications and intervene; apply pathophysiology and emergency-care knowledge to neurologic and infectious deterioration.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and escalation of suspected acute meningitis
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize acute fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status as a high-risk meningitis pattern requiring urgent evaluation while understanding that classic findings may be incomplete and no single absent sign reliably rules out bacterial meningitis.

options.A: Suspect acute meningitis and escalate for emergency medical evaluation because this symptom cluster can occur with bacterial meningitis.
options.B: Rule out meningitis because all clients with bacterial meningitis must have a petechial rash.
options.C: Treat the symptoms as an uncomplicated tension headache because neck stiffness and confusion are expected with benign headache disorders.
options.D: Rule out bacterial meningitis if one component of the classic triad is absent because all classic findings must occur together.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current WHO and CDC guidance describes acute meningitis as potentially presenting with rapid-onset fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. This constellation should trigger urgent evaluation because bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and clinical findings alone do not identify the exact pathogen. B is incorrect because a petechial or purpuric rash is associated particularly with meningococcal disease and is not required for all bacterial meningitis. C dangerously normalizes meningeal and neurologic findings. D is incorrect because the classic findings are frequently incomplete; absence of one component does not reliably exclude bacterial meningitis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Acute meningitis can present with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia and altered mental status; bacterial meningitis remains possible when the classic triad is incomplete, so a concerning symptom cluster requires urgent evaluation rather than rule-out from a missing single feature.
candidates.source_document_title: WHO Guidelines on Meningitis Diagnosis, Treatment and Care — Introduction/Clinical Presentation; Meningococcal Disease Symptoms and Complications; Bacterial Meningitis — StatPearls
candidates.source_locator: WHO guideline, section 1.5 Clinical presentation: acute meningitis is characterized by rapid onset of fever, neck stiffness, headache, photophobia and/or altered mental status; the classic combination should prompt strong suspicion, but all findings are not present in every case. CDC Meningococcal Disease Symptoms: fever, headache and stiff neck are common meningitis symptoms, often with confusion, nausea, photophobia or vomiting. NCBI StatPearls Bacterial Meningitis — History and Physical: fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status are the classic triad, but the complete triad is present in a minority of bacterial meningitis cases and absence of classic meningeal signs does not reliably rule disease out.
candidates.source_organization: World Health Organization; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); National Library of Medicine / NCBI

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize signs and symptoms of acute neurologic complications and intervene; apply pathophysiology and emergency-care knowledge to clients with changes in consciousness or seizures.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and escalation of suspected acute encephalitis
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize fever, headache, altered mental status, and new-onset seizure as a high-risk acute encephalitis/meningoencephalitis pattern requiring urgent evaluation while preserving a broad differential rather than attributing the seizure to primary epilepsy or requiring meningismus.

options.A: Suspect acute encephalitis or meningoencephalitis and escalate for urgent neurologic and infectious evaluation.
options.B: Assume a primary tension headache because fever and new seizures are expected complications of benign headache disorders.
options.C: Rule out encephalitis because neck stiffness is not described; meningeal signs must be present in every case.
options.D: Diagnose epilepsy as the sole cause because a first seizure excludes an acute inflammatory brain process.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI references describe fever, headache, altered mental status, and seizures as common manifestations of encephalitis. Encephalitis has a broad infectious and noninfectious differential, so the nurse should treat this as a neurologic emergency requiring urgent evaluation rather than infer a specific etiology from symptoms alone. B cannot explain the febrile encephalopathy and new seizure. C is incorrect because meningeal signs may be absent in encephalitis. D is incorrect because a first seizure occurring with fever and altered mental status may be secondary to an acute cerebral inflammatory process and does not establish primary epilepsy.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Fever, headache, altered mental status, and seizures are common findings in encephalitis and should prompt urgent evaluation; meningismus is not required and symptoms alone do not establish a specific cause.
candidates.source_document_title: Viral Encephalitis; Herpes Simplex Encephalitis
candidates.source_locator: Viral Encephalitis — History and Physical: common signs and symptoms include fever, headache, seizures, and altered mental status; evaluation requires consideration of a broad infectious and noninfectious differential. Herpes Simplex Encephalitis — History and Physical: typical features include altered mentation with evidence of brain inflammation such as fever, headache, seizures, or focal neurologic deficits; meningeal signs may occur but are present in fewer than half of cases.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret diagnostic/laboratory findings and recognize results that influence treatment decisions and risk reduction.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — antimicrobial susceptibility/MIC interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret MIC as an in-vitro growth-inhibition measurement that requires drug- and organism-specific susceptibility breakpoints and clinical context; do not choose therapy by simply selecting the smallest MIC number across different antimicrobials.

options.A: An MIC is the lowest tested drug concentration that inhibits visible microbial growth; it must be interpreted with the organism-drug breakpoint and clinical context rather than compared numerically across unrelated antibiotics.
options.B: The MIC is the highest antibiotic dose that can be administered safely to the client without toxicity.
options.C: The antibiotic with the lowest numeric MIC is always the best treatment choice, regardless of drug-specific breakpoints, infection site, or dosing.
options.D: An MIC directly measures the client's serum antibiotic concentration after a dose is given.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Standard antimicrobial susceptibility testing determines an MIC as the lowest concentration that inhibits visible growth under the test conditions. FDA interprets MIC results using organism- and antimicrobial-specific susceptibility breakpoints; for example, a susceptible category means the isolate's MIC falls at or below a susceptible breakpoint associated with achievable drug exposure for the recommended regimen/site. Therefore, MIC numbers from different drugs cannot be ranked as if lower always means clinically superior. B confuses microbiology susceptibility testing with a maximum tolerated dose. D confuses in-vitro susceptibility with therapeutic drug monitoring.
candidates.source_claim_supported: MIC is an in-vitro concentration-based susceptibility measurement; clinical interpretation depends on drug- and organism-specific breakpoints and exposure, so raw MIC numbers should not be compared across unrelated antibiotics as a universal ranking.
candidates.source_document_title: FDA-Recognized Antimicrobial Susceptibility Test Interpretive Criteria; MIC Determination; CLSI Harmonized Terminology Database
candidates.source_locator: FDA STIC — Category Definitions: susceptibility categories are defined by organism-antimicrobial MIC breakpoints and achievable exposure with recommended dosing. FDA Antimicrobial Resistance and Medical Devices — susceptibility methods determine the lowest drug concentration (MIC) that kills or slows/inhibits organism growth. EUCAST MIC Determination — broth microdilution methodology and MIC reading as the lowest concentration at which visible growth is inhibited/absent under specified test conditions. CLSI terminology database — MIC is used with breakpoint/cutoff frameworks rather than as a universal cross-drug rank.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration; European Committee on Antimicrobial Susceptibility Testing (EUCAST); Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute
candidates.source_version_date: FDA STIC pages current 2026; EUCAST MIC methodology current through 2025–2026; CLSI terminology database accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: obtain and interpret diagnostic specimens correctly and reduce risk from inaccurate laboratory results.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — blood-culture collection quality and interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Collect at least two appropriately filled adult blood-culture sets from separate venipuncture sites because diagnostic yield depends strongly on adequate blood volume and multiple sets help interpret possible skin-commensal contamination.

options.A: Multiple sets provide adequate blood volume to improve detection and help determine whether growth of a common skin commensal is more likely contamination rather than true bacteremia.
options.B: A second set is needed mainly to determine the maximum safe antibiotic dose for the client.
options.C: One set provides the same diagnostic volume and contamination information as multiple sets, so additional collections have little clinical value.
options.D: Multiple sets guarantee that every positive culture represents true bacteremia and eliminate the need for clinical correlation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's current adult blood-culture quality guidance states that diagnosis of bloodstream infection generally requires two or more sets to achieve adequate blood volume and that multiple sets are needed to evaluate possible contamination. For adults with suspected bloodstream infection, CDC recommends collecting two to four sets and at least two within the evaluation period, with the second set from a separate venipuncture site. A single set can provide insufficient volume and makes interpretation of possible skin-commensal contamination more difficult. D overstates the value of multiple sets because even a multi-set result still requires organism- and clinical-context interpretation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For adults with suspected bloodstream infection, multiple properly filled blood-culture sets improve diagnostic blood volume and allow interpretation of possible contamination; at least two sets from separate sites are recommended in standard adult collection practice.
candidates.source_document_title: Collect Adult Blood Culture Sets; Sub-Measure: Single-Set Blood Culture Rate; Primary Measure: Blood Culture Contamination Rate; Guidelines for Evaluating New Fever in Adult Patients in the ICU
candidates.source_locator: CDC Collect Adult Blood Culture Sets — 'Collect multiple sets to achieve the optimal volume': bloodstream-infection diagnosis generally requires two or more sets; two sets are required to assess a possible contaminant; standard practice is two to four sets for suspected adult bloodstream infection, with at least two sets collected and a separate venipuncture site for the second. CDC Single-Set Rate — one set lacks sufficient volume for reliable bacteremia diagnosis/contamination assessment. CDC Primary Measure — a common skin commensal in only one of multiple sets may represent probable contamination and requires clinical correlation. SCCM/IDSA fever guideline — collect at least two sets from different anatomical sites.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Division of Laboratory Systems; SCCM/IDSA
candidates.source_version_date: CDC collection page dated March 31, 2026; CDC quality-measure pages current through 2026; SCCM/IDSA guideline current and accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret diagnostic and laboratory findings and recognize how preliminary results affect ongoing evaluation and treatment.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — preliminary Gram-stain interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Use Gram-stain morphology as rapid preliminary microbiologic information that can inform early treatment while awaiting definitive organism identification and antimicrobial susceptibility results; do not equate gram-positive cocci in clusters with confirmed MRSA or a guaranteed drug response.

options.A: It provides rapid preliminary morphology consistent with organisms such as Staphylococcus and can inform initial therapy, but it does not replace definitive identification and susceptibility testing.
options.B: It definitively identifies methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and makes further culture or susceptibility testing unnecessary.
options.C: It determines the client's blood type and has no role in microbiologic treatment decisions.
options.D: It proves that any gram-positive antimicrobial will be clinically effective regardless of species, resistance pattern, infection site, or patient factors.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Gram staining rapidly classifies bacteria by staining characteristics and morphology; gram-positive cocci in clusters are commonly characteristic of Staphylococcus species. This preliminary information can help guide early antimicrobial decisions while more specific culture, biochemical, molecular, or susceptibility testing is completed. B is incorrect because Gram stain cannot distinguish MRSA from methicillin-susceptible S. aureus or reliably establish species by itself. C is unrelated. D overinterprets morphology as a susceptibility result.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Gram-positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain provide rapid preliminary evidence suggestive of Staphylococcus morphology and may inform empiric therapy, but Gram stain does not replace definitive identification or susceptibility testing.
candidates.source_document_title: Gram Staining; Gram-Positive Bacteria
candidates.source_locator: Gram Staining — Indications/Clinical Significance: Gram stain rapidly categorizes bacteria and provides preliminary identification that can guide immediate antibiotic decisions, while more specific methods provide species and resistance information. Normal and Critical Findings: gram-positive cocci in clusters are typically characteristic of Staphylococcus species. Gram-Positive Bacteria — Etiology: Staphylococcus forms clusters; further testing distinguishes species and resistance characteristics.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor and interpret laboratory values and recognize results that require further evaluation.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — ESR/inflammatory-marker interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret an elevated ESR as evidence compatible with a generalized inflammatory state, not as a disease-specific diagnosis; integrate the value with the client's clinical presentation and other diagnostic findings.

options.A: ESR is a nonspecific inflammatory marker and must be interpreted with the clinical picture and other testing rather than as proof of one disease.
options.B: An elevated ESR independently confirms bacterial infection and identifies the causative organism.
options.C: ESR is unaffected by age, sex, or noninfectious inflammatory conditions, so any elevation has one meaning.
options.D: An elevated ESR establishes malignancy and eliminates the need for additional diagnostic evaluation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ARUP Consult identifies ESR as a common inflammatory marker and emphasizes that inflammatory markers are nonspecific and are not diagnostic for a particular condition. ESR is influenced by multiple disease states and by factors such as age and sex, so the result must be interpreted with history, examination, and other tests. B and D falsely convert a nonspecific result into a definitive diagnosis. C contradicts the known physiologic and disease-related influences on ESR.
candidates.source_claim_supported: ESR is a nonspecific inflammatory marker influenced by clinical and physiologic factors and must be interpreted in context rather than used to diagnose a single infection, autoimmune condition, or malignancy by itself.
candidates.source_document_title: Inflammatory Markers — Choose the Right Test
candidates.source_locator: Introduction: CRP, ESR, and PCT are nonspecific inflammatory markers and are not diagnostic for any particular condition; use with other tests and the clinical picture. Laboratory Testing — Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate: ESR is an indirect measurement influenced by multiple disease states, changes more slowly than CRP, and normal values vary with age and sex. Quick Answers: inflammatory-marker results require careful interpretation because of assay/laboratory variation.

candidates.source_version_date: Last literature review May 2025; last update June 2025; current page accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: interpret laboratory trends and recognize findings that can indicate potential infection or physiologic deterioration.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — WBC differential/left-shift interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret bandemia/left shift as a reactive marrow pattern that can increase concern for acute infection—often bacterial—or inflammation, while avoiding use of the finding as a stand-alone etiologic diagnosis.

options.A: A left shift reflects release of immature granulocytes and can support concern for acute infection or inflammation, but it is not specific enough to diagnose bacterial infection by itself.
options.B: Bandemia proves a bacterial infection and identifies the responsible organism without culture or other evaluation.
options.C: A left shift is a normal finding unrelated to physiologic stress, infection, or inflammation.
options.D: Bandemia is specific for viral infection and argues against bacterial or inflammatory causes.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. A left shift refers to increased production and release of immature granulocytes such as band neutrophils. Current NCBI guidance notes that infection and inflammation can trigger release of band forms from marrow, and bacterial infections are commonly associated with left shift, but leukocyte patterns must be interpreted with the clinical picture and other laboratory data. B overstates specificity and ignores the need to identify the source and organism. C and D contradict the known reactive causes of band release.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Bandemia/left shift is release of immature granulocytes seen in reactive states including infection and inflammation; bacterial infection commonly produces this pattern, but the finding is not sufficiently specific to establish etiology by itself.
candidates.source_document_title: Leukocytosis; Neutrophilia; Laboratory Evaluation of Sepsis
candidates.source_locator: Leukocytosis — Etiology: in response to stress, infection, or inflammation, polymorphonuclear cells, band forms, and metamyelocytes may enter the circulation; leukocytosis has a broad differential and requires clinical context. Neutrophilia — Secondary Neutrophilia: bacterial infections are usually associated with left shift, but infection/inflammation includes broader causes. Laboratory Evaluation of Sepsis — left shift represents increased production/release of immature granulocytes and may support infection concern but should not be used alone to diagnose sepsis.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI StatPearls
candidates.source_version_date: Leukocytosis last updated June 15, 2026; current StatPearls 2026 edition pages accessed 2026-08-17
candidates.stem: A client's WBC differential shows increased band neutrophils, described as a left shift. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor laboratory trends and recognize changes that may indicate improvement or worsening of an inflammatory process.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — CRP versus ESR trend interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Use CRP as a relatively rapid inflammatory trend marker compared with ESR while recognizing that neither marker independently identifies the underlying cause of inflammation.

options.A: CRP generally changes more rapidly with acute inflammation, whereas ESR tends to rise and fall more slowly.
options.B: CRP and ESR have identical kinetics and can be interpreted interchangeably in every clinical situation.
options.C: ESR generally changes more rapidly than CRP and is therefore always preferred for short-term inflammatory trends.
options.D: A CRP elevation establishes the specific cause of inflammation without additional clinical evaluation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ARUP Consult notes that ESR depends on several plasma proteins with different half-lives and therefore increases and decreases more slowly than CRP. CRP is generally a more responsive marker of acute systemic inflammation, but both are nonspecific and must be interpreted in clinical context. B and C misstate their kinetics. D incorrectly converts a nonspecific inflammatory marker into a disease-specific diagnostic test.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CRP generally responds more rapidly to acute inflammatory change than ESR, while both remain nonspecific markers requiring clinical interpretation.
candidates.source_document_title: Inflammatory Markers — Choose the Right Test
candidates.source_locator: Laboratory Testing — Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate: because ESR depends on several proteins with varying half-lives, it increases and decreases more slowly than CRP; CRP is preferred over ESR in most situations. Introduction: CRP and ESR are nonspecific inflammatory markers and are not diagnostic for a particular condition.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: monitor invasive-device sites, recognize complications, and intervene to reduce risk from therapy-related adverse events.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — peripheral-IV phlebitis assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Use a standardized phlebitis scale to improve consistency of peripheral-IV complication assessment and documentation while continuing direct site examination and acting on clinically significant phlebitis findings according to evidence-based policy.

options.A: Standardize assessment and documentation of local phlebitis findings while the nurse continues direct inspection/palpation and follows clinical criteria and policy for catheter management.
options.B: Replace direct assessment of the IV site because the numeric grade alone determines whether phlebitis is present.
options.C: Diagnose catheter-related bloodstream infection solely from the phlebitis score without systemic assessment or microbiologic evaluation.
options.D: Determine the client's blood pressure and systemic perfusion rather than evaluate local IV-site complications.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. INS standards and related infusion-nursing literature use standardized phlebitis scales to promote consistent assessment and documentation of peripheral-IV complications. The scale complements—not replaces—direct site assessment. CDC recommends regular inspection/palpation of peripheral catheter sites and removal when signs of phlebitis such as warmth, tenderness, erythema, or a palpable venous cord develop. A scale does not independently diagnose bloodstream infection or substitute for the clinical assessment that guides site management.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Standardized phlebitis grading supports consistent assessment/documentation but does not replace direct IV-site examination; clinically significant phlebitis findings require catheter-management action according to policy/guidance.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Basic Care and Comfort: obtain basic physiologic measurements accurately and provide routine care adapted to client condition.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — accurate oral temperature measurement
candidates.educational_objective: For accurate oral temperature measurement, recognize that recent hot or cold intake can distort the reading and allow an appropriate waiting period before obtaining the measurement.

options.A: Wait before measuring orally because recent hot or cold intake can produce an inaccurate reading.
options.B: Measure immediately because beverage temperature does not affect sublingual temperature readings.
options.C: Assume the oral route is always the most accurate route regardless of recent intake or client condition.
options.D: Avoid the oral route permanently because oral temperature measurement is inappropriate in all clinical settings.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance states that recently consumed hot or cold food or beverages can falsely raise or lower an oral temperature. The cited nursing skills guidance recommends waiting 15–25 minutes after hot or cold intake before oral measurement. B ignores a known measurement artifact. C overstates one route as universally superior. D is incorrect because the oral route is appropriate for many cooperative clients when contraindications and interfering factors are absent.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Recent hot or cold oral intake can alter oral temperature measurements; waiting before measurement improves accuracy.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Skills — General Survey; Nursing Assistant — Demonstrate Reporting and Documentation of Client Data
candidates.source_locator: Nursing Skills, General Survey — Oral Temperature: recent hot/cold food or beverage can cause falsely elevated or decreased readings; oral temperature should be taken 15–25 minutes after hot/cold intake. Nursing Assistant, Oral Temperature section states the same timing and explains the sublingual route's susceptibility to recent intake.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCBI nursing texts accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Safety and Infection Prevention and Control: maintain invasive devices using aseptic technique and implement measures that reduce healthcare-associated infection risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — central-line dressing integrity
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain central-line site protection by promptly replacing any dressing that becomes loose, damp, or visibly soiled using appropriate aseptic site-care technique rather than waiting for the routine interval or removing an otherwise needed catheter solely for dressing failure.

options.A: Replace the compromised dressing promptly using appropriate aseptic catheter-site care according to facility policy.
options.B: Leave it in place until the routine scheduled dressing change because looseness alone is not an indication for replacement.
options.C: Tape over the loose edges without reassessing or replacing the dressing because preserving the old dressing is preferred.
options.D: Remove the central venous catheter solely because the dressing is loose, even if the catheter remains clinically indicated and the site has no other complication.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC recommends replacing a catheter-site dressing whenever it becomes damp, loosened, or visibly soiled and covering catheter sites with sterile gauze or a sterile transparent semipermeable dressing. A loose dressing compromises the protective barrier and should not be left until the next routine interval. B and C fail to restore an intact dressing. D overreacts: a loose dressing requires prompt dressing replacement, but catheter removal is based on catheter necessity and complications rather than looseness of the dressing alone.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A central-line dressing that becomes loose should be replaced promptly with an intact sterile dressing using appropriate catheter-site care; looseness alone does not automatically require removal of a clinically necessary catheter.
candidates.source_document_title: Guidelines for the Prevention of Intravascular Catheter-Related Infections — Summary of Recommendations; Prevention Strategies
candidates.source_locator: Catheter Site Dressing Regimens: use sterile gauze or sterile transparent semipermeable dressing to cover the site; replace catheter-site dressing if it becomes damp, loosened, or visibly soiled (Category IB). Central-line maintenance recommendations also emphasize continued assessment of catheter necessity and insertion-site condition.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Current CDC infection-control web guidance accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: obtain diagnostic specimens correctly, monitor for infection-related complications, and use laboratory results to reduce risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — wound culture specimen quality
candidates.educational_objective: When a wound swab culture is indicated, obtain the specimen from cleansed viable wound-bed tissue using pressure to express tissue fluid and avoid superficial exudate or necrotic material so the result better represents clinically relevant organisms.

options.A: Cleanse the wound, select viable wound-bed tissue, and rotate the swab over about 1 cm² with enough pressure to express wound fluid while avoiding pus, slough, eschar, necrotic material, and surface exudate.
options.B: Collect drainage from the surrounding skin before cleansing because surface exudate best represents organisms in viable wound tissue.
options.C: Swab necrotic tissue preferentially because devitalized material provides the most accurate sample of the organisms driving invasive infection.
options.D: Skip wound-bed assessment and culture every chronic wound routinely because bacterial growth on a swab confirms that the wound is infected.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI nursing guidance for wound-culture collection directs the nurse to irrigate and cleanse the wound to remove surface debris, identify approximately 1 cm² of viable tissue, and rotate the swab over that area with sufficient pressure to express wound fluid. The specimen should not be taken from pus, slough, eschar, necrotic tissue, or skin exudate. B and C increase the chance of sampling surface colonizers or nonviable material rather than the clinically relevant wound bed. D is incorrect because wound cultures are obtained when infection is suspected and bacterial presence on a chronic wound does not by itself establish clinical infection. Tissue sampling may be preferred when deeper or more definitive microbiologic assessment is needed.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For an indicated wound swab culture, cleansing followed by pressure swabbing of viable wound-bed tissue yields a more clinically appropriate specimen than superficial exudate or necrotic material; the culture result must still be interpreted in clinical context.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Skills — Chapter 20 Wound Care, 20.9 Checklist for Wound Culture
candidates.source_locator: Section 20.9 Checklist for Wound Culture, steps 9–20: irrigate with sterile normal saline to remove surface debris/exudate; wipe surface contaminants; identify a 1-cm² area of viable wound tissue; do not sample pus, slough, eschar, or necrotic tissue; rotate swab over the selected area for 5 seconds with sufficient pressure to express wound fluid; never collect exudate from the skin.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCBI Bookshelf nursing text accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide health teaching that supports appropriate medication use, prevention of infection, and risk-reducing health behaviors.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — patient antibiotic-use education
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients to use antibiotics exactly as prescribed, avoid sharing or saving leftover antibiotics, and seek professional guidance rather than independently shortening, extending, or reusing antimicrobial therapy.

options.A: I will take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed, will not share it or save leftover doses for another illness, and will contact my healthcare professional if I have questions or adverse effects.
options.B: I should stop the antibiotic on my own as soon as I feel better, even if the prescription instructions say to continue it.
options.C: I can save unused antibiotics for the next time I develop similar symptoms because this reduces unnecessary clinic visits.
options.D: If a family member develops similar symptoms, sharing my antibiotic is appropriate as long as we take the same dose.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's current antibiotic-use guidance advises clients to take antibiotics exactly as prescribed, not share them, not save them for later, and discuss questions or side effects with a healthcare professional. This wording is more accurate than a blanket instruction to 'finish every course no matter what,' because the prescribed duration itself may be changed by the treating clinician when clinically appropriate. B substitutes the client's own decision for the prescription. C and D can delay correct diagnosis and expose others to ineffective or harmful treatment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Safe patient-level antibiotic stewardship means taking antibiotics according to current prescription instructions, not sharing or saving them, and involving the healthcare professional in treatment changes rather than self-modifying therapy.
candidates.source_document_title: Healthy Habits: Antibiotic Do's and Don'ts; Antibiotic Use and Antimicrobial Resistance Facts
candidates.source_locator: Healthy Habits — 'Take antibiotics exactly as prescribed': take them exactly as prescribed; do not share antibiotics; do not save them for later; do not take antibiotics prescribed for someone else; contact a healthcare professional with questions. Antibiotic Use and Antimicrobial Resistance Facts — misuse includes taking the wrong antibiotic, wrong dose, or antibiotic for the wrong length of time; appropriate use is necessary to reduce harm and antimicrobial-resistance pressure.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Healthy Habits dated September 23, 2025; current CDC antibiotic-use resources accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: provide immunization education, promote preventive health practices, and reinforce age- and risk-appropriate vaccination.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — vaccine-preventable disease education
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that vaccination has substantially reduced vaccine-preventable disease burden, but continued age- and risk-appropriate vaccination and surveillance remain necessary to preserve protection and prevent resurgence.

options.A: Vaccination has prevented large numbers of illnesses, hospitalizations, and deaths, and staying up to date remains important because vaccine-preventable diseases can persist or reemerge when protection is insufficient.
options.B: Successful vaccination programs eliminate the need for continued immunization once disease incidence becomes low.
options.C: Vaccines are relevant mainly to diseases that no longer circulate and therefore provide little current public-health benefit.
options.D: Once a vaccine-preventable disease is controlled locally, surveillance and continued vaccination are unnecessary.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC reports that routine childhood vaccination has prevented hundreds of millions of illnesses and millions of hospitalizations and deaths in the United States. CDC also emphasizes that serious vaccine-preventable diseases remain a threat and that continued vaccination is needed to maintain protection and prevent reemergence or outbreaks. B and D ignore the need to sustain coverage after disease control or elimination targets are reached. C is false because multiple vaccine-preventable diseases continue to circulate and cause morbidity and mortality.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Vaccines have substantially reduced disease burden and saved lives, but ongoing recommended vaccination and surveillance remain necessary because vaccine-preventable diseases persist and can reemerge when coverage declines.
candidates.source_document_title: Vaccines and the Diseases they Prevent; Vaccine-Preventable Diseases — Global Immunization; Routine Immunizations on Schedule for Everyone (RISE)
candidates.source_locator: Vaccines and the Diseases they Prevent — routine vaccinations for children born 1994–2023 are estimated to prevent about 508 million illnesses, 32 million hospitalizations, and over 1.1 million deaths. Global Immunization — elimination/control sections: continued disease detection and vaccination are required to maintain elimination targets and prevent reemergence. RISE — routine immunization coverage remains an active public-health priority to protect against vaccine-preventable disease and disability.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Vaccines and Diseases dated August 10, 2024; Global VPD page current 2024–2026; RISE dated May 4, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance: assess health risks and provide preventive counseling, immunization education, and anticipatory guidance tailored to client circumstances.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — individualized pre-travel counseling
candidates.educational_objective: Individualize pre-travel health counseling to the traveler's medical history and specific itinerary, including recommended immunizations and destination-relevant food, water, vector, and infectious-disease precautions.

options.A: Use the destination, itinerary, trip duration, planned activities, health history, and immunization status to individualize vaccine, food/water, vector, and other infection-prevention advice.
options.B: Give every international traveler the same vaccine and prevention plan because destination-specific risks have little effect on recommendations.
options.C: Skip pre-travel counseling if the client feels healthy because preventive recommendations are needed only after illness develops abroad.
options.D: Focus only on routine vaccines because food, water, vector, and regional outbreak risks are outside the scope of pre-travel health counseling.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The CDC Yellow Book 2026 describes the pre-travel consultation as an individualized risk assessment based on the traveler's health background and trip details, including countries and regions visited, timing, duration, purpose, travel style, and planned activities. Risk management can include routine and travel vaccines, food and water precautions, vector-borne disease prevention, malaria prophylaxis when indicated, and counseling about other destination-specific exposures. B ignores major itinerary-dependent differences. C misses the preventive purpose of the consultation. D omits several core travel-health risks.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current CDC travel guidance requires individualized risk assessment and destination/itinerary-specific preventive counseling, including vaccines and exposure precautions rather than a universal travel plan.
candidates.source_document_title: CDC Yellow Book 2026 — The Pre-Travel Consultation; Food and Water Precautions for Travelers
candidates.source_locator: The Pre-Travel Consultation — Introduction and 'Assess individual risk': risk assessment incorporates health history plus itinerary, timing, duration, purpose, travel style, activities, and infectious-disease status at the destination. 'Manage risk — Vaccinations': routine/travel vaccines depend on destination and itinerary. Box 1.1.3 includes immunizations, malaria/vector risks, respiratory illness, and travelers' diarrhea/food-water counseling. Food and Water Precautions — contaminated food/water are important infectious risks and travelers should receive safe-food/water counseling.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: Yellow Book 2026 chapters published April 23, 2025; current pages accessed 2026-08-17
candidates.stem: A client is planning international travel. Which nursing recommendation best reflects current CDC pre-travel guidance?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: use therapeutic communication, respect client privacy and dignity, reduce barriers to care, and support clients experiencing stigma or discrimination.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — HIV stigma, confidentiality, and therapeutic communication
candidates.educational_objective: Reduce infection-related stigma by communicating respectfully and without judgment, protecting confidentiality, and recognizing that stigma can reduce willingness to seek testing, disclose relevant information, or engage in treatment and follow-up.

options.A: Use respectful, nonjudgmental communication, explain applicable confidentiality protections and testing procedures, and acknowledge that stigma can discourage people from testing and care.
options.B: Tell the client that stigma has little effect on healthcare use, so the concern should not affect the testing decision.
options.C: Discuss the client's possible diagnosis openly with staff who are not involved in care so the team can become more comfortable with HIV.
options.D: Avoid discussing stigma because bringing it up increases discrimination and interferes with clinical care.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC states that HIV stigma can discourage people from testing, disclosing their status, and accessing HIV services. CDC also recommends voluntary, noncoercive HIV screening and respectful, nonjudgmental risk assessment and counseling. Confidentiality must be protected according to applicable law and care processes. B dismisses a documented barrier to care. C violates the principle that private health information should not be disclosed to people without a care-related or legally permitted need to know. D prevents the nurse from addressing a real barrier to engagement.
candidates.source_claim_supported: HIV stigma can impede testing and care engagement; clinicians should use respectful, nonjudgmental communication and preserve confidentiality according to applicable law and clinical processes.
candidates.source_document_title: Stigma and HIV; Clinical Testing Guidance for HIV; STI and HIV Infection Risk Assessment
candidates.source_locator: Stigma and HIV — HIV stigma can discourage testing, status disclosure, and access to HIV services. Clinical Testing Guidance for HIV — routine screening should use an opt-out approach that can reduce stigma and must follow state testing laws. STI/HIV Infection Risk Assessment — effective interviewing and counseling require respect, compassion, and a nonjudgmental attitude; counseling should be empathetic and culturally appropriate.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
candidates.source_version_date: CDC HIV stigma page current under restored 2025 content; HIV testing guidance dated February 10, 2025; current pages accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: assess changes in psychosocial functioning, use therapeutic communication, support coping, and address stressors associated with illness and hospitalization.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — psychological effects of isolation precautions
candidates.educational_objective: While maintaining indicated transmission-based precautions, assess for isolation-related psychosocial distress and reduce it through clear education, therapeutic communication, regular human contact, dignity, and referral/support when needed.

options.A: Acknowledge the distress, explain the reason for precautions, maintain regular therapeutic contact and communication, and assess whether additional psychosocial support is needed.
options.B: Tell the client that isolation has no recognized psychological effects and that discussing anxiety may make adjustment more difficult.
options.C: Minimize staff contact beyond essential procedures because reducing interaction is part of the purpose of transmission-based precautions.
options.D: Discontinue the required isolation precautions solely because the client reports loneliness and anxiety.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Nursing infection-control guidance recognizes that isolation precautions can be associated with anxiety, depression, anger, loneliness, and stigma in some hospitalized clients. Education about the reason for precautions, emotional preparation, communication, and psychological support can reduce distress while infection-prevention measures remain in place. B dismisses a recognized potential effect. C unnecessarily compounds social isolation; precautions limit infection transmission, not therapeutic communication. D is unsafe because psychosocial distress should be addressed without independently discontinuing clinically indicated precautions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Isolation precautions may contribute to psychological distress in some clients; nurses should preserve indicated infection-control measures while providing education, communication, dignity and psychosocial support.
candidates.source_document_title: Nursing Fundamentals — Chapter 9 Infection
candidates.source_locator: Chapter 9 Infection — 'Psychological Effects of Isolation': transmission-based precautions can negatively affect mental well-being and behavior, including depression, anxiety, anger and stigma; client/family education when precautions begin is critical to reduce anxiety/distress, and preparing clients emotionally helps coping. WHO/NCBI infection-prevention guidance also notes possible social isolation, depression or anxiety during prolonged single-room isolation and recommends communication, dignity, respect and psychological support.
candidates.source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
candidates.source_version_date: Current NCBI nursing text accessed 2026-08-17
candidates.stem: A client has been on transmission-based isolation precautions for several days and says, 'I feel cut off from everyone and more anxious each day.' Which nursing response is most appropriate?

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: assess coping and psychosocial needs, use therapeutic communication, support adjustment to chronic illness, and facilitate appropriate resources/referrals.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — long-term adjustment to HIV
candidates.educational_objective: Support long-term HIV adjustment through continuing, nonjudgmental assessment of emotional, social, adherence, and structural needs and connection to appropriate mental-health, navigation, case-management, peer, and community resources.

options.A: Use ongoing nonjudgmental conversations to identify emotional, social, adherence, and structural barriers and connect the client with mental-health, case-management, navigation, peer/support-group, and other services as needed.
options.B: Limit support to one conversation at diagnosis because psychosocial needs generally end once antiretroviral therapy begins.
options.C: Focus only on whether doses are taken and avoid discussing mental health, stigma, relationships, housing, transportation, or social support.
options.D: Assume that viral suppression eliminates the need for continuing psychosocial assessment or support.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC's current HIV clinical-care guidance recommends regular conversations at every office visit to identify adherence barriers and links psychosocial barriers such as depression, substance use, negative beliefs about HIV, low quality of life, and lack of social support with the need for support services. CDC specifically identifies patient navigators, psychologists, support groups, adherence counselors, case managers, and referrals for structural barriers such as transportation, housing, childcare, and insurance. B, C, and D incorrectly treat HIV care as medication-only or time-limited support.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Long-term HIV care includes recurring assessment and support for psychosocial and structural barriers, not medication adherence alone; referrals and navigation/support services should be used as needs evolve.
candidates.source_document_title: Clinical Care of HIV — HIV Nexus
candidates.source_locator: 'Help your patients adhere to ART by engaging in regular conversations at every office visit': identify barriers and offer adherence/support services. 'Psychosocial barriers to adherence': mental health issues, substance use, negative HIV beliefs and lack of social support; refer to psychologists, support groups, adherence counselors, case managers and patient navigators. 'Structural barriers': transportation, housing, childcare and insurance; connect with navigation and support. 'Keeping patients in care': build supportive relationships and refer to needed mental-health/social services.
candidates.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: recognize acute neurologic complications and time-sensitive interventions for clients experiencing stroke.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — late-window EVT selection in acute ischemic stroke
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that late-window EVT is a time-sensitive treatment for selected acute ischemic stroke patients with large-vessel occlusion; contemporary selection integrates clinical status and vascular/brain imaging rather than applying a universal 24-hour rule or requiring one historic perfusion-mismatch profile in every case.

options.A: EVT can benefit selected patients presenting 6–24 hours after onset; eligibility uses vascular and brain imaging plus clinical factors, and treatment should proceed as rapidly as possible rather than assuming every late-window patient is eligible.
options.B: All patients with any ischemic stroke are eligible for EVT through 24 hours without regard to vessel occlusion, infarct burden, disability, or imaging findings.
options.C: Late-window EVT is available only when CT or MR perfusion demonstrates the exact DAWN or DEFUSE-3 mismatch profile; other imaging-selection strategies are no longer acceptable.
options.D: Because a 24-hour window exists for selected patients, time to reperfusion no longer affects outcome once the patient is within that window.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline recommends EVT for selected large-vessel-occlusion patients in the 6–24-hour window using clinical and imaging criteria. DAWN and DEFUSE-3 established benefit using advanced tissue-selection approaches, but subsequent large-core trials expanded the evidence base and the 2026 guideline no longer makes one specific perfusion-mismatch paradigm the universal explanation for late-window eligibility. Imaging must identify the occlusion and assess ischemic burden, and faster treatment remains important because reperfusion benefit is time dependent. B ignores selection criteria. C is too restrictive under current evidence. D falsely treats the late window as time-insensitive.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline supports EVT through 24 hours for selected LVO patients using clinical and imaging criteria, while preserving the time-sensitive nature of reperfusion and allowing a broader evidence-based imaging approach than a universal DAWN/DEFUSE-3 mismatch requirement.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 4.7.2 Endovascular Thrombectomy for Adults: recommendations for selected anterior-circulation proximal LVO patients presenting 6–24 hours after symptom onset based on clinical and imaging characteristics. Section 3.2 Initial, Vascular, and Multimodal Imaging Approaches and recommendation-support text: imaging identifies LVO and ischemic tissue burden; advanced tissue imaging was used in DAWN/DEFUSE-3 and many later trials, but multiple imaging approaches now inform selection. Supportive text emphasizes that EVT benefit is time dependent and evaluation/treatment should be performed as rapidly as possible.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published 2026; current guideline accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of medication therapeutic effects, evaluate response to therapy, and provide medication education.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — statin intensity and therapeutic response
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret statin intensity as the expected percentage reduction in LDL-C and recognize that high-intensity therapy targets at least a 50% reduction while individual response must be confirmed with follow-up lipid testing.

options.A: The statin regimen is expected to reduce LDL-C by at least 50%, although the actual response varies among patients and should be assessed with follow-up lipid testing.
options.B: The medication must be administered more frequently than moderate-intensity statins regardless of the specific drug.
options.C: The term refers primarily to medication cost rather than expected lipid lowering.
options.D: The classification guarantees that every client will reach the same absolute LDL-C value after treatment.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety dyslipidemia guideline classifies statin intensity by expected percentage LDL-C reduction: high-intensity therapy is expected to lower LDL-C by at least 50%, moderate-intensity by 30%–49%, and low-intensity by less than 30%. The guideline also emphasizes that actual percentage reduction varies in clinical practice and follow-up LDL-C assessment is needed to evaluate adherence and treatment effect. B and C misstate the classification. D turns an expected relative effect into a guaranteed identical absolute result.
candidates.source_claim_supported: High-intensity statin therapy is defined by an expected LDL-C reduction of at least 50%, but individual response varies and should be assessed rather than assumed.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
candidates.source_locator: Section 4.2.1.1 Statins, Synopsis and Table 6: statins are categorized by expected percent LDL-C reduction; high-intensity ≥50%, moderate-intensity 30%–49%, low-intensity <30%. The synopsis notes that magnitude of LDL-C lowering varies with patient population and adherence; follow-up LDL-C testing is used to assess adequacy of response and adherence.
candidates.source_organization: American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association and partner societies
candidates.source_version_date: Published March 13, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17
