candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of medication mechanisms, therapeutic effects, and client education.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — evolocumab mechanism of action
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate evolocumab's monoclonal-antibody mechanism from other LDL-lowering therapies: evolocumab binds PCSK9, reduces LDL-receptor degradation, and increases hepatic clearance of circulating LDL-C.

options.A: It binds circulating PCSK9 and prevents PCSK9-mediated degradation of hepatic LDL receptors, increasing receptor availability to clear LDL from the blood.
options.B: It blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption at the brush border and therefore works through the same mechanism as ezetimibe.
options.C: It directly dissolves existing atherosclerotic plaque after each injection rather than changing LDL-receptor activity.
options.D: It degrades hepatic PCSK9 messenger RNA through RNA interference, which is the mechanism of inclisiran rather than evolocumab.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current FDA labeling for evolocumab states that PCSK9 binds hepatic LDL receptors and promotes their degradation. Evolocumab is a monoclonal antibody that inhibits PCSK9 binding to LDL receptors, increasing the number of receptors available to clear LDL from the circulation and thereby lowering LDL-C. B describes intestinal cholesterol-absorption inhibition, not evolocumab. C is not the drug's mechanism. D describes the RNA-interference mechanism of inclisiran; both therapies ultimately increase hepatic LDL-receptor recycling/availability, but they act on PCSK9 through different mechanisms.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Evolocumab lowers LDL-C by binding/inhibiting PCSK9 and preventing PCSK9-mediated LDL-receptor degradation; this differs mechanistically from inclisiran's PCSK9 mRNA silencing despite a shared downstream increase in LDL-receptor availability.
candidates.source_document_title: REPATHA (evolocumab) injection Prescribing Information; LEQVIO (inclisiran) injection Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: REPATHA Section 12.1 Mechanism of Action: PCSK9 binds LDLR on hepatocytes and promotes LDLR degradation; evolocumab inhibits binding of PCSK9 to LDLR, increasing LDLRs available to clear LDL from blood and lowering LDL-C. LEQVIO Section 12.1: inclisiran is an siRNA that directs catalytic breakdown of PCSK9 mRNA, increasing LDL-receptor recycling and expression.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
candidates.source_version_date: REPATHA label updated January 22, 2026; current LEQVIO label accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: apply knowledge of medication mechanisms, therapeutic effects, and combination therapy.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — ezetimibe mechanism of action
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate ezetimibe from statins and PCSK9-directed therapies: ezetimibe lowers LDL-C by inhibiting NPC1L1-mediated cholesterol absorption at the small-intestinal brush border.

options.A: Ezetimibe inhibits the NPC1L1 sterol transporter at the small-intestinal brush border, reducing intestinal cholesterol absorption and delivery of cholesterol to the liver.
options.B: Ezetimibe inhibits hepatic HMG-CoA reductase and therefore works through the same primary mechanism as statins.
options.C: Ezetimibe binds circulating PCSK9 and prevents degradation of hepatic LDL receptors.
options.D: Ezetimibe directly removes cholesterol from established arterial plaque rather than altering cholesterol absorption or hepatic handling.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling states that ezetimibe localizes at the brush border of the small intestine and inhibits the NPC1L1 sterol transporter involved in intestinal uptake of cholesterol and phytosterols. This decreases delivery of intestinal cholesterol to the liver, reduces hepatic cholesterol stores, increases LDL-receptor activity, and lowers circulating LDL-C. B describes the statin mechanism rather than ezetimibe. C describes monoclonal-antibody PCSK9 inhibition such as evolocumab. D is not a labeled mechanism.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Ezetimibe lowers LDL-C by inhibiting NPC1L1-mediated intestinal cholesterol absorption, a mechanism distinct from statin-mediated HMG-CoA reductase inhibition and PCSK9-directed therapies.
candidates.source_document_title: EZETIMIBE tablets Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Section 12.1 Mechanism of Action: ezetimibe reduces blood cholesterol by inhibiting cholesterol absorption in the small intestine; its molecular target is the NPC1L1 sterol transporter involved in intestinal uptake of cholesterol and phytosterols. Ezetimibe localizes at the small-intestinal brush border, decreases delivery of intestinal cholesterol to the liver, reduces hepatic cholesterol stores, and increases LDL-receptor-mediated clearance.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: identify medication interactions, provide administration teaching, and reduce medication-related risk.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — cholestyramine drug interactions and timing
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients taking cholestyramine to separate other oral medications by at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after the resin because cholestyramine can bind medications in the gut and reduce their absorption.

options.A: Take other oral medications at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine to reduce the risk that cholestyramine will impair their absorption.
options.B: Take all oral medications at exactly the same time as cholestyramine because the resin does not bind other drugs in the gastrointestinal tract.
options.C: Inject cholestyramine subcutaneously because oral administration creates clinically important drug-binding interactions.
options.D: Timing is irrelevant because cholestyramine is systemically absorbed before it can affect other oral medications.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling states that cholestyramine may bind other concurrently administered drugs and impede their absorption. The label recommends taking other drugs at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine, or at as great an interval as possible. B and D contradict this labeled interaction. C is incorrect because cholestyramine is an oral resin that acts within the gastrointestinal tract rather than being given by injection.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Cholestyramine can bind concurrently administered oral drugs and reduce absorption; current labeling recommends separating other oral medications by at least 1 hour before or 4–6 hours after cholestyramine.
candidates.source_document_title: Cholestyramine for Oral Suspension, USP Prescribing Information
candidates.source_locator: Drug Interactions/Precautions: cholestyramine may bind other drugs given concurrently. Label recommendation: take other drugs at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine, or at as great an interval as possible, to avoid impeding absorption. The label also notes that cholestyramine is confined to the gastrointestinal tract rather than systemically absorbed.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: evaluate therapeutic medication effects, monitor response, and provide safe medication education.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — fenofibrate and severe hypertriglyceridemia
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize fenofibrate as a triglyceride-lowering option for adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia while avoiding the unsupported claim that treatment guarantees prevention of pancreatitis.

options.A: A substantial reduction in triglyceride-rich lipoproteins; fenofibrate is an evidence-based option for severe hypertriglyceridemia.
options.B: A primary antihypertensive effect with little expected change in triglycerides.
options.C: Selective LDL-C lowering with no clinically meaningful effect on triglycerides.
options.D: Guaranteed prevention of acute pancreatitis once triglycerides begin to fall.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling indicates fenofibrate as an adjunct to diet to reduce triglycerides in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia, defined in the label as triglycerides at least 500 mg/dL. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline identifies fibrates as a first-line triglyceride-lowering option in severe hypertriglyceridemia and notes expected triglyceride reductions of roughly 30% to 50%. B and C misstate the primary lipid effect in this scenario. D is too strong: although severe hypertriglyceridemia is associated with pancreatitis risk and triglyceride lowering is part of risk management, the fenofibrate label states that its effect on reducing pancreatitis risk has not been determined.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Fenofibrate is indicated and guideline-supported to lower triglycerides in severe hypertriglyceridemia; it should not be described as the only first-line therapy or as guaranteeing prevention of pancreatitis.
candidates.source_document_title: Fenofibrate Tablets Prescribing Information; 2026 ACC/AHA Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
candidates.source_locator: Fenofibrate label, Indications and Usage: adjunct to diet to reduce TG in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia (TG ≥500 mg/dL); limitation notes that the effect of fenofibrate on reducing pancreatitis risk has not been determined. 2026 dyslipidemia guideline, Triglyceride-Lowering Medications/Severe Hypertriglyceridemia: fibrates stimulate PPAR-alpha pathways, generally lower TG about 30%–50%, and are a first-line option for severe hypertriglyceridemia, particularly when TG is ≥500 mg/dL.
candidates.source_organization: U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed; American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association and partner societies

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: recognize common adverse effects, provide medication teaching, and distinguish expected effects from symptoms requiring further evaluation.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — niacin flushing management
candidates.educational_objective: Teach evidence-based strategies for niacin extended-release flushing: clinician-approved aspirin shortly before the dose, avoidance of common flushing triggers, appropriate titration, and continued attention to symptoms that could represent a cardiovascular emergency.

options.A: Ask the prescriber whether aspirin is appropriate; when approved, aspirin taken about 30 minutes before niacin can reduce flushing, and alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods should be avoided around dosing time.
options.B: Take niacin on a completely empty stomach and rapidly double the dose so tolerance develops faster.
options.C: Use any NSAID automatically before every dose because all NSAIDs are interchangeable with the labeled aspirin strategy.
options.D: Stop all cardiovascular evaluation during flushing because warmth and redness after niacin cannot overlap with symptoms that require urgent assessment.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling for niacin extended-release tablets states that flushing is common and may be minimized by aspirin, up to the recommended dose of 325 mg, taken about 30 minutes before niacin when appropriate. The label also advises avoiding alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around the time of dosing. B is incorrect because the dose should be titrated rather than rapidly doubled, and the label advises administration with a low-fat snack rather than on an empty stomach. C overgeneralizes the evidence to all NSAIDs; the current patient instructions specifically describe aspirin. D is unsafe because clients with cardiovascular disease must still distinguish flushing from symptoms of myocardial infarction or other urgent conditions.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Niacin extended-release flushing can often be reduced with clinician-approved aspirin about 30 minutes before dosing and by avoiding alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around the dose; rapid unsupervised dose escalation and blanket substitution of other NSAIDs are not supported by the label.
candidates.source_document_title: Niacin Extended-Release Tablets Prescribing Information and Patient Information
candidates.source_locator: Patient Counseling/Flushing: flushing is common and more likely with initiation or dose increases. Use of Aspirin Medication: aspirin up to the recommended dose of 325 mg approximately 30 minutes before dosing can minimize flushing. Diet: avoid alcohol, hot beverages, and spicy foods around dosing; take extended-release niacin with a low-fat snack. Patient information distinguishes flushing from possible myocardial-infarction symptoms.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: provide medication education, distinguish prescribed therapies from non-equivalent products, and evaluate therapeutic response.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — prescription icosapent ethyl versus OTC fish oil
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish prescription icosapent ethyl from nonprescription fish-oil supplements: it is a standardized EPA medication with defined dosing and evidence, and OTC products should not be substituted as if they were dose-for-dose equivalents.

options.A: This is a prescription EPA formulation with a defined dose and indication; nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not considered equivalent substitutes and may have variable fatty-acid content.
options.B: Any over-the-counter fish-oil capsule can be substituted dose-for-dose because all omega-3 products have standardized EPA content and identical evidence.
options.C: The medication is prescribed mainly to lower blood pressure and has little expected effect on triglycerides.
options.D: Icosapent ethyl is an EPA-plus-DHA product, so a rise in LDL-C from its DHA component is required for the medication to work.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current FDA labeling identifies icosapent ethyl as a prescription ethyl ester of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) indicated, among other labeled uses, as an adjunct to diet to reduce triglycerides in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia. The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline explicitly states that nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to prescription omega-3 medications and have variable fatty-acid content. B therefore makes an unsafe equivalence. C misstates the treatment purpose in this scenario. D is incorrect because icosapent ethyl contains EPA rather than an EPA/DHA combination.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Icosapent ethyl is a standardized prescription EPA product used to lower triglycerides; current guideline guidance distinguishes prescription omega-3 medications from variable-content nonprescription fish-oil supplements.
candidates.source_document_title: Icosapent Ethyl Capsules Prescribing Information; 2026 ACC/AHA Multisociety Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
candidates.source_locator: Icosapent ethyl label, Indications and Usage: ethyl ester of EPA indicated as adjunct to diet to reduce TG in adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia (≥500 mg/dL); Dosage and Administration: 4 g/day in divided doses with food. 2026 dyslipidemia guideline, Triglyceride-Lowering Medications: icosapent ethyl contains EPA only; nonprescription fish-oil supplements are not equivalent to or considered prescription medications and have variable fatty-acid content.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: understand medication indications, therapeutic effects, and client teaching.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — low-dose colchicine cardiovascular indication
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that the FDA-approved low-dose colchicine product LODOCO has a cardiovascular risk-reduction indication distinct from colchicine's traditional use for gout and distinct from LDL-lowering or antihypertensive therapy.

options.A: This low-dose colchicine product is FDA-approved to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular death in selected adults with established atherosclerotic disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors.
options.B: Its cardiovascular indication is to lower LDL-C directly and it should replace statin therapy when LDL-C remains elevated.
options.C: Its approved cardiovascular use is treatment of resistant hypertension through direct arterial vasodilation.
options.D: Its cardiovascular role is limited to acute treatment of gout flares that happen to occur in clients with coronary disease.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current FDA label for LODOCO identifies colchicine 0.5 mg once daily as indicated to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, coronary revascularization, and cardiovascular death in adults with established atherosclerotic disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors. B is incorrect because the indication is cardiovascular-event risk reduction, not direct LDL-C lowering or statin replacement. C is not a labeled indication. D incorrectly limits colchicine's cardiovascular use to gout treatment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: LODOCO 0.5 mg daily is an FDA-approved colchicine product for cardiovascular-event risk reduction in selected adults with established atherosclerotic disease or multiple cardiovascular risk factors; it is not an LDL-lowering or antihypertensive drug.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: safely administer time-critical medications and recognize treatment-window requirements for acute conditions.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — alteplase timing in acute ischemic stroke
candidates.educational_objective: For eligible adults with disabling acute ischemic stroke, treat intravenous thrombolysis as a time-critical intervention: alteplase should be administered as rapidly as safely possible within the 4.5-hour window rather than delayed simply because time remains.

options.A: Administer alteplase as quickly as possible once eligibility is established; benefit is time dependent even within the 4.5-hour treatment window.
options.B: Delay alteplase until the end of the 4.5-hour window because later administration within the window improves functional outcome.
options.C: Withhold thrombolysis because alteplase is used only for hemorrhagic stroke, not ischemic stroke.
options.D: Time from symptom onset is clinically unimportant once a client meets eligibility criteria for alteplase.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline recommends intravenous thrombolysis with either alteplase or tenecteplase for eligible adults presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset or last known well and emphasizes that treatment should be initiated as quickly as possible. B and D contradict the time-dependent benefit of reperfusion. C is incorrect because intravenous thrombolysis is a treatment for eligible acute ischemic stroke after hemorrhage has been excluded. The guideline also allows extended-window thrombolysis in selected patients using advanced imaging, but that does not weaken the urgency of treatment in the standard 4.5-hour window.
candidates.source_claim_supported: In eligible adults with acute ischemic stroke presenting within 4.5 hours, alteplase remains a recommended IV thrombolytic option and should be given as quickly as possible because treatment benefit is time dependent.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 4.6.1 Thrombolysis Decision-Making, COR 1: in adults eligible for IV thrombolysis within 4.5 hours, treatment should be initiated as quickly as possible while ensuring safe administration and avoiding unnecessary imaging-related delays. Section 4.6.2, COR 1: either tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg or alteplase 0.9 mg/kg is recommended in eligible adults within 4.5 hours. Section 4.6.3: selected patients beyond 4.5 hours may be considered using advanced imaging criteria.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published 2026; current guideline accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: coordinate interdisciplinary care, use specialized resources, and support evidence-based systems that improve client outcomes.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — organized stroke-unit care
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize organized inpatient stroke-unit care as a multidisciplinary care model associated with improved survival, independence, and discharge/home-living outcomes compared with conventional ward care.

options.A: Greater likelihood of survival, independence, and living at home after follow-up because organized stroke-unit care integrates specialized multidisciplinary assessment, treatment, and rehabilitation.
options.B: No meaningful difference in survival or independence compared with conventional ward care once acute reperfusion decisions are complete.
options.C: Worse functional outcomes because geographically colocated stroke units delay rehabilitation and multidisciplinary care.
options.D: A shorter hospital stay is the main proven benefit, whereas mortality and disability outcomes are unchanged.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline states that organized inpatient stroke-unit care reduces death, disability, and institutionalization. The supporting systematic review found that patients cared for in organized stroke units were more likely to survive, be independent, and live at home at follow-up; benefits were seen across age, sex, stroke type, and severity. B and C contradict this evidence. D is incorrect because the guideline notes no clear effect on length of stay while showing better survival and independence outcomes.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Organized inpatient stroke-unit care improves clinically important outcomes such as survival and independence relative to conventional ward care and is characterized by coordinated specialized multidisciplinary management.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 5.1 Stroke Units — Synopsis: organized stroke-unit care reduces death, disability, and institutionalization; key characteristics include specialized multidisciplinary care, caregiver involvement, staff specialization, early/intensive therapy, and treatment protocols. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: updated systematic review of 29 trials/5902 participants found patients in organized inpatient stroke units more likely to survive, be independent, and live at home, with no clear effect on length of stay.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published 2026; current guideline accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: recognize changes requiring rapid escalation, coordinate interdisciplinary care, and use emergency response systems appropriately.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — stroke-alert activation and rapid team coordination
candidates.educational_objective: Activate the stroke response promptly when acute focal neurologic deficits are recognized so a coordinated team can complete rapid assessment, imaging, and treatment decisions without avoidable delay.

options.A: Mobilize a coordinated stroke team for rapid assessment, brain imaging, and time-sensitive treatment decisions without waiting for a complete diagnostic workup before the response begins.
options.B: Replace bedside neurologic assessment because the stroke team will determine whether the deficits are real after imaging is complete.
options.C: Delay imaging until all laboratory and specialty consultations are completed so the diagnostic sequence is exhaustive before treatment decisions are made.
options.D: Use the alert only when stroke has already been definitively diagnosed, not when acute focal neurologic deficits are first recognized.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline emphasizes expeditious evaluation and treatment, organized stroke protocols, and immediate availability of a stroke team because reperfusion benefit is highly time dependent. Stroke-alert activation begins the coordinated response when stroke is suspected; it does not replace nursing assessment or require definitive diagnosis first. B, C, and D would create inappropriate delay or misunderstand the purpose of the emergency pathway.
candidates.source_claim_supported: A stroke alert is an emergency systems-of-care activation used to mobilize rapid coordinated assessment, imaging, and treatment decisions for suspected acute stroke before a definitive diagnosis is fully established.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Initial evaluation and stroke-systems sections: evaluation and initial treatment of suspected stroke should be performed expeditiously; organized protocols and availability of a stroke team speed clinical assessment, diagnostic studies, and early management decisions. Section 4.6.1 further emphasizes initiating eligible thrombolysis as quickly as possible and avoiding unnecessary diagnostic delays.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published 2026; current guideline accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: coordinate interdisciplinary and telehealth resources, arrange consultation and transfer, and use systems that improve access to timely care.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — telestroke consultation and transfer coordination
candidates.educational_objective: Use telestroke as a systems-of-care resource that brings remote stroke expertise to hospitals without on-site specialists and supports rapid imaging interpretation, reperfusion decisions, and transfer planning while local clinicians continue hands-on care.

options.A: It gives the local team rapid remote access to stroke expertise and imaging review to support thrombolysis, triage, and transfer decisions when on-site specialists are unavailable.
options.B: It replaces all in-person nursing, emergency, radiology, and follow-up care for the remainder of the hospitalization.
options.C: It is useful mainly in large academic centers and offers little benefit to remote hospitals without local neurologists.
options.D: It should be used only after reperfusion-treatment decisions are complete because telemedicine has little role in acute stroke evaluation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline states that telestroke bridges gaps in access to stroke expertise, particularly in remote locations. In the emergency setting, telestroke and teleradiology support timely review of brain imaging, thrombolytic decision-making, and triage or transfer for endovascular thrombectomy when appropriate. B overstates telemedicine as a replacement for local hands-on care. C reverses its equity/access purpose. D is incorrect because acute treatment decisions are a central telestroke use.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Telestroke provides remote specialist consultation and imaging-based decision support for acute stroke, improving access to timely thrombolysis and transfer/triage decisions in hospitals lacking on-site stroke expertise.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 2.8 Telemedicine — Synopsis: telestroke bridges access gaps for remote patients; in acute ED care, teleradiology/telestroke enable timely brain-imaging review, thrombolytic decision-making, and timely treatment. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text: telestroke supports hospitals without on-site neurological expertise and can aid triage/transfer for EVT or allow appropriate local care.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published January 26, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: perform focused screening and assessments that identify aspiration risk and complications before initiating care activities that could increase harm.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake
candidates.educational_objective: Before oral intake after acute stroke, use the facility's validated dysphagia-screening process to identify swallowing risk and trigger further evaluation when needed while recognizing that screening reduces risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia.

options.A: Complete an approved bedside dysphagia screen before oral intake; if the screen is abnormal, restrict oral intake and arrange further swallowing evaluation according to the stroke protocol.
options.B: Offer a small amount of water first because formal screening has little role in identifying aspiration risk after stroke.
options.C: Skip dysphagia screening if the client speaks clearly because swallowing impairment occurs only when aphasia is present.
options.D: Assume that passing a bedside screen guarantees that aspiration and hospital-acquired pneumonia cannot occur.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline states that bedside dysphagia screening before oral intake has inherent clinical logic because it can identify patients at risk, guide additional definitive swallowing assessment, and inform nutritional management. Observational data suggest screening may reduce pneumonia, but the guideline also emphasizes that screening does not prevent every episode of aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia and that no single screening method has been proven superior. B initiates oral intake before screening. C falsely links dysphagia only to aphasia. D overstates the protective value of a passed screen.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Post-stroke dysphagia screening before oral intake can identify patients at risk and guide further swallowing/nutritional evaluation; it may reduce pneumonia risk but does not guarantee prevention of aspiration or pneumonia and no single screening method is universally superior.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 5.2 Dysphagia — Synopsis: bedside screening may help prevent aspiration and pneumonia through early identification of at-risk patients, but screening/formal evaluation/oral-intake restrictions do not prevent all aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1–3: there is inherent logic in screening for dysphagia before oral intake; screening may reduce pneumonia in observational studies, guide additional definitive testing, and aid nutritional management; no specific screening method has proven superiority.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: implement interventions based on identified aspiration risk, monitor response to treatment plans, and recognize changes requiring reassessment.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — individualized aspiration precautions for post-stroke dysphagia
candidates.educational_objective: Implement post-stroke dysphagia precautions according to the individualized swallowing evaluation—using appropriate positioning, texture/viscosity, pacing, cueing, and supervision—and continue monitoring because modified diets do not eliminate aspiration risk.

options.A: Follow the individualized swallowing plan for posture/positioning, food texture and liquid consistency, pacing, cueing, and supervision during oral intake, and reassess if swallowing status changes.
options.B: Use the same thickened-liquid level and chin-tuck position for every client with post-stroke dysphagia regardless of the swallowing evaluation.
options.C: Encourage rapid eating so the meal is completed before fatigue develops, even if the client coughs or requires repeated swallows.
options.D: Assume texture modification eliminates aspiration risk, so ongoing observation and reassessment are unnecessary once the diet order is written.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. ASHA guidance emphasizes individualized dysphagia management based on swallowing assessment, including posture/positioning, compensatory strategies, bolus or diet-texture modification, pacing/cueing, and patient/caregiver education. Texture-modified foods and thickened liquids do not eliminate aspiration or pneumonia risk, and reassessment may be needed when clinical status changes. B applies one strategy to every patient even though postural and consistency recommendations depend on swallowing physiology. C may increase risk when fatigue, impulsivity, coughing, or multiple swallows are present. D incorrectly treats diet modification as a guarantee of airway protection.
candidates.source_claim_supported: For a stroke patient with confirmed dysphagia who is permitted oral intake, aspiration-risk reduction requires individualized swallowing strategies and diet/positioning recommendations with ongoing monitoring; no single posture or consistency is appropriate for all patients and modification does not eliminate aspiration risk.
candidates.source_document_title: Adult Dysphagia Practice Portal; 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: ASHA Adult Dysphagia — intervention may include compensatory swallowing strategies, posture considerations, bolus consistency modification, pacing/cueing, education, and reassessment; Diet Texture Modifications: texture/thickened-liquid changes must be individualized and may not eliminate aspiration or pneumonia risk. AHA/ASA 2026 Section 5.2 Dysphagia: swallowing evaluation and management should identify at-risk patients and guide appropriate oral/nutritional management, while aspiration risk can persist despite screening or restrictions.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: use appropriate organizational and referral resources, coordinate transfers, and participate in quality-improvement systems.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — interpreting stroke-center certification for referral and transfer
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret Comprehensive Stroke Center certification as evidence that a hospital has met an advanced, externally reviewed stroke-care framework with stroke-specific standards, evidence-based care processes, and performance measurement, while continuing to verify real-time transfer capability for the individual client.

options.A: The hospital has met Joint Commission advanced stroke-certification requirements that include core disease-specific standards plus additional stroke-specific requirements, evidence-based clinical practice processes, and performance measurement.
options.B: Any hospital can use the CSC designation regardless of stroke resources, patient volume, standardized care processes, or certification review.
options.C: CSC is a basic rehabilitation-only designation and does not indicate an advanced acute-stroke program.
options.D: CSC certification means performance measurement is unnecessary once the initial certification review is passed.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The Joint Commission classifies Comprehensive Stroke Center certification as an advanced stroke certification developed with the American Heart Association/American Stroke Association. Advanced certification requires the core Disease-Specific Care requirements plus additional clinically specific requirements, use of evidence-based clinical practice guidelines, and ongoing performance measurement. B, C, and D contradict the certification framework. Specific transfer decisions still depend on the patient's clinical needs and the receiving hospital's current capabilities and availability; certification does not replace real-time transfer assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Joint Commission CSC certification is an advanced stroke-care certification requiring compliance with disease-specific and stroke-specific standards, evidence-based care processes, and performance measurement; it is not an unrestricted label available to any hospital.
candidates.source_document_title: Stroke Certification; What Is Certification?; 2026 Stroke Certification Standards

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — interdisciplinary post-stroke rehabilitation planning
candidates.educational_objective: Coordinate early interdisciplinary rehabilitation assessment after stroke because recovery needs can span mobility, self-care, communication, swallowing, cognition, and psychosocial function and require an individualized plan and appropriate post-acute level of care.

options.A: Stroke can produce different combinations of physical, functional, communication, cognitive, and psychosocial impairments, so coordinated multidisciplinary assessment helps determine the appropriate rehabilitation needs and level of care.
options.B: A single discipline can reliably address every post-stroke impairment, making coordinated rehabilitation assessment unnecessary.
options.C: Only motor weakness affects rehabilitation planning; communication, cognition, swallowing, and activities of daily living do not alter the rehabilitation plan.
options.D: Rehabilitation assessment should generally be deferred until after discharge because in-hospital interdisciplinary evaluation has no association with functional recovery.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline notes that patients have highly variable impairments and individualized needs and recommends a comprehensive multidisciplinary approach to determine the appropriate intensity and modality of rehabilitation. In-hospital interdisciplinary rehabilitation evaluation is associated with improved functional outcomes. B and C ignore the multidimensional effects of stroke. D contradicts the guideline's support for inpatient interdisciplinary assessment and early rehabilitation planning.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Post-stroke rehabilitation planning should use multidisciplinary assessment because impairments and recovery needs vary across functional domains; inpatient interdisciplinary evaluation helps determine the appropriate rehabilitation level and is associated with improved functional recovery.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 5.7 Rehabilitation — Synopsis: patients with stroke have highly variable degrees of impairment and diverse individualized needs; a comprehensive multidisciplinary program is critical for assessing appropriate rehabilitation intensity and modality. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1: organized stroke units commonly include interdisciplinary rehabilitation assessment; inpatient interdisciplinary evaluation for the appropriate level of rehabilitation is associated with improved functional outcomes and guidelines support multidisciplinary inpatient evaluation.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
candidates.source_version_date: Published January 26, 2026; accessed 2026-08-17

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — early individualized post-stroke rehabilitation planning
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate early rehabilitation assessment and planning—which should begin during hospitalization—from indiscriminate very-early high-dose mobilization; rehabilitation timing and intensity must be individualized to the client's condition.

options.A: Begin interdisciplinary rehabilitation assessment and individualized planning during hospitalization, while tailoring mobilization intensity and timing to the client's medical and neurologic status rather than prescribing high-dose mobilization within the first 24 hours for everyone.
options.B: Postpone all rehabilitation assessment until after hospital discharge because early inpatient planning has no demonstrated relationship to functional recovery.
options.C: Require intensive out-of-bed mobilization within the first 24 hours for every stroke client because greater early mobilization doses consistently improve functional outcome.
options.D: Limit rehabilitation planning to clients with mild stroke because clients with moderate or severe deficits do not benefit from multidisciplinary assessment.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline supports comprehensive multidisciplinary rehabilitation assessment during hospitalization to determine the appropriate intensity and modality of rehabilitation. In-hospital interdisciplinary evaluation is associated with improved functional outcomes. However, the guideline also states that very early mobilization within 24 hours has not shown functional benefit, and one randomized trial found worse outcomes with high-dose very-early mobilization. B incorrectly delays planning. C converts early planning into an unsupported universal high-dose mobilization protocol. D incorrectly restricts rehabilitation assessment by stroke severity.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Early inpatient multidisciplinary rehabilitation assessment and planning are supported after acute stroke, but this should not be conflated with universal intensive mobilization within the first 24 hours; mobilization timing and dose should be individualized.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 5.7 Rehabilitation — Synopsis: patients have diverse individualized needs and a comprehensive multidisciplinary program is critical for selecting rehabilitation intensity/modality; in-hospital interdisciplinary evaluation is associated with improved functional outcomes. The same synopsis states that very early (<24 hours) mobilization has not shown functional benefit and high doses produced worse outcomes in one RCT. Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1 supports multidisciplinary inpatient evaluation for the appropriate rehabilitation level.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized stroke discharge and transition planning
candidates.educational_objective: Plan stroke discharge as an early, dynamic, individualized transition process that integrates rehabilitation/service needs, medications and secondary prevention, follow-up and safety/self-management planning, and caregiver education/readiness.

options.A: Use an individualized, evolving plan based on patient and family needs that addresses postacute rehabilitation and services, medication and secondary-prevention education, follow-up, safety and self-management needs, and caregiver readiness before transition.
options.B: Use the same discharge template for every stroke survivor because functional deficits, home environment, caregiver support, and rehabilitation needs do not change the transition plan.
options.C: Wait until the day of discharge to begin planning because early needs assessment does not affect selection of postacute services or caregiver preparation.
options.D: Focus only on the discharge date and medication list because rehabilitation placement, recurrent-stroke education, caregiver training, and follow-up are handled after the client leaves the hospital.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. A 2026 AHA scientific statement on nursing stroke care states that discharge planning should begin early, remain dynamic, and be guided by patient and family needs assessments; predischarge rehabilitation assessment is important for selecting the appropriate postacute setting and services. Current AHA nursing guidance also emphasizes education about lifestyle changes, medication adherence, recurrent-stroke symptom recognition, self-management and secondary prevention, and preparation of caregivers before discharge. B, C, and D fail to individualize the transition or defer essential planning until too late.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Stroke discharge planning should begin early, remain individualized and dynamic, incorporate rehabilitation/postacute service selection and secondary-prevention/self-management education, and prepare patients and caregivers for the transition rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all last-day process.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — individualized discharge planning/caregiver preparation for transition to home
candidates.educational_objective: Select an individualized post-stroke caregiver education plan that combines practical skill-building with psychoeducational support and includes reassessment after discharge as caregiver needs change.

options.A: Use an individualized plan that combines practical skill-building with psychoeducational support and reassess caregiver needs after discharge.
options.B: Provide a standardized written packet focused on stroke facts and defer practical skills training until home services begin.
options.C: Limit teaching to psychoeducation during hospitalization because practical skills are best learned only after discharge.
options.D: Teach only the client unless the caregiver requests training, then provide the same material used for all families.

candidates.rationale: The AHA/ASA stroke rehabilitation guideline recommends caregiver interventions that combine skill building with psychoeducational strategies, are tailored to the individual caregiver's needs, and include postdischarge assessment with interventions adjusted as needs change. Therefore, option A is the best plan. A standardized information-only approach (B), psychoeducation without skill building (C), and client-only or one-size-fits-all caregiver teaching (D) do not match these recommendations.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized stroke caregiver interventions combining skill-building and psychoeducational strategies, plus postdischarge reassessment and tailoring to changing caregiver needs. Currentness was cross-checked against the AHA/ASA 2025 rehabilitation access policy statement and the 2026 acute ischemic stroke guideline, which continue to reference the adult stroke rehabilitation guideline for poststroke rehabilitation practice.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — recognizing and explaining an appropriate palliative-care referral/consultation for a client with serious stroke
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that palliative care after severe stroke can begin early and continue through recovery to address symptoms, values/goals communication, and patient-family support rather than being restricted to hospice or the final days of life.

options.A: Palliative care is generally reserved for the final days of life after disease-directed treatment has stopped.
options.B: Palliative care can be integrated now to address symptoms, communication about values and goals, and support for the client and family throughout recovery.
options.C: Palliative care is mainly used to determine hospice eligibility and should replace rehabilitation planning once consulted.
options.D: Palliative care should be delayed until the prognosis is certain so that recovery-focused care is not undermined.

candidates.rationale: The American Heart Association's 2024 scientific statement on palliative and end-of-life care in stroke emphasizes that palliative care should be integrated from the initial hospitalization and throughout stroke recovery, not limited to end-of-life. Core palliative-care skills include symptom management, effective communication, and understanding patient values and goals, while support extends to patients and families. Therefore, B is the best response. A and D incorrectly delay palliative care, and C incorrectly reduces palliative care to hospice and frames it as a replacement for rehabilitation rather than care that can be integrated across recovery.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Items 1, 2, and 9 directly support integrating palliative care from initial hospitalization through all phases of stroke recovery rather than limiting it to end-of-life; item 7 directly supports communication, symptom management, and attention to patient values and goals. The same AHA material identifies support for patients and families as part of the palliative approach.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Management of Care — Performance Improvement (Quality Improvement) using stroke process-measure data
candidates.educational_objective: Use stroke performance-measure data for structured quality improvement by reviewing eligible cases against the measure's defined criteria and exclusions rather than treating the metric as a substitute for individualized care or as proof of individual fault.

options.A: Review eligible ischemic-stroke cases against the STK-2 discharge-prescribing criteria and documented exclusions to identify process gaps for improvement.
options.B: Assume every ischemic-stroke discharge without an antithrombotic prescription represents an error, regardless of documented reasons for nonprescribing.
options.C: Use the aggregate STK-2 rate to determine which individual bedside nurse caused each missed prescription without reviewing the records.
options.D: Replace individualized discharge decisions with the measure numerator so that all stroke clients receive the same medication plan.

candidates.rationale: The Joint Commission's current STK-2 measure evaluates ischemic-stroke patients prescribed antithrombotic therapy at discharge and includes a pathway for documented reasons for not prescribing therapy. A quality-improvement review should therefore examine eligible cases against the defined measure criteria and exclusions to identify process gaps. B ignores valid documented exclusions, C attributes causation from an aggregate measure without case review, and D misuses a performance measure as a substitute for individualized clinical decision-making.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly defines STK-2 as a stroke process-performance measure based on antithrombotic prescribing at discharge and explicitly accounts for documented reasons for nonprescribing, supporting case review against measure criteria rather than automatic classification of every nonprescription as an error.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — preventing pulmonary complications in acute stroke by recognizing dysphagia/aspiration risk before oral intake
candidates.educational_objective: For a client with acute ischemic stroke, ensure dysphagia screening is completed before oral intake to identify aspiration risk and guide safe nutrition and medication administration.

options.A: Perform or ensure completion of a bedside swallow screen before giving liquids, food, or oral medications.
options.B: Offer a small amount of water first; arrange swallowing assessment only if coughing or choking occurs.
options.C: Allow thin liquids while withholding solid food because liquids are less likely than solids to be aspirated after stroke.
options.D: Keep the client permanently NPO because bedside screening cannot eliminate all aspiration or pneumonia risk.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline recommends bedside dysphagia screening before oral intake of liquids or food. Its dysphagia section explains that screening can identify patients at risk and may help reduce pneumonia incidence, while also emphasizing that screening does not prevent every episode of aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia. Therefore, the nurse should ensure screening occurs before oral intake. B and C expose an unscreened client to oral intake, and D overstates the limitation of screening by converting it into a permanent NPO requirement.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports completing bedside dysphagia screening before oral intake in acute ischemic stroke and supports the rationale that screening identifies aspiration risk without claiming that screening prevents every aspiration or pneumonia event.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 5, In-Hospital Management of AIS: General Supportive Care → 5.2 Dysphagia. Recommendation: bedside swallow screening before oral intake of liquids and foods is recommended. Synopsis and Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 1: screening may identify patients at risk for aspiration/pneumonia, observational data suggest screening may reduce pneumonia incidence, and screening should precede oral intake; screening does not prevent all aspiration or hospital-acquired pneumonia.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — recognition and management principles for post-stroke seizure
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that unprovoked seizures can occur after the acute stroke period and that antiseizure treatment after such a seizure is individualized rather than universally prophylactic or automatically lifelong.

options.A: Post-stroke seizures occur only during the first week after a stroke, so this event is unrelated to the prior stroke.
options.B: An antiseizure medication may reasonably be initiated after an unprovoked post-stroke seizure, with the drug and duration individualized to the client.
options.C: Every client with ischemic stroke should receive prophylactic antiseizure medication even if no seizure has occurred.
options.D: A fixed lifelong antiseizure regimen is required after any post-stroke seizure regardless of seizure recurrence, adverse effects, or client factors.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline states that seizures may occur early within the first week or later as unprovoked post-stroke seizures. After an unprovoked post-stroke seizure, starting an antiseizure medication is reasonable, but medication selection and duration should be individualized according to patient-specific factors. Routine prophylactic antiseizure medication for patients who have not had a seizure is not supported by sufficient evidence. Therefore, B is the best answer. A incorrectly excludes late seizures, C promotes unsupported universal prophylaxis, and D invents a fixed lifelong duration.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports the occurrence of both early and later post-stroke seizures, individualized antiseizure treatment after an unprovoked post-stroke seizure, and the absence of sufficient evidence for routine prophylactic antiseizure medication in seizure-free stroke patients.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
candidates.source_locator: Section 6, In-Hospital Management of AIS: Treatment of Acute Complications → 6.5 Seizures. candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — stroke-risk assessment, disease prevention, and counseling about modifiable health behaviors
candidates.educational_objective: Identify modifiable stroke-prevention targets, including tobacco cessation, physical activity, blood-pressure control, and blood-glucose management, while distinguishing them from nonmodifiable factors such as age and family history.

options.A: I can lower my risk by stopping tobacco use, being physically active, and working with my health care team to control blood pressure and blood sugar.
options.B: My family history is the main risk factor I can change, so lifestyle changes have little role if stroke runs in my family.
options.C: Age is a modifiable risk factor, so reducing age-related risk is more important than controlling blood pressure or tobacco exposure.
options.D: Once diabetes is present, managing blood sugar no longer contributes to the health factors used to reduce stroke risk.

candidates.rationale: The American Heart Association/American Stroke Association 2024 primary-prevention guidance identifies tobacco use, physical inactivity, high blood pressure, and blood-glucose management among important modifiable or manageable factors for cardiovascular and brain health. Family history and age are not modifiable. Therefore, A correctly identifies changeable targets for stroke prevention. B incorrectly treats family history as changeable and dismisses modifiable behaviors, C incorrectly labels age as modifiable, and D incorrectly dismisses blood-glucose management after diabetes develops.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports tobacco cessation, physical activity, blood-pressure control, and blood-glucose management as actionable stroke-prevention targets and distinguishes family history as a risk factor that informs risk rather than a behavior that can be changed.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — stroke-risk assessment in a client with atrial fibrillation to reduce thromboembolic complications
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that CHA₂DS₂-VASc estimates thromboembolic stroke risk in atrial fibrillation and contributes to anticoagulation decision-making without diagnosing atrial fibrillation or replacing individualized risk-benefit assessment.

options.A: It estimates the client's risk of thromboembolic stroke and helps inform decisions about stroke-prevention therapy, including oral anticoagulation.
options.B: It confirms the diagnosis of atrial fibrillation by grading the severity and duration of the client's rhythm disturbance.
options.C: It primarily estimates the client's risk of major bleeding if oral anticoagulation is prescribed.
options.D: It replaces assessment of bleeding risk, patient preferences, and other clinical factors when anticoagulation is considered.

candidates.rationale: The 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS atrial fibrillation guideline identifies CHA₂DS₂-VASc as a validated clinical score used to estimate stroke/thromboembolic risk in patients with atrial fibrillation. Stroke-risk assessment helps guide selection of stroke-prevention therapy, including oral anticoagulation, but the score is only an estimate and does not replace assessment of bleeding risk, patient preferences, or other clinical factors. It is not a diagnostic test for atrial fibrillation and is not primarily a bleeding-risk score. Therefore, A is the best answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports use of CHA₂DS₂-VASc to estimate stroke/thromboembolic risk in atrial fibrillation and to inform stroke-prevention/anticoagulation decisions while preserving individualized assessment of bleeding risk and patient preferences.
candidates.source_document_title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation

Section 6.2, Risk-Based Selection of Oral Anticoagulation: stroke-prevention therapy is guided by stroke risk, bleeding risk, and individual preferences; stroke scores are estimates rather than substitutes for individualized assessment.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — secondary prevention of recurrent stroke after an existing cerebrovascular event
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that secondary stroke prevention requires individualized evaluation of stroke cause plus management of modifiable vascular and lifestyle risk factors to reduce future stroke risk.

options.A: Secondary prevention should be individualized to the cause of the stroke and includes management of vascular risk factors and health behaviors that can reduce recurrence risk.
options.B: Once the acute stroke has resolved, recurrence risk is negligible, so additional risk-factor management usually adds little benefit.
options.C: A recurrent stroke is generally expected to be milder than the first, so prevention efforts can be deferred unless new symptoms develop.
options.D: Secondary prevention is essentially the same for every stroke survivor, regardless of the stroke mechanism, comorbidities, or treatment preferences.

candidates.rationale: The AHA/ASA secondary stroke-prevention guideline emphasizes that prevention strategies depend on the ischemic stroke or TIA subtype and that vascular risk-factor management, including hypertension, diabetes, smoking cessation, lipids, diet, and physical activity, is important for preventing future events. Care plans should be tailored to the individual client. Therefore, A is correct. B minimizes a clinically important recurrence risk, C falsely assumes a recurrent stroke will be milder, and D contradicts the guideline's etiology-specific and individualized approach.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized, etiology-informed secondary prevention and management of modifiable vascular and lifestyle risk factors to reduce future stroke risk after ischemic stroke or TIA.
candidates.source_document_title: 2021 Guideline for the Prevention of Stroke in Patients With Stroke and Transient Ischemic Attack
candidates.source_locator: Top 10 Take-Home Messages, items 1–4: secondary-prevention strategies depend on ischemic stroke/TIA subtype; diagnostic workup should identify etiology and treatment targets to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke; vascular risk-factor management including diabetes, smoking cessation, lipids, and especially hypertension remains extremely important; healthy diet and physical activity are important for preventing a second stroke; goals should be tailored to the individual patient. Professional Heart Daily guideline summary states the guideline provides evidence-based recommendations for prevention of future stroke among survivors of ischemic stroke or TIA.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — lipid management to reduce recurrent atherosclerotic events after ischemic stroke
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize lipid-lowering therapy, with statin therapy as the foundation, as part of secondary prevention after atherosclerotic ischemic stroke while avoiding one-size-fits-all LDL targets that ignore ASCVD risk and stroke mechanism.

options.A: Lipid management is relevant only to coronary disease, so prior ischemic stroke does not support continued lipid-lowering therapy.
options.B: For clinical atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, statin therapy is a foundation of secondary prevention, with treatment goals and any additional lipid-lowering therapy individualized to the client's risk.
options.C: After an ischemic stroke, lipid-lowering therapy is avoided because lowering LDL cholesterol increases recurrent stroke risk.
options.D: A single LDL cholesterol target applies to every stroke survivor regardless of whether the stroke was atherosclerotic or of another mechanism and regardless of overall ASCVD risk.

candidates.rationale: The 2026 ACC/AHA multisociety dyslipidemia guideline identifies statin therapy as the foundation of lipid-lowering treatment for secondary prevention in clinical ASCVD. It also uses risk-based LDL-C and non-HDL-C goals and allows additional lipid-lowering therapy according to the degree of risk, LDL lowering needed, and patient preferences. Therefore, B is correct for a client with an atherosclerotic ischemic stroke. A incorrectly limits lipid management to coronary disease, C reverses the evidence-based purpose of LDL lowering, and D ignores the guideline's risk-based and individualized approach.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports statin-based lipid lowering for secondary prevention in clinical ASCVD and a risk-stratified rather than universal approach to LDL-C goals and additional therapy. The stem specifies an atherosclerotic ischemic stroke so the ASCVD secondary-prevention framework applies without assuming every stroke mechanism is atherosclerotic.
candidates.source_document_title: 2026 ACC/AHA/AACVPR/ABC/ACPM/ADA/AGS/APhA/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia

candidates.blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — long-term blood-pressure control to reduce recurrent stroke risk
candidates.educational_objective: For a neurologically stable stroke survivor with hypertension, recognize the current secondary-prevention blood-pressure goal of less than 130/80 mm Hg and the need to individualize antihypertensive therapy.

options.A: Work toward a blood pressure below 130/80 mm Hg, with the antihypertensive regimen individualized to the client's comorbidities and preferences.
options.B: Maintain chronically elevated blood pressure after stroke because lowering blood pressure increases recurrent-stroke risk in stable outpatients.
options.C: Treat blood pressure only if new focal neurologic symptoms develop because hypertension management is relevant mainly during an acute stroke.
options.D: Use the same antihypertensive drug regimen for every stroke survivor because stroke mechanism and comorbidities do not affect treatment selection.

candidates.rationale: The 2025 AHA/ACC adult hypertension guideline states that neurologically stable patients with prior stroke or TIA benefit from a blood-pressure goal below 130/80 mm Hg for secondary stroke prevention. It also emphasizes that antihypertensive regimens should account for comorbidities, medication class, and patient preference. Therefore, A is correct. B and C incorrectly discourage long-term blood-pressure control, and D ignores individualized treatment selection.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports a long-term blood-pressure goal below 130/80 mm Hg for neurologically stable clients with prior stroke/TIA and supports individualized antihypertensive regimen selection rather than a universal drug plan.
candidates.source_document_title: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults

Recommendation-Specific Supportive Text 2 supports benefit of the <130/80 mm Hg goal after prior stroke/TIA.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — safe assisted mobility and transfer support for a stroke survivor with weakness and impaired balance
candidates.educational_objective: Reduce post-stroke falls by using individualized risk assessment and matching transfer assistance, supervision, and mobility aids to the client's current deficits while continuing safe mobility practice.

options.A: Use an individualized fall-risk assessment, follow the recommended mobility aid and transfer technique, and provide the level of assistance or supervision indicated by the assessment.
options.B: Use the same fall precautions for every stroke client because individualized assessment does not meaningfully change mobility planning.
options.C: Keep the client on bed rest until independent balance has completely returned so that falls cannot occur during rehabilitation.
options.D: Permit unassisted transfers once the client can stand briefly, even if the prescribed mobility aid and supervision level have not been reassessed.

candidates.rationale: Current stroke-rehabilitation guidance recommends screening all people with stroke for fall risk, performing a comprehensive assessment when risk is identified, and implementing an individualized fall-prevention plan. The plan may include safe-transfer training and recommended mobility aids, with strategies based on the client's specific impairments. Therefore, A is best. B ignores individualized risk factors, C unnecessarily restricts rehabilitation and mobility, and D advances independence without reassessment of the client's current fall risk and support needs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports individualized post-stroke fall-risk screening/assessment, individualized prevention planning, safe-transfer training, and use/reassessment of appropriate mobility aids rather than universal precautions or mobility restriction.
candidates.source_document_title: Rehabilitation, Recovery and Community Participation Following Stroke, 7th Edition 2025 — Falls Prevention and Management
candidates.source_locator: Part Two: Delivery of Stroke Rehabilitation to Optimize Functional Recovery → Section 5, Falls Prevention and Management. Recommendations 1–3: screen all individuals with stroke for fall risk using validated tools; assess medical, physical, cognitive, medication-related and environmental factors; perform comprehensive interdisciplinary assessment for those at risk; implement an individualized falls-prevention plan based on findings. Recommendation 3.2: provide skills training for safe transfers and mobility. Recommendation 3.4: educate regarding recommended and appropriate mobility aids and transfer devices. Section 4.1 Clinical Considerations also states that gait aids, wheelchairs, and other assistive devices should be evaluated on an individual basis and reassessed as appropriate.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — therapeutic communication adapted to a client with post-stroke aphasia
candidates.educational_objective: Communicate with a client who has post-stroke aphasia by allowing time and using clear adult-level language plus individualized multimodal supports without assuming cognitive incapacity.

options.A: Use short adult-level sentences, speak at a comfortable pace and volume, allow extra response time, and use writing, pictures, or gestures when helpful.
options.B: Speak loudly and rapidly so the client receives more information before becoming frustrated by the communication difficulty.
options.C: Direct questions primarily to the family because aphasia indicates that the client is unable to understand spoken language or participate in decisions.
options.D: Avoid alternative communication methods so the client must practice spoken language during every interaction until verbal fluency returns.

candidates.rationale: ASHA guidance for adults with communication disorders recommends simple but adult language, slower speech, short sentences, adequate time to communicate, and multimodal supports such as pictures, writing, and gestures when useful. Aphasia does not automatically imply cognitive impairment or absent comprehension. Therefore, A is best. B adds unnecessary loudness and speed, C wrongly assumes incapacity and bypasses the client, and D removes compensatory communication methods that can support effective participation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports adult-level simplified language, appropriate pace/volume, extra response time, multimodal communication supports, and avoidance of the assumption that aphasia means cognitive incapacity.
candidates.source_document_title: Aphasia — ASHA Practice Portal; Tips for Communicating With Adults Who Have a Speech or Language Disorder
candidates.source_locator: ASHA Practice Portal → Aphasia → Differential Diagnosis: aphasia does not imply cognitive deficits; Partner Approaches → Conversational Coaching and Supported Conversation for Adults With Aphasia: communication partners may use drawing, gesturing, cueing, confirming, summarizing and multimodal communication. ASHA communication tips → 'To help someone understand you better': keep voice at a comfortable level, use simple but adult words, slow speech, short sentences, and pictures/gestures/writing; 'To help someone express themselves better': give time to communicate and invite drawing, writing, pointing, or gesturing as needed.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — integrating family history with modifiable stroke-risk counseling
candidates.educational_objective: Distinguish nonmodifiable stroke-risk information, such as family history, from modifiable prevention targets and use both appropriately in primary-prevention counseling.

options.A: Family history still helps identify stroke risk, while prevention efforts can focus on modifiable factors such as blood pressure, tobacco use, physical activity, and blood-glucose management.
options.B: Family history should be ignored because only factors that can be changed are relevant when assessing stroke risk.
options.C: A family history of stroke means lifestyle and medical risk-factor management are unlikely to alter the person's overall risk.
options.D: Family history becomes clinically relevant only after a person has already experienced a stroke or transient ischemic attack.

candidates.rationale: The AHA/ASA 2024 primary-prevention guidance lists family history among common stroke risk factors and separately emphasizes actionable health factors and behaviors such as blood-pressure control, tobacco avoidance, physical activity, and blood-glucose management. A nonmodifiable factor can still be important for risk assessment even though it cannot itself be changed. Therefore, A is best. B incorrectly discards useful risk information, C promotes unsupported fatalism, and D incorrectly delays consideration of family history until after a cerebrovascular event.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports considering family history as part of stroke-risk assessment while focusing prevention counseling on actionable vascular and lifestyle factors.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — lifestyle counseling for primary stroke prevention
candidates.educational_objective: Counsel adults without prior stroke to use evidence-based primary-prevention lifestyle strategies, including a Mediterranean-style diet, regular physical activity, and reduction of prolonged sedentary behavior.

options.A: Follow a Mediterranean-style eating pattern, engage in regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity as appropriate, and reduce prolonged sedentary behavior.
options.B: Rely on a low-fat diet alone and avoid structured physical activity because exertion can increase stroke risk in otherwise healthy adults.
options.C: Focus only on body weight and disregard diet quality or sedentary behavior if the client's weight remains in the desired range.
options.D: Delay lifestyle changes until hypertension or diabetes develops because lifestyle counseling has little role in primary stroke prevention before disease appears.

candidates.rationale: The 2024 AHA/ASA primary-prevention guideline recommends a Mediterranean dietary pattern for adults without prior cardiovascular disease and emphasizes regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. It also recommends identifying and counseling about prolonged sedentary behavior because sedentary time is associated with higher stroke risk. Therefore, A best matches current guidance. B incorrectly discourages activity and overstates the value of a low-fat diet alone, C ignores diet quality and sedentary behavior, and D delays primary prevention until disease develops.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports the combination of Mediterranean-style eating, regular physical activity, and reduction of prolonged sedentary behavior for primary stroke prevention without claiming that any single lifestyle change guarantees prevention.
candidates.source_document_title: 2024 Guideline for the Primary Prevention of Stroke — Top Things to Know
candidates.source_locator: Top Things to Know → item 3: recommends a Mediterranean diet for adults without prior cardiovascular disease and notes little stroke-risk impact from low-fat diets; item 4: physical activity is important for stroke-risk reduction, prolonged sedentary behavior is associated with increased risk, and counseling to avoid sedentary behavior is recommended in addition to regular moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
candidates.source_organization: American Heart Association/American Stroke Association

candidates.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity: nursing care that promotes and supports emotional, mental and social well-being during stressful events. candidates.blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — family-role adjustment and caregiver support after stroke
candidates.educational_objective: Support family adjustment after stroke by acknowledging role changes and caregiver stress, assessing support needs, and linking caregivers with individualized education and community resources.

options.A: Acknowledge the role changes and stress, assess the family's support needs, and connect the caregiver with education and community or respite resources.
options.B: Reassure the spouse that caregiver stress usually resolves once the client is medically stable, so additional support is rarely needed.
options.C: Focus discharge teaching only on the client's physical needs because family adjustment is outside the nursing plan of care.
options.D: Provide one general caregiver handout and avoid follow-up questions so the family can adapt independently.

candidates.rationale: American Stroke Association caregiver guidance notes that stroke can create major role changes and new responsibilities, that caregiving can be stressful and frustrating, and that caregivers may need help from family, community resources, respite services, home health, and stroke support groups. Nursing support should therefore acknowledge the transition, assess needs, provide education, and facilitate appropriate resources. B minimizes caregiver burden, C excludes an important part of psychosocial care, and D substitutes one-time generic information for individualized support.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Directly supports acknowledging caregiver role changes and stress and connecting stroke caregivers with individualized education, emotional support, and community/respite resources rather than assuming medical stability eliminates family support needs.

candidates.source_locator: Sections 'What should a stroke caregiver do?' and 'Is there assistance for caregivers?': caregiver responsibilities vary with the survivor's unique needs; role changes and new skills may be needed; caregiving can be stressful and frustrating; caregivers should rely on others when needed; community resources include home health, personal-care support, respite care, meal programs, and stroke support groups for education and emotional support.
