candidates.blueprint_topic: Skin integrity / comfort measures
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize a moist radiation skin reaction and provide prompt assessment plus radiation-team-directed gentle skin/wound care rather than vigorous cleansing or unsupervised adhesive/topical treatment.

options.A: Notify the radiation oncology team, assess the skin for severity and infection concerns, and follow the team's gentle cleansing and prescribed dressing plan for the moist reaction.
options.B: Scrub the moist area vigorously during bathing to remove loose skin and reduce bacterial growth.
options.C: Apply an adhesive bandage and any over-the-counter antibiotic ointment available without first checking the radiation skin-care plan.
options.D: Reassure the client that wet, painful skin breakdown does not need to be reported because it is an expected finding that cannot be treated.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI defines a moist reaction as radiation-related skin peeling that becomes moist and painful; sores or ulcers may develop and can lead to infection. NCI advises clients to report skin changes promptly and states that the health care team may direct how to keep a peeling, painful, wet area clean and dry and may prescribe special dressings or antibiotics when indicated. B is incorrect because vigorous scrubbing can further injure damaged skin. C is incorrect because unapproved adhesives and self-selected topical products should not be placed over irradiated skin without the radiation team's plan. D is incorrect because a moist reaction requires assessment and directed supportive care rather than dismissal.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Moist reaction is peeling, moist, painful irradiated skin with possible sores/infection; skin changes should be reported; the team directs cleaning and prescribed dressings/treatment; adhesives and trauma to the field should be avoided.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Nutrition / symptom management
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate cancer cachexia from simple inadequate intake and support individualized multidisciplinary management that includes, but is not limited to, dietitian-guided nutrition intervention.

options.A: Cachexia is a complex wasting syndrome that is not fully reversed by nutrition alone; care should address symptoms and medical contributors while using individualized nutrition support, often with a registered dietitian.
options.B: Cachexia is caused only by inadequate calorie intake, so increasing food intake is sufficient to reverse the syndrome in most clients.
options.C: Nutrition support has no role in cachexia, so dietary assessment and symptom-related eating problems should not be addressed.
options.D: Every client with cachexia should receive the same high-calorie meal plan regardless of appetite, symptoms, cancer type, or goals of care.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI describes cancer cachexia as a wasting syndrome with loss of skeletal muscle and fat that, unlike simple malnutrition, cannot be reversed with nutrition support alone. Inflammation, metabolic changes, reduced intake, and symptom burden may contribute. NCI recommends multidisciplinary management and notes that registered dietitians can provide individualized nutrition counseling and strategies. B is incorrect because inadequate calories are not the sole mechanism and increased intake alone does not reliably reverse cachexia. C is incorrect because nutrition assessment and support remain clinically useful even though they are not sufficient by themselves. D is incorrect because nutrition intervention should be individualized rather than a single universal meal plan.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Cancer cachexia is multifactorial and not reversed by nutrition support alone; individualized multidisciplinary care and registered-dietitian nutrition support remain appropriate.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Activity-rest balance / energy conservation
candidates.educational_objective: Teach balanced energy conservation for cancer-related fatigue by combining prioritization and short planned rest with individualized safe activity rather than complete inactivity or indiscriminate overexertion.

options.A: Plan short rest periods and prioritize the activities that matter most, but balance rest with an individualized level of physical activity rather than remaining completely inactive.
options.B: Complete bed rest is the preferred fatigue-management strategy because physical activity reliably worsens cancer-related fatigue.
options.C: Ignore fatigue when planning the day and complete all usual activities at the same pace regardless of symptoms.
options.D: Avoid discussing activity with the healthcare team because fatigue-management strategies do not need to be individualized.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI recommends planned rest, prioritizing the most important activities, and doing activities when energy is highest. NCI also supports individualized physical activity and exercise because activity can reduce cancer-related fatigue and help maintain function; complete inactivity is not the general goal. B is incorrect because routine complete bed rest can promote deconditioning and is not NCI's recommended fatigue strategy. C is incorrect because pacing and prioritization are appropriate when fatigue interferes with function. D is incorrect because activity should be individualized to the client's condition, treatment, safety, and functional ability.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Cancer-related fatigue management includes planned rest, prioritization and scheduling of important activities, plus individualized physical activity/exercise rather than complete inactivity.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize early upper-extremity lymphedema symptoms after axillary lymph-node dissection and prioritize prompt assessment and comparison of the affected limb rather than delaying evaluation or starting unassessed treatment.

options.A: Assess and compare both arms for swelling and other changes and promptly arrange evaluation for possible lymphedema.
options.B: Reassure the client that heaviness and tightness are expected after axillary surgery and require evaluation only if the swelling becomes severe.
options.C: Encourage immediate heavy resistance exercise with the affected arm before any assessment is completed.
options.D: Assume the symptoms prove lymphedema and begin tight compression wrapping without evaluation or fitting by the healthcare team.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI states that lymph-node removal increases lymphedema risk after breast-cancer treatment and advises clients to report even slight changes such as a heavy, full, or tight feeling and swelling. When an arm is affected, evaluation includes examination and comparison with the other limb; additional testing may be used to evaluate causes of swelling. B is incorrect because early symptoms should be reported rather than dismissed until severe. C is incorrect because exercise should be individualized and safe; new symptoms warrant assessment before an unsupervised heavy program. D is incorrect because symptoms do not establish the diagnosis by themselves and compression garments or wraps should be appropriately selected and taught by the healthcare team or certified lymphedema therapist.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Axillary lymph-node removal increases lymphedema risk; early heaviness, tightness and swelling should be reported and assessed; limb comparison is part of evaluation; exercise and compression should be individualized and appropriately supervised.

candidates.educational_objective: Manage peristomal irritant skin injury from stool leakage by promptly changing the leaking pouching system, assessing the skin and barrier fit, and ensuring a close-fitting barrier opening rather than patching the leak.

options.A: Gently cleanse the peristomal skin, reassess the pouching-system fit so the barrier opening fits closely around the stoma, and replace the leaking system rather than taping over the leak.
options.B: Reapply the leaking pouch and reinforce the edges with additional tape so the appliance can remain in place despite the leak.
options.C: Cut the new barrier opening substantially larger than the stoma so more peristomal skin remains exposed to the stool.
options.D: Ignore the skin beneath the barrier because persistent burning and leakage do not require assessment until the next routine pouch change.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. WOCN identifies stool undermining the skin barrier as a cause of peristomal moisture-associated irritant skin damage. Its clinician and consumer guides direct prompt pouch/barrier change when there is burning or leakage, assessment of the skin and adhesive side of the barrier, and sizing the barrier opening to fit closely around the stoma base. WOCN also explicitly states to change a leaking pouch rather than reinforce it with additional tape. B is incorrect because taping over a leak leaves the cause and skin exposure uncorrected. C is incorrect because an oversized opening exposes more peristomal skin to effluent rather than creating the close fit WOCN recommends. D is incorrect because burning and leakage are specific triggers for immediate pouch-system assessment and change.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Effluent leakage can cause peristomal irritant skin damage; burning or leakage warrants prompt pouch-system change and skin/barrier assessment; the barrier opening should fit closely around the stoma base; leaking pouches should be changed rather than reinforced with tape.

candidates.educational_objective: Apply the current USPSTF breast-cancer screening recommendation by identifying biennial mammography from ages 40 through 74 for the population covered by the average-risk screening recommendation and distinguishing screening from high-risk or symptom-directed evaluation.

options.A: Screen with mammography every 2 years from age 40 through age 74 while she remains within the population covered by the recommendation.
options.B: Wait until age 50 because routine screening mammography is not recommended for average-risk women in their 40s.
options.C: Use annual breast MRI as the routine primary screening test for all average-risk women in their 40s.
options.D: Do not screen unless breast symptoms develop because mammography is intended only for diagnostic evaluation.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The USPSTF final recommendation dated April 30, 2024 recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years (Grade B). The recommendation applies to average-risk persons in the covered population, including those with some common risk factors such as family history or dense breasts, but not to people with certain high-risk conditions such as BRCA-associated syndromes, prior high-dose chest radiation at a young age, previous breast cancer, or high-risk breast lesions. B is outdated because the current recommendation begins at age 40. C is incorrect because MRI is not the routine primary screening modality recommended for all average-risk women in their 40s. D is incorrect because screening is intended for asymptomatic people; symptoms require diagnostic evaluation rather than waiting for routine screening.
candidates.source_claim_supported: USPSTF recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 years and defines the population to whom the recommendation applies and important exclusions for high-risk conditions.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Immunization / cancer prevention / family education
candidates.educational_objective: Explain the cancer-prevention purpose and current routine schedule of HPV vaccination for an immunocompetent preteen, including why vaccination is given before likely HPV exposure and why it applies regardless of sex.

options.A: HPV vaccination is routinely recommended at age 11–12 years because it prevents new HPV infections that can cause cancers later in life; when started at ages 9–14, the routine series is 2 doses 6–12 months apart.
options.B: HPV vaccination should be delayed until adulthood because it works best only after a person has already been exposed to HPV.
options.C: HPV vaccine is used to treat an existing HPV infection, so it is started only after an HPV-related lesion or abnormal screening result develops.
options.D: HPV vaccination is recommended only for girls because HPV-related cancers do not occur in boys or men.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current CDC child/adolescent immunization schedule notes routine HPV vaccination at age 11–12 years, with vaccination permitted starting at age 9. For people who initiate vaccination at ages 9–14 years, the routine schedule is 2 doses at 0 and 6–12 months; immunocompromised persons require a 3-dose series. CDC also states that HPV vaccination prevents new HPV infections rather than treating existing infection or disease and protects against HPV infections that cause cancers in both females and males. B is incorrect because vaccination is most beneficial before exposure. C reverses prevention and treatment. D is incorrect because HPV causes cancers in both men and women and vaccination is recommended for all preteens.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC currently supports routine HPV vaccination at ages 11–12, a 2-dose 0 and 6–12 month series when initiated at ages 9–14 for immunocompetent persons, prevention of new HPV infection rather than treatment, and cancer-prevention benefit for both males and females.

candidates.educational_objective: Counsel a long-term older smoker that tobacco cessation remains an effective cancer-risk-reduction intervention regardless of age or smoking duration and should not be replaced by screening alone.

options.A: Quitting now still lowers your risk of smoking-related cancers and other diseases; benefits occur even after many years of smoking, so cessation support is still worthwhile.
options.B: You are correct; cancer risk no longer changes once a person has smoked for several decades.
options.C: Quitting is useful only for people younger than 40 because older adults do not gain meaningful health benefit from cessation.
options.D: Continuing to smoke is reasonable if you undergo cancer screening because screening eliminates the additional cancer risk from ongoing tobacco exposure.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC states that quitting smoking lowers the risk for multiple cancers and that this benefit applies regardless of age, how long a person has smoked, or how much the person has smoked. NCI likewise states that people who quit smoking, regardless of age, reduce their risk of smoking-related disease and cancer compared with people who continue to smoke. B and C are incorrect because cessation benefit is not restricted to short-term or younger smokers. D is incorrect because cancer screening does not neutralize the carcinogenic effects of continued tobacco exposure; cessation and appropriate screening address different aspects of risk and prevention.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Smoking causes multiple cancers; quitting reduces cancer risk compared with continued smoking; meaningful benefit remains regardless of age and after long smoking duration.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Family-history risk assessment / genetic counseling referral
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize an early-onset colorectal/endometrial family pattern that may suggest Lynch syndrome and initiate referral for genetic counseling before genetic-testing and individualized risk-management decisions.

options.A: Recognize a possible hereditary cancer pattern and recommend referral for cancer genetic counseling to assess whether evaluation for Lynch syndrome is appropriate.
options.B: Reassure the client that hereditary cancer is unlikely because the client has not personally developed cancer.
options.C: Advise the client to order a direct-to-consumer genetic test and make screening decisions independently from the result.
options.D: Use only the usual average-risk screening approach because colorectal or endometrial cancer diagnosed before age 50 does not affect hereditary-risk assessment.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current CDC guidance identifies colorectal cancer diagnosed before age 50 in a family member and uterine/endometrial cancer before age 50 as findings that can raise concern for hereditary colorectal cancer and Lynch syndrome. CDC states that genetic counseling may be recommended for a family history of colorectal cancer, especially when relatives were diagnosed before age 50, and that counseling helps determine whether genetic testing is appropriate. NCI likewise lists early-age cancer and family patterns involving colon and endometrial cancers as features suggesting a hereditary cancer syndrome. B is incorrect because an unaffected person can still have inherited susceptibility. C is incorrect because testing and interpretation should be guided by personal/family history and genetic counseling rather than self-directed screening decisions from an uncontextualized consumer test. D ignores two age- and cancer-pattern findings that specifically warrant hereditary-risk assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Early-onset colorectal cancer and endometrial cancer in relatives are hereditary-cancer warning patterns; family colorectal cancer before 50 can warrant genetic counseling for possible Lynch syndrome; genetic counseling precedes testing decisions.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Therapeutic communication / coping / psychosocial assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Respond therapeutically to acute distress after a cancer diagnosis by validating emotion, assessing understanding and support needs, and pacing/repeating information to preserve comprehension and participation in care.

options.A: Acknowledge the client's distress, assess what the client understands and needs now, and review important information in small amounts with opportunities to repeat and clarify it while offering psychosocial support as needed.
options.B: Provide all treatment details immediately in one uninterrupted session because emotional distress should not change how information is communicated.
options.C: Reassure the client that there is no reason to be frightened and redirect the conversation away from emotional concerns.
options.D: Give all future information only to the family because acute distress means the client can no longer participate in health care decisions.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI notes that a new cancer diagnosis can produce heightened distress that impairs attention and cognitive processing. NCI communication guidance recommends responding to emotion, limiting emotionally charged information at each interaction, repeating important information, checking understanding, and avoiding long detailed explanations when the patient is not ready to absorb them. Psychosocial assessment and referral are appropriate when clinically significant distress is identified. B risks information overload. C uses premature reassurance and dismisses the client's expressed emotion. D unnecessarily removes the client from communication and decision-making rather than adapting communication to the client's current needs and preferences.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Distress around diagnosis can impair attention and information processing; communication should acknowledge emotion, limit information per interaction, repeat/check understanding, and connect clients with psychosocial support when distress warrants it.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Anxiety / coping / psychosocial assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Respond to fear of cancer recurrence by validating the concern, assessing its functional and care impact, supporting recommended follow-up, and facilitating psychosocial help when anxiety becomes difficult to manage.

options.A: Acknowledge the fear, assess how much it is affecting daily function and follow-up care, encourage the client to keep the recommended follow-up plan, and offer psychosocial support or counseling if needed.
options.B: Tell the client there is no reason to worry because completing treatment guarantees that the cancer will not recur.
options.C: Support canceling the scan because avoiding cancer-related reminders is the best way to reduce fear of recurrence.
options.D: Explain that fear of recurrence is abnormal after treatment and by itself proves the client has a psychiatric disorder.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI describes fear of cancer recurrence as a common survivorship concern and notes that follow-up scans and other medical tests can trigger substantial anxiety or 'scanxiety.' NCI advises survivors to tell the healthcare team about recurrence fears, maintain follow-up care, and seek counseling when fear becomes more than they can manage. Psychosocial assessment should consider how distress affects functioning and care. B is incorrect because treatment completion does not guarantee that recurrence is impossible. C reinforces avoidance of recommended follow-up rather than addressing the fear. D incorrectly pathologizes a common survivorship concern without assessing its severity or impact.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Fear of recurrence is common after treatment and may intensify around scans/follow-up; survivors should discuss it with the healthcare team, maintain follow-up care, and may need psychosocial support when fear interferes with coping or function.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Coping / self-concept / therapeutic support
candidates.educational_objective: Respond therapeutically to cancer-related guilt and self-blame by assessing its effect on coping and relationships, avoiding reinforcement of blame, and facilitating appropriate emotional and social support.

options.A: Acknowledge the guilt without reinforcing self-blame, explore how it is affecting coping and relationships, and offer counseling or support resources if the feelings are difficult to manage.
options.B: Tell the client that guilt is useful because self-blame is necessary to prevent cancer from recurring.
options.C: Avoid discussing the guilt because emotional reactions after cancer treatment have little relevance to survivorship care.
options.D: Explain that withdrawing from friends is the healthiest way to manage guilt until the feeling disappears on its own.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI states that many people with cancer experience guilt and may blame themselves for lifestyle choices they believe contributed to cancer. NCI advises that having cancer is not the person's fault and recommends sharing feelings with trusted people, counselors, support groups, or the healthcare team. NCI also recognizes guilt/self-blame and avoidance of people as possible cancer-related post-traumatic stress symptoms, so persistent or disruptive distress warrants assessment and support. B reinforces unsupported causal blame and incorrectly links guilt with recurrence prevention. C dismisses a recognized psychosocial need. D promotes isolation even though NCI identifies social and professional support as potential coping resources.
candidates.source_claim_supported: NCI recognizes cancer-related guilt and self-blame, advises against blaming oneself for cancer, supports expression of feelings and counseling/support-group resources, and identifies guilt/self-blame and social avoidance among possible cancer-related stress symptoms.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize significant caregiver burden when caregiving demands exceed available resources and respond by assessing caregiver capacity and connecting the family with individualized practical, respite, and psychosocial support.

options.A: Assess the caregiver's current demands, available resources, and ability to perform care safely, then help identify support that matches the needs, such as sharing tasks, respite care, or social-work/counseling resources.
options.B: Encourage the spouse to continue all caregiving duties alone because accepting outside help generally increases caregiver burden.
options.C: Reassure the spouse that severe exhaustion is an expected part of caregiving and needs no intervention unless the client is hospitalized.
options.D: Focus only on the client's symptoms because caregiver sleep loss, work strain, and concerns about managing medications are unrelated to safe home care.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI defines caregiver burden as stress or strain that occurs when caregiving demands exceed the resources available to the caregiver. Cancer caregivers can have emotional, social, financial, work-related, and health needs, and NCI emphasizes recognizing caregiver roles and challenges, asking what help is needed, sharing tasks, seeking support, and using respite or professional resources when appropriate. In this scenario, severe sleep loss plus concern about medication mistakes makes an assessment of caregiving capacity and available support clinically important. B is incorrect because NCI encourages caregivers to accept help and share responsibilities rather than assuming they must do everything alone. C inappropriately normalizes potentially unsafe exhaustion. D is incorrect because NCI treats caregiver well-being and ability to perform caregiving tasks as relevant to cancer care.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Caregiver burden occurs when caregiving demands exceed available resources; cancer caregivers may experience emotional, social, financial, employment, and health strain; clinicians should recognize caregiver needs and support task-sharing, respite, counseling/social-work, and other resources as appropriate.

candidates.educational_objective: Explain that palliative sedation is an end-of-life comfort intervention for otherwise refractory suffering, with deliberate lowering of consciousness directed toward symptom relief rather than intentionally shortening life or causing death.

options.A: Palliative sedation may deliberately lower consciousness to relieve otherwise refractory suffering; its intent is comfort and symptom relief, not to shorten life or cause death.
options.B: Palliative sedation is used mainly to shorten the dying process after symptoms become difficult to control.
options.C: Palliative sedation is routinely used for clients in the last days of life even when symptoms remain adequately controlled with other palliative measures.
options.D: Once palliative sedation is chosen, decisions about hydration, nutrition, and other life-sustaining treatments are automatically determined by the sedation decision.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI defines palliative sedation as deliberate pharmacologic lowering of consciousness to relieve symptoms that are unacceptably distressing and refractory to optimal palliative-care interventions. NCI states that the goal is relief of intractable suffering and that the intent is not to shorten life; the NCI Dictionary likewise states that palliative sedation is not meant to shorten life or cause death. B is incorrect because intentionally causing or hastening death is not the goal of palliative sedation. C is incorrect because palliative sedation is reserved for selected refractory symptoms rather than routine use for every dying client. D is incorrect because NCI states that decisions about potentially life-sustaining treatments such as artificial hydration or nutrition are distinct from the decision to use palliative sedation and require separate review of goals, benefits, harms, and preferences.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Palliative sedation deliberately lowers consciousness to relieve extreme or refractory suffering when other treatment has not adequately controlled symptoms; its intent is comfort rather than shortening life or causing death; decisions about other life-sustaining treatments remain separate.

candidates.educational_objective: Verify that a client considering a randomized phase 3 cancer treatment trial understands random assignment, the role of standard-treatment comparison, and the continuing voluntary right to withdraw after consent.

options.A: I may receive either the investigational treatment or the standard treatment because assignment is by chance, and I can still choose to leave the study later.
options.B: Because this is phase 3, I am guaranteed to receive the investigational treatment if I sign the consent form.
options.C: If I am assigned to the standard-treatment group, I will receive no active cancer treatment because the comparison group is always untreated.
options.D: Once I sign the consent form, I must remain in the trial until the study ends even if I later change my mind.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NCI states that phase 3 treatment trials compare an investigational treatment with the current standard treatment. In randomized trials, assignment is by chance; neither the participant nor the doctor chooses the treatment group. NCI informed-consent guidance also states that research participation is voluntary and that a participant may leave the study after signing the consent form. B is incorrect because enrollment does not guarantee assignment to the investigational arm. C is incorrect because, in the basic cancer-treatment trial design described by NCI, the control group receives standard treatment rather than no treatment; NCI also notes that placebos are rarely used in cancer treatment trials and are not routinely substituted for effective standard therapy. D is incorrect because signing the consent form does not surrender the participant's right to withdraw.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Phase 3 cancer treatment trials compare investigational and standard treatment; randomization assigns participants by chance rather than participant/physician choice; cancer treatment trials generally preserve active standard treatment in the comparison structure; informed consent is voluntary and participants retain the right to withdraw.

candidates.educational_objective: Explain the labeled role of rifaximin in reducing recurrence of overt hepatic encephalopathy and recognize that current label evidence supports its use with lactulose without inventing an ammonia-binding mechanism or implying reversal of underlying liver disease.

options.A: Rifaximin is indicated to reduce overt hepatic encephalopathy recurrence, and current label data show fewer breakthrough episodes with rifaximin plus lactulose than with rifaximin alone.
options.B: Rifaximin binds circulating ammonia directly in the bloodstream and removes it through the kidneys, making intestinal therapy unnecessary.
options.C: Rifaximin restores hepatic detoxification and reverses the chronic liver disease responsible for the encephalopathy.
options.D: Rifaximin has no labeled role in hepatic encephalopathy recurrence and is used only to treat systemic bacterial infections.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current XIFAXAN prescribing information explicitly indicates rifaximin for reduction in the risk of overt hepatic encephalopathy recurrence in adults. In the label's Trial 2, clients receiving rifaximin plus lactulose experienced fewer breakthrough overt hepatic encephalopathy episodes than clients receiving rifaximin monotherapy, supporting the continued role of lactulose rather than presenting rifaximin as a replacement for it. B is incorrect because the label does not describe direct binding of circulating ammonia with renal elimination as rifaximin's mechanism; Section 12.1 identifies rifaximin as an antibacterial. C is incorrect because rifaximin does not reverse the underlying chronic liver disease. D directly contradicts the labeled hepatic encephalopathy indication. The final item deliberately does not claim that the clinical benefit is proven specifically by 'reducing ammonia-producing bacteria,' because that mechanistic statement is not established in the current label.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current label directly supports rifaximin's indication to reduce overt hepatic encephalopathy recurrence, identifies rifaximin as an antibacterial, and reports fewer breakthrough overt HE episodes with rifaximin plus lactulose than with rifaximin monotherapy in Trial 2; it does not establish direct plasma ammonia binding or reversal of underlying liver disease.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Medication mechanism, therapeutic effect, and electrolyte monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that spironolactone treats cirrhotic ascites by antagonizing aldosterone-driven distal sodium retention and recognize the need to monitor for hyperkalemia and changes in renal or volume status.

options.A: It antagonizes aldosterone in the distal nephron, promoting sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium; secondary aldosteronism commonly contributes to fluid retention in cirrhosis.
options.B: It acts primarily as a loop diuretic in the thick ascending limb and increases potassium excretion to correct the fluid retention of cirrhosis.
options.C: It reverses portal hypertension by dissolving hepatic fibrosis, thereby eliminating the need for ongoing ascites management.
options.D: It is used because cirrhotic ascites is usually caused by aldosterone deficiency, so spironolactone replaces the missing hormone.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current spironolactone label identifies spironolactone and its active metabolites as aldosterone antagonists that competitively bind receptors at the aldosterone-dependent sodium-potassium exchange site in the distal renal tubule. This increases sodium and water excretion while potassium is retained. The label specifically states that secondary aldosteronism is usually involved in edematous states including hepatic cirrhosis and that spironolactone provides effective therapy for edema and ascites in these conditions. B incorrectly assigns the mechanism of a loop diuretic and incorrectly states that spironolactone increases potassium excretion. C is incorrect because spironolactone does not reverse cirrhotic fibrosis or cure portal hypertension. D reverses the pathophysiology: the relevant problem is secondary hyperaldosteronism, not aldosterone deficiency. Because spironolactone retains potassium, the current label warns about hyperkalemia and directs serum-potassium monitoring as well as monitoring of volume status and renal function.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current spironolactone label directly supports its use for cirrhosis-associated edema, aldosterone-antagonist mechanism, sodium/water excretion with potassium retention, the role of secondary aldosteronism in hepatic cirrhosis, and monitoring for hyperkalemia, renal function, and volume status.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Medication combination, electrolyte effects, and laboratory monitoring
candidates.educational_objective: Explain why spironolactone and furosemide may be used together for cirrhotic ascites while recognizing that complementary potassium effects do not eliminate the need for electrolyte, renal-function, volume-status, and clinical-response monitoring.

options.A: The two diuretics act at different nephron sites and have complementary potassium effects, but electrolyte and renal monitoring are still required because either hypo- or hyperkalemia and excessive diuresis can occur.
options.B: Using both medications guarantees a normal serum potassium level, so potassium and renal-function testing are unnecessary once the combination is started.
options.C: Both medications are potassium-wasting loop diuretics, so the combination is used primarily to intensify potassium loss.
options.D: Both medications work by blocking aldosterone receptors, so combining them adds no mechanism distinct from spironolactone alone.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AASLD identifies aldosterone antagonists such as spironolactone and loop diuretics such as furosemide as the principal diuretics used for cirrhotic ascites and advises dose adjustment according to tolerance and blood testing. Current DailyMed labeling shows that spironolactone antagonizes aldosterone in the distal nephron, promotes sodium and water excretion while retaining potassium, and can cause hyperkalemia. Current furosemide labeling shows a different diuretic mechanism involving inhibition of sodium and chloride reabsorption including in the loop of Henle and specifically warns that hypokalemia and other fluid/electrolyte disturbances can occur, especially in cirrhosis. Therefore, the combination provides complementary diuretic actions and opposing potassium tendencies, but it does not guarantee normokalemia or remove the need for renal and electrolyte monitoring. B overstates the balancing effect and is unsafe. C incorrectly classifies spironolactone as a loop diuretic and potassium-wasting drug. D incorrectly assigns spironolactone's aldosterone-antagonist mechanism to furosemide.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AASLD supports combined use of spironolactone and furosemide for cirrhotic ascites with laboratory/tolerance-based adjustment. Current labels confirm their distinct nephron mechanisms and opposite potassium tendencies—spironolactone potassium retention/hyperkalemia risk and furosemide potassium loss/hypokalemia risk—while both require ongoing safety monitoring.

candidates.educational_objective: Explain that IV albumin after large-volume paracentesis is used to reduce post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and related complications while ongoing hemodynamic, renal, electrolyte, and fluid-status monitoring remains necessary.

options.A: Albumin is given to reduce the risk of post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and related complications after removal of a large volume of ascitic fluid.
options.B: Albumin replaces the ascitic fluid inside the peritoneal cavity so that abdominal fluid cannot accumulate again.
options.C: Albumin reverses the cirrhosis and portal hypertension that caused the ascites, preventing the need for future ascites management.
options.D: Once albumin is infused, further assessment of blood pressure, renal function, electrolytes, and fluid status is unnecessary.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD materials identify prevention of post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction as a key indication for albumin after large-volume paracentesis in cirrhosis. AASLD notes that circulatory dysfunction following removal of large volumes of ascites is associated with clinically important complications, including renal and electrolyte consequences, and current cirrhosis management resources pair large-volume paracentesis with albumin replacement when indicated. B is incorrect because IV albumin is an intravascular plasma-expanding therapy; it does not replace ascitic fluid within the peritoneal cavity or prevent ascites from ever recurring. C is incorrect because albumin does not reverse cirrhotic fibrosis or cure portal hypertension. D is incorrect because albumin does not eliminate the need for continued postprocedure assessment of hemodynamic status, renal function, electrolytes, and overall fluid balance. The final item intentionally avoids requiring a numeric albumin dose or fluid-volume threshold because the tested construct is the purpose of therapy rather than dose calculation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance directly supports IV albumin after large-volume paracentesis as a strategy to reduce post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction and associated complications in cirrhosis; albumin does not cure cirrhosis or eliminate the need for postprocedure monitoring.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Medication indication, response evaluation, and coagulation-laboratory interpretation
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret an incomplete INR response to phytonadione in cirrhosis by distinguishing correctable vitamin K deficiency from liver-related synthetic dysfunction and by recognizing that INR alone does not reliably quantify bleeding risk in cirrhosis.

options.A: Persistent INR elevation may reflect liver-related impairment of clotting-factor synthesis rather than correctable vitamin K deficiency; repeated large phytonadione doses are not warranted simply because the INR remains high.
options.B: Any prolonged INR in cirrhosis proves vitamin K deficiency, so phytonadione should be repeated until the INR reaches a universal normal target.
options.C: A prolonged INR in cirrhosis directly quantifies bleeding risk, so failure to normalize it means major bleeding is inevitable.
options.D: Phytonadione is contraindicated whenever chronic liver disease is present, even when a true vitamin K deficiency is contributing.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Phytonadione is indicated when hypoprothrombinemia is caused by vitamin K deficiency or interference with vitamin K activity. Current DailyMed labeling specifically states that repeated large doses are not warranted in liver disease if the initial response is unsatisfactory and that failure to respond may indicate a condition inherently unresponsive to phytonadione. AASLD explains that prolonged PT/INR is common in liver dysfunction because liver-derived coagulation factors are reduced, but INR measures only procoagulant factors and does not account for simultaneous reductions in anticoagulant factors. Therefore, INR alone is not a reliable measure of bleeding risk in cirrhosis and there is no universal target INR for routine correction. B incorrectly assumes every elevated INR is vitamin K deficiency and invents a universal correction target. C overstates INR as a direct bleeding-risk measure. D is incorrect because phytonadione can be appropriate when genuine vitamin K deficiency or interference is present; chronic liver disease itself is not a blanket contraindication.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Phytonadione is appropriate for vitamin K-deficiency/interference states, but an unsatisfactory response in liver disease does not justify repeated large doses. In cirrhosis, INR prolongation can reflect impaired hepatic synthesis and INR alone is not a reliable bleeding-risk measure or a universal target for correction.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Antidote mechanism, medication education, and prevention of hepatic injury
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that acetylcysteine reduces acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by maintaining/restoring glutathione and supporting detoxification of the reactive metabolite rather than by increasing toxic metabolism, blocking gastrointestinal absorption, or repairing necrotic liver tissue.

options.A: It maintains or restores hepatic glutathione and can provide an alternate substrate for conjugation and detoxification of acetaminophen's reactive metabolite.
options.B: It increases cytochrome P450 conversion of acetaminophen to its reactive metabolite so the drug can be eliminated more rapidly.
options.C: It directly regenerates hepatocytes that have already undergone necrosis, reversing established structural liver injury.
options.D: It works mainly by preventing gastrointestinal absorption of acetaminophen after the medication has entered the bloodstream.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current ACETADOTE prescribing information states that acetylcysteine reduces the extent of liver injury after acetaminophen overdose and probably protects the liver by maintaining or restoring glutathione levels or by acting as an alternate substrate for conjugation with, and detoxification of, the reactive acetaminophen metabolite. B is incorrect because increasing formation of the reactive metabolite would increase rather than reduce hepatotoxic risk. C is incorrect because acetylcysteine is used to prevent or lessen hepatic injury; the label does not state that it regenerates necrotic hepatocytes or reverses established structural injury. D is incorrect because IV acetylcysteine is a systemic antidote and its labeled mechanism is not blockade of gastrointestinal acetaminophen absorption. The final item uses the mechanism directly stated in the current label and does not require an unsourced metabolite name, time cutoff, or dose threshold.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current ACETADOTE label directly supports its role in preventing or lessening acetaminophen-related hepatic injury and its mechanism through maintenance/restoration of glutathione or alternate-substrate detoxification of the reactive metabolite.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Aseptic/sterile technique during an invasive bedside procedure
candidates.educational_objective: Maintain infection prevention during paracentesis by using appropriate skin antisepsis, allowing the antiseptic to dry, establishing a sterile field, and preserving sterile gloves and equipment throughout peritoneal access.

options.A: Prepare the insertion site with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine, allow the antiseptic to dry, apply a sterile drape, and maintain sterile gloves and equipment for the procedure.
options.B: Use clean gloves without a sterile field because paracentesis is performed at the bedside rather than in an operating room.
options.C: Use sterile technique only when ascitic fluid is being collected for diagnostic testing; therapeutic fluid removal can be performed with clean technique.
options.D: After skin antisepsis, allow nonsterile equipment to contact the prepared field because the antiseptic alone prevents procedure-related contamination.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current StatPearls paracentesis procedure review describes skin antisepsis with povidone-iodine or chlorhexidine, application of a sterile drape, and use of sterile gloves as part of the technique. These precautions apply to paracentesis as an invasive entry into the peritoneal cavity, whether the procedure is diagnostic or therapeutic. B is incorrect because bedside location does not eliminate the need for a sterile field and sterile technique. C is incorrect because the need for sterile technique is not limited to diagnostic fluid sampling; therapeutic paracentesis uses the same percutaneous access to the peritoneal space. D is incorrect because skin antisepsis does not make nonsterile equipment acceptable within the sterile procedural field. The final item tests specific infection-prevention actions rather than a vague statement that the procedure should simply be 'sterile.'
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current NCBI StatPearls paracentesis procedure directly supports skin antisepsis, drying of antiseptic, sterile draping, sterile gloves, and maintenance of sterile procedural technique for peritoneal access.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize new confusion and asterixis after TIPS as possible post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy requiring prompt focused assessment and escalation rather than assuming a benign postprocedure effect or shunt occlusion.

options.A: These findings are concerning for post-TIPS hepatic encephalopathy and require prompt focused assessment and communication with the treating team.
options.B: These findings are an expected harmless effect of portal decompression and do not require evaluation unless they persist for several weeks.
options.C: These findings prove that the TIPS is occluded because hepatic encephalopathy occurs only when portal decompression has failed.
options.D: These findings are best explained by routine venous-access discomfort and are unrelated to the physiologic effects of portosystemic shunting.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AASLD identifies hepatic encephalopathy as a well-known and clinically important complication after TIPS. TIPS redirects portal blood into the systemic circulation and reduces first-pass hepatic clearance of neurotoxins, so new disorientation and asterixis after the procedure are compatible with hepatic encephalopathy and warrant prompt assessment rather than reassurance. Current NCBI guidance also identifies TIPS and other portosystemic shunts as causes of hepatic encephalopathy and lists confusion, disorientation, altered attention, and asterixis among clinically relevant findings. B is incorrect because new neurologic changes are not a harmless expected finding to ignore. C is incorrect because hepatic encephalopathy can occur with a functioning TIPS and does not by itself prove shunt occlusion. D is incorrect because venous-access discomfort does not explain a new encephalopathic mental-status change and asterixis. The final item narrows the construct to one high-value post-TIPS complication instead of bundling encephalopathy, access-site bleeding, and shunt-patency surveillance into a single recall answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AASLD and NCBI directly support hepatic encephalopathy as a major post-TIPS complication caused in part by portosystemic diversion and reduced hepatic clearance; new disorientation and asterixis are compatible with hepatic encephalopathy and require clinical evaluation.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition of postprocedure bleeding and rapid escalation
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize worsening abdominal pain with tachycardia and hypotension after percutaneous liver biopsy as possible hemorrhage and prioritize immediate focused assessment and escalation rather than reassurance, ambulation, or discharge.

options.A: Suspect post-biopsy hemorrhage, perform an immediate focused assessment, and promptly notify the treating team for further evaluation and management.
options.B: Reassure the client that these findings are expected after liver biopsy and continue routine observation without escalation.
options.C: Encourage ambulation because movement will reduce the pain and improve blood pressure after the procedure.
options.D: Prepare the client for discharge because bleeding complications are excluded once the biopsy needle has been removed.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI procedural guidance identifies bleeding as an important complication of liver biopsy and notes that severe or persistent abdominal or shoulder pain, tachycardia, hypotension, hemodynamic instability, and falling hemoglobin can signal post-biopsy hemorrhage. Early recognition is imperative and may require resuscitation, imaging, interventional radiology, or surgical consultation depending on severity. B is incorrect because the combination of worsening pain and hemodynamic changes is not a benign expected recovery pattern. C is unsafe because a potentially bleeding client requires assessment and stabilization rather than ambulation. D is incorrect because significant bleeding can present during the observation period or later; removal of the needle does not eliminate hemorrhagic risk. The final item deliberately removes the source's overstatement that right-side positioning itself should be understood as a proven mechanism for reducing bleeding.
candidates.source_claim_supported: NCBI directly supports post-liver-biopsy bleeding as a clinically important complication and identifies worsening pain, tachycardia, hypotension/hemodynamic instability, and hemoglobin decline as warning findings requiring prompt recognition and management.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Sterile device access and recognition of catheter-site infection
candidates.educational_objective: Teach safe care of an indwelling peritoneal drainage catheter by maintaining sterile technique during drainage, avoiding reuse of single-use components, and promptly reporting local or systemic findings that may indicate infection.

options.A: Use sterile technique when draining the catheter and promptly report increasing pain, redness, warmth, swelling, fever, or fluid around the catheter site.
options.B: Clean technique is sufficient for catheter drainage because the device is intended for repeated home use.
options.C: Reuse single-use drainage components if they appear clean because this does not increase contamination risk.
options.D: Persistent redness or drainage around the catheter is expected and does not require assessment unless the catheter stops draining completely.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The official BD PeritX peritoneal catheter instructions state that sterile technique should be used when placing and draining the catheter. The manufacturer also instructs patients to contact the clinician if infection is suspected and identifies pain, erythema/redness, warmth, swelling, fever, or fluid around the catheter site as possible infection findings. B is incorrect because repeated home drainage does not convert the procedure to clean technique; the device instructions explicitly require sterile technique for drainage. C is incorrect because the manufacturer identifies the relevant components as single use and warns that reuse may contribute to cross-contamination. D is incorrect because persistent or worsening redness, fluid, pain, warmth, swelling, or fever can indicate infection and should not be dismissed. AASLD separately notes that permanent indwelling peritoneal catheters may be considered for palliative/end-of-life relief in cirrhosis but their infection risk limits broader use. The final item focuses on concrete device-care teaching rather than a generic statement about long-term catheter infection risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Official device instructions require sterile technique for PeritX catheter drainage, warn against reuse/cross-contamination, and identify specific local/systemic findings that may indicate catheter infection; AASLD recognizes infection risk as a limiting factor for permanent indwelling peritoneal catheters in cirrhosis.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Fall-risk recognition and injury prevention in cognitive/neuromuscular impairment
candidates.educational_objective: Prevent injury in hepatic encephalopathy by recognizing disorientation, asterixis, and unsteady mobility as indications for individualized fall precautions and assisted/supervised ambulation.

options.A: Implement individualized fall precautions and assist or supervise mobility because the client's cognitive and neuromuscular deficits increase injury risk.
options.B: Encourage independent ambulation to determine whether the unsteadiness resolves once the client begins walking.
options.C: Discontinue fall precautions once vital signs are stable because hepatic encephalopathy does not meaningfully affect coordination or judgment.
options.D: Use fall precautions only if the client progresses to coma because earlier hepatic encephalopathy does not impair safe mobility.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Hepatic encephalopathy can impair attention, orientation, judgment, and neuromuscular function; current NCBI guidance lists asterixis, bradykinesia, ataxia, and other coordination abnormalities among its manifestations. Contemporary evidence also links covert or overt hepatic encephalopathy and cirrhosis-related cognitive dysfunction with increased falls. Because this client already demonstrates disorientation, asterixis, and unsteadiness, individualized fall precautions and assisted/supervised mobility are appropriate. B is unsafe because an unsteady, cognitively impaired client should not be used to 'test' independent ambulation. C is incorrect because normal vital signs do not remove the neurologic and cognitive contributors to fall risk. D is incorrect because fall risk is not restricted to coma or the most advanced grade of encephalopathy; impaired cognition and motor control can occur earlier. The final item bases the safety intervention on observed deficits rather than assuming that every client with cirrhosis has the same fall risk.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Hepatic encephalopathy can impair cognition and coordination and cause asterixis/ataxia; current literature links these deficits with increased falls, supporting fall precautions when the client demonstrates disorientation and unsteady mobility.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: reduce complications from health conditions and treatments, recognize signs of deterioration or bleeding, and reinforce risk-reduction teaching consistent with the treatment plan.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Risk reduction for portal-hypertension complications and recognition of bleeding
candidates.educational_objective: Teach that prevention of first esophageal-variceal hemorrhage relies on evidence-based portal-pressure or endoscopic prophylaxis when indicated, while new hematemesis or melena requires urgent evaluation rather than lifestyle-only prevention strategies.

options.A: Evidence-based prevention may include a prescribed nonselective beta blocker or endoscopic variceal ligation when appropriate; vomiting blood or passing black stools requires urgent evaluation.
options.B: The main proven prevention strategy is to avoid coughing or straining; medication or endoscopic prophylaxis is generally unnecessary.
options.C: Daily aspirin should be started routinely because its antiplatelet effect protects fragile varices from rupturing.
options.D: No preventive treatment is useful before a first hemorrhage, so management begins only after active bleeding occurs.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD portal-hypertension guidance supports nonselective beta blockers and, in appropriate variceal settings, endoscopic variceal ligation as established strategies to reduce the risk of a first variceal hemorrhage. AASLD also emphasizes earlier portal-pressure management in clinically significant portal hypertension rather than relying on unsupported behavioral rules. Hematemesis or melena in a client with varices can represent acute variceal bleeding and requires urgent evaluation. B is incorrect because avoiding coughing or straining is not an evidence-based substitute for indicated portal-pressure or endoscopic prophylaxis. C is incorrect because aspirin is not routinely prescribed to prevent variceal rupture and antiplatelet therapy must be considered in the context of an individual client's indication and bleeding risk. D is incorrect because primary prophylaxis is a recognized component of variceal management before a first hemorrhage. The final item does not prescribe which prophylactic option is best for every client; selection depends on variceal characteristics, clinical context, contraindications, preferences, and current hepatology guidance.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance supports primary prophylaxis of variceal hemorrhage with nonselective beta blockers and/or endoscopic variceal ligation in appropriate patients and does not support substituting unproven strain/cough avoidance rules for evidence-based management.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Blood-product appropriateness, coagulation interpretation, and prevention of unnecessary transfusion
candidates.educational_objective: Evaluate blood-product orders in cirrhosis by recognizing that an isolated prolonged INR does not reliably quantify bleeding risk and that prophylactic plasma should not be given solely to normalize INR without a clinically supported indication.

options.A: Clarify the indication with the treating team because INR alone does not reliably predict bleeding risk in cirrhosis, there is no universal target INR for routine correction, and prophylactic plasma may worsen portal hypertension.
options.B: Administer plasma until the INR reaches the normal laboratory range because any prolonged INR in cirrhosis directly predicts procedural bleeding.
options.C: Request repeated plasma transfusions whenever the INR rises, even without bleeding, because transfusion risk is negligible compared with an abnormal coagulation value.
options.D: Assume the procedure must be canceled permanently because a prolonged INR caused by cirrhosis cannot be evaluated using any other clinical information.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD guidance explains that PT/INR in cirrhosis reflects reduced liver-derived procoagulant factors but does not account for simultaneous deficiencies in anticoagulant factors; INR alone therefore is not a reliable measure of bleeding risk. AASLD further states that attempts to correct PT/INR with plasma can exacerbate portal hypertension, so prophylactic plasma transfusion is not recommended and a universal target INR does not exist. The nurse should therefore clarify a plasma order whose sole stated purpose is normalization of an isolated INR rather than automatically administering the product. B is incorrect because it treats INR as a direct bleeding-risk measure and invents a target. C ignores clinically important transfusion and volume-related risks and substitutes a laboratory number for individualized assessment. D is incorrect because procedural decisions in cirrhosis incorporate procedure-specific risk and other clinical modifiers rather than using INR alone. This item does not imply that plasma is never appropriate: AASLD notes that blood products may have roles in active bleeding or hemorrhagic shock depending on the clinical situation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AASLD directly supports that INR alone is not a reliable bleeding-risk measure in cirrhosis, there is no universal target INR for routine correction, and prophylactic plasma transfusion to normalize INR is not recommended because it may worsen portal hypertension; transfusion decisions require clinical context.

Same article → Table 1/Take Home Points: fresh frozen plasma and PCC should be restricted and may be considered in hemorrhagic shock. AASLD 'Back to Basics: The Conundrum of Coagulopathy in Cirrhosis' → 'Periprocedural Considerations' and Take-home points: elevated INR alone does not accurately reflect bleeding risk and clinical/procedural modifiers must be considered.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Standard and Contact Precautions for fecal-oral infection risk
candidates.educational_objective: Apply CDC isolation guidance by using Contact plus Standard Precautions for a hospitalized patient with hepatitis A who is fecally incontinent, while reinforcing hand hygiene and fecal-contamination control because HAV is transmitted primarily by the fecal-oral route.

options.A: Use Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions, with meticulous hand hygiene and measures to prevent fecal contamination of the environment.
options.B: Use Standard Precautions only because hepatitis A never requires additional transmission-based precautions in adults.
options.C: Use Airborne Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily spread by inhalation of respiratory aerosols.
options.D: Use Droplet Precautions because hepatitis A is primarily transmitted by respiratory secretions during coughing and sneezing.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies hepatitis A as primarily transmitted by the fecal-oral route. In CDC Appendix A, viral hepatitis A generally requires Standard Precautions, but diapered or incontinent patients require Contact Precautions in addition to Standard Precautions. CDC also notes that healthcare-associated hepatitis A transmission has been associated with fecal incontinence and inadequate hand hygiene, making meticulous hand hygiene and environmental contamination control directly relevant in this scenario. B is incorrect because fecal incontinence is the specific condition that changes the precaution requirement from Standard alone to Contact plus Standard. C and D are incorrect because hepatitis A is not primarily transmitted by airborne or respiratory-droplet routes. The final item deliberately includes fecal incontinence in the stem so that Contact Precautions are uniquely indicated rather than creating ambiguity with uncomplicated hepatitis A, for which Standard Precautions are generally sufficient.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports fecal-oral transmission of HAV, Standard Precautions for uncomplicated hepatitis A, Contact plus Standard Precautions for diapered or incontinent hepatitis A patients, and the importance of hand hygiene and control of fecal contamination in healthcare settings.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Multidisciplinary transplant evaluation, client education, and barrier mitigation
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that psychosocial and caregiver assessment is a core part of liver-transplant evaluation used to identify modifiable barriers, assess adherence and support needs, and develop interventions that promote safe wait-list and post-transplant care.

options.A: These areas are assessed to identify barriers that could affect transplant success and to develop supports or treatment plans when problems can be addressed.
options.B: Any history of a mental health disorder automatically excludes a client from liver transplantation, regardless of treatment or stability.
options.C: The caregiver interview is used mainly to judge the client's social worth and is not related to practical post-transplant care needs.
options.D: Psychosocial assessment is optional because transplant candidacy is determined only by laboratory values and imaging results.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current AASLD/AST adult liver-transplant candidate-evaluation guideline includes a dedicated psychosocial evaluation. It recommends assessing adherence to medical directives and mental-health stability, evaluating whether adequate caregiver/social support is available for the wait-list and postoperative period, and helping identify strategies to mitigate social and financial barriers when they are found. The guideline explains that the purpose of psychosocial assessment is to identify areas requiring intervention and to support successful transplantation, not simply to exclude candidates. B is incorrect because the guideline states that even serious mental-health disorders are not absolute contraindications when appropriate treatment, stability, and support can be achieved. C is incorrect because caregiver assessment focuses on practical assistance such as transportation, medication management, and postoperative support and should not be used as a proxy for social worth. D is incorrect because liver-transplant evaluation is explicitly multidisciplinary and includes psychosocial as well as medical assessment. The final item teaches the purpose of psychosocial evaluation without stigmatizing mental illness or presenting social support as an automatic binary eligibility rule.
candidates.source_claim_supported: The current AASLD/AST guideline directly supports comprehensive psychosocial evaluation of adherence, mental health, caregiver/social support, and modifiable barriers as part of liver-transplant candidate assessment and explicitly rejects automatic exclusion based on mental-health diagnosis alone.
candidates.source_document_title: AASLD AST Practice Guideline on Adult Liver Transplantation: Candidate Evaluation

'Rationale and Background' under the same section: goal is to identify psychosocial areas requiring intervention; relevant domains include adherence, caregiver support, cognitive capacity, psychiatric/substance-use issues, illness understanding, coping, and treatment understanding. Later Psychosocial guidance: mental-health disorders are not absolute contraindications when treated/stabilized and adequate support is available.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Client education and care coordination related to transplant allocation
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that the current MELD score is an OPTN medical-urgency tool used to help prioritize most liver-transplant candidates age 12 and older, while recognizing that actual organ allocation also follows status, exception, donor, and logistical rules.

options.A: For most liver-transplant candidates age 12 and older, MELD is a calculated medical-urgency score used to help assign transplant priority; actual organ offers also follow OPTN rules for status, exceptions, donor factors, and logistics.
options.B: MELD determines liver allocation solely by how long a client has been waiting, regardless of medical urgency or donor characteristics.
options.C: MELD is used only for alcohol-related liver disease and is not used for candidates with other causes of end-stage liver disease.
options.D: MELD is designed primarily to predict long-term post-transplant graft survival rather than pretransplant medical urgency.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current OPTN materials state that MELD is a calculated formula used to assign priority to most liver-transplant candidates age 12 and older based on medical urgency. The current adult MELD calculation was updated effective July 13, 2023 to improve prediction of wait-list mortality and currently incorporates bilirubin, creatinine, INR, sodium and albumin, with sex included for adult calculation. However, MELD is not the only factor in an individual organ offer: OPTN liver-allocation policy also incorporates special status categories, exception scores, donor characteristics, geography/logistics, and the sequence of the match run. B is incorrect because waiting time alone does not determine priority. C is incorrect because MELD is not limited to alcohol-related disease. D is incorrect because MELD's allocation role is based on pretransplant medical urgency/wait-list risk, not primarily on long-term graft survival after transplantation. The final item replaces the outdated MELD-Na wording and avoids claiming that MELD alone completely determines every allocation decision.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current OPTN/HRSA sources directly support MELD as a medical-urgency priority score for most liver candidates age 12 and older, confirm the updated adult MELD inputs and 2023 policy change, and show that actual liver allocation follows broader OPTN match rules rather than MELD or waiting time alone.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Communicable-disease reporting and jurisdiction-specific legal requirements
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize acute hepatitis B as a reportable/nationally notifiable condition and follow the applicable state or local reporting law and facility process rather than assuming a universal direct-to-CDC reporting workflow.

options.A: Follow the facility and state/local reporting process to ensure the case is reported to the appropriate health department, because acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions even though the exact reporting workflow is jurisdiction-specific.
options.B: Send the client's complete medical record directly to CDC because individual nurses are universally required to notify CDC themselves.
options.C: Do not initiate any reporting process because only chronic hepatitis B, not acute hepatitis B, is nationally notifiable.
options.D: Treat reporting as optional unless the client specifically requests that the diagnosis be sent to public health authorities.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC states that acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and that acute, chronic, and perinatal hepatitis B are nationally notifiable conditions. However, CDC also states that cases should be reported to health departments as specified by state, territorial, or local regulations and that rules governing whether health care providers, facilities, and laboratories report hepatitis B vary by jurisdiction. Therefore, the nurse should follow the applicable state/local law and facility process to ensure the case reaches the appropriate health department. B is incorrect because national notification to CDC occurs through public-health surveillance systems; there is no universal rule requiring an individual bedside nurse to send a complete record directly to CDC. C is incorrect because acute hepatitis B is nationally notifiable. D is incorrect because communicable-disease reporting is governed by law/regulation rather than being optional based on client preference. The final item preserves the national reportability of acute hepatitis B while avoiding the legally inaccurate assumption that every nurse in every state has the same direct reporting duty or workflow.
candidates.source_claim_supported: CDC directly supports that acute hepatitis B is reportable in all jurisdictions and nationally notifiable, while specific provider/facility/laboratory reporting duties and workflows are determined by state, territorial, or local regulations and health-department processes.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Targeted screening and education for high-risk health behaviors
candidates.educational_objective: Respond to a positive alcohol-use screen by obtaining a structured, nonjudgmental history and facilitating further assessment or referral when indicated, while recognizing that a screening result alone does not diagnose alcohol use disorder.

options.A: Use a nonjudgmental, structured follow-up history to clarify amount and pattern of alcohol use and arrange further assessment or referral for alcohol use disorder when indicated.
options.B: Document alcohol use disorder as confirmed solely because the screening result is positive, without further assessment.
options.C: Avoid discussing alcohol further because asking detailed questions is likely to worsen stigma and does not affect liver-disease management.
options.D: Limit further evaluation to clients who already have advanced alcohol-associated cirrhosis because screening is not useful earlier in liver disease.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AASLD guidance recommends routine screening for harmful alcohol use and identifies validated tools such as the NIAAA single alcohol screening question and AUDIT-C. AASLD also states that a positive screen should be followed by a more detailed, structured alcohol history and formal assessment for alcohol use disorder rather than being treated as a diagnosis by itself. A nonjudgmental, normalized interview style is recommended because stigma and defensiveness can reduce disclosure. B is incorrect because a positive screening result does not by itself establish alcohol use disorder. C is incorrect because alcohol history is clinically important in the diagnosis and management of liver disease, and a respectful approach is preferred rather than avoidance. D is incorrect because AASLD recommends routine screening across clinical settings and emphasizes early identification of harmful alcohol use. The final item tests the correct nursing response to a positive screen rather than merely asking whether alcohol can contribute to liver disease.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance directly supports routine validated alcohol-use screening, structured follow-up after a positive screen, nonjudgmental history taking, and the distinction between screening and formal diagnosis of alcohol use disorder.
candidates.source_document_title: Beyond 'How Much Do You Drink?': A Structured Approach to Screening and Assessing Alcohol Use

candidates.blueprint_topic: Advance directives, self-determination, and integration of goals into the plan of care
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that advance care planning should begin proactively in cirrhosis, can continue alongside liver-transplant evaluation and disease-directed treatment, and should document the client's values, goals, surrogate decision-maker, and future treatment preferences before decision-making capacity is lost.

options.A: No. Advance care planning is an ongoing process for discussing and documenting values, goals, a surrogate decision-maker, and future treatment preferences; it can occur alongside transplant evaluation and disease-directed care.
options.B: Yes. Advance care planning is appropriate only after transplant-directed treatment has been stopped and the client has chosen hospice care.
options.C: Advance care planning should wait until hepatic encephalopathy causes loss of decision-making capacity so the family can make decisions then.
options.D: Only specialty palliative-care clinicians should discuss advance care planning; hepatology and transplant-team clinicians should avoid these conversations.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AASLD defines advance care planning as a proactive, ongoing, collaborative process of medical decision-making that includes identifying surrogate decision-makers, discussing illness and prognosis, eliciting values and treatment preferences, and documenting goals through advance directives. AASLD specifically states that disease-directed care, including liver-transplant evaluation and listing, does not preclude palliative care and that hepatology clinicians should provide basic advance care planning. Current AASLD guidance also recommends starting advance care planning early in cirrhosis and preferably before hepatic decompensation or loss of decision-making capacity. B is incorrect because advance care planning and palliative care can coexist with transplant-directed or other disease-directed treatment; hospice is a distinct, comfort-focused model. C is incorrect because waiting until decision-making capacity is lost defeats a central purpose of advance planning. D is incorrect because AASLD encourages hepatology clinicians and other members of the care team to participate in primary palliative care and advance care planning rather than reserving these discussions exclusively for specialists.
candidates.source_claim_supported: AASLD directly supports proactive, iterative advance care planning in cirrhosis; early documentation of values, goals and surrogate decision-makers; participation by hepatology clinicians; and continued ACP/palliative care during liver-transplant evaluation or other disease-directed treatment.
