candidates.blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention teaching and early recognition of postoperative infection
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients after joint replacement to recognize and promptly report wound or joint findings that may indicate surgical or prosthetic joint infection rather than assuming infection risk ends at discharge or requires high fever.

options.A: I will promptly report increasing redness or pain around the incision, cloudy or new wound drainage, increasing joint swelling or persistent worsening pain, or fever because these may indicate infection.
options.B: Drainage and increasing redness are expected during recovery, so I should wait until the joint becomes unusable before contacting the surgical team.
options.C: Once the incision is closed, an implanted joint can no longer become infected, so infection monitoring is needed only in the hospital.
options.D: Persistent joint pain after replacement rules out infection because prosthetic joint infection always causes a high fever before other symptoms appear.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC identifies redness and pain around a surgical site, cloudy wound drainage, and fever as warning findings of surgical site infection, including infections involving implanted material such as a hip replacement. AAOS patient guidance on joint-replacement infection also emphasizes early recognition of incision redness, joint swelling, persistent pain and other infection findings because prosthetic joint infection can require substantial additional treatment. B delays evaluation of concerning wound changes. C is incorrect because prosthetic joint infections can occur after hospital discharge and may present later. D is incorrect because infection does not require a high fever to be present before local or pain-related findings become clinically important. The final item focuses on source-supported postoperative recognition and escalation rather than bundling multiple perioperative prophylaxis protocols into one answer.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current CDC and AAOS sources directly support recognition and prompt reporting of local wound/joint and systemic findings compatible with infection after joint replacement and establish that implanted material can be involved in SSI.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention practices during surgical wound care
candidates.educational_objective: Prevent postoperative wound contamination by performing hand hygiene before and after wound care and limiting unnecessary contact with the incision or dressing by visitors and caregivers.

options.A: I will clean my hands before and after caring for the wound, and I will ask family or visitors not to touch the incision or dressing unnecessarily.
options.B: Hand hygiene is needed only if the dressing is visibly soiled because a closed surgical incision cannot become contaminated.
options.C: Family members can touch the incision or dressing without cleaning their hands as long as they do not have a fever.
options.D: I should avoid asking healthcare workers to clean their hands before wound care because gloves make hand hygiene unnecessary.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. CDC surgical-site-infection guidance instructs patients to clean their hands before and after caring for a surgical wound and advises that family and friends should not touch the wound or dressings unnecessarily. CDC hand-hygiene guidance also identifies wound-dressing changes as a specific time when hand cleaning is indicated. B is incorrect because hand hygiene is required around wound care even when visible soil is absent. C creates avoidable contamination risk and ignores hand-hygiene recommendations. D is incorrect because gloves do not replace hand hygiene; CDC guidance requires hand cleaning at appropriate points before and after patient or wound contact. The final item is intentionally distinct from V2-Q1863: Q1863 tests recognition of infection findings, whereas this item tests prevention of contamination during wound care.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current CDC sources directly support hand hygiene before and after wound care, limiting unnecessary visitor contact with surgical wounds/dressings, and the principle that glove use does not eliminate indicated hand hygiene.
candidates.source_document_title: Surgical Site Infection Basics; About Hand Hygiene for Patients in Healthcare Settings; CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices

CDC 'About Hand Hygiene for Patients in Healthcare Settings' → When patients and visitors should clean their hands: before and after changing wound dressings or bandages. CDC Core Infection Prevention and Control Practices → Hand Hygiene: perform hand hygiene before aseptic tasks, after patient/environment contact and after glove removal.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition of evolving limb-threatening complications after trauma
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize acute compartment syndrome as an evolving emergency requiring serial neurovascular assessment and urgent escalation for worsening pain or passive-stretch pain even when distal pulses remain palpable.

options.A: Treat the change as possible evolving compartment syndrome, perform an immediate focused neurovascular reassessment, and urgently notify the treating team rather than waiting for pulse loss or paralysis.
options.B: Continue routine monitoring because a warm foot and palpable pulse rule out clinically significant compartment pressure.
options.C: Wait for pallor, paralysis, or pulselessness before escalating because these are the earliest reliable findings of acute compartment syndrome.
options.D: Document the pain as expected fracture discomfort because compartment syndrome can be excluded after one earlier normal assessment.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Acute compartment syndrome is an evolving clinical emergency and cannot be excluded by one earlier normal examination. Current AAOS guidance emphasizes vigilance in traumatized extremities, while authoritative NCBI reviews support serial examinations because no single examination finding is perfectly sensitive or specific. Worsening pain out of proportion to the injury, pain with passive stretch, increasing analgesic requirements, paresthesias, and tense swelling are important warning findings. A palpable distal pulse does not exclude compartment syndrome because arterial pressure may remain greater than compartment pressure until late in the process. B is incorrect because preserved warmth or pulses do not reliably rule out the condition. C is unsafe because pallor, paralysis, and pulselessness are generally late findings and waiting for them risks irreversible muscle and nerve injury. D is incorrect because acute compartment syndrome is dynamic; serial reassessment is required when symptoms evolve. The final item replaces the source's static '6 Ps' recall with a time-linked deterioration scenario that tests early recognition and escalation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AAOS and NCBI sources directly support acute compartment syndrome as a limb-threatening evolving complication after trauma, serial clinical reassessment, early concern for worsening pain or passive-stretch pain, and the fact that palpable pulses do not exclude the diagnosis.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Infection-prevention teaching for percutaneous orthopedic hardware
candidates.educational_objective: Teach clients with external fixation to follow their prescribed pin-site care protocol and promptly report findings suggestive of pin-site infection or hardware problems, recognizing that no single cleansing regimen is universally established for all patients.

options.A: I will follow the pin-site care instructions prescribed by my orthopedic team and report increasing redness, drainage, pain, swelling, fever, or a loose pin rather than inventing my own cleaning schedule or solution.
options.B: All external-fixator pin sites require the same cleansing solution and frequency, so I can use any standard internet protocol instead of the plan given by my care team.
options.C: Pin sites do not need ongoing assessment once I leave the hospital because infection occurs only during the initial placement procedure.
options.D: Drainage or increasing redness around a pin is expected and should be ignored unless the entire fixator becomes unstable.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance emphasizes that pin-site care is important for external fixation, but available techniques vary and evidence does not support one universal cleansing protocol for every patient. Therefore, clients should follow the specific pin-site instructions provided by the orthopedic team rather than substitute an unapproved solution or schedule. Pin-site infection is a recognized complication, and ongoing assessment for erythema, drainage, pain, soft-tissue problems, or hardware loosening is important. B is incorrect because no single universal pin-care regimen has been established as superior. C is incorrect because pin-site infection and soft-tissue problems remain possible while the external fixator is in place and require ongoing monitoring. D is unsafe because new or increasing drainage or erythema can indicate pin-site infection and should prompt clinical review. The final item preserves infection-prevention teaching while removing the source's unsupported implication that one fixed cleaning frequency applies to all external fixators.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI guidance directly supports individualized pin-site care rather than a universal cleansing protocol, ongoing monitoring for pin-site infection and soft-tissue problems, and reporting clinically concerning findings to the treating team.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Postoperative precautions and prevention of prosthetic dislocation
candidates.educational_objective: Follow surgeon- and approach-specific hip precautions when they are prescribed after total hip arthroplasty, while recognizing that routine strict posterior precautions are not a universal requirement for every client.

options.A: I will follow the prescribed restrictions, including avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction across the midline, and internal rotation for the period my surgical team specifies.
options.B: All clients with hip replacement require these exact restrictions for the same duration regardless of surgical approach, implant stability, or surgeon protocol.
options.C: Because I feel little pain, I can ignore the prescribed precautions and cross my legs or deeply flex the hip whenever it is comfortable.
options.D: The precautions are intended to prevent blood clots rather than reduce positions that may increase dislocation risk after this posterior approach.

candidates.rationale: A is correct because the stem explicitly states that this client's surgeon prescribed posterior hip precautions. Contemporary randomized evidence shows that routine strict precautions after posterior-approach total hip arthroplasty are not necessarily required for every patient, so the nurse should not teach them as a universal rule. When posterior precautions are prescribed, common restrictions used in trials include avoiding hip flexion beyond 90 degrees, adduction across the midline, and internal rotation for the surgeon-specified period. B is incorrect because current evidence does not support presenting the same restrictions and duration as mandatory for every total-hip-replacement client. C is unsafe because the client should follow the individualized postoperative plan rather than use pain absence as permission to disregard prescribed restrictions. D is incorrect because these movement restrictions are intended to reduce provocative hip positions related to dislocation risk, not to serve as venous-thromboembolism prophylaxis. The final item preserves the clinically recognizable posterior-precaution movements while explicitly avoiding an outdated universal-precautions claim.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current randomized evidence directly supports the specific posterior restriction set when precautions are prescribed and, equally importantly, shows that routine strict precautions should not be generalized as mandatory for every posterior-approach THA patient; NCSBN supports individualized postoperative precaution teaching under Reduction of Risk Potential.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Fall-risk reduction, safe ambulation, and medication-related impairment after orthopedic surgery
candidates.educational_objective: Prevent falls after total knee replacement by reassessing dizziness and mobility, using prescribed assistive devices and assistance, and accounting for opioid-related impairment before allowing independent ambulation.

options.A: Do not ambulate alone; reassess the dizziness and mobility, and use the prescribed assistive device and staff assistance until balance, strength, and medication effects make independent ambulation safe.
options.B: Walk independently now because early ambulation eliminates fall risk after joint replacement.
options.C: Avoid all future ambulation because any postoperative dizziness means the client should remain on bed rest for the rest of recovery.
options.D: Use furniture for support instead of the prescribed walker because assistive devices increase the chance of falling.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AAOS guidance after total knee replacement emphasizes fall prevention during early recovery and advises use of a cane, crutches, walker, handrails, or another person's assistance until balance, flexibility, and strength improve. Current oxycodone labeling warns that the medication may impair mental or physical abilities and the June 2026 Medication Guide specifically lists sleepiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, and trouble walking among clinically relevant effects or warning symptoms. In a client who is currently dizzy after oxycodone, independent ambulation should be deferred until the nurse reassesses safety and provides appropriate assistance. B is incorrect because early mobility is beneficial but does not eliminate fall risk. C is an unnecessary extreme; safe assisted mobility is part of recovery when clinically appropriate. D is unsafe because furniture is not a substitute for prescribed mobility aids. The final item tests a specific nursing safety decision rather than a vague statement about postoperative fall risk.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Assignment, delegation, supervision, and evaluation of delegated care
candidates.educational_objective: Apply the NCSBN delegation process by assessing the client, task and delegatee, verifying jurisdiction/facility rules, communicating clearly, and providing appropriate supervision and evaluation.

options.A: First assess the client and task, verify that delegation is permitted by jurisdiction and facility policy and appropriate for the delegatee, give clear directions, and provide needed supervision and evaluation.
options.B: Delegate the task solely because it is routine, without assessing the client's current condition or the delegatee's competence.
options.C: Assume that delegation rules are identical in every state and facility, so local law and policy do not need to be checked.
options.D: Transfer all responsibility for the outcome to the assistive personnel once the task is delegated, eliminating the RN's need to supervise or evaluate.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCSBN delegation guidance describes delegation as a structured process involving the employer or nurse leader, the individual licensed nurse, and the delegatee. It emphasizes the responsibilities associated with delegation, effective communication, oversight, and the need for licensed nurses to know the laws and rules in the jurisdiction where they practice. A routine task is not automatically appropriate for every client or delegatee, so B is unsafe. C is directly contradicted by NCSBN, which states that jurisdictions differ in delegation laws and regulations. D is incorrect because delegation does not erase the licensed nurse's responsibilities for the delegation decision, communication, supervision, and evaluation. The final item deliberately avoids asserting that routine ambulation is universally delegable to a particular role in every jurisdiction; instead, it tests the safe delegation process itself.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current official NCSBN guidance directly supports a structured delegation process, jurisdiction-specific scope awareness, communication, oversight and evaluation rather than automatic task transfer or transfer of all responsibility.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize when postoperative mobility deficits make a planned home discharge unsafe and coordinate physical-therapy and discharge-planning reassessment to establish an appropriate level of support or care setting.

options.A: Communicate that the current discharge plan may be unsafe and coordinate reassessment with physical therapy and the discharge/case-management team to determine additional training, support, or a different discharge setting.
options.B: Discharge the client as planned because postoperative mobility goals do not affect readiness for home care.
options.C: Tell the client to practice the stairs alone after arriving home because rehabilitation should begin only after hospital discharge.
options.D: Cancel all future physical therapy because needing assistance before discharge indicates that rehabilitation is unlikely to help.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AAOS patient guidance after total knee replacement includes functional discharge goals such as safe transfers, ambulation with an appropriate assistive device, and stair negotiation when stairs are part of the discharge environment. AAOS also notes that if these goals cannot be achieved or adequate help is unavailable, direct discharge home may be unsafe and temporary rehabilitation or skilled-nursing care may be needed. NCSBN places discharge planning, referrals, multidisciplinary collaboration, and continuity of care within Management of Care. B ignores functional safety. C sends an unready client into an avoidable fall-risk situation. D is incorrect because physical therapy is part of restoring mobility and function; failure to meet goals indicates a need for additional assessment/support, not abandonment of rehabilitation. The final item tests the nurse's role in coordinating a safe discharge rather than simply recalling that physical therapy is beneficial.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AAOS guidance directly supports functional mobility goals as part of discharge readiness after total knee replacement and the possibility that clients who cannot meet them need additional rehabilitation/support; NCSBN supports nursing coordination of discharge and referrals.

candidates.educational_objective: Recognize occupational therapy as the appropriate interdisciplinary referral when orthopedic clients need help adapting dressing, bathing, toileting, equipment use, or other daily activities despite adequate basic ambulation.

options.A: Occupational therapy, to assess daily-task performance and teach adaptive techniques or equipment for dressing, toileting, bathing, and home function.
options.B: Respiratory therapy, because difficulty with dressing and bathing after hip surgery primarily indicates impaired ventilation.
options.C: No rehabilitation referral, because the ability to walk with a walker means the client is independent in all activities of daily living.
options.D: Physical therapy only, because occupational therapy does not address self-care, adaptive equipment, or home-task performance.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AOTA defines occupational therapy as helping people participate in the daily activities they need and want to perform. OT services include evaluation and intervention for activities of daily living such as bathing and dressing, adaptive equipment, caregiver training, home safety/accessibility, and return to meaningful routines. This client has adequate basic ambulation but remains limited in self-care tasks, making occupational-therapy evaluation directly relevant. B does not match the functional problem described. C incorrectly equates ambulation with independence in all ADLs. D is incorrect because AOTA explicitly includes ADLs and adaptive equipment within occupational-therapy practice. The final item distinguishes a true OT referral need from the preceding physical-therapy discharge-readiness item rather than asking only for a definition of the profession.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AOTA sources directly support OT assessment/intervention for ADLs, adaptive equipment, home function and musculoskeletal conditions; NCSBN supports nursing identification and coordination of appropriate referrals.

candidates.educational_objective: Individualize joint-replacement discharge planning by assessing the home environment and available support, arranging equipment or services, and resolving fall and self-care barriers before discharge.

options.A: Assess the home and support barriers with the client and interdisciplinary team, arrange needed equipment or assistance, and modify the discharge plan so identified safety needs are addressed before the client is sent home.
options.B: Use the same standard discharge plan as every other joint-replacement client because home layout and caregiver availability do not affect safety.
options.C: Advise the client to leave the rugs and bathroom unchanged because environmental modifications do not influence fall risk during recovery.
options.D: Discharge the client without discussing help at home because social support is unrelated to postoperative self-care and mobility.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AAOS joint-replacement guidance recommends planning the home environment before and after surgery, including secure handrails or grab bars, a stable shower bench or chair, removal of loose rugs and cords, and arranging help with activities during early recovery when needed. AAOS also notes that an alternative discharge setting may be appropriate when the client cannot safely care for themselves at home or lacks needed support. NCSBN places individualized discharge planning, referrals, resource coordination, and continuity of care within Management of Care. B is incorrect because discharge planning should reflect the client's actual functional and environmental circumstances. C contradicts established fall-prevention recommendations. D ignores a major determinant of safe postoperative recovery. The final item is distinct from V2-Q1870: Q1870 tests whether mobility goals have been met, whereas this item tests whether the home environment and support system are adequate.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AAOS sources directly support home-safety modifications and planning for assistance after joint replacement; NCSBN supports individualized discharge planning and coordination of necessary resources.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Referral planning, payer requirements, and continuity of skilled care at home
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize that Medicare home health referral after orthopedic surgery requires both homebound status and a qualifying skilled-service need, together with practitioner certification and a plan of care, rather than mobility limitation alone.

options.A: Communicate the need for a home-health referral and ensure the discharge team verifies the full Medicare requirements, including homebound status, skilled-service need, practitioner certification/plan of care, and required documentation.
options.B: Assume the client automatically qualifies for home health solely because a walker is used, without verifying skilled-service or certification requirements.
options.C: Exclude home health because clients who can leave home occasionally for medical care can never meet the Medicare homebound definition.
options.D: Refer only after all rehabilitation goals are completed because Medicare home health cannot include skilled physical therapy during recovery.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current CMS guidance states that Medicare home health coverage requires the patient to be confined to the home, under the care of a physician or allowed practitioner, receive services under an established and periodically reviewed plan of care, and need qualifying skilled care such as intermittent skilled nursing, physical therapy, or speech-language pathology (or a continuing OT need under the applicable rules). CMS defines homebound status using both the need for supportive devices/another person's help or a condition making leaving home inadvisable and the additional requirement that the patient normally cannot leave home and that leaving requires considerable and taxing effort. Limited absences for medical care or certain infrequent reasons do not automatically disqualify the patient. B is incomplete because a walker alone does not establish all eligibility criteria. C is incorrect because permitted limited absences can coexist with homebound status. D is incorrect because skilled PT is an expressly covered qualifying service when other requirements are met. The final item tests referral coordination and accurate eligibility screening rather than presenting mobility limitation alone as sufficient.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current CMS and Medicare.gov sources directly support the complete home-health eligibility framework, including homebound status, skilled-service need, plan-of-care/certification requirements, and the fact that limited absences do not automatically negate homebound status.

Medicare.gov 'Home Health Services Coverage' → Who's eligible: part-time/intermittent skilled need plus homebound criteria; limited medical or infrequent absences do not automatically disqualify.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Resource coordination, medical-equipment orders, and payer-related discharge planning
candidates.educational_objective: Coordinate medically necessary DME for discharge by ensuring an appropriate provider order for home use and working with eligible suppliers/payer processes without guaranteeing coverage or cost before requirements are verified.

options.A: Ensure the medically necessary walker is ordered for home use and coordinate with the discharge team and an appropriate Medicare-enrolled DME supplier rather than promising coverage before requirements are verified.
options.B: Tell the client that any walker purchased from any retailer is automatically covered by Medicare without a provider order or supplier requirements.
options.C: Delay arranging the walker until after discharge because DME cannot be coordinated while the client is still hospitalized.
options.D: Guarantee that Medicare will pay the entire cost because all medically useful equipment is covered at 100 percent.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current Medicare guidance states that Part B covers medically necessary walkers as durable medical equipment when a provider prescribes the equipment for use in the beneficiary's home. Medicare also directs beneficiaries to use doctors and DME suppliers enrolled in Medicare and to clarify supplier participation/assignment and cost responsibility. The nurse's role is to coordinate the order and discharge resource process and help verify requirements; the nurse should not guarantee a specific coverage amount before eligibility and supplier details are confirmed. B is incorrect because a provider order and supplier requirements matter. C unnecessarily delays equipment needed for a safe discharge. D is incorrect because Medicare DME commonly involves deductible/coinsurance and other coverage details rather than universal 100-percent payment. The final item tests coordination of a real discharge resource and avoids duplicating prior questions about the functional benefit of walkers or home fall-proofing.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current Medicare/CMS sources directly support medically necessary provider-ordered home-use walkers, Medicare-enrolled supplier requirements, order/documentation requirements and the need to verify cost/assignment details rather than promising universal coverage.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment → Management of Care: protect client rights, confidentiality and privacy; follow legal/ethical requirements; document and communicate client information appropriately.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Client privacy, legal disclosure requirements, and documentation in work-related injury care
candidates.educational_objective: Protect client privacy in workers' compensation cases by following applicable law and facility privacy procedures, recognizing that some disclosures may occur without authorization but that employer access is not automatically unlimited.

options.A: Follow the facility's privacy process and applicable workers' compensation law to determine what information may or must be disclosed; do not release the entire record merely because the employer requested it.
options.B: Send the entire record immediately because any workers' compensation claim gives an employer unlimited access to all protected health information.
options.C: Refuse every workers' compensation disclosure unless the client signs a HIPAA authorization, even when a disclosure is specifically authorized or required by applicable law.
options.D: Give the employer an informal verbal summary from memory because verbal disclosures are not subject to privacy requirements.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current HHS guidance explains that the HIPAA Privacy Rule permits covered entities to disclose protected health information for workers' compensation purposes without individual authorization when the disclosure is authorized by, and to the extent necessary to comply with, workers' compensation or other applicable law. HHS also emphasizes significant variation among state workers' compensation laws. An employer's request by itself does not create unlimited access to an entire medical record; the covered provider should follow the applicable legal authority and facility privacy procedures. B is incorrect because workers' compensation does not create blanket employer access to all PHI. C is too absolute because HIPAA expressly permits certain workers' compensation disclosures without authorization when authorized or required by law. D is incorrect because verbal PHI disclosures are still subject to privacy requirements. The final item tests a realistic privacy decision and avoids implying that workers' compensation documentation or disclosure rules are identical in every jurisdiction.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current HHS guidance directly supports legally authorized workers' compensation disclosures without universal authorization, jurisdiction-specific limits, and the principle that an employer request does not by itself authorize unrestricted disclosure of the entire medical record.
candidates.source_document_title: Disclosures for Workers' Compensation Purposes; HIPAA Workers' Compensation FAQ 324; Employers and Health Information in the Workplace
candidates.source_locator: HHS 'Disclosures for Workers' Compensation Purposes' → Disclosures Without Individual Authorization: PHI may be disclosed as authorized by and to the extent necessary to comply with workers' compensation or similar law; state-law variability is explicitly noted. HHS FAQ 324 → covered entities may disclose PHI without authorization for workers' compensation adjudication as authorized by applicable law. HHS 'Employers and Health Information in the Workplace' → if an employer asks a health care provider directly for information, the provider generally cannot disclose it without authorization unless another law permits or requires disclosure.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Documentation, legal/benefit processes, and interdisciplinary communication
candidates.educational_objective: Document objective impairment-related functional findings for disability evaluation while recognizing that the nurse or treating clinician provides evidence rather than making the legal Social Security disability determination.

options.A: Document objective clinical findings and the client's observed functional limitations, and explain that the Social Security disability determination is made by the appropriate adjudicating agency using the full medical and nonmedical evidence.
options.B: Document that the client is legally disabled based only on the client's request because the nurse's statement determines Social Security eligibility.
options.C: Avoid documenting functional limitations because disability decisions are based only on the diagnosis name and not on work-related function.
options.D: Tell the client that medical evidence is irrelevant because Social Security evaluates disability without reviewing health records or functional information.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current SSA guidance states that disability adjudication considers medical and nonmedical evidence about the nature and severity of impairments and how they affect the person's ability to perform work-related physical and mental activities. Medical sources provide clinical evidence and information about what a claimant can still do despite impairments; SSA explicitly states that the medical source is not asked or expected to make the legal disability decision. Disability Determination Services develops the evidence and makes the initial determination under SSA rules. B improperly assigns the legal determination to the nurse. C is incorrect because functional abilities such as sitting, standing, walking, lifting, carrying, reaching, stooping, and other work demands are central to SSA evaluation. D is incorrect because SSA actively develops and reviews medical evidence. The final item distinguishes objective clinical documentation from the adjudicator's legal eligibility determination.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current SSA sources directly support objective medical/functional evidence as part of disability evaluation and explicitly separate the treating medical source's evidence role from the agency's legal disability determination.

SSA 'Part II - Evidentiary Requirements' → evidence must establish the impairment and whether the claimant can perform work-related activities. SSA DDS definition → DDS considers medical evidence and work-related abilities and physicians are not asked to decide disability. SSA 'How We Decide If You Are Disabled' → residual functional capacity evaluates remaining abilities such as sitting, standing, walking, lifting, carrying, pushing/pulling and postural activities.

candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Physiological Adaptation: recognize and manage acute, chronic or life-threatening physical health conditions; apply pathophysiology and identify manifestations or complications of altered body-system function.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Pathophysiology and manifestations of reduced bone strength
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize a fracture after minimal trauma in an older adult as a possible manifestation of osteoporosis caused by reduced bone strength and understand that osteoporosis may be clinically silent before fracture.

options.A: A low-trauma fracture can be a sign of osteoporosis because reduced bone mass or altered bone structure decreases bone strength and increases fracture susceptibility; bone-health evaluation is warranted.
options.B: A fracture from standing height rules out osteoporosis because osteoporotic fractures occur only after high-energy trauma.
options.C: Osteoporosis primarily affects skin and soft tissue, so it would not explain increased skeletal fragility after a minor fall.
options.D: If the client had no bone pain before the fall, osteoporosis can be excluded because osteoporosis is usually painful before a fracture occurs.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance defines osteoporosis as a bone disease in which bone mineral density and bone mass decrease or bone quality/structure changes, reducing bone strength and increasing fracture risk. Osteoporosis is often silent until a fracture occurs, and affected bones may fracture after minor trauma such as a fall from standing height that would not normally break healthy bone. Therefore, this low-trauma wrist fracture should prompt consideration of osteoporosis and appropriate bone-health evaluation rather than being dismissed as ordinary trauma. B is incorrect because minor falls are a recognized mechanism of osteoporotic fragility fractures. C is incorrect because osteoporosis is a skeletal disease. D is incorrect because osteoporosis commonly causes no symptoms before fracture. The final item converts the source's definition recall into clinical recognition of the pathophysiologic consequence of impaired bone strength without requiring an unnecessary DXA threshold.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS sources directly support reduced bone mass/quality and decreased bone strength as the basis of osteoporosis, low-trauma fracture susceptibility, the silent nature of disease before fracture, and follow-up evaluation after an older adult sustains a fragility-type fracture.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Differentiation of inflammatory and degenerative joint disease manifestations
candidates.educational_objective: Differentiate rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis by recognizing symmetric inflammatory small-joint disease, prolonged morning stiffness that improves with movement, and systemic symptoms such as fatigue.

options.A: The pattern is more consistent with rheumatoid arthritis because the joint involvement is symmetric and inflammatory, with prolonged morning stiffness and systemic symptoms.
options.B: The pattern is more typical of osteoarthritis because osteoarthritis usually causes prolonged morning stiffness and symmetric inflammatory swelling of small joints.
options.C: Rheumatoid arthritis is unlikely because it does not cause fatigue or symptoms outside a single weight-bearing joint.
options.D: The pattern excludes inflammatory arthritis because morning stiffness that improves with movement occurs only with mechanical joint disease.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current American College of Rheumatology guidance describes rheumatoid arthritis as an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis that commonly causes symmetric involvement of small joints in the hands, wrists, and feet, with pain, swelling, stiffness, and morning stiffness that may last more than an hour and improve with movement. NIAMS likewise describes symmetric joint involvement, stiffness after waking or prolonged rest, fatigue, and occasional systemic symptoms, while using a broader threshold of longer than 30 minutes rather than requiring one exact cutoff in every patient. In contrast, NIAMS describes osteoarthritis as a degenerative joint disease in which pain commonly occurs with joint use and may improve with rest, while morning or post-rest stiffness is usually less than 30 minutes. B reverses these characteristic patterns. C is incorrect because fatigue and multijoint symmetric disease are well recognized in RA. D is incorrect because prolonged morning stiffness that improves with activity supports inflammatory rather than purely mechanical disease. The final item uses a symptom cluster rather than treating any single stiffness-duration threshold as independently diagnostic.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current ACR and NIAMS sources directly support the rheumatoid-arthritis symptom pattern used in the stem and distinguish it from the shorter, more mechanical stiffness pattern commonly seen in osteoarthritis without requiring one universal duration cutoff for RA diagnosis.
candidates.source_document_title: Rheumatoid Arthritis; Osteoarthritis

NIAMS 'Rheumatoid Arthritis' → Symptoms: symmetric involvement, pain/swelling/warmth, stiffness lasting longer than 30 minutes after waking/rest and fatigue. NIAMS 'Osteoarthritis' → Symptoms: pain with joint use that may improve with rest and morning/post-rest stiffness usually lasting less than 30 minutes.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition and escalation of a life-threatening post-trauma complication
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize new respiratory compromise, neurologic change, and petechiae 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone fracture as possible fat embolism syndrome and prioritize urgent escalation and supportive management.

options.A: Recognize possible fat embolism syndrome, immediately escalate the change in condition, and support oxygenation and other urgent care as prescribed while further evaluation occurs.
options.B: Treat the petechiae as an uncomplicated medication allergy and delay respiratory evaluation unless wheezing develops.
options.C: Reassure the client that respiratory and neurologic changes are expected 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone fracture and require only routine monitoring.
options.D: Exclude fat embolism syndrome because all three classic manifestations must occur simultaneously in every affected client before urgent action is justified.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance describes fat embolism syndrome as a serious multisystem complication most commonly associated with orthopedic trauma and long-bone fractures. It typically manifests 24 to 72 hours after the initial insult and can involve respiratory distress or hypoxemia, neurologic changes, and a petechial rash. The classic triad is clinically useful but is not present in every patient, so urgent recognition should not wait for a perfectly complete triad. Management is primarily supportive and focuses on prompt respiratory and hemodynamic support while other causes are evaluated. B is unsafe because the simultaneous respiratory and neurologic deterioration after a long-bone fracture makes a simple allergy assumption inappropriate. C incorrectly normalizes a potentially life-threatening complication. D is incorrect because absence of a complete triad does not exclude FES. The final item preserves the source's supported 48-hour timing but tests urgent nursing recognition and escalation rather than a label-recall question.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI and peer-reviewed sources directly support the timing, long-bone-fracture association, respiratory/neurologic/petechial manifestations, incomplete-triad possibility, and supportive urgent management used in the item.
candidates.source_document_title: Fat Embolism; Fat embolism syndrome

PMC review 'Fat embolism syndrome' → Clinical presentation: typically 24-72 hours after injury; classic triad of respiratory distress, neurologic dysfunction and petechial rash does not occur in all patients.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pathophysiology of tissue repair after fracture
candidates.educational_objective: Describe typical secondary fracture healing as overlapping hematoma/inflammatory, soft-callus, hard-callus, and remodeling phases while recognizing that healing speed depends on biological and mechanical factors.

options.A: Healing proceeds through overlapping stages that begin with hematoma and inflammation, progress through granulation tissue and a soft callus, then a mineralized bony callus, followed by long-term remodeling.
options.B: Every fracture heals through one instantaneous stage, so callus formation and remodeling do not occur.
options.C: The healing sequence is identical in speed for every fracture regardless of blood supply, stability, fracture pattern, age, or health factors.
options.D: Blood supply has little relationship to fracture repair because healing occurs independently of vascular and cellular responses.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI fracture-healing guidance describes secondary bone healing as a dynamic process with overlapping stages: hematoma formation and inflammation, granulation or fibrocartilaginous soft-callus formation, development and mineralization of a bony/hard callus, and subsequent remodeling toward mature lamellar bone. B is incorrect because fracture repair is progressive rather than instantaneous. C is incorrect because healing speed and outcome vary with local and systemic factors, including fracture stability, vascular supply, infection, age, health conditions, nutrition, smoking, and fracture characteristics. D is incorrect because blood supply and angiogenesis are important to successful fracture repair, and impaired vascular supply can contribute to delayed union or nonunion. The final item preserves the source's valid sequence but clarifies that the phases overlap and avoids teaching a universal healing timeline.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI sources directly support the overlapping secondary fracture-healing sequence and the importance of blood supply, mechanical stability, fracture characteristics and patient factors rather than one universal timeline.
candidates.source_document_title: Fracture Healing Overview; Health Alterations — Chapter 10: Musculoskeletal System Alterations
candidates.source_locator: NCBI StatPearls 'Fracture Healing Overview' → Definition/Introduction and Issues of Concern: secondary healing progresses through overlapping hematoma formation, granulation/fibrocartilaginous callus, bony callus formation and bone remodeling; Clinical Significance: vascular supply and mechanical environment are major determinants and impaired blood supply can delay union. NCBI Open RN Chapter 10 → 'Stages of Bone Healing': hematoma, granulation tissue, soft callus, osteoblastic/hard bone formation and remodeling; healing time varies with age, health, severity and fracture location.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Pathophysiology of ischemic bone complications after fracture
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that femoral-head osteonecrosis after a femoral-neck fracture results from disruption of blood supply to living bone, causing ischemic bone death and possible structural collapse.

options.A: The fracture can disrupt vessels that supply the femoral head; prolonged loss of blood flow can cause ischemia and death of bone tissue, with later structural collapse.
options.B: Osteonecrosis occurs because the fracture causes excessive blood flow to the femoral head, which makes the bone overgrow and collapse.
options.C: Osteonecrosis is an expected stage of normal fracture healing and does not reflect impaired circulation to living bone.
options.D: The complication affects only the surrounding muscles because adult bone tissue does not require an ongoing blood supply.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NIAMS explains that osteonecrosis, also called avascular necrosis, occurs when blood flow to part of a bone is disrupted, resulting in death of living bone tissue and possible later collapse of the affected bone or joint surface. Femoral-neck fractures are clinically important because blood vessels supplying the femoral head travel along the neck and can be injured, particularly in displaced intracapsular fractures. B reverses the pathophysiology. C is incorrect because osteonecrosis is a complication, not a normal healing stage. D is incorrect because bone is living tissue that depends on vascular perfusion. The final item keeps the source's correct mechanism but applies it to the clinically relevant femoral-neck-fracture context without adding an unsupported incidence estimate or implying that every femoral-neck fracture will develop osteonecrosis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS and NCBI sources directly support disrupted bone blood flow as the mechanism of osteonecrosis and the specific vulnerability of femoral-head perfusion after displaced femoral-neck fracture.
candidates.source_document_title: Osteonecrosis; Femoral Neck Fractures
candidates.source_locator: NIAMS 'Osteonecrosis' → Overview: living bone requires blood supply; disruption of blood flow causes death of bone tissue and may lead to bone/joint collapse. NCBI StatPearls 'Femoral Neck Fractures' → Introduction/Pathophysiology: femoral-head blood supply runs along the femoral neck; displaced femoral-neck fractures can tear ascending cervical/retinacular vessels and compromise perfusion, leading to osteonecrosis or nonunion.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition of posture-dependent neurologic symptoms from lumbar canal narrowing
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize walking- or standing-induced leg symptoms relieved by sitting or lumbar flexion as suggestive of neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis while preserving appropriate neurologic and vascular differential assessment.

options.A: The posture-dependent pattern is suggestive of neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis and warrants focused neurologic and vascular assessment rather than being dismissed as normal aging.
options.B: The symptoms rule out spinal stenosis because lumbar extension and standing usually relieve nerve-root compression.
options.C: The pattern proves a vascular cause and makes examination of pulses, neurologic function, or the spine unnecessary.
options.D: No further evaluation is needed because bilateral leg numbness with walking is an expected consequence of aging.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance describes neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis as leg pain, numbness, tingling, or weakness that is characteristically aggravated by walking, standing, and lumbar extension and relieved by sitting or forward flexion. The 'shopping cart' posture is a classic example of flexion-related relief. However, the pattern is suggestive rather than by itself diagnostic; vascular claudication and other causes should remain in the differential, and pedal pulses plus neurologic examination are appropriate. B reverses the typical positional physiology. C is incorrect because the pattern does not prove a vascular cause and does not eliminate focused examination. D is unsafe because new exertional neurologic symptoms require evaluation. The final item therefore preserves the source's high-yield positional pattern without presenting it as an absolute diagnosis from symptoms alone.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI sources directly support the posture-dependent neurogenic-claudication pattern of lumbar spinal stenosis and the need to preserve vascular and neurologic differential assessment rather than treating the symptom pattern as an absolute diagnosis.
candidates.source_document_title: Spinal Stenosis and Neurogenic Claudication; Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
candidates.source_locator: NCBI StatPearls 'Spinal Stenosis and Neurogenic Claudication' → Pathophysiology/History and Physical: symptoms worsen with prolonged standing, walking and lumbar extension and improve with sitting or forward flexion. NCBI StatPearls 'Lumbar Spinal Stenosis' → History and Physical: neurogenic claudication is aggravated by ambulation/extension; forward flexion or the shopping-cart posture relieves symptoms; pedal pulses should be checked to help evaluate vascular claudication.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition of nerve-root symptoms and escalation for emergent spinal compression
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize dermatomal radiating leg pain and sensory change as lumbar radiculopathy that may be caused by disc herniation, while assessing neurologic deficits and cauda-equina red flags rather than assuming a definitive diagnosis from symptoms alone.

options.A: The pattern is compatible with lumbar radiculopathy, which may result from disc herniation; assess motor strength, reflexes, sensation, and urgent red flags such as new bowel or bladder dysfunction or saddle anesthesia.
options.B: The symptom pattern proves a herniated disc and makes further neurologic assessment unnecessary.
options.C: Radiating pain and numbness indicate neurologic improvement, so no additional evaluation is needed unless the back pain resolves.
options.D: A cardiac disorder is the most likely explanation for a dermatomal leg-pain pattern after lifting, so spinal causes do not need consideration.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance describes lumbar radiculopathy as radiating pain with sensory changes and sometimes weakness or reflex abnormalities in a nerve-root distribution. Disc herniation is a common cause because disc material can compress or inflame a lumbar nerve root, but the symptom pattern alone does not prove one specific structural cause. The nurse should perform a focused neurologic assessment and identify red flags such as progressive motor deficit, saddle anesthesia, or new bowel/bladder dysfunction that raise concern for cauda equina or other emergent compression. B overstates diagnostic certainty and omits safety assessment. C misclassifies neurologic symptoms as improvement. D is inconsistent with the described nerve-root pattern and mechanism. The final item preserves the source's disc-radiculopathy concept while preventing diagnostic anchoring and adding clinically important red-flag assessment.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI sources directly support lumbar radiculopathy as a nerve-root symptom pattern, disc herniation as an important possible cause, and focused assessment for motor/sensory/reflex abnormalities and cauda-equina red flags.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition and assessment of neuropathic pain after amputation
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize phantom limb pain as genuine post-amputation neuropathic pain, validate and assess the client's symptoms, and distinguish it from residual-limb pain that may require evaluation for local pathology.

options.A: Acknowledge that phantom limb pain is a real post-amputation pain phenomenon, assess its characteristics and impact, and communicate the need for individualized pain management while continuing to monitor the residual limb for separate causes of pain.
options.B: Explain that pain cannot originate from an absent limb, so the symptom is imaginary and does not require pain assessment.
options.C: Treat every report of phantom pain as proof of a surgical-site emergency even when the residual limb examination is reassuring.
options.D: Assure the client that phantom limb pain always disappears within 24 hours and therefore does not need follow-up.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance defines phantom limb pain as pain or discomfort perceived in a limb that no longer exists and describes contributions from peripheral nerve changes, spinal sensitization, and cortical reorganization. The pain is genuine and should be assessed and managed. At the same time, clinicians should distinguish phantom limb pain from residual-limb pain, which originates from the remaining limb and may reflect surgical trauma, neuroma, ischemia, skin breakdown, infection, or other local pathology; the two can coexist. B is invalidating and physiologically incorrect. C overstates phantom pain as automatic evidence of an acute surgical complication. D is incorrect because onset, duration, frequency, and persistence vary widely and symptoms may continue long after amputation. The final item therefore validates the client's pain while preserving assessment for separate residual-limb causes.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI and VA sources directly support phantom limb pain as a real post-amputation pain phenomenon, its neurologic basis, variable course, and the need to distinguish it from residual-limb pathology.
candidates.source_document_title: Phantom Limb Pain; Phantom Sensation and Phantom Pain After Amputation

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of diagnostic testing for fracture risk
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that central DXA measures bone mineral density and that T-score interpretation is appropriate for postmenopausal women and men age 50 or older, while younger populations are evaluated differently.

options.A: The scan measures bone mineral density, usually at the hip and spine; in a postmenopausal adult the result is commonly expressed as a T-score and contributes to osteoporosis and fracture-risk assessment.
options.B: The scan measures serum calcium and replaces the need for any imaging of bone density.
options.C: The scan primarily measures muscle strength and joint inflammation rather than bone mineral density.
options.D: A T-score is the standard interpretation for every child and younger adult regardless of age or sex.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. NIAMS states that a bone mineral density test measures calcium and other minerals in bone and that central dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA/DEXA) is the most common BMD test, usually measuring the hip and spine. BMD testing can help identify or diagnose osteoporosis, estimate fracture risk, and monitor treatment. For postmenopausal women and men age 50 or older, results are generally interpreted with a T-score comparing BMD with that of a healthy young adult. B is incorrect because DXA is an imaging-based BMD test, not a serum-calcium measurement. C misstates what DXA measures. D is incorrect because NIAMS describes use of a Z-score rather than a T-score in premenopausal women and men younger than 50, and pediatric interpretation also differs. The final item specifies a 68-year-old postmenopausal client so the T-score statement is directly applicable and avoids universalizing T-score use across age groups.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS sources directly support DXA as a BMD measurement tool, common hip/spine assessment, use in osteoporosis/fracture-risk evaluation, and age/sex-appropriate use of T-scores versus Z-scores.
candidates.source_document_title: Bone Mineral Density Tests: What the Numbers Mean; Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take
candidates.source_locator: NIAMS 'Bone Mineral Density Tests: What the Numbers Mean' → What is a BMD test?: measures minerals in bone; What tests are used?: central DXA is the most common BMD test and usually measures hip/spine; What is a T-score?: postmenopausal women and men age 50 or older receive T-score interpretation, while premenopausal women and men younger than 50 receive Z-scores. NIAMS 'Osteoporosis: Diagnosis, Treatment, and Steps to Take' → Diagnosis: DXA at hip/spine is a reliable method to diagnose osteoporosis and predict fracture risk.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of multivariable fracture-risk assessment
candidates.educational_objective: Explain that FRAX combines multiple clinical risk factors with optional femoral-neck BMD to estimate 10-year fracture probability and should be interpreted alongside clinical judgment rather than as a bone-density-only or fully comprehensive model.

options.A: FRAX estimates 10-year fracture probability using multiple clinical risk factors and can incorporate femoral-neck bone mineral density when available; it is not based on bone density alone.
options.B: FRAX uses only the DXA T-score, so age, prior fracture, smoking, glucocorticoid exposure, and other clinical factors do not affect the calculation.
options.C: FRAX is a genetic test that estimates fracture risk from inherited variants without using clinical history.
options.D: FRAX replaces clinical judgment because every risk factor is modeled in complete dose- and severity-specific detail.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. The current official FRAX/FRAXplus calculator estimates 10-year fracture probability using individualized clinical risk factors including age, sex, weight, height, previous fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, glucocorticoid use, rheumatoid arthritis, secondary osteoporosis, and alcohol use, with femoral-neck BMD entered when available. The calculator can also be used without a BMD value. B incorrectly reduces FRAX to bone density alone. C misclassifies FRAX as genetic testing. D is incorrect because official FRAX documentation notes important limitations: several risk factors are entered as yes/no variables and dose-response or fracture-number/severity effects are not fully represented, so clinical judgment remains necessary. The final item emphasizes what FRAX adds beyond DXA while avoiding unsupported treatment thresholds or country-specific intervention cutoffs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current official FRAX/FRAXplus resources directly support the multivariable inputs, optional femoral-neck BMD, 10-year probability purpose, and limitations requiring clinical judgment.
candidates.source_document_title: FRAXplus Calculation Tool; FRAX Calculation Tool and FAQ

FRAX FAQ/Notes on risk factors → dose-response for prior fractures, smoking, glucocorticoids and alcohol is not fully captured and clinical judgment is needed.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of mineral and bone-turnover laboratory abnormalities
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize the combination of vitamin D deficiency, hypophosphatemia, low/low-normal calcium, secondary hyperparathyroidism, elevated alkaline phosphatase, bone pain, and proximal muscle weakness as a pattern compatible with osteomalacia rather than routine fracture healing or osteoporosis alone.

options.A: The pattern is compatible with impaired bone mineralization from vitamin-D-deficiency osteomalacia and warrants further clinical evaluation and treatment of the underlying deficiency.
options.B: The findings are the expected laboratory pattern of uncomplicated fracture healing and therefore require no evaluation for metabolic bone disease.
options.C: Low phosphate and elevated alkaline phosphatase exclude a mineralization disorder because osteomalacia occurs only when all serum minerals are elevated.
options.D: The findings establish isolated osteoporosis because osteoporosis and osteomalacia have identical biochemical patterns and mechanisms.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Osteomalacia is characterized by impaired mineralization of bone matrix. Current NCBI/Endotext sources describe vitamin-D-deficiency osteomalacia as commonly showing low 25-hydroxyvitamin D with low or low-normal calcium, low phosphate, secondary hyperparathyroidism, and elevated alkaline phosphatase, although the exact biochemical pattern varies with stage and cause and no single laboratory value is diagnostic. Bone pain and proximal muscle weakness are recognized clinical manifestations. B is incorrect because this pattern should not be normalized as routine fracture healing. C reverses the expected mineral-abnormality relationship. D is incorrect because osteoporosis primarily reflects reduced bone mass/strength and routine mineral studies may be normal, whereas osteomalacia is a mineralization defect. The final item replaces the unsupported claim that calcium and phosphorus must be routinely monitored during fracture healing with clinically meaningful laboratory interpretation.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI sources directly support the mineralization defect, symptom pattern and biochemical findings used in the item while explicitly preventing any single laboratory result from being treated as independently diagnostic or as routine fracture-healing monitoring.
candidates.source_document_title: Disorders in the Action of Vitamin D; Osteomalacia
candidates.source_locator: NCBI Endotext 'Disorders in the Action of Vitamin D' → Table 1, biochemical parameters in hypocalcemic/vitamin-D-deficiency osteomalacia: calcium low to low-normal, phosphorus low, iPTH elevated, bone-specific alkaline phosphatase elevated. NCBI StatPearls 'Osteomalacia' → History and Physical: diffuse bone pain and proximal muscle weakness; Evaluation: no single laboratory finding is specific, but hypophosphatemia and/or hypocalcemia with increased alkaline phosphatase are typical, and 25(OH)D is the best marker of vitamin-D status.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of autoimmune laboratory findings in clinical context
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret rheumatoid factor as supportive rather than definitive evidence in rheumatoid arthritis and recognize that a negative RF does not exclude the disease when clinical findings remain compatible.

options.A: A negative rheumatoid factor does not rule out rheumatoid arthritis; the result must be interpreted with the clinical pattern and other findings such as anti-CCP antibodies, inflammatory markers, and imaging when indicated.
options.B: A negative rheumatoid factor excludes rheumatoid arthritis, so no additional rheumatologic evaluation is appropriate.
options.C: Rheumatoid factor is diagnostic by itself, so only a positive RF can establish rheumatoid arthritis regardless of symptoms.
options.D: Rheumatoid factor has no useful role in rheumatoid arthritis evaluation and should never be considered with other clinical information.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance states that rheumatoid arthritis has no single diagnostic test. Rheumatoid factor is one useful laboratory finding, but not every person with RA tests positive, and some people without RA or with other diseases can have a positive RF. Anti-CCP antibodies, inflammatory markers, the history and physical examination, and imaging may all contribute to evaluation. Therefore, a negative RF does not exclude RA in a client with a compatible inflammatory joint pattern. B and C incorrectly treat RF as an all-or-none diagnostic test. D is incorrect because RF can support the diagnosis when interpreted appropriately. The final item converts the source's abstract sensitivity/specificity statement into a practical interpretation problem without requiring memorization of a numerical test-performance percentage.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS guidance directly supports the limitations of RF testing, the fact that negative RF does not exclude RA, and the need to interpret RF with clinical findings and additional laboratory/imaging information.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of nonspecific inflammatory laboratory markers
candidates.educational_objective: Interpret elevated ESR and CRP as evidence supporting systemic inflammation while recognizing that these markers are nonspecific and require correlation with clinical findings and other diagnostic data.

options.A: The elevated markers support the presence of inflammation but do not identify a specific diagnosis by themselves; they must be interpreted with the clinical examination and other testing.
options.B: The elevated ESR and CRP confirm rheumatoid arthritis regardless of the joint pattern, autoantibody results, or other possible causes of inflammation.
options.C: ESR and CRP are unrelated to inflammatory disease and therefore should be ignored when evaluating joint symptoms.
options.D: Once ESR and CRP are elevated, no additional laboratory, imaging, or clinical assessment is needed because the cause has been established.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NIAMS guidance describes ESR and CRP as laboratory measures of inflammation that can help evaluate rheumatoid arthritis and monitor disease activity, but rheumatoid arthritis has no single diagnostic test and diagnosis relies on the history, physical examination, laboratory findings, and imaging as appropriate. Elevated inflammatory markers therefore support an inflammatory process but are not disease-specific. B incorrectly treats nonspecific markers as diagnostic for RA. C denies their established clinical role. D incorrectly substitutes inflammatory-marker elevation for a complete diagnostic evaluation. The final item focuses on appropriate laboratory interpretation and avoids unsupported numerical cutoffs.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NIAMS guidance directly supports ESR and CRP as inflammatory markers used within a broader rheumatoid-arthritis evaluation rather than as stand-alone disease-specific diagnostic tests.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Interpretation of joint-fluid findings and recognition of inflammatory or infectious patterns
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize a relatively clear, low-leukocyte, mononuclear-predominant synovial-fluid pattern as compatible with non-inflammatory osteoarthritis while preserving appropriate evaluation for infection, crystals, and other causes when clinically indicated.

options.A: The fluid pattern is non-inflammatory and is compatible with osteoarthritis, although the overall clinical picture and any needed crystal, Gram-stain, or culture results still guide the differential diagnosis.
options.B: The findings prove septic arthritis because any joint effusion with leukocytes should be treated as bacterial infection regardless of the cell pattern or culture.
options.C: The fluid pattern is typical of rheumatoid arthritis because inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis have essentially identical synovial-fluid profiles.
options.D: Synovial fluid analysis has no diagnostic value in a swollen joint and should not influence evaluation for infection, crystals, or inflammatory disease.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current NCBI guidance describes osteoarthritis synovial fluid as non-inflammatory, commonly clear or only slightly turbid with a relatively low leukocyte count and predominantly mononuclear cells. In contrast, inflammatory arthritis generally has higher synovial leukocyte counts, and septic arthritis often has a markedly inflammatory, neutrophil-predominant pattern. However, synovial-fluid interpretation is not based on one count alone; crystal analysis, Gram stain, culture, the clinical examination, and the presence of prosthetic hardware or other modifying factors may change interpretation. B incorrectly treats all leukocytes as proof of infection. C erases the inflammatory/non-inflammatory distinction. D denies the established diagnostic role of arthrocentesis. The final item avoids using a single WBC threshold as an absolute rule-out for septic arthritis.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current NCBI sources directly support the non-inflammatory synovial-fluid pattern typical of osteoarthritis, the distinction from inflammatory/septic patterns, and the need to integrate cell count with culture, Gram stain, crystal analysis and clinical context rather than rely on one absolute cutoff.
candidates.source_document_title: Osteoarthritis; Synovial Fluid Analysis; Septic Arthritis
candidates.source_locator: NCBI StatPearls 'Osteoarthritis' → History and Physical/Evaluation: OA effusions are non-inflammatory; if synovial fluid is obtained, leukocyte count is generally below the inflammatory range and predominantly mononuclear. 'Synovial Fluid Analysis' → normal/non-inflammatory, inflammatory, infectious and crystal-analysis categories; Gram stain/culture are used when infection is considered. 'Septic Arthritis' → Evaluation: synovial fluid cell count/differential, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis are central; lower WBC values can occur in some infections, so no single count universally excludes septic arthritis.

candidates.blueprint_topic: Mobility assistance, assistive-device teaching, and prevention of device-related injury
candidates.educational_objective: Use axillary crutches safely by bearing weight through the handgrips rather than the axillae, ensuring individualized fit, and following the prescribed weight-bearing status for the injured extremity.

options.A: I will support my body weight through my hands on the handgrips rather than leaning on my armpits, and I will use crutches adjusted to my height and the weight-bearing plan prescribed for my injured leg.
options.B: I should rest my body weight on the axillary pads because pressure in the armpits is the main way crutches are designed to support me.
options.C: Crutches are one standard size for adults, so fitting them to my height is unnecessary as long as I can reach the floor.
options.D: Once I have crutches, I can choose any weight-bearing amount on the injured leg without following the provider's restrictions.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current MedlinePlus guidance instructs clients using axillary crutches to let the hands carry body weight rather than the armpits and to have the crutches adjusted to the client's height. Excess pressure in the axilla can injure nerves and blood vessels. MedlinePlus also states that the treating provider determines how much weight the client may place on the injured leg, such as non-weight-bearing, touch-down, partial weight-bearing, or weight-bearing as tolerated. B creates avoidable neurovascular pressure. C is incorrect because crutch fit is individualized. D is unsafe because the prescribed weight-bearing restriction depends on the injury and treatment plan. The final item tests safe assistive-device use without imposing one gait sequence or one weight-bearing status on every client.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current MedlinePlus guidance directly supports handgrip weight bearing, avoidance of axillary pressure, individualized crutch fit, and adherence to the prescribed weight-bearing status.
candidates.source_document_title: Using crutches
candidates.source_locator: MedlinePlus 'Using crutches' → Crutch Basics: let the hands carry weight, not the armpits; ensure crutches are adjusted to height. Walking and Turning: the provider determines the allowed weight-bearing status, including non-weight-bearing, touch-down, partial weight-bearing, or weight-bearing as tolerated. candidates.blueprint_topic: Comfort, swelling reduction, skin protection, and self-care with immobilization
candidates.educational_objective: Teach safe home cast care by keeping the cast dry, avoiding insertion of objects, using elevation to reduce swelling as directed, and promptly reporting neurovascular warning signs.

options.A: I will keep the cast dry, elevate the leg as instructed while swelling is prominent, avoid putting objects inside the cast to scratch, and contact the orthopedic team for increasing tightness, numbness, tingling, or inability to move my toes.
options.B: If the cast itches, I can slide a coat hanger inside to scratch as long as I do not break the cast.
options.C: It is safe to soak a standard plaster or fiberglass cast in bath water because the padding is designed to remain wet.
options.D: Increasing numbness or loss of active toe movement is expected while swelling resolves, so I should wait until the next routine visit.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. Current AAOS cast-care guidance advises keeping a cast dry unless the treating team specifically confirms waterproof materials, avoiding objects inside the cast to scratch because they can injure the skin, and elevating the injured extremity during the early swelling period. AAOS also identifies increased pain/tightness, numbness or tingling, excessive distal swelling, and loss of active finger or toe movement as warning signs that require prompt clinical contact or urgent evaluation. B risks skin injury. C can damage cast material or leave damp padding against the skin unless the cast is specifically designed as waterproof. D delays evaluation of possible pressure-related neurovascular compromise. The final item integrates home comfort care with recognition of complications rather than teaching cast care as a passive checklist.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AAOS guidance directly supports keeping the cast dry, avoiding inserted objects, elevation for swelling, and prompt reporting of neurovascular warning signs.
candidates.source_document_title: Care of Casts and Splints
candidates.source_locator: AAOS OrthoInfo 'Care of Casts and Splints' → Getting Used to a Splint or Cast: elevate the injured extremity to reduce swelling during the early post-injury period. candidates.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Reduction of Risk Potential: recognize unexpected changes or complications after procedures/treatments, perform focused assessment, use precautions to prevent additional harm, and intervene or escalate appropriately.
candidates.blueprint_topic: Recognition and escalation of postoperative prosthetic complications
candidates.educational_objective: Recognize sudden severe pain, inability to bear weight, and limb deformity after total hip arthroplasty as possible prosthetic dislocation and prioritize immobilization, focused neurovascular assessment, and urgent orthopedic evaluation.

options.A: Suspect prosthetic hip dislocation, limit movement of the affected limb, perform a focused neurovascular assessment, and arrange urgent orthopedic evaluation rather than attempting to reposition the hip independently.
options.B: Encourage the client to walk on the leg to see whether the prosthetic components return to position with weight bearing.
options.C: Reassure the client that sudden severe pain and leg deformity are expected during early hip-replacement recovery and can wait for routine follow-up.
options.D: Manually rotate and flex the hip until the leg lengths look equal because nursing reduction is the preferred first response.

candidates.rationale: A is correct. AAOS identifies dislocation as a recognized complication of total hip arthroplasty, with greatest risk during the first months while tissues are healing; reduction is a medical procedure, not a nursing maneuver. Current NCBI guidance describes hip dislocation as typically producing sudden severe pain, inability to ambulate or bear weight, and visible deformity such as shortening and abnormal rotation, and recommends a thorough neurovascular examination. B and D risk further tissue, nerve, vascular, or prosthetic injury. C delays evaluation of a potentially urgent postoperative complication. The source's original routine-abduction-pillow claim was not retained because contemporary evidence does not support presenting abduction pillows or identical movement restrictions as universally necessary after every total hip arthroplasty.
candidates.source_claim_supported: Current AAOS and NCBI sources directly support prosthetic dislocation as an early postoperative risk, the acute pain/weight-bearing/deformity presentation, and the need for urgent clinical evaluation rather than bedside self-reduction.
candidates.source_document_title: Total Hip Replacement; Posterior Hip Dislocation
candidates.source_locator: AAOS OrthoInfo 'Total Hip Replacement' → Possible Complications of Surgery → Dislocation: prosthetic ball can come out of the socket; risk is greatest in the first few months while tissues heal; treatment generally requires closed reduction and sometimes further surgery. NCBI StatPearls 'Posterior Hip Dislocation' → History and Physical: sudden painful pop, inability to ambulate or bear weight, visible shortening/abnormal rotation; perform and document a thorough neurovascular examination.
